statement: In one controlled study (McCann et al., 1994), lumbar cerebrospinal fluid 5-HIAA, the main breakdown product of serotonin, was lower in 30 people who had used MDMA at least 25 times than in 28 controls: 10.3 (SD 3.1) against 15.2 (7.9) ng/ml, about a third lower (editors' calculation), F(1, 54) = 11.6, p = .001 after adjustment for age and height. The difference depended on sex: 46% lower in women (12 against 11 people), marked significant, and 20% lower in men (18 against 17), not marked significant. 5-HIAA was not related to the number of MDMA exposures (r = -0.2, p = .33), the duration or frequency of use, or the time since last use; the authors attribute the larger difference in women to greater exposure (about 115 occasions against 85 for men, at lower body weight), an explanation that sits against the absence of any relation with the number of exposures. The MDMA group had used other drugs far more often (for example cocaine 80% against 29%, LSD and other hallucinogens 87% against 32%), which was not adjusted for, although the Discussion describes the groups as matched for other drug use; no one was measured before use; and the authors write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from cerebrospinal fluid data alone. Prolactin responses to L-tryptophan and pain sensitivity showed no group differences, and the MDMA group scored as less impulsive and less hostile on two personality scales.
plain: One 1994 study measured a breakdown product of serotonin in spinal fluid. It was about a third lower in 30 people who had used MDMA many times than in 28 people who had not, clearly in the women but not in the men. The MDMA group had also used many other drugs far more often, which was not taken into account, and nobody was measured before they started. A lower level cannot show whether serotonin nerve cells were damaged.

statement: In cross-sectional studies, people who use ecstasy score lower on average than people who do not on some memory and executive tests, but the size of the difference is uncertain and the pattern differs across tasks and studies. A 2026 meta-analysis, whose confidence was rated critically low, pooled four or five small studies per comparison: overall learning and memory was lower in people abstinent for at least 6 months (g -1.37, 95% CI -2.65 to -0.09; I2 96%) and in people currently using (g -1.06, -1.98 to -0.15; I2 95%) than in MDMA-naive comparison groups, while the intervals for the verbal-memory subtests all included zero (Ung et al., 2026). A 2009 review of 33 studies of executive function and visuospatial memory, also rated critically low, pooled no effect sizes and found differences mainly in updating information in working memory and in visuospatial tasks with high executive demand, little evidence of impaired shifting or inhibition, and contradictory results on access to long-term memory; most of the updating studies came from the review's own authors, with overlapping samples (Murphy et al., 2009). Narrative reviews report larger pooled differences from the same meta-analytic literature while themselves describing marked variation between individual studies, which they put down to lifetime dose, sample size and method (Parrott, 2011, 2013). In almost every study both groups had used other drugs, most often cannabis, and people were tested once, after use had begun, so differences that predate use cannot be excluded.
plain: On average, people who use ecstasy score lower on some memory and thinking tests than people who don't. How much lower is very uncertain, and results differ a lot between studies and tasks. Almost all studies tested people once, after they had started, and most also used other drugs such as cannabis, so the tests cannot show that ecstasy caused the difference.

Murphy et al. (2009): 33 studies, no pooling; computation span differences in 7 of the 9 updating studies, all but one of them by combinations of the review's own authors and with overlapping samples.

statement: In the one study read that selected people who had used ecstasy but little else (Halpern et al., 2011), 52 people from the Salt Lake City all-night dance scene who had used ecstasy (a median of 43.5 lifetime episodes; last use a median of 121 days earlier), screened for other drugs by interview and by breath, urine and hair tests, were compared with 59 people from the same scene who had not used it. Memory measures did not differ after adjustment (verbal learning, difference -0.5, 95% CI -4.2 to 3.2). Of the 40 measures reported from the 15-test battery, four differed between the whole groups at p < .05 without correction for multiple comparisons (vocabulary, digit symbol, spatial span forward, non-dominant-hand pegboard) and two more stood at exactly p = .05 (Raven's matrices, digits backwards); in the 22 people with more than 50 episodes, scores were lower on a strategy-application test (79.5% against 88.5% of brief items, p = .003, virtually unchanged after adjustment for verbal IQ and depression), and more lifetime episodes went with fewer brief items within the ecstasy group (r = -0.37); the same subgroup was also slower with the non-dominant hand (p = .003) and scored lower on vocabulary (p = .04). The authors read the lower vocabulary as a difference that predates use, and the strategy finding as possibly reflecting impulsivity that may also predate use. For the heavier-use subgroup, the study reports how large an effect it could exclude on the 14 measures on which the two groups did not differ: a large effect (d 0.8) on all 14, and a medium effect (d 0.5) on 5 of them, with one bound at exactly 0.50 and the remaining 8 from 0.53 to 0.76, although the authors say many; only 6 people had used 150 times or more. The groups also differed in parents' education, ethnicity, number of all-night parties and cannabis use. Two commentaries read the same results in opposite ways (Parrott, 2011; Lyvers, 2011).
plain: One US study picked people who had used ecstasy but hardly any other drugs, checked with breath, urine and hair tests, and compared them with people from the same dance scene who had never used it. Memory did not differ, and most of the other scores were similar. People who had used it more than 50 times did worse on one planning test. Nobody was tested before they started, and medium-sized differences could not be ruled out on most tests.

outcome: Scores on a battery of 15 neuropsychological tests (40 reported measures)
magnitude: 52 vs 59; memory after adjustment, e.g. verbal learning (CVLT trials 1 to 5) difference -0.5 (95% CI -4.2 to 3.2); whole groups: 4 of 40 measures at p < .05 (uncorrected), 2 more at exactly p = .05; more than 50 episodes (n = 22) vs none: strategy application 79.5% vs 88.5% brief items, difference 8.7 (3.1 to 14.4), p = .003; within the ecstasy group r = -0.37 with log lifetime episodes; heavier use, on the 14 measures with no significant difference: d 0.8 excluded on all 14, d 0.5 on 5, one bound exactly 0.50 and 8 from 0.53 to 0.76 (values from Table 4).

statement: In the one prospective cohort read (Schilt et al., 2007, in the Netherlands), 58 young adults who started using ecstasy after a first test and 60 who did not showed no significant difference overall on 12 test scores before any use, in one multivariate test (F(12, 96) = 0.73, p = .72); the scores were not compared one by one at baseline. At retest, after very little use (a median of 1.5 tablets in total; last use a median of about 8 weeks before), verbal learning improved less in those who started (immediate recall +0.86 against +3.90 words; adjusted difference 2.23, 95% CI 0.17 to 4.29, p = .03), delayed recall changed by -0.52 against +0.65 words (0.63, 0.05 to 1.22, p = .03), and more showed any decline in recognition (22% against 7%; odds ratio 5.87, p = .02); nine other scores did not differ. All scores stayed within the normal range. The delayed-recall difference remained after excluding everyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines (43 against 57 people). The groups differed in cannabis use (higher before and after in those who started) and in cocaine use at follow-up, and in time between tests (11.1 against 19.1 months), and in the wider cohort people who started scored higher on sensation seeking. Two further prospective datasets are known here only through a narrative review (Parrott, 2013): one of them (de Win et al., 2008) reports this same Netherlands cohort, which the review presents as a separate study, and the other is cited as Wagner et al. (2013) but has no entry in that review's reference list, so it cannot be identified; the review also gives this cohort's retest interval as 18 to 36 months, against the 11.1 and 19.1 months the primary paper reports.
plain: A Dutch study tested young people before they had ever used ecstasy, and again 1 to 2 years later. Those who had started, mostly with very little use, improved less on a word-memory test than those who had not. All scores stayed in the normal range. The groups also differed in cannabis and cocaine use and in how long they waited between tests, so this does not show that ecstasy caused it.

statement: Whether test scores recover after people stop using ecstasy has not been established. In a 2026 meta-analysis rated critically low confidence (Ung et al., 2026; 14 studies, 5 in the pooled memory analysis), people abstinent for at least 6 months did not differ from people currently using on overall learning and memory (g 0.03, 95% CI -0.35 to 0.41; I2 80%), and both groups scored lower than MDMA-naive groups (abstinent g -1.37, -2.65 to -0.09; current g -1.06, -1.98 to -0.15); the effect of abstinence longer than 6 months was not tested, although the abstract and conclusion state that longer abstinence did not bring greater improvement. Of the unpooled memory studies, two case-control studies found deficits after 12 to 24 months of abstinence, and one small, poor-quality 2-year cohort found memory improved in people who stopped and worsened in people who continued. For executive function, two small prospective studies of poor quality found neither improvement nor deterioration after 18 months of abstinence, and seven case-control studies found no significant difference between abstinent and MDMA-naive groups, four of them by one author and sharing the same abstinent participants, so those seven rest on at most four independent samples. In every study the MDMA groups had also used other drugs, and only one had a drug-naive comparison group; exposure was self-reported in 12 of 14 studies; 9 of 14 were rated poor quality; and the study with the longest abstinence also had the lowest use, so length of abstinence and amount of use cannot be separated across studies.
plain: Do memory and thinking scores recover after people stop using ecstasy? Nobody knows yet. In one review, people who had stopped for at least 6 months scored about the same as people still using, and both scored lower than people who had never used. But the studies were small and weak, compared different people, and did not test longer breaks.

statement: In adults who use ecstasy regularly and are abstinent when scanned, binding of radioligands to the serotonin transporter is lower than in people who do not use it, most consistently and most markedly in the cerebral cortex. Four cross-sectional PET studies with the selective tracer [11C]DASB, all read in full here, agree: in 23 people abstinent on average 4.7 months against 19 who had not used ecstasy, specific binding was 68% lower in occipital, 55% in dorsolateral prefrontal, 51% in parietal and 48% in temporal cortex and 40% in hippocampus, with smaller differences in thalamus (23%), caudate (14%) and putamen (13%) (McCann et al., 2005); in 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair, abstinent a median of 38 days, against 50 others, binding was lower throughout the cortex (17% to 46%) and in the hippocampus (21%, or 31% after correction for brain volume) and unchanged in striatum, pallidum, thalamus and midbrain (Kish et al., 2010); in 14 people whose use was mainly MDMA against 21 who used neither MDMA nor hallucinogens, binding was 56% lower in neocortex, 32% in amygdala and 19% in pallidostriatum, with the midbrain unchanged (Erritzoe et al., 2011); and in 13 people against 13, binding was lower across cortical regions in a mixed model (F=25.65, p<0.001) though no single region survived correction, with subcortical values identical (Urban et al., 2012). With the older SPECT tracer [123I]beta-CIT, which also binds the dopamine transporter, one study found lower binding only in the women with heavy use (Reneman et al., 2001), and the one prospective cohort found no change after a median of 2 tablets (de Win et al., 2008); in 12 men abstinent for at least a year there was no difference, in a study with no comparison group of people currently using and with only one cortical region measured (Selvaraj et al., 2009). Every study but the cohort is cross-sectional with no pre-use scan, exposure is self-reported, and the ecstasy groups used more cannabis, alcohol, tobacco and other stimulants, although the largest study found the same reduction in the people whose hair was negative for methamphetamine and cocaine. What a lower binding signal means for nerve cells is disputed: it can follow loss of terminals, lower transporter expression or internalization, and no imaging tracer measures damage directly. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Brain scans of people who use ecstasy show less of a marker that sits on the endings of serotonin nerve cells. The difference is clearest in the outer layer of the brain, where it is about a fifth to two thirds lower than in people who do not use ecstasy. The scans were taken when people had been off the drug for weeks or months. Nobody was scanned before they started, and the groups also used more cannabis, alcohol, tobacco and other stimulants. A lower signal does not by itself show that nerve cells were harmed: the marker can also fall if cells make less of it.
population: Adults who use ecstasy recreationally, mostly moderate to heavy lifetime use, abstinent from 2 weeks to several months when scanned
exposure: Recreational ecstasy (MDMA) use
comparator: People who have not used ecstasy, or who use other drugs but not ecstasy
outcome: Serotonin transporter binding measured with PET or SPECT
magnitude: Cortical differences of about 17% to 68% depending on region, tracer and sample, largest in occipital cortex; hippocampus 21% to 40% lower; subcortical regions unchanged in three of the four PET studies (the fourth found pallidostriatum 19% and amygdala 32% lower). Editors' calculation of standardized differences from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g, 95% interval): McCann et al. (2005) occipital -2.16 (-2.93 to -1.40), hippocampus -1.26 (-1.93 to -0.60), thalamus -0.62 (-1.24 to 0.00), caudate -0.40 (-1.02 to 0.21); Urban et al. (2012) occipital -1.11 (-1.93 to -0.28), medial prefrontal -0.87 (-1.68 to -0.07), caudate 0.00 (-0.77 to 0.77). Reported effect sizes in the largest study: occipital 1.14 and insular 1.10 (Kish et al., 2010). Percentages from studies whose cortical binding values are near zero (Urban et al., 2012) are not interpretable and are not used.

risk_of_bias.note: High at the level of each study (self-selected groups, self-reported exposure, no pre-use scan, more cannabis, alcohol, tobacco and other stimulant use in the ecstasy groups), but these bear mainly on the cause of the difference, which this claim does not assert. inconsistency.note: The four PET studies with the selective tracer agree on the cortical difference. The disagreements are explained and are stated in the claim: the SPECT tracer is not selective and found a difference only in women; the prospective cohort studied a median of 2 tablets; the one study of people abstinent for a year measured only one cortical region and had no current-use group.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded as a difference in a measured binding signal, which is what was measured. Whether that signal means loss of nerve terminals is a separate, contested question and is rated there.

imprecision.note: The cortical differences are large relative to the spread (editors' standardized differences about -0.9 to -2.2 with intervals excluding zero) in samples of 13 to 49 per group. The subcortical null results are imprecise, and the claim says they are unchanged rather than equivalent.

publication_bias.note: Not formally assessable; the one review read here searched a single database and did not test for it. Null results are published in this field (two of the studies here report them), which is some reassurance.

large_effect.note: Not applied: these are group differences in a surrogate marker between small selected samples (METHODS §6.3).

dose_response.note: Not applied here; the dose relation is a separate claim and would be circular as an upgrade for this one.

grade.reasoning: Observational imaging evidence starts low. It is rated for the direction of the difference, which four independent laboratories report with the same selective tracer, with the largest reduction in the same region (occipital cortex) and with exposure verified in hair in the largest study; it is therefore not downgraded for inconsistency or risk of bias, which bear on causation rather than on the association as worded. The size of the difference is less certain than the direction: every comparison is unadjusted, the groups differ in other drug use, cortical binding is low and noisy, and the percentages differ by tracer and binding measure; for the size a strict reading gives very low certainty.

statement: A 2002 report in Science that a common recreational dose regimen of MDMA caused severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity in primates was retracted in September 2003, its authors reporting that a labelling error meant all but one animal had received methamphetamine instead; both documents have now been read. The report described squirrel monkeys and baboons given three doses of 2 mg/kg at 3-hour intervals, recorded that 2 of the 10 animals given the regimen died and 2 more could not complete it, claimed losses of striatal dopamine markers larger than the losses of serotonin markers, and concluded that people who take repeated doses over several hours are at high risk of severe brain dopamine injury and possible parkinsonism later in life; it also argued that the doses were lower than human doses once adjusted by interspecies scaling, which the same authors denied having used when they replied to critics three months before the retraction. The notice states that the drug given to all but one animal came from a bottle labelled MDMA that contained methamphetamine, that the two bottles were ordered on the same date for the same amount and processed and delivered by the supplier on the same day with different labels, that brains frozen from two animals that died contained methamphetamine and amphetamine and no trace of MDMA, that the bottle labelled methamphetamine was found to contain MDMA, and that the error came to light only after the authors failed to extend the finding to oral dosing and then failed to reproduce it with a new, authenticated batch. The notice does not say which animal received MDMA or what that animal showed; it states that the serotonin findings of earlier studies are not called into question and that whether MDMA damages dopamine neurons in primates remains uncertain. A case study of the 50 largest US newspapers with searchable archives found that 26 (52%) covered the publication and 20 (40%) the retraction; of the 26 that covered the publication, 14 (54%) covered the retraction, and 6 newspapers covered only the retraction. Retraction stories were shorter on average (mean 396 against 482 words), and all 20 stated both that the original findings had suggested that one night's use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism and that a mix-up of compounds made them erroneous. The difference in coverage between the two events was not tested by the authors. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In 2002 a study said that one night's worth of ecstasy damaged monkeys' brains. A year later it was withdrawn: the monkeys had been given the wrong drug by mistake. Of 50 big US newspapers, 26 wrote about the study and 20 about the withdrawal.

magnitude: Publication covered by 26 of 50 newspapers (52%; editors' calculation, Wilson 95% CI 38.5% to 65.2%) and the retraction by 20 of 50 (40%; 27.6% to 53.8%); 14 of the 26 that covered the publication also covered the retraction (54%; 35.5% to 71.2%), and 6 of 50 (12%) covered only the retraction. Mean lengths 482 words (SD 303) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193) for retraction stories. Neither difference was tested by the authors; editors' calculations give exact McNemar p=0.24 for the coverage difference (12 against 6 discordant newspapers) and Welch p=0.25 for the word counts.

statement: Whether MDMA damages dopamine neurons in people has not been shown. The primate report that put the question on the agenda in 2002 was retracted after its authors found that all but one animal had received methamphetamine; as described in the 2021 case study read here, evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not appeared since, although that statement is made without citing human studies. In the 2003 exchange that preceded the retraction, the critics cited imaging and post-mortem reports of normal dopamine markers in people who used MDMA heavily, a description that does not hold for one of the studies they cite (McCann et al., 1994, below), and the study's authors replied that cerebrospinal fluid homovanillic acid is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity and that groups unselected for pattern of use would not be expected to show differences. The one primary human study of a dopamine marker read here found cerebrospinal fluid HVA, a dopamine metabolite, lower in the MDMA group after adjustment (19.4 against 27.4 ng/ml; p = .01), but only in women (18.7 against 34.8) and not in men (22.1 against 24.6), with a very wide spread in the control women; on unadjusted unequal-variance tests the overall difference was not clear (editors' calculation, p about .07) (McCann et al., 1994). A review of molecular imaging to November 2015, read in full, lists one animal and five human studies of the dopamine system and finds no consistent effect: of three studies of the dopamine transporter, one reported striatal binding 13% higher than in people who used other drugs but not ecstasy (p=0.045) and 20% lower in those who had also used amphetamines recently than in those who had not (p=0.007), which its authors read as an amphetamine effect, and two found no difference; dopamine D2/3 binding (16% to 19% lower, not significantly) and release did not differ significantly in 9 people who had stopped; and dopamine-synthesis capacity measured with [18F]dopa was 9% higher in the putamen than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021) but no different from polydrug controls (Vegting et al., 2016; the primary studies were not read here). The retraction notice itself, now read, states that the serotonin findings of earlier studies are not called into question, that dose regimens in the range of those used by some people but not yet tested might still produce dopamine neurotoxicity in primates as they do in rodents, and that the question remains uncertain (Ricaurte et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.

debate.question: Does recreational MDMA use damage dopamine nerve cells in people?
debate.evidence_yes: The case for a dopamine effect rested on the 2002 primate report of severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity after what its title called a common recreational dose regimen, and on its authors' argument that the pattern of dosing, not only the amount, decides which transmitter systems are affected, so that three doses given over several hours produced damage to both dopamine and serotonin systems while more widely spaced, higher doses produced serotonin damage alone; this is the reply by Ricaurte and colleagues in the same exchange (Mithoefer et al., 2003). They also pointed to mouse evidence of MDMA-related dopamine neurotoxicity, and argued that human studies which ignore patterns of use would not be expected to show differences in dopamine markers. That report was retracted in September 2003 (Barnett & Doblin, 2021), so this side of the argument no longer has its primary support. The one human dopamine marker read here points the same way: cerebrospinal fluid homovanillic acid was lower in the MDMA group after adjustment (19.4 against 27.4 ng/ml, p = .01), and its authors read that, with the lower 5-HIAA, as consistent with damage to dopamine as well as serotonin neurons at high doses (McCann et al., 1994). The difference was carried by the 12 women, was not marked significant in Table 4 for the group as a whole, and is a metabolite rather than a measure of nerve cells. The retraction notice, now read in full, leaves the question open on its authors' own account: it states that dose regimens in the range of those used by some people, but different from those tested so far, might still produce dopamine neurotoxicity in primates as they do in rodents, that lasting effects of MDMA on dopaminergic function in humans have been reported and that some people with a history of MDMA use have developed parkinsonism (Ricaurte et al., 2003). It cites no human imaging for those statements, and the sources it cites were not read here.
debate.evidence_no: The critics cited human studies finding normal dopamine with reduced serotonin in people who used MDMA heavily: two in vivo imaging studies of the dopamine transporter, one post-mortem examination, and earlier work by the same research group reporting dopamine metabolites in cerebrospinal fluid that were not reduced (Mithoefer et al., 2003) - a description that does not hold for one of the studies cited, in which that metabolite was lower in the MDMA group and in women (McCann et al., 1994). They also argued that the high mortality among the primates showed the regimen was not a common recreational one; how many animals died is itself disputed in the sources read (one in the 2003 reply, two in the 2021 case study), and neither source read the 2002 paper. The newspaper case study states that evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not appeared in the years since the retraction (Barnett & Doblin, 2021), a statement it makes without citing any human study. A review of molecular imaging to November 2015, read in full, supplies what that statement lacks: one animal and five human studies of the dopamine system, with no consistent effect. Three studies of the dopamine transporter found no reduction in people who used ecstasy; one of them reported striatal binding 13% higher than in people who used other drugs (p=0.045, effect size 2.92) and 20% lower in those who had also used amphetamines recently than in those who had not (p=0.007), which its authors read as an effect of amphetamine rather than of MDMA. Dopamine D2/3 binding (16% to 19% lower, not significantly) and release did not differ significantly in 9 people who had stopped, and dopamine-synthesis capacity was 9% higher in the putamen than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021, effect size 1.10) but no different from polydrug controls (Vegting et al., 2016). All are small and cross-sectional and none was read in the original.
debate.neither_can_show: Of the human studies on either side, only one cerebrospinal fluid study was read for this claim (McCann et al., 1994), and neither the 2002 paper nor its retraction notice is among the sources. Both documents are partisan: one letter is from people who ran and defended the study, the other from an organization that funds MDMA therapy research and asked for an investigation. The critics' description of the cerebrospinal fluid literature is not accurate for at least one study they cite, in which the dopamine metabolite homovanillic acid was lower in the MDMA group overall and in women (see card sc_mithoefer_2003). A statement that evidence has not materialized is an argument from silence: no systematic search is reported behind it. The retraction notice, now read, does not say which animal received MDMA or what that animal showed, so nothing survives from the 2002 report even in principle. The human dopamine studies that do exist are known here only through a review that searched one database and appraised none of them; they are small, cross-sectional, and in the one case where both comparisons were made, the difference against drug-naive controls disappeared against people who used other drugs.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The claim that recreational MDMA damages dopamine neurons in people rested on a study that was withdrawn because the animals had mostly received a different drug (Barnett & Doblin, 2021). The only primary human dopamine-marker study read here found a lower metabolite in spinal fluid, clear only in women (McCann et al., 1994), which cannot show damage to nerve cells. That is not the same as showing that MDMA leaves dopamine systems untouched: apart from that one study, the human studies cited on both sides have not been read here, and they were unselected for pattern of use (Mithoefer et al., 2003), and a metabolite in spinal fluid is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of damage to dopamine nerve cells, as the primate study's authors argued (Mithoefer et al., 2003). Since that reading, a review of molecular imaging has been read in full: across five human studies it finds no consistent dopamine effect, at second hand and without appraisal of the studies (Vegting et al., 2016), and the authors of the retracted report themselves wrote in their notice that the primate question remains uncertain (Ricaurte et al., 2003). The honest position is that the question is open, that what human evidence exists points away from a dopamine effect, and that the burden rests with anyone asserting either answer.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Dopamine transporter or vesicular transporter imaging, and post-mortem dopamine markers, in people with documented heavy MDMA use and little stimulant use, against matched controls, with the pattern of use recorded and repeat measurement over abstinence; and a systematic search of the human literature published since 2003. The 2016 review supplies part of that search, to November 2015, from a single database and without appraising the studies; the primary dopamine imaging studies it lists (by McCann, Reneman, Tai and Weinstein and their colleagues, 2002 to 2011) have not been read here yet.

verification.flag_note: Still rests on letters, a media case study, one cerebrospinal fluid study and a review's tabulation; stays at draft. The retraction notice has now been read (sc_ricaurte_2003) and the human dopamine imaging is described from a review read in full (sc_vegting_2016); the primary dopamine imaging studies (McCann et al., 2008; Reneman et al., 2002; Tai et al., 2011; Weinstein, 2010) have not been read and should be obtained before this claim rises.

statement: Whether recreational ecstasy use causes lasting damage to the serotonin system in people, and whether any such damage explains the lower test scores found in people who use it, is contested and not settled by the sources read here. On one side, four PET studies with the same selective tracer, read in full, report lower serotonin transporter binding in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus of people who use ecstasy, by about a fifth to two thirds depending on region, with the difference graded by years of use and largest dose and with exposure verified in hair in the largest of them (McCann et al., 2005; Kish et al., 2010; Erritzoe et al., 2011; Urban et al., 2012), and reviews report lower memory and executive scores in many studies, often related to lifetime use; one controlled study found cerebrospinal fluid 5-HIAA about a third lower, clearly in women only (McCann et al., 1994); and the one prospective cohort read found a smaller gain in verbal learning after very little use (Schilt et al., 2007). On the other, the 5-HIAA difference was unrelated to amount or recency of use and confounded by much heavier use of other drugs; the prospective cohort's scores stayed in the normal range and its groups differed in cannabis and cocaine use; the study that selected people who used little else found memory unchanged and most tests similar (Halpern et al., 2011); the one prospective cohort, which scanned people before they had ever used ecstasy, found no change in transporter binding after a median of 2 tablets, and 12 men abstinent for at least a year did not differ from men who used other drugs or none (de Win et al., 2008; Selvaraj et al., 2009); traits such as impulsivity predict who starts; and the reviews' descriptions of individual studies are at points inaccurate. The two reviews with systematic searches were rated critically low confidence (Murphy et al., 2009; Ung et al., 2026), and authors on both sides call for prospective studies with brain measures. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does ecstasy damage the brain's serotonin system for good? Experts disagree, and the papers read here are opinion pieces and reviews, not new studies. Nobody has tested people before they started using, so a difference found later could have been there all along.

Transporter binding figures now come from the primary studies: cortical reductions of 17% to 46% and hippocampus 21% in 49 people with hair-verified use against 50 (Kish et al., 2010); 48% to 68% across cortical regions and 40% in hippocampus in 23 against 19 (McCann et al., 2005); 56% in neocortex, 32% in amygdala and 19% in pallidostriatum in 14 against 21 (Erritzoe et al., 2011); lower across cortical regions in a mixed model in 13 against 13 (Urban et al., 2012); against no change after a median of 2 tablets in the prospective cohort (de Win et al., 2008) and no difference in 12 men abstinent at least a year (Selvaraj et al., 2009).

No difference at follow-up in transporter binding in any region (for example thalamus -0.001, 95% CI -0.077 to 0.076) or in brain metabolites; small differences in diffusion and perfusion measures (each group's change from baseline under 5%). Before anyone had used ecstasy the groups did not differ on any imaging measure, on substance use or on transporter genotype.

risk_of_bias.note: The narrative reviews, letters and commentaries appraise nothing and select partisanly; the primary studies are cross-sectional or, in one case, a small cohort, with confounding by other drug use (cards sc_mccann_1994, sc_halpern_2011, sc_schilt_2007); both systematic reviews are rated critically low confidence.

inconsistency.note: Counted once, under risk of bias: the disagreement is about the interpretation of a largely shared body of cross-sectional studies, not about separate findings.

indirectness.note: The outcome of interest, lasting damage to nerve cells, is inferred from binding signals, a metabolite and test scores; the imaging evidence is now read in the primary studies, but a binding signal remains a surrogate that can fall without loss of terminals, and no PET or SPECT tracer measures damage directly.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable from these sources, though their selection of studies is unsystematic on both sides.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness. Worded as insufficient evidence, which is what the sources support: their own authors call for prospective studies with brain measures.

debate.question: Does recreational ecstasy use cause lasting damage to the brain's serotonin system in people, and does that damage explain the lower test scores found in people who use it?
debate.evidence_yes: A narrative review sets out the case: serotonergic neurotoxicity after MDMA is well established in laboratory animals; most human imaging studies report lower serotonin transporter binding in people abstinent from ecstasy, by 19% to 46% across cortical regions and 21% in the hippocampus in one study of 49 people against 50 (as summarized), related to lifetime use and surviving control for other drug use; a group preferring MDMA showed reductions while a group preferring hallucinogens showed none; memory and higher cognitive differences appear in many studies, with meta-analytic differences of about 0.3 to 1.0 SD, and are reported in relation to lifetime dose; and lower binding goes with poorer memory in two imaging studies (Parrott, 2013). A letter adds that differences appear even in people who use almost no other drugs, and reads this as showing damage under conditions the author calls protective (Parrott, 2011). The author of a cross-sectional imaging study holds that MDMA's serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates is well established, that he knows of no evidence that humans are less vulnerable, and that incident use was followed by increased impulsivity in a prospective cohort (Cowan, 2012). Primary studies read here add: cerebrospinal fluid 5-HIAA about a third lower in people who had used MDMA many times, clearly in women (McCann et al., 1994); a smaller gain in verbal learning in people who started using, against people who did not, in a cohort tested before first use (Schilt et al., 2007); and lower learning and memory scores in people abstinent for at least 6 months, as in people currently using, against MDMA-naive groups (Ung et al., 2026). The best-controlled study on this page also has one positive finding: in its heavier-use subgroup, fewer brief items on a strategy-application test (79.5% against 88.5%, difference 8.7, 95% CI 3.1 to 14.4, p = .003, virtually unchanged after adjustment for verbal IQ and depression), with more lifetime episodes going with fewer brief items within the ecstasy group (r = -0.37) (Halpern et al., 2011); its own authors read it as possibly reflecting impulsivity that may predate use. The imaging evidence has since been read in the primary studies and is stronger than the second-hand account suggested: four independent PET studies with the same selective tracer find lower cortical and hippocampal transporter binding in people currently using ecstasy, the largest of them in 49 people whose use was confirmed in hair and in whom the reduction held among those whose hair was negative for methamphetamine and cocaine and was not explained by brain volume, cortical thickness, hormones, genotype or sex (Kish et al., 2010); the reduction is graded by lifetime tablets, years of use and largest dose (Erritzoe et al., 2011; Kish et al., 2010); and in one study the fall in transporter binding was matched region by region by a rise in 5-HT2A receptor binding, the pattern expected if cortical serotonin signalling were reduced (Urban et al., 2012).
debate.evidence_no: Only one cohort read here tested people before they began using, and only after very little use (Schilt et al., 2007); the other studies cannot exclude differences that predate use; traits such as impulsivity and weaker executive control are linked to lower serotonergic function and to heavier substance use, and decision-making predicted first ecstasy use in a prospective study, so the heaviest-using groups would score lower even with no drug effect (Lyvers, 2011). In the study designed to remove confounding by other drugs, the commentary counts only one of 15 tests as clearly different, and only in the heavier-use subgroup (Lyvers, 2011); that study's own tables show four of 40 measures differing in the whole group at p < .05 with two more at exactly p = .05, and, in the heavier-use subgroup, the strategy test and the non-dominant-hand pegboard at p = .003 and vocabulary at p = .04 (Halpern et al., 2011). The commentary argues that transporter binding in people who use ecstasy appears to recover with abstinence, unlike the persistent reductions reported years after fenfluramine (Lyvers, 2011); the recovery rests on a single-time-point comparison of people currently using with people who had stopped, and the statements about how widely fenfluramine was prescribed and why it was withdrawn come from a legal and technical book rather than from a research report. Re-analysis of one imaging study's raw data, combining the MDMA group with controls, found no association between exposure and brain activation (as reported by Cowan, 2012). Not every imaging study finds reductions, and a prospective cohort of people with very low use found no transporter difference (Parrott, 2013). The animal literature itself admits an interpretation without loss of nerve terminals, and the field has been criticized for lacking a clear definition of neurotoxicity (Parrott, 2013). In the primary studies read here: the study that selected people who used little else found memory unchanged and most measures similar, with a large effect (d 0.8) excluded on each of the 14 measures its equivalence analysis covers, though a medium effect only on 5 of them (Halpern et al., 2011); the 5-HIAA difference was unrelated to number of exposures, duration, frequency or recency of use, and the MDMA group had used cocaine and hallucinogens far more often (McCann et al., 1994); and the prospective cohort's scores stayed in the normal range, with groups that differed in cannabis and cocaine use and in time between tests (Schilt et al., 2007). The brain scans of that same cohort, now read, found no change in transporter binding or brain metabolites after a median of 2 tablets, and the groups had been indistinguishable on every imaging measure before anyone used ecstasy, which is the only direct test of the objection that such differences predate use (de Win et al., 2008); 12 men abstinent for at least a year showed no difference from men who used other drugs or none (Selvaraj et al., 2009); and the review of this literature lists down-regulation or internalization of the transporter, lower protein expression and competition from released serotonin, alongside loss of neurones, as explanations that imaging cannot separate, noting that no PET or SPECT tracer measures toxicity directly (Vegting et al., 2016).
debate.neither_can_show: The reviews, letters and commentaries describe individual studies in ways that differ from one another and, at points, from the studies' own tables. Only the Dutch cohort tested people before they started, after very little use, and its brain-imaging results are known here only second-hand; no other design read here can separate a difference that follows use from one that preceded it. Binding signals and test scores are surrogates: both can change without any loss of nerve cells, and neither side reports post-mortem or structural evidence in people. Group averages are reported without saying how many individuals fall outside the normal range, and the reviews report no formal assessment of publication bias. The two sides also select differently: the review omits the published critiques, and the commentary omits the transporter imaging studies. Reading the imaging studies themselves does not remove the central gap: nobody has been scanned while using ecstasy and again after a long break, so every statement about recovery compares different people; the prospective cohort that did scan people before use studied a median of 2 tablets with a tracer its authors call too insensitive for small changes; cortical binding values in two of the studies lie close to zero, so percentage reductions from them are not interpretable; and the exposure in every study is what the person remembered taking.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). From the sources read so far (primary studies and reviews read in full, and the narrative reviews and letters), two things are reported consistently: a difference in serotonin transporter binding between people who use ecstasy and people who do not, now read in the primary studies: four PET studies with the same selective tracer find lower cortical and hippocampal binding, the largest with use confirmed in hair, graded by years of use and largest dose (Erritzoe et al., 2011; Kish et al., 2010; McCann et al., 2005; Urban et al., 2012), while the one cohort scanned before first use found no change after a median of 2 tablets (de Win et al., 2008) and the one study of men abstinent for a year found no difference (Selvaraj et al., 2009); and a modest average difference in memory and executive test scores (Kish et al., 2010; Parrott, 2013). Neither establishes lasting damage to nerve cells, and neither is shown to be caused by ecstasy: the designs cannot do it, the exposure is self-reported, and other drug use and pre-existing differences run in the same direction. The strongest argument on the yes side is the relation of both measures to lifetime use (Erritzoe et al., 2011; Kish et al., 2010; Parrott, 2013); the strongest on the no side is that the one study designed to remove confounding by other drugs found almost nothing (Halpern et al., 2011). The authors on both sides agree that prospective studies are needed (Cowan, 2012; Lyvers, 2011; Parrott, 2013), which is the clearest signal of where this stands.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that measure serotonin transporter binding and cognition in people before first use and repeatedly afterwards, with use verified biologically, a retested group who do not start, and pre-specified outcomes; repeat scanning of the same people over years of abstinence to see whether binding and scores change together; within-person studies of controlled administration with the same measures; and post-mortem studies of structural markers in people with documented long-term use. None of the studies read here reports any of these: the one prospective cohort measured brains before use but followed people only through a median of 2 tablets, and no one has yet been scanned during use and again after a long break.

statement: In adults with moderate or severe PTSD who had stopped their psychiatric medicines (two phase 3 trials from one sponsor: 90 adults with severe PTSD in MAPP1, 104 with moderate to severe PTSD in MAPP2), MDMA given in three sessions within an intensive manualized therapy, compared with an inactive placebo given with the same therapy, lowered clinician-rated PTSD symptom scores (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80, baseline means about 44 and 39) at 18 weeks by 11.9 points more in MAPP1 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 points more in MAPP2 (4.1 to 13.7); both arms improved substantially (in MAPP2, by 23.7 and 14.8 points). Analyses that kept scores recorded after people stopped treatment, a worst-case imputation of MAPP1's missing scores and a tipping-point analysis in MAPP2 still showed a significant difference (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2's supplement). Among completers (MAPP1) and those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2), 67% vs 32% and 71% vs 48% no longer met PTSD criteria; counting everyone randomized (for MAPP1, everyone dosed), 61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% (editors' calculation). Functional impairment improved slightly more with MDMA (SDS difference 1.2 points on a 0 to 10 scale in MAPP2, and 1.4 in MAPP1 by the amended study report as the sponsor's briefing document gives it). The two trials share their sponsor, design and therapy manual, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors; in MAPP2, the only trial that asked, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified their group at the end of the study, MAPP1 did not assess blinding, and neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, so how much of the difference is due to MDMA itself is uncertain; the trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks, and the only later data, a single observational follow-up visit analysed in the FDA's briefing document, were judged by the FDA not designed to evaluate durability; no trial in the sources read compares MDMA-assisted therapy with a trauma-focused psychotherapy. The FDA's reviewers, re-tabulating the sponsor's study reports, give the same estimates and call the changes clinically meaningful (their threshold is 10 points), while judging that functional unblinding and expectation bias, which they cannot quantify, probably affected them, the in-session monitors probably knowing allocation too; the FDA's advisory committee voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two trials run for the same sponsor, adults with PTSD had three long therapy sessions with either MDMA or a dummy pill, plus the same talking therapy before and after. About 4 months later, PTSD scores had dropped more with MDMA: about 9 to 12 points more on a 0 to 80 scale. Of the people who finished, about 7 in 10 on MDMA no longer had PTSD, against 3 to 5 in 10 on the dummy pill. In the second trial, most people could tell which pill they had (the first trial did not ask), and neither trial reports measuring what people expected, so part of the difference may come from their expectations. These trials report nothing after 4 months; the only later check, reported by the US regulator, was one visit it said was not designed to show whether the benefit lasts. No study we read compared MDMA with standard PTSD talking therapy, and the regulator's expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show that the treatment works.
population: Adults with DSM-5 PTSD of at least 6 months, CAPS-5 of 35 or more (MAPP1) or 28 or more (MAPP2), after washout of psychiatric medicines; people with current substance use disorders (MAPP1) or most substance use disorders (MAPP2), personality disorders or cardiovascular disease excluded, and in MAPP2 also people at high suicide risk
exposure: MDMA in three 8-hour sessions about a month apart, within a manualized therapy of three preparatory and nine integration sessions with a two-person team
comparator: Inactive placebo with the identical therapy
outcome: Change in CAPS-5 total severity from baseline to 18 weeks (primary); loss of PTSD diagnosis; SDS functional impairment
magnitude: MAPP1 (de jure MMRM, n = 89): difference 11.9 CAPS-5 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4), d 0.91 (0.44 to 1.37) as printed (it equals the completers' raw difference of 10.5 points over their pooled SD; the model difference over the same SD gives about 1.03, editors' calculation); registry least-squares means −24.5 vs −12.64. MAPP2 (n = 103): −23.7 (−26.94 to −20.44) vs −14.8 (−18.28 to −11.28); difference −8.9 (−13.70 to −4.12), d 0.7. Loss of diagnosis among completers (MAPP1) and those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2): 28/42 (67%) vs 12/37 (32%) and 37/52 (71.2%) vs 20/42 (47.6%); with everyone randomized as denominator (for MAPP1, the 46 and 44 dosed; editors' calculation): 60.9% vs 27.3% (difference 33.6 points, 14.3 to 52.9) and 69.8% vs 39.2% (30.6, 12.4 to 48.8). Remission 14/42 vs 2/37 and 24/52 vs 9/42. SDS: MAPP2 difference −1.20 (−2.26 to −0.14); MAPP1 P = 0.0116, d 0.43 (−0.01 to 0.88) in the publication, but −1.36 (−2.46 to −0.25), P = 0.0167, in the FDA's table from the clinical study report. Responder P values are nominal (MAPP2 response P = 0.0708).

risk_of_bias.note: Very serious: unblinding with a participant-reported outcome and no reported measure of expectancy, shared by both trials and of unknown size against differences of comparable order.

grade.reasoning: Two randomized, prospectively registered phase 3 trials (193 in the modified intention-to-treat sets, 90 and 103), starting high. Risk of bias, two levels (very serious): in both trials the outcome-measurement domain of RoB 2 is high, because the CAPS-5, although rated by blinded independent assessors, rests on what participants report, and most participants very probably knew their group (in MAPP2's end-of-study survey 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it, mostly from effects felt or not felt; MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only anecdotes); neither trial reports a measure of expectancy, and the assessors' guesses were not recorded. This bias runs toward a larger difference (expectation on MDMA, disappointment on placebo, which the MAPP2 authors themselves name as a possible reason for the 8 vs 1 placebo dropouts, 5 of them after the first session); it is shared by both trials, so their agreement does not reduce it; and its size cannot be estimated from these papers, while the differences it would have to explain are of a comparable order (8.9 and 11.9 points, lower limits 4.1 and 6.3). METHODS §6.3 rates down when the biases that remain could plausibly change the estimate materially, as here (the FDA's reviewers reach the same view, add that the in-session monitors probably knew allocation too and say the bias cannot be quantified, and 9 of the 11 voting members of its advisory committee judged the data unable to show effectiveness); that the bias is unlikely to explain all of the difference argues against very low, not for moderate (the first reader's strict reading; both second readers). The sponsor's oversight of data collection, analysis and interpretation is carried by the status (replicated by the same team), not by a further level. Missing outcome data are not a further reason to rate down: analyses keeping scores recorded after people stopped treatment, MAPP1's worst-case imputation and MAPP2's tipping-point analysis all kept a significant difference (sponsor's briefing document; MAPP2 supplement); they do not address unblinding. Inconsistency not rated down: both trials found differences in the same direction with overlapping intervals (d 0.91 and 0.7). Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial populations, to the comparison with placebo plus the same therapy and to 18 weeks. Imprecision not rated down: both intervals exclude no difference, though their lower ends (4.1 and 6.3 points) are small relative to the 10-point change agreed with the FDA as clinically meaningful for an individual. Publication bias not rated down: both registered phase 3 trials are published. The relation stays 'reduces': randomization supports causal language about the package that was assigned (MDMA against placebo within the same therapy), which the site uses for randomized evidence at low certainty; how much of the difference is due to MDMA's pharmacology is the question of the contested claim in section 14.

statement: Both phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD compared MDMA with an inactive placebo. In MAPP2, the only one that asked, most participants identified their group at the end of the study: of the 96 who answered, 49 of 52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33 of 44 (75.0%) on placebo correctly identified their group, most citing effects they felt or did not feel (Bang blinding index 0.92 and 0.55, editors' calculation; 1 means everyone right, 0 chance); MAPP1 did not assess blinding and reports only that at least 9 of 90 participants (10%) had guessed wrongly when told their allocation. MAPP2's supplementary tables add that one of the eight placebo participants with missing outcome data had stopped treatment because they believed they were receiving placebo. The outcome assessors were independent and blinded to treatment and visit, but whether they could guess allocation was not reported, and the primary outcome, a clinician interview, rests on what participants report. Expectancy was not measured in MAPP2 and no measure is reported for MAPP1, and the MAPP2 authors' arguments that it was mitigated are indirect. The trials therefore cannot separate MDMA's pharmacological effect from participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations: how much of the 9- to 12-point difference reflects these is unknown. Two commentaries that welcomed the first trial (one also relaying the sponsor's announcement of the second) did not discuss whether the blind held and give no blinding data (Nutt & de Wit, 2021; Madero & Alvarez, 2023), and a 2025 study reports, citing news reports, that the FDA advisory committee raised the difficulty of maintaining the blind given MDMA's psychoactive effects (Earleywine et al., 2025), which the committee's minutes confirm: members said functional unblinding and expectation bias may have played a role in the results, and some said these biases alone could explain the short-term difference. The FDA's briefing document reports MAPP2's survey by degree of certainty (78.8% of the MDMA arm were positive they had received MDMA, against 43.2% of the placebo arm positive they had received placebo), judges that the in-session monitors could probably tell allocation too, and records that the FDA had doubted the blind since 2016, when it suggested niacin or low-dose MDMA as comparators and the sponsor preferred inert placebo, and that it asked for MAPP2's survey in October 2020, after MAPP1 had ended. A second critique of MAPP1 argued from its figures that up to 90% of participants may have guessed their group and that an inactive placebo distributes placebo and nocebo effects unequally, adding no data of its own (Burke & Blumberger, 2021); the sponsor's own briefing document for the committee describes its safeguards for the outcome ratings but reports neither the blinding survey nor any measure of expectancy (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). Certainty: low. Status: single study (MAPP2 is the only trial with a blinding survey).
plain: Both big MDMA trials used a dummy pill with no effects. In the second trial, people were asked at the end which pill they thought they had: 94 in 100 on MDMA and 75 in 100 on the dummy pill guessed right, mostly from what they felt. About 8 in 10 of those on MDMA were sure of it, and one person stopped taking part because they believed they had the dummy pill. The first trial did not ask. The people who scored PTSD did not know who had what, but the scores came from what people told them, the US regulator thinks the therapists in the room could probably tell too, and neither trial reports measuring what people expected. The regulator's expert panel said this may have affected the results. So we cannot tell how much of the extra benefit came from MDMA itself.
population: Adults with moderate or severe PTSD in the two MAPS-sponsored phase 3 trials (MAPP1, 90; MAPP2, 104)
exposure: MDMA in three sessions with manualized therapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same therapy
outcome: Participants' identification of their allocation (blinding integrity); assessor blinding; measurement of expectancy
magnitude: MAPP2 end-of-study survey: correct 49/52 (94.2%) on MDMA and 33/44 (75.0%) on placebo; wrong 1/52 (1.9%) and 9/44 (20.5%); could not tell 2/52 (3.8%) and 2/44 (4.5%); Bang index (correct minus wrong over all respondents) 0.92 and 0.55 (editors' calculation). MAPP1: not assessed; at unblinding at least 7/44 (15.9%) on placebo and 2/46 (4.3%) on MDMA had believed they were in the other group (anecdotal). Expectancy: not measured in MAPP2; no measure reported for MAPP1. Degree of certainty (FDA, Table 9): positive 41/52 (78.8%) and think 8/52 (15.4%) on MDMA; positive 19/44 (43.2%) and think 14/44 (31.8%) on placebo. Therapists' and assessors' guesses: not reported (the FDA judges the in-session monitors probably aware). MAPP2's own Supplementary Table S6 gives the same figures, with 1/52 (1.9%) on MDMA positive they had placebo and 2/44 (4.5%) on placebo positive they had MDMA; 1 of the 8 placebo participants with missing data stopped because they believed they had placebo (Table S3). MAPP1, Burke & Blumberger's derivation: at most 81/90 (90%) correct.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about the trials' blinding (METHODS §6.3: descriptive claims start low). The figures come from one end-of-study survey in one trial (96 respondents of 104 randomized, 7 placebo participants missing), taken after participants had experienced their outcomes, which mixes recognition of drug effects with perceived benefit; MAPP1 offers only anecdote; the FDA's Table 9 reproduces the same survey from the clinical study report and is not independent of it. The consequence drawn (that the trials cannot separate MDMA's effect from expectancy and unblinding) follows from the design: an inactive placebo, a participant-reported outcome and no measure of expectancy. The size of any resulting bias is not estimable from these papers.

statement: In the two phase 3 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (99 people given MDMA and 95 given an inactive placebo, with the same therapy, during about 3 to 4 months of treatment), MDMA compared with placebo increased common, mostly mild or moderate, short-lived adverse events: muscle tightness in 58.5% vs 25.5% (MAPP2) and 61% vs 14% (MAPP1, registry; 63% vs 11% in the article's supplementary table), which the FDA's pooled table splits into jaw clenching or tightness (with bruxism, 57.6% vs 14.7%) and other muscle tightness (21.2% vs 9.5%), and more often decreased appetite, nausea, hyperhidrosis, feeling cold, restlessness, mydriasis, bruxism and nystagmus, with transient rises in blood pressure and pulse during sessions, which in the FDA's outlier analysis reached a systolic pressure of 180 mm Hg or more in 6 of 99 people on MDMA and none of 95 on placebo; in the sponsor's pooled table, peak systolic pressure reached 160 mmHg or more in 14% of participants at the starting dose level (first session) and in about 21% at each later session, against 4% on placebo at any session (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). Serious adverse events were rare and occurred only on placebo (2 of 44 in MAPP1, none in MAPP2); severe events occurred in 5 of 53 vs 2 of 51 and mild cardiac events, mostly palpitations, in 7 vs 1 (MAPP2), and severe events in both trials together in 9.1% vs 9.5% (the sponsor's pooled table). Across the sponsor's wider programme, serious adverse events occurred in 10 of 226 people given MDMA in six pooled phase 2 and 3 studies (none of them in the two randomized trials) and in 8 more given MDMA in other studies, among them serious suicidal ideation in 2 and a suicide attempt 28 days after the last session (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). Suicidal ideation was common in both arms and never rose above baseline; active ideation with some intent emerged in 2 MDMA and 1 placebo participant in MAPP2. No events were coded as misuse or abuse potential, but because positive drug effects went unrecorded (see below), the FDA judges the trials unable to inform abuse potential; its pooled table lists binge drinking in 2 vs 0 participants besides the substance-use events noted below, and in the open-label extension, once such effects were recorded from 2023, euphoric mood was recorded in 3 people (7%). How events were recorded limits these figures: expected effects such as euphoria were intentionally not solicited as adverse events (MAPP1), and the MAPP1 registry lists no term for euphoria; across the programme, the FDA reports, effects judged neutral, positive or favourable were not systematically collected as adverse events, against its advice of 2017; events were collected by site staff (therapists, in MAPP1), who were probably aware of allocation (as the FDA also judges), and graded for severity by the site physician (MAPP2); phase 3 had no laboratory tests on dosing days and no scheduled post-dose ECGs, blood pressure was measured three times per session, and the QT assessment was incomplete (FDA); relatedness was not assessed except for serious events (MAPP2); attribution to MDMA rested on a twofold difference in frequency, and the sponsor's own briefing document confirms that subjective effects were collected only when reported as adverse events and that no ECGs or laboratory tests followed dosing; the MAPP1 registry lists substance-use events in 3 vs 0 participants, which the article's supplementary table identifies as cannabis use and, by the twofold rule, counts among the events related to MDMA; and the trials excluded cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and (in MAPP2) high suicide risk and ended at 18 weeks, too few people and too short to show rare or delayed harms such as later misuse; the FDA judges that the cardiovascular risk cannot be determined from so small a database, and the follow-up visit's protocol reviewed medical history rather than adverse events. Two commentaries describe the safety profile favourably without numbers (Nutt & de Wit, 2021; Madero & Alvarez, 2023); at the FDA's advisory committee, which voted 10 to 1 that the benefits did not outweigh the risks (as the BMJ also reports; Mahase, 2024), members cited the missing laboratory and cardiac data, inadequate data on abuse liability and diversion, hyponatremia and the risk of boundary violations (the committee's minutes); a 2025 study, citing news reports, says the committee also questioned the long-term safety data and raised therapists' conduct during the trials, and its unsourced statement that the FDA's rejection cited weaknesses in safety documentation and in the reporting of adverse events matches the FDA reviewers' pre-meeting briefing, though the decision letter itself was not read (Earleywine et al., 2025). Certainty: moderate (for the increase in common adverse events). Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two trials, 99 people took MDMA and 95 took a dummy pill, in a clinic, with therapy. MDMA often caused short-lived side effects: a tight or clenched jaw (about 58 in 100 people, against 15 in 100 on the dummy pill), less appetite, feeling sick, sweating and feeling cold. Blood pressure and pulse went up during sessions; 6 in 100 people on MDMA reached very high blood pressure, and nobody on the dummy pill did. No serious side effects were seen on MDMA; two people on the dummy pill had one. Thoughts of suicide were common in both groups and did not go up. But the trials did not record pleasant effects, like feeling very happy, did no blood tests on treatment days, and were too small and short to show rare harms or misuse later on.
population: Adults with moderate or severe PTSD in the two MAPS-sponsored phase 3 trials (MAPP1, 90; MAPP2, 104), excluding cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and (in MAPP2) high suicide risk
exposure: MDMA in three supervised 8-hour sessions with manualized therapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same therapy
outcome: Treatment-emergent adverse events from the first experimental session to the last integration session (common, severe, serious, cardiac, suicidality and misuse-related events), as recorded
magnitude: MAPP2 (53 vs 51): muscle tightness 58.5% vs 25.5% (editors' difference 33.0 points, 95% CI 15.1 to 50.9); nausea 45.3% vs 21.6%; decreased appetite 35.8% vs 9.8%; hyperhidrosis 34.0% vs 5.9%; severe events 9.4% vs 3.9%; serious 0 vs 0; cardiac 7 vs 1; psychiatric 83.0% vs 72.5%; events of special interest 11.3% vs 5.9%. MAPP1 (46 vs 44; registry counts over about 18 weeks): muscle tightness 28 vs 6 (editors' difference 47.2 points, 29.9 to 64.6); decreased appetite 24 vs 5; nausea 14 vs 5; hyperhidrosis 10 vs 1; serious events 0 vs 2; suicidality events of special interest 3 (6.5%) vs 5 (11.4%); abuse-potential events 0 vs 0; substance use 3 vs 0, cannabis use per the supplement, whose table gives muscle tightness as 29 (63.0%) vs 5 (11.4%). FDA pooled MAPP1 and MAPP2 (99 vs 95; first session to study termination): bruxism and jaw tightness 57.6% vs 14.7%; other muscle tightness 21.2% vs 9.5%; decreased appetite 43.4% vs 10.5%; nausea 38.4% vs 16.8%; hyperhidrosis 28.3% vs 4.2%; substance use 3 vs 0; binge drinking 2 vs 0; systolic pressure 180 mm Hg or more 6.1% vs 0 (risk difference 6.1, 95% CI 1.4 to 10.8), 140 or more 67.7% vs 22.1% (45.6, 33.1 to 58.0); heart rate 110 or more and at least 10 above baseline 23.2% vs 0; C-SSRS rising from 3 or less to 4 or 5 in 4/98 vs 3/93. Sponsor's pooled tables (same 99 vs 95): severe 9.1% vs 9.5%; discontinuation of study drug for adverse events 1 vs 5; peak systolic 160 mmHg or more 14.1% (starting dose level, first session), 21.3% and 21.7% (second and third sessions) vs 4.2% (placebo, any session), 140 mmHg or more 45.5%, 61.7% and 56.5% vs 26.3% (the FDA's table gives 22.1% for placebo); serious suicidal ideation 4.1% vs 3.2%, without denominators (they match the FDA's 4/98 and 3/93), while the text names four participants with such scores in each arm. MAPP2 supplement: post-dose extremes on MDMA only (systolic 180 mmHg or more 1 event, diastolic 110 or more 4, pulse above 110 26, temperature 38 °C or more 4; none on placebo); dissociation 3 vs 0.

grade.reasoning: Two randomized trials, starting high. Risk of bias, one level: adverse events were collected by site therapists who were probably aware of allocation, expected drug effects were not solicited as adverse events (MAPP1) and, across the programme, positive or neutral effects were not systematically collected (FDA), relatedness was not assessed and attribution rested on a twofold difference; these affect what was counted, though they could not plausibly create differences as large as those in muscle tightness, appetite, nausea and sweating. Inconsistency not rated down: the same events dominate both trials. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the treatment period and the trial populations. Imprecision not rated down for the common events, whose intervals are far from no difference; serious, severe and cardiac events, suicidality and misuse are too few to compare, and the claim says so rather than claiming no increase (METHODS §6.3). The FDA's pooled re-analysis (99 vs 95) confirms the excess of common events and adds the vital-sign outliers; its findings that positive effects such as euphoria went unrecorded, against its 2017 advice, and that phase 3 had no laboratory tests on dosing days or post-dose ECGs limit what the trials can show about abuse potential and organ toxicity, not the direction of the increase in common events. Both trials are from one sponsor, hence replicated by the same team.

statement: The US Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee, meeting on 4 June 2024 on Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA (midomafetamine) capsules with a psychological intervention for PTSD, voted 9 to 2 that the available data did not show the drug to be effective and 10 to 1 that its benefits, with the FDA's proposed risk-mitigation programme, did not outweigh its risks (the FDA's final summary minutes, approved on 26 July 2024). Members cited functional unblinding, unmanaged expectation bias and selection bias; a follow-up too confounded to show durability; the lack of a factorial design separating the drug from the psychotherapy, and the therapists' unblinding and power of suggestion; and, on safety, missing laboratory, QTc and cardiac data, inadequate data on abuse liability and diversion, hyponatremia and the risk of boundary violations; the two members voting yes weighed the large effect sizes. The FDA reviewers' own briefing document, pre-decisional, had put the same issues to the committee: in MAPP2 94% of the MDMA arm and 75% of the placebo arm guessed their allocation and the in-session monitors could probably tell it too; the only outcome after 18 weeks came from an observational visit the FDA judged not designed to evaluate durability; no study separated the effect of the psychotherapy; the QT assessment was incomplete and phase 3 had no laboratory tests on dosing days; and the sponsor had not recorded positive drug effects such as euphoria as adverse events, against the FDA's advice of 2017, which the reviewers said limited the assessment of abuse potential. The decision itself is known only second-hand: as described in a BMJ news report and two later papers, the FDA declined in August 2024 to approve the application and, according to the company, asked for another phase 3 trial (the month is given by a 2025 commentary citing CNN; the decision letter was not read); the BMJ, published on 13 August 2024, says the decision came before the three phase 2 retractions by Psychopharmacology (see the retraction claim in this section). A 2025 paper, citing news reports and an article in JAMA, calls the vote split, and its unsourced statement that the rejection cited weaknesses in safety documentation and in adverse-event reporting is consistent with the reviewers' briefing but not shown by it. The BMJ also states, without a source, that the research in the three retracted papers did not form part of the application; the FDA's briefing bases efficacy on the phase 3 trials and lists phase 2 studies among the sources of its safety data, without naming the retracted analyses or the study site (MP4) behind the retractions; the sponsor's own briefing document for the committee likewise cites none of the three analyses and lists the phase 2 study MP-4 among the 17 studies supporting the drug's safety but not among the six it pooled for its safety analyses (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). The same document dates the FDA's agreement on the phase 3 design (a Special Protocol Assessment, July 2017) and Breakthrough Therapy Designation (August 2017), the final part of the rolling application to December 2023 and the FDA's filing of it, with Priority Review, to February 2024. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In June 2024 the US medicines regulator's (FDA's) expert panel voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show that MDMA therapy works for PTSD, and 10 to 1 that its benefits did not outweigh its risks. Panel members worried that most people knew which pill they had, that the later check could not show whether the benefit lasts, and that some safety data, such as blood tests, heart tests and the drug's pleasant effects, were never collected. In August 2024 the FDA said no; the company says it asked for another large trial. We have read the panel's record and the regulator's briefing, not its final letter.

statement: On 10 August 2024, as described in the journal's three retraction notices (read in full on the publisher's pages), Psychopharmacology retracted three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, published online in 2019 and 2020: a pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials that set out the design and rationale for the phase 3 trials, a pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials, and an analysis of how stopping medicines classified as reuptake inhibitors affected treatment response. The editors state that they had been informed of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one study site (MP4), that the authors confirmed knowing of these violations when they submitted but had neither disclosed them to the journal nor removed that site's data, and that a potential competing interest was not fully declared (authors affiliated with MAPS or its wholly owned subsidiary MAPS PBC; the notices state that MAPS fully funded and provided the MDMA used and that MAPS PBC organised the trial). Of the authors who responded to the publisher, most disagreed with the retractions (6 of 8, 4 of 5 and 3 of 4). The notices do not describe the violations, say when the editors were informed or how much of the analysed data came from the site, and do not mention the phase 3 trials; the BMJ, citing a New York Times report and a 2019 statement by MAPS, says reports suggest that an investigator at one study site had an unethical sexual relationship with a trial participant. The sponsor's briefing document for the FDA committee, prepared for its meeting of 4 June 2024, two months before the retractions, states that one participant in the phase 2 study MP-4 sustained serious harm from significant breaches of boundaries, unethical conduct and sexual misconduct, which it presents among the risks of impairment during MDMA's altered mental state; the event, it says, was reported to the sponsor after the study had ended and was investigated, with no evidence of misconduct with other participants at the site; MP-4 was a single-site study in Canada with 6 participants in its first stage (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In August 2024 a journal withdrew three earlier studies from the research programme behind the MDMA therapy trials. It said the authors knew of serious rule-breaking at one study site and did not tell it, and had not fully declared their ties to the sponsor. Most of the authors who answered the journal disagreed. The journal did not say what the rule-breaking was. The company's own papers for the regulator, written two months before, say one person in that study was seriously harmed by sexual misconduct.
