statement: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD is cost-effective in the United States has been examined, in the sources read, only in models funded by the sponsor or co-written by an author who declares financial ties to it, described in two commentaries (the sponsor's model and an earlier model second-hand; the critics' own model as outputs without its inputs); according to the 2025 critique, the answer turns mainly on the comparator and the price of the drug. As described by its critics, the sponsor-funded model compared MDMA-assisted therapy with the same therapy given with a dummy pill (placebo), priced the drug at 36,000 US dollars for the full course, therapy excluded (48,376 dollars for the whole treatment), counted only PTSD-specific health-care costs, drew on 17 months of trial follow-up (including an observational follow-up that the FDA judged not designed to evaluate durability) and found about 84,000 dollars per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) over five years, under its threshold of 150,000 dollars. The critics' earlier models (2020, 2022), whose base-case comparator brings no new costs and no change in health, gave net savings at five years at a treatment cost of 11,537 dollars; re-run with the sponsor's drug price, payers would break even only after about 8.4 years (3.8 years in their 2022 analysis), and with the drug at 10,500 dollars the result is about 160 dollars per QALY over five years, with cost savings at any drug price below 10,320 dollars. These figures are reported without the model's inputs or any uncertainty range. The critique's second author has the same name and the same University of California San Francisco departments as the first author of both phase 3 trials, a link the critique does not mention (editors' comparison). An earlier model with an overlapping author, quoted in a 2023 commentary, projected 43,000 to 106,000 deaths averted and 109 to 266 billion dollars in net savings over 10 years if access were extended to 25% to 75% of eligible patients with chronic and severe PTSD. The sponsor's briefing document for the FDA committee gives no result for the trials' self-reported, sponsor-developed measure of health-care use or for the health-economics data collected in its follow-up study, and classes the trials' quality-of-life measure (EQ-5D-5L) as suggestive of benefit in both trials although its MAPP2 P value was 0.0557 (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). The critics note that no trial has compared MDMA-assisted therapy with standard PTSD treatments, and no independent economic evaluation is among these sources. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: According to two critics of the company's study, who also have money ties to the company, whether MDMA therapy is good value depends mostly on its price and on what it is compared with. The company's study compared it with the same talking therapy plus a dummy pill. The critics say it should be compared with the treatments people would otherwise get, and that at a much lower price it could even save money. No independent study of its value for money was among the papers read.
population: People with PTSD in the United States who would be eligible for MDMA-assisted therapy (as modelled)
exposure: MDMA-assisted therapy at the modelled drug prices
comparator: The same therapy with placebo (sponsor's model) or standard care assumed to bring no new costs or health change (critics' model)
outcome: Incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year; time for payers to break even; net savings
magnitude: Sponsor's model (second-hand): about 84,000 US dollars per QALY over five years against placebo-therapy, threshold 150,000. Critics' earlier models (2020, 2022): net savings at five years at a treatment cost of 11,537 dollars; break-even at 3.8 years in the 2022 analysis, at a much lower drug price. Critics' new runs of their model: break-even about 8.4 years at the sponsor's 36,000-dollar drug cost; about 160 dollars per QALY over five years at a 10,500-dollar drug price; dominant at any drug price below 10,320 dollars. Earlier model by an overlapping author (second-hand): 43,000 to 106,000 deaths averted, 3.3 to 8.2 million QALYs and 109 to 266 billion dollars in net savings over 10 years with access extended to 25% to 75% of eligible patients with chronic and severe PTSD. No interval is given for any figure.

statement: Whether the phase 3 trials show that MDMA itself, given within an intensive therapy, is an effective and acceptably safe treatment for PTSD is contested, and the sources read here cannot settle it. Two randomized trials from one sponsor (MAPP1, 90 adults; MAPP2, 104) found larger falls in PTSD symptom scores with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy at 18 weeks (11.9 and 8.9 CAPS-5 points; see the efficacy claim in section 12) and no serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment. Against this, in MAPP2, the only trial that asked, most participants identified their group, and neither trial reports a measure of expectancy; the comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy; the trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks, and the only later data, from an observational follow-up visit, were judged by the FDA not designed to evaluate durability (the sponsor presents them as evidence of durability); expected drug effects were not solicited as adverse events (MAPP1) and, the FDA reports, positive drug effects went unrecorded across the programme, against its advice of 2017; in 2024 the US regulator declined approval (as reported) after its advisory committee voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness and 10 to 1 that the benefits did not outweigh the risks, citing functional unblinding and expectation bias (the committee's minutes); and three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme, including the one that set out the rationale for the phase 3 trials, were retracted because the authors had not disclosed protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one site, or removed that site's data, and had not fully declared competing interests (the retraction notices). The regulator's briefing document and the committee's minutes were read; its decision letter was not. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Is MDMA, given with talking therapy, a good and safe treatment for PTSD? Not settled. Two trials run for the same sponsor found that PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill and the same therapy, over about 4 months, with no serious side effects on MDMA. But in the second trial most people could tell which pill they had, and neither trial reports measuring what they expected. MDMA was not compared with standard PTSD talking therapy, and the only later check was one visit that the regulator said could not show whether the benefit lasts. In 2024 the regulator's expert panel voted against the treatment and the regulator said no, and a journal withdrew three earlier studies from the same programme because rule-breaking at one study site was not disclosed.
population: Adults with PTSD considered for MDMA-assisted therapy
exposure: MDMA in three sessions within a manualized therapy
comparator: The same therapy with placebo; trauma-focused psychotherapy; the course of PTSD after treatment ends
outcome: PTSD symptoms beyond the trial period and harms in clinical use attributable to MDMA itself
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of MDMA separate from expectancy, or beyond 18 weeks: the only later data, an observational visit attended by 137 of 195 randomized, cannot separate a lasting effect from self-selection, unblinding and interim treatments (FDA). The trials' between-group differences at 18 weeks are 11.9 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 (4.1 to 13.7) CAPS-5 points; 94% and 75% of MAPP2 participants identified their allocation. Advisory committee votes: yes 2, no 9 on effectiveness; yes 1, no 10 on benefit-risk.

grade.reasoning: Rated for the question as posed, which goes beyond what the trials measured. Starting high (randomized trials). Risk of bias, two levels, as in the efficacy claim: unblinding (measured in MAPP2, not assessed in MAPP1) with a participant-reported outcome and no reported measure of expectancy, a bias shared by both trials and of unknown size against differences of comparable order. Indirectness, one level: the question concerns MDMA's own contribution, durability beyond 18 weeks, comparison with existing psychotherapy and harms in clinical use, none of which the trials measured directly. The short-term comparison with placebo plus the same therapy is rated separately (low, section 12), as is the rise in common adverse events (moderate, section 12). Contested (METHODS §6.4): credible published critiques and the 2024 regulatory events change the interpretation of the trials.

debate.question: Do the phase 3 trials show that MDMA, given with therapy, is an effective and acceptably safe treatment for PTSD?
debate.evidence_yes: Two prospectively registered, randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials with central randomization and blinded independent assessors found larger falls in clinician-rated PTSD symptom scores with MDMA than with placebo plus identical therapy at 18 weeks: 11.9 points (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) in 90 adults with severe PTSD and 8.9 points (4.1 to 13.7) in 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD; 67% vs 32% of completers (MAPP1) and 71% vs 48% of those in the 18-week analysis (MAPP2) no longer met PTSD criteria (61% vs 27% and 70% vs 39% of everyone randomized, for MAPP1 everyone dosed, editors' calculation) (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The registered primary outcomes are those reported, and analyses that included off-treatment data agreed. The benefit was seen in people with long-standing PTSD, high rates of depression and the dissociative subtype (in MAPP1, 6 participants on MDMA and 13 on placebo), and again in a more diverse second sample, where only 1 of 53 people stopped treatment on MDMA against 8 of 51 on placebo; in that trial the placebo arm had more women (82% vs 60%), and female sex went with better outcomes in both arms, an imbalance that if anything favours placebo (Mitchell et al., 2023). In the two phase 2 trials in which the systematic review judged the blind maintained or partly maintained, both with a low-dose MDMA comparator, the active doses lowered CAPS scores significantly more than the comparator in one (26 participants) and not significantly in the other (12 participants); these are the review's second-hand accounts of Mithoefer et al. (2018) and Oehen et al. (2013) (Brett & Bynum, 2025). No serious adverse event occurred among the 99 people given MDMA; common effects were short-lived and mostly mild; suicidal ideation never rose above baseline in either arm; no events were coded as misuse (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). Proponents can also point to longer follow-up: according to two critics of the sponsor's cost-effectiveness model, that model drew on 17 months of follow-up from MAPP2 and its extension study (MPLONG) and documented less health-care use after MDMA treatment, though no outcome figures are given in that critique (Marseille & Mitchell, 2025); the FDA's own analysis of that follow-up gives them: at a single visit 6 months to more than 2 years after treatment, among the 137 of 195 randomized who attended, CAPS-5 differences between the original arms of 14.7 (MAPP1) and 11.96 (MAPP2) points, which the FDA says might indicate a true drug effect (FDA, 2024b). The sponsor's interim report of the same follow-up adds that, of those assessed, 68% vs 33% had lost the diagnosis and 39% vs 11% were in remission both at the end of the trial and at follow-up (75% vs 41% and 45% vs 16% among MAPP2's participants, who were still blinded) (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). The differences at 18 weeks also survived a worst-case treatment of MAPP1's missing values (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024) and a tipping-point analysis in MAPP2 (Mitchell et al., 2023). The trial's authors argue that phase 3 drug trials are designed to isolate the drug against placebo with the same therapy and that no flawless comparator exists (Mitchell, Coker, et al., 2021). A systematic review counted five of six MAPS-linked randomized trials as finding significant benefit (Brett & Bynum, 2025). Two commentaries welcomed the first trial's efficacy and safety, without giving blinding or adverse-event data; one author of each declares an interest in MDMA treatment research or in the sponsor's trials (Nutt & de Wit, 2021; Madero & Alvarez, 2023). The FDA's reviewers, re-tabulating the sponsor's study reports, took both trials as positive and the changes as clinically meaningful, and two of the eleven voting members of its advisory committee judged the data to show effectiveness, citing the large effect sizes (FDA, 2024b; FDA, 2024c).
debate.evidence_no: Most participants identified their group where this was asked: in MAPP2, 94% on MDMA and 75% on placebo identified it at the end of the study, mostly from the effects they felt or did not feel; MAPP1 did not assess blinding; neither trial reports a measure of expectancy; and the outcome, although rated by blinded assessors, rests on participants' reports (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023). The MAPP2 authors' arguments that expectancy was mitigated are indirect: five of the eight placebo participants who stopped did so after the first session. Both trials were funded by one sponsor, which designed, analysed and helped write them, and 18 of MAPP2's 19 named authors are also MAPP1 authors (editors' comparison); a systematic review whose search keywords included MAPS, with no stated way of combining them, found no randomized trial without a link to MAPS (Brett & Bynum, 2025). The comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy, and the placebo-with-therapy arm also improved substantially (by 14.8 points in MAPP2); critics argue that a breakthrough claim needs benchmarking against first-line psychotherapies, which on cross-trial figures reach similar or greater symptom reductions with half or less of the therapy time (Halvorsen et al., 2021). The trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks, and the FDA judged the only later data, a single observational visit, not designed to evaluate durability: attendance was self-selected by those who had done better, MAPP1 participants had been told their allocation, and many had other treatments in the interval, some of them MDMA from outside the study (FDA, 2024b). The sponsor's own briefing document reports none of these interim treatments, adds that 32 of MAPP1's placebo participants received open-label MDMA in an extension study (whether before their follow-up visit is not stated) and gives the follow-up's scores only in figures (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). A second critique of MAPP1 argued that an inactive placebo distributes placebo and nocebo effects unequally (Burke & Blumberger, 2021), and in MAPP2 one placebo participant stopped treatment because they believed they had placebo (Mitchell et al., 2023). Expected effects such as euphoria were not solicited as adverse events (MAPP1), and across the programme positive or neutral effects were not collected, against the FDA's advice of 2017, nor were laboratory tests or post-dose ECGs done on dosing days in phase 3 (FDA, 2024b); events were collected by site therapists, whom the FDA judges probably aware of allocation, and the trials excluded people with cardiovascular disease, most substance use disorders and (in MAPP2) high suicide risk; the MAPP1 registry lists substance-use events in 3 of 46 participants on MDMA and none on placebo, identified in the trial's supplement as cannabis use (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021); in the phase 2 study MP-4, by the sponsor's own account, one participant sustained serious harm from significant breaches of boundaries, unethical conduct and sexual misconduct (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). On 10 August 2024 Psychopharmacology retracted three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme, among them the pooled analysis that set out the design and rationale for the phase 3 trials, because the authors knew of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one site (MP4) when they submitted but neither disclosed them nor removed that site's data, and because competing interests were not fully declared (Mithoefer et al., 2024; Jerome et al., 2024; Feduccia et al., 2024). In August 2024 the FDA declined to approve the application, according to a 2025 commentary citing a CNN report (Marseille & Mitchell, 2025); before that, its advisory committee had voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness and 10 to 1 that the benefits did not outweigh the risks, citing functional unblinding, unmanaged expectation bias and selection bias, a follow-up too confounded to show durability, the lack of a factorial design separating the drug from the psychotherapy, and missing laboratory, cardiac and abuse-liability data, as the BMJ summarized (FDA, 2024c; Mahase, 2024); the FDA's reviewers had judged that the therapists in the sessions could probably tell allocation too and that the psychotherapy's contribution had never been separated from the drug's (FDA, 2024b); news reports cited by a 2025 study describe the same concerns (Earleywine et al., 2025).
debate.neither_can_show: With an inactive placebo, neither the trials nor their critics can separate MDMA's pharmacological effect from participants' knowledge of their allocation and their expectations, and no trial reports a measure of expectancy or the assessors' guesses. Two trials of under 200 people followed for 18 weeks cannot show rare harms, later misuse or durability, and the longer follow-up (MPLONG) is an observational visit that, in the FDA's analysis, cannot separate a lasting drug effect from self-selection, unblinding and the other treatments received in the interval. No trial in the sources read compared MDMA-assisted therapy with a first-line psychotherapy, so the cross-trial comparisons of effect sizes and remission rates made by both sides rest on different control conditions and populations. The regulator's decision letter was not read; its briefing document and the committee's minutes do not mention the MP4 site, and no source shows whether the problems behind the phase 2 retractions reach the phase 3 data.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In two trials from one sponsor (Mitchell, Bogenschutz, et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2023), MDMA within an intensive therapy led to larger short-term falls in PTSD symptom scores than placebo with the same therapy, without serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment (low certainty for that comparison and moderate for the rise in common adverse events; see the efficacy and adverse-event claims in section 12). How much of the difference is due to MDMA rather than to unblinded expectation, whether it lasts beyond 18 weeks (the one observational follow-up suggests a persisting difference but cannot show that it is due to MDMA; FDA, 2024b; Lykos Therapeutics, 2024), how it compares with trauma-focused psychotherapy and what harms appear in wider use are not answered by the papers read here. The two commentaries that welcomed the first trial (Madero & Alvarez, 2023; Nutt & de Wit, 2021) did not examine the weaknesses on which the later doubts centre. The FDA's own reviewers (FDA, 2024b) and its advisory committee (9 to 2 against on effectiveness; FDA, 2024c) placed the central weakness in the same place. Missing from this reading: the regulator's decision letter (its briefing document and the committee's minutes are now read), the sponsor's cost-effectiveness analysis and a peer-reviewed report of the long-term follow-up of the phase 3 participants (MPLONG), known here only from the FDA's analysis and the sponsor's interim account.
debate.what_would_settle_it: An independent, preregistered trial with an active comparator that mimics MDMA's noticeable effects (or several doses), expectancy measured before treatment and blinding during it, assessors' guesses recorded, adverse events collected by staff outside the therapy team, and follow-up of at least 12 months; a trial against a trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time; publication of the phase 3 long-term follow-up for both arms, with the treatments received after the trial, the timing of open-label crossover and illicit MDMA use; and the regulator's full review and decision letter. Also: independent analysis of individual-participant data from both phase 3 trials, and the phase 2 analyses re-run without the MP4 site.

statement: At a single observational follow-up visit (MPLONG), as described in the FDA's briefing document (its own analyses of the sponsor's data; the published trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks), held 6 months to more than 2 years after treatment (median 23.4 months after the last session for MAPP1 participants, 8.5 months for MAPP2), the 137 phase 3 participants who enrolled and were assessed (56 of 91 randomized in MAPP1, 81 of 104 in MAPP2) still showed a difference between the original arms: CAPS-5 had fallen from baseline by 30.3 vs 15.6 points (MAPP1) and 28.0 vs 16.1 points (MAPP2), differences of 14.7 and 12.0 points that the FDA reports without intervals; from week 18 to the visit the MDMA arms improved by a further 5.5 (95% CI 1.1 to 10.0) and 3.6 (1.1 to 6.1) points, and the placebo arms changed little (+0.3 and -0.7). The FDA judged that the follow-up was not designed to evaluate durability: it had no prespecified analysis or error control; enrolment was voluntary and those who enrolled had done better by the end of the trials (CAPS-5 20.2 vs 30.9); MAPP1 participants knew their allocation before the visit; in the interval most participants had other psychotherapy, 12 had ketamine-assisted therapy, and 13 people from the MDMA arms and 7 from the placebo arms reported taking MDMA obtained outside the study; and when the FDA set aside scores after such drug use, the further improvement on MDMA was no longer distinguishable from zero in MAPP2 (-2.0, 95% CI -4.6 to 0.6), though it remained in MAPP1 (-4.9, -9.3 to -0.5) until the imputed scores were penalized. The sponsor's own briefing document presents the same visit as evidence of durability, adds that of those assessed 68% vs 33% had lost the diagnosis and 39% vs 11% were in remission both at the end of the trial and at follow-up (75% vs 41% and 45% vs 16% among MAPP2's participants, who were still blinded), shows the scores only in figures with a nominal P value, and reports neither the interim treatments nor the illicit MDMA use it collected; it also lists 32 of MAPP1's placebo participants as treated with open-label MDMA in an extension study from March 2021, without saying whether before their follow-up visit (Lykos Therapeutics, 2024). Many members of the FDA's advisory committee found the follow-up too confounded to judge durability. Whether the benefit of MDMA-assisted therapy over placebo with the same therapy lasts beyond 18 weeks is therefore not established. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Months to years after the trials, people who had MDMA still had lower PTSD scores than people who had the dummy pill. But only about 7 in 10 people came back for this one check, those who came back had done better, people from the first trial knew which pill they had had, and many had other treatments in between, some of them MDMA from outside the study. The US regulator said this check was not designed to show whether the benefit lasts.
population: Adults with PTSD from the two phase 3 trials (MAPP1, MAPP2) who enrolled in the observational follow-up study MPLONG and were assessed (137 of 195 randomized)
exposure: MDMA in three sessions within the trials' manualized therapy, with no further doses in the study
comparator: Placebo with the same therapy (the original randomized arm)
outcome: CAPS-5 total severity at a single follow-up visit 6 months to more than 2 years after the parent trial, and its change from week 18
magnitude: Effectiveness subset (FDA Table 8): least-squares mean change in CAPS-5 from parent-trial baseline at the follow-up visit, MAPP1 -30.31 on MDMA (n = 27) vs -15.61 on placebo (n = 29), MAPP2 -28.01 (n = 44) vs -16.05 (n = 37); between-arm differences -14.7 and -11.96 (FDA, no interval); at week 18 in the same subsets -8.8 and -9.0 (editors' calculation from Table 8). Change from week 18 to the visit: -5.51 (95% CI -9.95 to -1.07) and -3.60 (-6.10 to -1.09) on MDMA, +0.34 (-3.90 to 4.59) and -0.69 (-3.43 to 2.05) on placebo. FDA tipping-point analysis (scores after interim ketamine, 5-MeO-DMT or MDMA use treated as missing, mITT): -2.02 (-4.61 to 0.57) in MAPP2 and -4.93 (-9.32 to -0.53) in MAPP1 at no penalty. Attendance 56 of 91 and 81 of 104 randomized; median interval 23.4 (7.9 to 32.4) and 8.5 (6.0 to 22.8) months after the last treatment. Sponsor's briefing document (interim study report; 71 vs 66 assessed): durable responder 89% vs 59%, durable loss of diagnosis 68% vs 33%, durable remission 39% vs 11% (MAPP2 only, 44 vs 37: 89% vs 57%, 75% vs 41%, 45% vs 16%), without intervals; counting everyone dosed who was not assessed as not durable (99 vs 95), loss of diagnosis about 48% vs 23% and remission about 28% vs 7% (editors' calculation; counts inferred from the rounded percentages); enrolled 30 of 46 and 30 of 44 (MAPP1), 45 of 53 and 37 of 51 (MAPP2); follow-up from the parent study median 12.7 months (6.0 to 32.9), mean 15.9 and 15.8.

evidence.locator: Items 7 and 8
evidence.extracted: As corrected, MPLONG enrolled people who had received at least one dose of investigational product, drug or placebo, and its protocol included a review of medical history (not of adverse events), one C-SSRS and one administration of the primary efficacy measure.

evidence.locator: 6.9.1 MPLONG Disposition (p. 68); Figure 22 (p. 69); 6.9.3 and Tables 16 and 17 (pp. 70-71)
evidence.extracted: Enrolment by arm: MAPP1 30 on MDMA and 30 on placebo, MAPP2 45 and 37; 69 of 75 and 66 of 67 enrolled completed; among enrollees, men 42.7% vs 25.4%, earlier sertraline 33.3% vs 16.4%, CAPS-5 at the end of the parent study 15.9 vs 24.9 and SDS 3.0 vs 4.3; follow-up from the parent study mean 15.9 and 15.8 months, median 12.7 (6.1 to 32.7) and 12.7 (6.0 to 32.9). Editors' subtraction from the 46 and 44 treated in MAPP1 and 53 and 51 in MAPP2: 16 and 14, and 8 and 14, not enrolled.

evidence.locator: 6.9.4, 1st paragraph and the paragraph after Figure 23 (p. 72); Figure 24 and its notes (p. 73); 6.9.5 summary paragraph (pp. 74-75); 6.10, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 75)
evidence.extracted: The sponsor concludes that MPLONG provides evidence of durability of the treatment effect and that results were similar whether the visit came within a year or later (windows 6 to 12, 13 to 18, 19 to 24 and more than 24 months: 34, 10, 17 and 10 vs 31, 11, 10 and 13 participants); its P value (< 0.0001) is nominal and descriptive, the source is the interim study report, and no mean difference with an interval is given in text or tables.

evidence.locator: 6.8 MPLONG Study Design, 1st to 4th paragraphs (pp. 67-68); 6.8.1 (p. 68); Table 29, MAPPUSX row (p. 121), and its footnote d (p. 127)
evidence.extracted: MPLONG was observational and voluntary (participants were strongly encouraged to join, at least 6 months after their last session): MAPP1's participants enrolled after its database lock and unblinding, MAPP2's stayed blinded until its database lock and their MPLONG visit; interim psychotherapy, medicines and illicit MDMA use were collected but are not reported in the document; 32 MAPP1 placebo participants received open-label MDMA in the extension study MAPPUSX, from March 2021 (whether before or after their follow-up visit is not stated); the results come from an interim study report.

risk_of_bias.note: Self-selected attendance by better-off participants, MAPP1 unblinded before the visit, functional unblinding, interim treatments including MDMA from outside the study, single visit at variable times, no prespecified analysis.

inconsistency.note: Both trials' subsets show a persisting difference.

indirectness.note: The claim is limited to the trials' follow-up population and says durability is not established.

imprecision.note: No interval for the between-arm difference at follow-up; subsets of 27 to 44 per arm; the further improvement on MDMA loses significance in a sensitivity analysis.

large_effect.note: Not applicable: the comparison is not protected by randomization at follow-up.

grade.reasoning: MPLONG is an observational study (as the FDA describes it) of self-selected subsets of the randomized arms, so the comparison at follow-up is no longer protected by randomization and is rated as observational evidence, starting low. Risk of bias, one level: those who enrolled had done better by the end of the trials, MAPP1 participants knew their allocation, nearly all participants could tell their allocation anyway, most had other psychotherapy in the interval and some had ketamine or MDMA from outside the study, the visit came at times ranging from 6 to 32 months, and nothing was prespecified. Imprecision, one level: the FDA gives no interval for the between-arm difference at follow-up, the subsets are small, and the further improvement on MDMA is not robust to the FDA's sensitivity analysis. Rated instead as follow-up of randomized arms (starting high), the same problems would need at least three levels of downgrading and the certainty would also be very low. The evidence is seen through the regulator's re-analysis of the sponsor's data and through the sponsor's own summary of the same interim study report, which adds the durable-response percentages but none of the interim-treatment data; the study report itself was not read. The claim says only that durability is not established, which the evidence shows directly.

statement: In 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had recently completed detoxification (one open-label feasibility study in the UK, all White British, with no comparison group), an eight-week course of ten psychotherapy sessions that included two MDMA sessions was followed, 3 months after treatment, by self-reported drinking at least two WHO risk levels lower than at baseline in 9 of the 14 (64%; 95% CI 35% to 87%), which the authors' Bayesian analysis restates as a success rate of 55% to 63%; self-reported craving, a four-item sleep score and self-compassion also improved in the 13 or 14 with data, while quality of life did not change significantly after correction (11 with data). The trial registry places the drinking baseline before detoxification, the outcomes were self-reported by people who knew they had taken MDMA, the two-level endpoint was not a registered outcome, and the registered 6- and 9-month results are not in this report, so none of these changes can be attributed to MDMA. No randomized or otherwise controlled trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in alcohol use disorder was among the sources read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small UK study, 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had just been through detox had a talking-therapy course with two MDMA sessions. Three months later, 9 of the 14 reported drinking much less than at the start (which seems to mean before detox). There was no group without MDMA, and drinking was self-reported, so we cannot tell whether MDMA helped.
population: Adults aged 18 to 65 (registry) with a primary DSM-5 diagnosis of alcohol use disorder who had completed detoxification; excluded: psychotic, bipolar I or personality disorders, serious suicide risk, cardiovascular or severe liver disease, regular ecstasy use, other drug dependence, and antidepressants unless stopped
exposure: An eight-week recovery-based psychotherapy course of ten sessions, two of them with MDMA, with an overnight stay after each MDMA session
comparator: None: each participant's own baseline (for drinking, apparently drinking before detoxification, per the registry)
outcome: Reduction of at least two WHO drinking risk levels (Timeline Followback) 3 months after treatment; craving (PACS, OCDS), sleep, quality of life (SF-36), self-compassion and empathy at 3 months
magnitude: Two-level WHO risk reduction: 9 of 14 (proportion .64; binomial test against 50%, P = .423; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87); mean posterior success rate 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with a Beta(1,3) prior (editors' check: posterior means 0.625 and 0.556). Three months vs baseline: PACS −5.50 (95% CI 0.5 to 13; n = 13); OCDS obsessive −5.00 (2.00 to 8.50) and compulsive −5.00 (1.00 to 9.00); four-item sleep score −2.00 (n = 14); Self-Compassion Scale +12.1 (9.09 to 14.4; n = 13); no SF-36 subscale significant after Bonferroni correction (n = 11). Within-group changes only.

evidence.locator: Results › Bayesian analysis of World Health Organization drinking risk level at 3 months follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 9 of 14 reached a two-level reduction in WHO drinking risk at 3 months; binomial test against 50%: proportion .64, P = .423, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87; mean posterior 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with the sceptical Beta(1,3) prior.

evidence.locator: Results › Drinking behavior at 3 months follow-up, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 legend
evidence.extracted: At 3 months vs baseline (n = 13): PACS total difference 5.50 (95% CI .5 to 13), P = .031; OCDS obsessive 5.00 (2.00 to 8.50), P = .006; OCDS compulsive 5.00 (1.00 to 9.00), P = .021; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

evidence.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Quality of life, Sleep and Self-compassion, 1st paragraphs; Fig. 3 legend
evidence.extracted: SF-36 (n = 11): no subscale significant after Bonferroni correction; four PSQI-derived sleep items (n = 14): difference 2.00, P = .041; Self-Compassion Scale (n = 13): +12.1 (95% CI 9.09 to 14.4), P < .001.

evidence.locator: Abstract › Methods; Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Fourteen participants with alcohol use disorder who had recently undergone detoxification completed the eight-week course of ten sessions, two with MDMA; 8 men and 6 women, mean age 48, all White British.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Single-group open-label phase 1 study, actual start 18 April 2018, first submitted 31 January 2019 (retrospective registration); drinking registered as change by Timeline Followback from pre-detoxification (screening) levels to session 10 and 3, 6 and 9 months; no two-level WHO endpoint registered; questionnaires registered at 3, 6 and 9 months; no results posted.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors call the study an open-label trial with a small population, acknowledge possible Type I error inflation, call the findings hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of efficacy, and ask for randomized placebo-controlled trials that measure de-blinding and expectancy, and for long-term follow-up.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors compare the 55% to 63% success rate with 68% of patients reaching a two-level WHO risk reduction at the end of treatment in secondary analyses of the COMBINE study and Project MATCH: a comparison across studies, not within this one.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison group, pre-detoxification baseline, unblinded self-report, unregistered endpoint.

imprecision.note: Fourteen participants.

grade.reasoning: One single-arm open-label study of 14 people; for the question of effect it is non-randomized, so it starts low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical): no comparison group; a drinking baseline that the registry places before detoxification, so a fall after detoxification is expected whatever the treatment; self-reported outcomes from people who knew they had taken MDMA; unexplained missing questionnaire data; an unregistered endpoint, with the registered 6- and 9-month results unreported. Imprecision one level: 14 people, with a 95% interval from 35% to 87% for the endpoint. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to this population and time point; publication bias not assessable from one study. The relation is 'insufficient evidence': the design cannot show whether MDMA-assisted therapy changes drinking, and the statement only describes what was observed.

verification.flag_note: The original report of the same 14 participants (Sessa et al., 2021, J Psychopharmacol, doi 10.1177/0269881121991792) is not free and was not read; its safety and 9-month drinking data should be added before this claim is shown.

statement: In autistic adults with marked to very severe social anxiety (one randomized pilot trial at a single California site: 8 randomized to MDMA and 4 to an inactive placebo, of whom 7 and 4 were analysed), two MDMA sessions within psychotherapy, compared with placebo with the same psychotherapy, were followed one month later by a larger fall in interview-rated social anxiety (Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale: −44.1 vs −19.3 points; difference 24.8, 95% CI 1.9 to 47.9; P = 0.037), and the difference was similar at 6 months (P = 0.036). Participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions, two dose groups were pooled (in the registry the lower-dose group improved more), and the interval runs from a trivial to a very large difference, so the evidence is insufficient to say how much, if at all, MDMA reduces social anxiety in autistic adults. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial, 12 autistic adults with strong social anxiety had talking therapy with MDMA or a dummy pill. Social anxiety dropped more with MDMA, but almost everyone could tell which pill they had, and the trial was too small to show how big any benefit is.
population: Autistic adults aged 21 or older (ADOS-2 Module 4) with an LSAS of 60 or more, MDMA-naive by self-report, physically healthy and psychologically stable
exposure: MDMA in two blinded 8-hour sessions about a month apart (two dose subgroups, pooled), with three preparatory sessions including mindfulness skills and three integrative sessions after each
comparator: Inactive placebo (lactose) with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Change in Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale total from baseline to one month after the second session (primary) and to 6 months
magnitude: LSAS change −44.1 (SD 14.8; n = 7) vs −19.3 (18.8; n = 4); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037; 95% CI of the difference 1.92 to 47.87 (editors' recalculation 1.8 to 47.8); placebo-subtracted d 1.4, printed CI −0.074 to 2.874 (editors' approximation 0.04 to 2.76). Six months: −47.7 (14.7) vs −23.3 (18.0), P = 0.036. Fall of 20 points or more: 6 of 7 vs 2 of 4. Registry results by dose group: lower-dose group −51.0, higher-dose group −39.0, placebo −19.3.

evidence.locator: Results › Clinical response, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3
evidence.extracted: Six months: placebo change −23.3 (18.0), MDMA −47.7 (14.7); t(9) = 2.454, P = 0.036; within the MDMA group, primary endpoint to 6 months P = 0.307; a fall of 20 points or more in 6 of 7 on MDMA vs 2 of 4 on placebo (Table 3; the text gives 6 of 8).

evidence.locator: Results › Blinding, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Participants guessed their treatment wrongly in one of 8 placebo sessions and in none of the 15 MDMA sessions (correct in 22 of 23); the two therapists were wrong in 2 and 1 of 8 placebo sessions and in 2 of 15 MDMA sessions each.

evidence.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image); Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of 8 randomized to MDMA, one was withdrawn after randomization because they had been enrolled with hypertension and a recent substance use disorder within the exclusion window; 7 MDMA and 4 placebo participants were analysed, without imputation; the two dose subgroups were combined.

evidence.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396 (API v2) › Status; Results › Outcome Measures
evidence.extracted: Registered 6 December 2013, before the start on 11 April 2014; LSAS change to one month after session 2 posted by group: lower-dose MDMA group −51.0 (8.19), higher-dose group −39.0 (17.57), placebo −19.3 (18.77); posted denominators 4, 4 and 3, while weights of 3 and 4 reproduce the paper's pooled MDMA values (editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors call the sample small, too small to compare doses, consider blinding with an inactive placebo adequate because one participant and both investigators made incorrect guesses, and acknowledge that observable MDMA effects might contribute to efficacy.

imprecision.note: Eleven analysed; very wide interval.

grade.reasoning: One randomized trial: starts high. statement: In couples in which one partner had PTSD (two small uncontrolled studies sharing an author: 6 White heterosexual couples in which both partners took MDMA twice within a condensed course of cognitive-behavioral conjoint therapy, and 8 US veteran couples in which only the veteran took MDMA twice within an eight-session brief version), clinician-rated PTSD symptoms fell after treatment (CAPS-5, scale 0 to 80: from about 41 to 19 in the first study, with 5 of 6 patients no longer meeting PTSD criteria; a mean fall of 16 points from 39 in the second, with 3 of 8 no longer meeting criteria and a rebound of about 6 points by 6 months), and both partners' relationship satisfaction rose (in the second study it partly fell back, and one partner's worsened). All couples completed treatment and no serious adverse event was reported. Neither study had a comparison group, the conjoint therapy improves PTSD without MDMA, and in the veteran study loss of diagnosis was about as frequent as with the brief therapy alone in an earlier trial in the same population, so whether MDMA adds anything is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In two small studies, couples in which one partner had PTSD had couples therapy that included MDMA sessions. PTSD and relationship scores improved, and no one had a serious side effect. But neither study had a group without MDMA, and this couples therapy also helps without it, so we do not know if MDMA added anything.
population: Couples (married or committed, almost all heterosexual) in which one partner had chronic PTSD on the CAPS-5 and the other did not; severe relationship aggression or intimate partner violence and current substance use disorders excluded; psychiatric medicines stopped for the PTSD partner (and, in the first study, both partners)
exposure: Two MDMA sessions within cognitive-behavioral conjoint therapy for PTSD: both partners dosed within the full 15-session protocol condensed into 7 weeks (first study), or only the partner with PTSD dosed within an 8-session brief protocol with integration sessions drawing on couple therapy (second study)
comparator: None: change from baseline in each study
outcome: CAPS-5 PTSD severity and diagnosis; relationship satisfaction (Couples Satisfaction Index) and other relational measures; adverse events; up to 6 months
magnitude: First study (6 couples; model-estimated means): CAPS-5 41.42 (SD 5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months (within-group d 2.10 and 2.25); registry: CAPS-5 change −25.7 (SD 13.89); Couples Satisfaction Index, patients 105.37 to 127.00 (d 0.82) and partners 98.10 to 125.34 (d 0.64) after treatment. Second study (8 veteran couples): CAPS-5 39.13 (10.56) at baseline, mean fall 16.1 (SD 11.4) during treatment, response 5 of 8, loss of diagnosis 3 of 8, remission 2 of 8, rebound 6.3 points by 6 months; satisfaction d 1.83 (veterans) and 1.29 (partners) during treatment, rebound d −0.68 and −0.47; reliable improvement in 10 of 16 people and reliable deterioration in 1 partner.

evidence.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
evidence.extracted: Six couples: CAPS-5 41.42 (5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after, 17.43 (17.14) at 3 months and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months (estimated means); B = −4.64, P < .001; within-group d 2.10, 1.88 and 2.25; all but one patient had a sustained remission of the clinician-assessed PTSD diagnosis.

evidence.extracted: Couples Satisfaction Index: patients 105.37 (13.39) to 127.00 after treatment and 130.78 at 6 months, B = 4.55, P < .05, d 0.82 to 1.22; partners 98.10 (50.81) to 125.34 and 130.10, B = 5.73, P < .05, d 0.64 to 0.80; one patient satisfied at baseline was dissatisfied afterwards.

evidence.locator: 2. Results, 1st paragraph; 3. Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: All six couples completed the protocol and there were no serious adverse events; the authors state that the lack of randomization or a control condition severely limits the conclusions.

evidence.extracted: Posted results: CAPS-5 at the primary endpoint 16.3 (13.71), change −25.7 (13.89), n = 6; all 6 patients and all 6 partners had at least one non-serious adverse event up to 2 months after the last MDMA session; no serious events or deaths.

evidence.locator: Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes and Relationship Quality Outcomes, 1st paragraphs; Tables 1 and 2
evidence.extracted: Same six couples: the patient's posttraumatic growth rose as rated by patients (B = 7.30) and partners (B = 7.63), both P < 0.001; perceived support and social intimacy rose for both partners (intimacy B = 4.12 and 3.10); relationship depth did not change; the printed SORTS means duplicate another measure's values (card reporting issue).

evidence.locator: RESULTS › PTSD symptom severity, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 note
evidence.extracted: Eight veterans: CAPS-5 39.13 (10.56) at baseline; during treatment d = −1.25, mean fall 16.1 points (SD 11.4; range 3 to 34); response 5 of 8, loss of diagnosis 3 of 8, remission 2 of 8; rebound during follow-up of 6.3 points (d = 0.29).

evidence.locator: RESULTS › Relationship satisfaction, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Relationship satisfaction (CSI-32): d = 1.83 for veterans and 1.29 for partners during treatment, mean rise 27.9 (31.8) and 19.8 (23.1); rebound d = −0.68 and −0.47 during follow-up; reliable improvement in 10 of 16, reliable deterioration in 1 partner.

evidence.locator: Introduction (untitled opening section), 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors report that CBCT without MDMA has shown large reductions in PTSD symptoms (gs 1.28 to 1.71, citing Monson et al., 2024) and that their eight-session brief CBCT, without MDMA, reduced PTSD in veterans (ds 1.05 to 1.12; Morland et al., 2022) with smaller relationship gains; these figures are second-hand.

evidence.locator: DISCUSSION, 2nd and 7th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Loss of diagnosis (37.5%) and remission (25%) were lower than in the phase 3 MDMA trials and, the authors say, closer to brief CBCT without MDMA in the same population; the open-label design, small sample and lack of a comparison condition preclude causal inference.

evidence.locator: RESULTS › Safety › AEs and Medication management, 1st paragraphs; RESULTS › Feasibility and acceptability
evidence.extracted: All couples completed every session; no serious adverse events; every veteran had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event; one veteran's second MDMA session was rescheduled after a cocaine-positive urine test.

risk_of_bias.note: Critical: no comparison; base therapy effective without MDMA.

imprecision.note: Fourteen couples in two studies.

grade.reasoning: Two uncontrolled studies (14 couples in all), non-randomized: start low. Risk of bias two levels (ROBINS-I critical in both): no comparison group, and the base therapy is an established treatment that improves PTSD on its own, so MDMA's contribution cannot be separated from the therapy, time or expectation; outcomes unblinded. Imprecision one level: 6 and 8 couples. Inconsistency not rated down: both studies improved, though the second rebounded. Status 'replicated by the same team' because the studies share an author (Anne C. Wagner) and a related protocol; the second sample is independent. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' about any added effect of MDMA.

statement: In adults with severe PTSD and no current alcohol use disorder (the first phase 3 trial, MAPP1; 82 of 90 with data), MDMA-assisted therapy compared with placebo plus the same therapy was followed by small changes in self-reported hazardous drinking (AUDIT, scale 0 to 40: −1.0 vs +0.4 points; P = 0.04 without adjustment, P = 0.52 after adjusting for the MDMA group's higher baseline) and drug use (DUDIT, scale 0 to 44: −1.4 vs −0.8; P = 0.55) by the end of the study. The questionnaires asked about the past 12 months at baseline but only about the time since treatment ended at the end, the outcomes were exploratory and self-reported in a trial where most participants probably knew their allocation, and people with current substance use disorders other than mild alcohol or cannabis use disorder were excluded. The evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy changes alcohol or drug use in people with PTSD; drug-use scores did not rise in either group. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one PTSD trial of 90 people, those who had MDMA therapy did not clearly change their drinking or drug use compared with those who had a dummy pill. But almost no one had a drinking or drug problem to begin with, and people reported their own use.
population: Adults with severe PTSD (CAPS-5 of 35 or more) in MAPP1; current mild alcohol or cannabis use disorder (or moderate in early remission) allowed and other substance use disorders within 12 months excluded; in the analysed set none had a current alcohol use disorder
exposure: MDMA in three sessions within manualized therapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same therapy
outcome: Change in AUDIT and DUDIT scores from baseline to study termination
magnitude: AUDIT change −1.02 (SD 3.52; n = 42) vs +0.40 (2.70; n = 40), unadjusted P = 0.0436, Hedges' g 0.45; adjusted for baseline AUDIT, P = 0.52. DUDIT change −1.36 (3.00) vs −0.78 (5.39), P = 0.5452, g 0.13. Baseline AUDIT 4.26 vs 2.83 (Table 1; P = .10).

risk_of_bias.note: Exploratory self-report; changed recall window; analysis-dependent result.

imprecision.note: Small differences with wide uncertainty.

grade.reasoning: From a randomized trial: starts high. Risk of bias two levels (RoB 2 high for measurement and for selection of the reported result): exploratory self-reported questionnaires, a recall window that changed between the two measurements, probable unblinding, complete-case data, and a result that depends on whether the baseline imbalance is adjusted for. Imprecision one level: small differences on long scales and a wide range of plausible effects for drug use. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to people with PTSD without current substance use disorders. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' because neither a change nor its absence is shown with precision.

statement: In the small trials of MDMA-assisted therapy outside PTSD read for this page (anxiety with a life-threatening illness, 13 on MDMA and 5 on placebo; social anxiety in autistic adults, 8 and 4; major depression, 12 open-label; couples, 6 and 8 couples open-label), no serious adverse event was attributed to MDMA and no participant stopped treatment because of side effects. During sessions MDMA was followed more often than placebo by jaw clenching (11 of 13 vs 1 of 5), thirst (11 of 13 vs 2 of 5), sweating (9 of 13 vs 0 of 5) and headache (8 of 13 vs 1 of 5), and in autistic adults by anxiety (6 of 8 vs 1 of 4); in the following week by fatigue and needing more sleep (12 of 13 each vs 3 and 2 of 5); blood pressure, pulse and temperature rose during sessions without needing treatment. Suicidal ideation was recorded as an adverse event in 2 of 8 autistic adults on MDMA (and 1 of 4 on placebo), and worsening suicidal ideation in 4 to 6 of 12 people with depression; 2 of those 12 received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for anxiety and insomnia after dosing. Side effects were mostly collected as spontaneous reports or by the treating therapists, and with at most 13 people on MDMA per trial, rare or delayed harms could not be detected. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In small trials of MDMA therapy for problems other than PTSD, no one had a serious side effect from MDMA. Short-lived effects such as a tight jaw, thirst, sweating, headache and tiredness were common. These trials were too small to show rare harms.
population: Adults in published trials of MDMA-assisted therapy outside PTSD that were read in full: anxiety with a life-threatening illness, social anxiety in autistic adults, major depressive disorder, and couples in which one partner had PTSD
exposure: MDMA in two (occasionally three) supervised sessions within psychotherapy
comparator: Inactive placebo with the same psychotherapy in two trials; none in the open-label studies
outcome: Adverse events, expected reactions, vital signs and suicidal ideation during and after MDMA sessions
magnitude: Anxiety with a life-threatening illness (MDMA 13, placebo 5): during sessions jaw clenching 11 vs 1, thirst 11 vs 2, dry mouth 9 vs 1, perspiration 9 vs 0, headache 8 vs 1; in the next 7 days fatigue 12 vs 3, needing more sleep 12 vs 2, insomnia 9 vs 2; peak temperature 37.3 vs 36.9 °C. Autistic adults (8, 4): anxiety 6 vs 1, difficulty concentrating 5 vs 1; suicidal ideation 2 vs 1; peak systolic pressure, pulse and temperature higher on MDMA (maximum pulse 114, maximum temperature 37.7 °C). Depression (12, open-label): 46 adverse events in 10 participants, none serious; worsening suicidal ideation in 4 to 6. Veteran couples (8 dosed): headache 6 of 8 within 7 days, raised blood pressure 3 of 8. Serious adverse events attributed to MDMA: none among the 58 people given MDMA in these five studies (counting the 5 placebo participants of the life-threatening-illness trial who later took MDMA open-label).

evidence.locator: Table 4; Results, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: During the two blinded sessions, MDMA (13) vs placebo (5): jaw clenching 11 vs 1, thirst 11 vs 2, dry mouth 9 vs 1, perspiration 9 vs 0, headache 8 vs 1; in the following 7 days fatigue 12 vs 3, needing more sleep 12 vs 2, insomnia 9 vs 2; reactions decreased over the week.

evidence.locator: Results, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Treatment-emergent adverse events infrequent and nearly equal between groups; serious events only from cancer recurrence or progression (one death about a year after stopping, unrelated to MDMA); only peak temperature differed (37.3 vs 36.9 °C); no serious suicidal ideation or behaviour; no discontinuation because of adverse effects related to MDMA.

evidence.locator: Results › Safety, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Tables 4 and 5
evidence.extracted: No serious adverse events; during sessions anxiety in 6 of 8 on MDMA vs 1 of 4 on placebo and difficulty concentrating 5 vs 1; one severe headache on MDMA; suicidal ideation as an adverse event in 2 of 8 vs 1 of 4, pre-existing in medical history; depressed mood 2 of 8 vs 0.

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic measurements, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Mean peak systolic blood pressure (P = 0.021), pulse (P = 0.015) and temperature (P < 0.001) higher on MDMA; maximum pulse 114 bpm, maximum temperature 37.7 °C; no systolic pressure above 180 or diastolic above 110 mmHg; blood pressure back to pre-drug levels by session end.

evidence.locator: Results › Safety, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: 46 adverse events in 10 of 12, 15 moderate and 31 mild, none serious, no discontinuations; most common headache, increased suicidal ideation and jaw muscle tightness; benzodiazepines and zopiclone for 2 participants after dosing; worsening intensity of suicidal ideation in 6 participants (12 events).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 7th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Suicidal ideation given as 33.3% in the comparison with MAPP1; adverse events were reported to the therapy team, which may have led to under-reporting.

evidence.locator: RESULTS › Safety › AEs, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: No serious adverse events; every veteran had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event; headache 75.0%, feeling warm 37.5%, increased blood pressure 37.5%, nausea, decreased appetite and sadness 25.0% each within 7 days of an MDMA session; no high suicide risk on the C-SSRS.

evidence.locator: 2. Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: All six couples completed the protocol; no serious adverse events; the most common reactions after MDMA sessions were diminished appetite, anxiety, headache and jaw tightness.

risk_of_bias.note: Spontaneous or therapist-recorded side effects; possible under-reporting.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about what was recorded in these trials: starts low. Risk of bias one level: side effects were collected as spontaneous reports or by the treating therapists, which the depression trial's authors say may have led to under-reporting, and the counts of suicidal ideation differ within one paper; this could materially change the figures. Imprecision is not rated down separately because the claim gives counts and states that rare or delayed harms could not be detected. Status 'replicated': the same pattern of short-lived sympathomimetic and mood reactions, without serious adverse events attributed to MDMA, was recorded by independent teams in the United States and Norway. To be joined with the other reader's claim from the cross-indication reviews.

statement: In adults with moderate to severe anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, almost all with cancer (one randomized pilot trial at a single California clinic: 13 on MDMA, 5 on an inactive placebo), two MDMA sessions within manualized psychotherapy, compared with placebo with the same psychotherapy, were followed one month later by a larger fall in self-reported trait anxiety (STAI-Trait, scale 20 to 80: −23.5 vs −8.8 points; difference 14.7, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9, editors' calculation; P = 0.056). The difference was not statistically significant and its interval runs from no difference to a very large one; the MDMA group started 5 points more anxious, and participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions. After the placebo group crossed over to MDMA, scores stayed lower at 6 and 12 months, with no control group left. The evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy reduces anxiety in people with a life-threatening illness. A Cochrane review of the same trial reached the same conclusion, with intervals it computed more conservatively (trait anxiety −14.7 points, 95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), and found no treatment-related serious adverse events (Schipper et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small trial, 18 adults with anxiety linked to cancer or another serious illness had talking therapy with either MDMA or a dummy pill. A month later, anxiety had dropped more in the MDMA group, but the difference could be chance, and most people could tell which pill they had.
population: Adults with a life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness (17 of 18 with neoplasms), life expectancy of at least 9 months, STAI-Trait of 45 or more and anxiety mainly related to the illness, off psychiatric medicines; excluded: ongoing first-line treatment such as initial chemotherapy, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, brain tumours, diabetes, psychotic and bipolar I disorders
exposure: MDMA in two blinded day-long sessions 2 to 4 weeks apart within manualized non-directive psychotherapy (three preparatory sessions and integration sessions after each)
comparator: Inactive placebo (lactose) with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Change in STAI-Trait from baseline to one month after the second session (primary); secondary anxiety, depression, sleep and well-being measures; uncontrolled follow-up to 12 months after crossover
magnitude: STAI-Trait change −23.5 (SD 13.2; n = 13) vs −8.8 (14.7; n = 5), P = 0.0558; Hedges' g 1.03, printed with a 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31 that cannot be right (editors' approximate interval −0.05 to 2.12); raw difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9 (editors' calculation, pooled t(16) = 2.06). Of 20 uncorrected secondary comparisons, only posttraumatic growth and mindfulness reached P = 0.04. After crossover, uncontrolled (n = 17): STAI-Trait 61.1 at baseline, 33.6 at 6 months and 34.2 at 12 months.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 (STAI Trait row)
evidence.extracted: STAI-Trait change from baseline to one month after the second blinded session: −23.5 (SD 13.2) on MDMA vs −8.8 (14.7) on placebo, P = 0.0558; endpoint 38.9 vs 48.6; Hedges' g 1.03 printed with a 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31. Editors' calculation: difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9; approximate CI for g −0.05 to 2.12.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Placebo change scores ranged from −1 to −35 (median −3); excluding the one placebo participant with −35, a post hoc comparison gave P = 0.0066; the prespecified comparison gave P = 0.0558.

evidence.locator: Table 1
evidence.extracted: Baseline STAI-Trait 62.5 (7.3) on MDMA vs 57.4 (5.2) on placebo; history of PTSD 11 of 13 (84.6%) vs 2 of 5 (40.0%); the primary analysis compared unadjusted change scores.

evidence.locator: Results, 8th paragraph
evidence.extracted: At the end of each blinded session participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions (86.1%) and the co-therapists in 32 of 36 (88.9%).

evidence.locator: Table 2; Results, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Secondary outcomes at the primary endpoint: posttraumatic growth (P = 0.04) and mindfulness (P = 0.04) favoured MDMA; STAI-State (P = 0.10), BDI-II (P = 0.36), PSQI (P = 0.05), MADRS (P = 0.41), GAF (P = 0.52) and self-compassion (P = 0.21) did not differ significantly; no correction for about 20 tests.

evidence.locator: Table 3; Results, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: After both groups had received three MDMA sessions (n = 17, no control group): STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) at baseline, 36.4 (9.5) at treatment exit, 33.6 (8.3) at 6 months and 34.2 (10.3) at 12 months; F(3,48) = 51.39.

evidence.extracted: 18 randomized (13 MDMA, 5 placebo), single US centre, 2015 to 2018; mean age 54.9, 77.8% women; life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness, STAI-Trait above 45, life expectancy of at least 9 months; placebo of lactose (listed as an active placebo group); two blinded sessions with nine non-drug psychotherapy sessions; funded by MAPS; blinding high risk (more than 80% guessed correctly; outcomes mostly self-reported); primary outcome prespecified in NCT02427568.

evidence.extracted: STAI-T −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83), BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33), 18 participants, endpoint 1 month after the second session; very low certainty (one level for risk of bias, two for imprecision).

evidence.locator: Methods › Data collection and analysis › Measures of treatment effect, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Mean differences were computed from change scores, with standard errors assuming no correlation between pre- and post-treatment values, which the authors note widens the confidence intervals.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (secondary outcomes), Wolfson 2020 rows; Table 4 (adverse events), Wolfson 2020 rows; Results › Effects of interventions › Entactogens (MDMA) › Secondary outcomes, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: GAF 75.1 (SD 9.9) on MDMA against 72.8 (7.7) on placebo 1 month after two sessions, p = 0.52; FACIT subscales p 0.15 to 0.87; no treatment-related serious or grade 3 or 4 adverse events; jaw clenching 11 (84.6%) against 1 (20.0%), thirst 11 against 2, dry mouth 9 against 1, perspiration 9 against 0, headache 8 against 1; the reactions were short and mostly resolved by the end of the session or during the following week.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: All included trials were crossover trials; all outcomes after more than 3 months were measured after crossover, so no controlled long-term comparison is possible.

risk_of_bias.note: Participant-reported outcome with allocation evident; baseline imbalance with unadjusted analysis.

imprecision.note: Five controls; interval includes no difference.

grade.reasoning: One randomized trial: starts high. Risk of bias two levels (very serious, RoB 2 high for the measurement of the outcome): the primary outcome is self-reported while participants identified their allocation in 86% of sessions and expectancy was not measured; the MDMA group also started with higher anxiety and change scores were not adjusted for baseline, which could favour MDMA through regression to the mean. Imprecision two levels: 18 participants with only 5 controls, and the 95% interval of the difference runs from about −0.5 to 30 points. Indirectness not rated down because the claim is restricted to the trial population and endpoint. The relation is 'insufficient evidence' because neither an effect nor its absence is shown with precision.

statement: In 12 adults with moderate to severe major depressive disorder, mostly recurrent (one open-label proof-of-principle study in Norway, with no comparison group), two MDMA sessions about a month apart within a psychotherapy programme of about eleven sessions were followed, about 8 weeks after the second session, by a fall in clinician-rated depression (MADRS, scale 0 to 60: from 29.6 to 10.3, as corrected in a corrigendum; change −19.3, 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7), with 9 of 12 meeting both response and remission thresholds; functional impairment also fell. There were no serious adverse events, but worsening suicidal ideation was recorded as an adverse event in 4 to 6 of the 12 (the paper gives both figures) and 2 received benzodiazepines and zopiclone after dosing. The raters were not blind, almost all participants were self-referred, entry required a high score, and there was no control group, so the fall cannot be attributed to MDMA; the 7-month follow-up was not read. A network meta-analysis of randomized trials reporting depressive symptoms, whose MDMA trials enrolled mostly people with PTSD rather than depression, found a larger reduction with high-dose MDMA-assisted therapy than in the placebo arms of psychedelic trials (5.3 points on the HAMD-17, 95% credible interval 2.26 to 8.32), but could not show a difference from the placebo arms of antidepressant trials (1.5 points, −2.79 to 5.78, an indirect comparison; Hsu et al., 2024). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study in Norway, 12 adults with depression had two MDMA sessions with talking therapy. About two months later, depression scores had dropped a lot, and 9 of the 12 were much better. But there was no group without MDMA, and the people rating depression knew everyone had taken it.
population: Adults with DSM-5 major depressive disorder (single or recurrent, without psychotic features; current episode 12 weeks to 2 years) and a MADRS of 20 or more; excluded: psychotic disorders, mania, personality disorders, eating disorders with purging, substance use disorders, serious suicide risk and cardiovascular risk; psychotropic medicines tapered
exposure: MDMA in two open-label day-long sessions about 4 weeks apart within MDMA-assisted therapy (three preparatory and six integration sessions)
comparator: None: change from baseline
outcome: Change in MADRS from baseline to about 8 weeks after the second session (primary); Sheehan Disability Scale; response and remission; adverse events
magnitude: MADRS 29.6 (SD 4.9) at baseline and 10.3 (8.3) at the outcome visit (corrigendum; first printed as 9.7, SD 10.0); change −19.3 (SD 8.3), bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7, P < 0.001; responders (fall of 50% or more) 9 of 12 and remitters (MADRS 12 or less) 9 of 12; SDS 21.3 to 9.7, change −11.7 (95% CI −7.6 to −15.8). Adverse events: 46 in 10 of 12 participants (15 moderate, 31 mild), none serious; worsening intensity of suicidal ideation in 6 participants (12 events) by the Results, suicidal ideation in 33.3% by the Discussion; benzodiazepines and zopiclone for 2 participants within 2 days after dosing.
