statement: In the clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy reviewed up to 2024, almost all in PTSD (outside PTSD, one randomized trial each in 12 autistic adults with social anxiety and in 18 people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, plus small open-label studies and a case series), MDMA compared with placebo or low-dose MDMA increased common side effects during sessions and in the following week, such as jaw clenching or muscle tightness, anxiety, reduced appetite, nausea, sweating, feeling cold and headache, which the reviews describe as mostly mild to moderate and largely transient. A 2024 meta-analysis found higher odds of any expected reaction during sessions in phase 2 trials (odds ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.49) and of any treatment-emergent adverse event in the two phase 3 trials (3.51, 2.76 to 4.46), although its any-event percentages cannot be shares of participants; in the life-threatening-illness trial, jaw clenching occurred in 11 of 13 people on MDMA and 1 of 5 on placebo. The meta-analysis found no difference in psychiatric adverse events (phase 2), in suicidality or cardiac events of special interest (phase 3) or in dropping out, and a network meta-analysis found no excess of severe adverse events; a 2022 review found one serious adverse event related to MDMA in the studies it covered (more frequent premature heartbeats, present before treatment, needing a night of hospital monitoring). The record of harms is weak: most studies relied on spontaneous reports, no trial reported harms adequately by the CONSORT Harms 2022 standard, 56% of the non-serious and 4 of the 13 serious adverse events listed in the trial registries were missing from the publications (the 4 all in MDMA groups), and the meta-analysis found too little data on risks beyond active treatment, from small and highly selected samples. Certainty: low (for the increase in common side effects). Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In trials, mostly for PTSD, MDMA often caused side effects such as a tight jaw, tight muscles, worry, less appetite, feeling sick, sweating or feeling cold. These were more common than with a dummy pill or a very small dose, and they mostly passed within a week. Few serious problems were recorded, but many trials only noted problems people mentioned themselves, some recorded problems never made it into the published papers, and there is too little information on what happens later.
population: People treated in clinical trials of MDMA-assisted therapy: mostly adults with PTSD; also autistic adults with social anxiety, people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, people with alcohol use disorder (open-label) and couples in which one partner has PTSD
exposure: MDMA in one to three sessions within psychotherapy
comparator: Inactive placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy
outcome: Side effects and adverse events during and after treatment, serious adverse events, adverse events of special interest, withdrawal, and completeness of harms reporting
magnitude: Colcott 2024 (8 randomized trials, 298 participants, in the meta-analyses; 13 studies, 333 participants, in the review): phase 2, any expected reaction during sessions OR 1.67 (1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the following 7 days OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety OR 4.84 and jaw clenching OR 4.72 during sessions (Fig. 2; the Discussion prints the two the other way round); phase 3, any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5% (unit unclear), 13 named TEAEs more frequent; no difference in phase 2 TEAEs or psychiatric TEAEs, phase 3 suicidality or cardiac AESIs, or withdrawal. Registers against publications: 1487 against 661 non-serious events (5 trials), 13 against 9 serious events (8 trials). Life-threatening illness trial (Schipper 2024, Table 4): jaw clenching 11/13 (84.6%) against 1/5 (20.0%), thirst 11/13 against 2/5, perspiration 9/13 against 0/5; no treatment-related serious adverse events. Autistic adults (Breeksema 2022, Table 1): acute anxiety 6/8 against 1/4.

evidence.locator: Results › Study selection, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 13 studies with 333 unique participants; 8 randomized trials (298 participants) in the meta-analyses: seven in PTSD and one in autistic adults with social anxiety (Danforth 2018, 12); non-randomized studies in PTSD, couples with one partner with PTSD, alcohol use disorder (14) and a Swiss case series.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Results › Systematic review: reporting of side effects, 1st paragraph; Results › Phase two studies, side effects during and 7 days following medication sessions; Fig. 2 (forest-plot values); Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Phase 2 side effects were the protocols' spontaneously reported reactions, a subset of adverse events expected from studies in healthy volunteers, recorded during and for 7 days after sessions. Any such reaction during sessions OR 1.67 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the 7 days after OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety (OR 4.8) and jaw clenching (OR 4.7) during sessions more likely with MDMA (Fig. 2 prints 4.84 and 4.72; the Discussion text gives them the other way round); the review describes the side effects as largely transient and mild or moderate in severity.

evidence.locator: Results › Phase three studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Phase 3: any treatment-emergent adverse event OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5%; more likely with MDMA: muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, excessive perspiration, feeling cold, restlessness, dilated pupils, jaw clenching or tight jaw, uncontrolled eye movements, feeling jittery, non-cardiac chest pain or discomfort, blurred vision, chills.

evidence.locator: Results › Phase three studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st paragraph, against Table 1 (Mitchell 2021 and 2023 rows) (editors' comparison)
evidence.extracted: The any-event proportions cannot be shares of participants: 16% of MDMA participants with any TEAE in phase 3, while Table 1 lists muscle tightness alone in 63% and 58.5% of the MDMA arms; the unit of analysis is not stated, so the pooled any-event odds ratios indicate direction only.

evidence.locator: Results › Phase two studies › Treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE); Phase three studies › Adverse event of special interest (AESI); Phase 2 and 3 studies › Withdrawal
evidence.extracted: No difference in any TEAE or psychiatric TEAE in phase 2 (lower odds of TEAEs with MDMA in the PTSD subgroup, two studies with low-dose controls); no difference in suicidality or cardiac adverse events of special interest in phase 3 and no events of abuse, misuse or diversion reported; no difference in withdrawal.

evidence.locator: Results › Comparison of adverse events published versus reported on ClinicalTrial.gov; Results › Adherence to CONSORT Harms 2022; Results › Risk of bias, 1st paragraph; Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Registers listed 1487 non-serious adverse events against 661 in the articles (5 trials) and 13 serious events against 9 (8 trials); the 4 unpublished serious events were in MDMA groups (CNS metastases, clavicle fracture, syncope, suicidal behaviour); no trial reached adequate CONSORT Harms 2022 adherence (median 50%, range 21% to 64%); 7 of 8 trials at high risk of bias for side effects; 11 of 13 studies used passive monitoring.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Conclusions only for acute and short-term side effects, with insufficient data on longer-term risks beyond active treatment; a limited number of studies with highly selective samples, largely small studies sponsored by a single advocacy group; side effects likely to be more frequent outside controlled trials.

evidence.locator: Table 4 (adverse events), Wolfson 2020 rows; Table 3 (serious and grade 3/4 events); Results › Effects of interventions › Entactogens (MDMA) › Secondary outcomes, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Life-threatening illness trial (13 MDMA, 5 placebo): jaw clenching 11 (84.6%) against 1 (20.0%), thirst 11 (84.6%) against 2 (40.0%), dry mouth 9 (69.2%) against 1 (20.0%), perspiration 9 (69.2%) against 0, headache 8 (61.5%) against 1 (20.0%); no treatment-related serious or grade 3 or 4 adverse events; the reactions were short and mostly resolved by the end of the session or during the following week.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Danforth et al. (2018) row; Results › MDMA › Adverse events › Social anxiety
evidence.extracted: Autistic adults with social anxiety (8 MDMA, 4 placebo): acute anxiety 6 (75%) against 1 (25%), difficulty concentrating 5 (63%) against 1 (25%); 2 of 8 on MDMA and 1 of 4 on placebo reported depressed mood, suicidal ideation and panic attack after the first session; no serious adverse events.

evidence.locator: Results › MDMA › Physiological effects; Results › MDMA › Quality appraisal
evidence.extracted: Nine MDMA studies reported mild, transient rises in blood pressure, temperature and heart rate during sessions, none needing intervention; one MDMA-related serious adverse event (more frequent premature ventricular contractions, present at baseline, one night of hospital monitoring, resolved; Mithoefer 2018); 11 MDMA studies recorded adverse events only when spontaneously reported.

evidence.locator: Results › All cause discontinuation and severe adverse event
evidence.extracted: In the network meta-analysis of depressive symptoms, no intervention, MDMA included, was associated with more all-cause discontinuation or severe adverse events than the placebo arms of psychedelic trials.

risk_of_bias.note: Side effects mostly recorded from spontaneous reports by staff who probably knew the allocation; 7 of 8 trials at high risk of bias for this outcome.

indirectness.note: The claim covers trials across indications, but the evidence comes mostly from PTSD trials of one sponsor's protocol and is seen through systematic reviews.

imprecision.note: Not rated down for the common effects, whose differences are large and consistent at trial level; the pooled any-event intervals are probably too narrow and are not relied on.

publication_bias.note: Registered adverse events missing from publications would bias towards fewer reported harms, not create the observed increase; stated in the claim rather than rated down.

grade.reasoning: Randomized comparisons start high. Rated down once for risk of bias (spontaneous, probably unblinded recording) and once for indirectness (a claim across indications resting mostly on PTSD trials of one sponsor, seen through systematic reviews). Certainty applies to the increase in common side effects; rare, serious or delayed harms cannot be assessed from these trials, which the claim says. The causal verb is used because the comparisons are randomized and the effects are those expected pharmacologically, although the reviews themselves describe them as associations. Most trials share the sponsor and protocol, hence replicated by the same team. This overlaps the phase 3 adverse-event claim in this section, which rests on the trial reports read directly.

statement: What happens after MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD ends is known from the sponsor's phase 2 programme only through two follow-ups without a comparison group. In the first US trial, 16 of the 19 people treated with MDMA were reassessed 17 to 74 months (mean about 45) after their last MDMA session: their mean CAPS score was similar to that 2 months after their second MDMA session (23.7 against 24.6; mean change −0.9 points, 95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, editors' calculation), but individual scores moved widely in both directions; 2 of the 16 scored above the trial's entry threshold again, which the authors count as relapse; 3 of the 19 were not reassessed; and at follow-up 8 of 19 were in psychotherapy and 12 of 19 took psychiatric medicines. On a questionnaire written by the investigators, all 19 reported some benefit and none reported harm from taking part; 8 reported some cannabis use and 1 psilocybin use, all of whom had used these before the trial, and 1 reported using ecstasy once (Mithoefer et al., 2013). In pooled open-label data from four other phase 2 trials, corrected after an ethical violation by two therapists at one site and under an expression of concern, mean CAPS-IV scores 12 months after treatment were lower than at the end of treatment (35.3 against 42.5 on a 0 to 136 scale; 58 participants), by which time everyone had received full-dose MDMA (Ponte et al., 2021, and its correction, 2025). The sponsor's pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials (Jerome et al., 2020) is among the retracted papers described in this section and is not used; the follow-up of the phase 3 trials is the subject of a separate claim in this section. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: In one small early trial, 16 of 19 people were checked again about 4 years later. On average their PTSD scores were about the same as soon after treatment, but some people got much better and some much worse, and 2 had moderate-to-severe PTSD again. Many were also getting other therapy or medicines, and there was no comparison group. In four other early trials, scores a year later were a little lower than at the end of treatment, again with no comparison group, and the results had to be corrected after an ethics breach by two therapists at one site.
population: Adults with chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD treated with MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in the sponsor's phase 2 trials (first US trial, 19 treated with MDMA; four later trials pooled, 59 after the correction)
exposure: Two or three MDMA sessions within manualized psychotherapy (randomized stage or open-label crossover)
comparator: None at follow-up: the same participants' scores at the end of treatment
outcome: PTSD symptom severity (CAPS-IV) 12 months and 17 to 74 months after treatment; relapse (CAPS above 50); later psychotherapy and psychiatric medicines; self-reported benefit, harm and drug use during follow-up
magnitude: First US trial (Mithoefer 2013): CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) 2 months after the second MDMA session and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, n = 16, matched t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; editors' calculation from Table 2: mean change −0.9 (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9), SD of individual changes 31.5, 6 of 16 improved and 3 worsened by 10 points or more; CAPS above 50 in 2 of 16 (13%), or 5 of 19 (26%) counting the 3 not reassessed as negative outcomes; at follow-up 8 of 19 in psychotherapy (16 of 19 at enrolment) and 12 of 19 on psychiatric medicines (12 of 19 at entry). Questionnaire: 19 of 19 some benefit, 0 of 19 harm; cannabis 8, psilocybin 1 (all with earlier use), ecstasy once 1. Four pooled phase 2 trials, corrected (Ponte 2021; correction 2025): CAPS-IV least-squares means 88.22 at baseline, 42.46 at treatment exit and 35.28 at 12 months; treatment exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008, N = 58.

evidence.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 1st to 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Original trial: 20 randomized (12 MDMA, 8 placebo with the same psychotherapy); 7 of 8 placebo participants crossed over to open-label MDMA, so 19 were treated with MDMA; follow-up added by protocol amendment; CAPS and IES-R completed by 16 of the 19 (one lost after moving, two declined, one of them having had the smallest earlier response and fearing symptoms would be triggered); CAPS 17 to 74 months after the final MDMA session (mean 45.4, SD 17.3, n = 17).

evidence.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
evidence.extracted: CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) at 2 months and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; IES-R 19.8 (19.5) and 22.1 (21.8), p = 0.72; 2 of 16 completers (13%) above 50 at follow-up, the cut-off for entry to the original study, which the authors call relapse to moderate-to-severe PTSD; counting the 3 non-completers as negative outcomes too, 5 of 19 (26%).

evidence.locator: Table 2 (editors' calculation)
evidence.extracted: Editors' calculation from the 16 completers' individual scores, which reproduce Table 1's means and SDs: mean change from 2 months to follow-up −0.9 points (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, paired t −0.11), SD of individual changes 31.5; 6 improved by 10 points or more and 3 worsened by 10 points or more (the two relapses from 16 to 60 and from 6 to 91). For the 8 participants who later had a third MDMA session, the 2-month score was taken before it.

evidence.locator: Results › Participation in psychotherapy; Results › Psychiatric medications; Table 4; Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: In psychotherapy at enrolment 16 of 19, at follow-up 8 of 19; on psychiatric medicines 12 of 19 at entry and at follow-up. The authors state there was no meaningful control group at follow-up, that natural history or uncontrolled variables could explain the results, and that later psychotherapy and medicines are the most important confounder and preclude a definite conclusion about long-term benefit.

evidence.locator: Results › LTFU questionnaire results for 19 PTSD subjects › Degree of benefit, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period
evidence.extracted: On the investigators' own follow-up questionnaire, all 19 MDMA-treated participants reported some benefit and none reported harm from taking part; cannabis use by 8 (once to occasionally) and psilocybin mushrooms by 1, all of whom reported use before enrolment; 1 participant reported using ecstasy once, in an attempt at a therapeutic setting, and found it unsatisfactory.

evidence.locator: Methods and materials › Study design, 2nd paragraph; Footnotes › Conflict of interest
evidence.extracted: The follow-up CAPS was administered in person or by phone by the same independent rater as in the original trial; the sponsor paid this rater, who is the second author, and played a role in the study design, data analysis and writing.

evidence.locator: Corrected Table 3; Summary of corrections made › Open-label endpoints, 1st paragraph (revised text)
evidence.extracted: Corrected open-label analysis of the four pooled trials (N = 58): CAPS-IV least-squares means 88.22 at baseline, 42.46 at treatment exit and 35.28 at 12-month follow-up; treatment exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008.

evidence.locator: Results › Open-Label Endpoints: Treatment Exit and Long-Term Follow-Up, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 note; Method › Participants and Procedure, 6th paragraph; Method › Measures › PTSD Symptoms, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: After the blinded endpoint, participants given the control dose or 75 mg crossed over to full-dose open-label sessions and the other full-dose participants had one further open-label session (MP-9 had no third session); because all participants had received active-dose MDMA in either the blinded or open-label segments, groups were pooled for treatment exit and the 12-month follow-up, which took place after the final open-label session, so these comparisons are within-person and uncontrolled. CAPS-IV total severity scores range from 0 to 136.

evidence.locator: Notice, 2nd to 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Expression of concern (3 December 2024): an ethical violation by a pair of therapists who treated 4 of the 6 MP-4 participants caused a protocol deviation; the authors had not told the journal at submission in December 2019, although the violation was publicly announced in May 2019; the data of those therapists are removed by correction; the journal judged the non-disclosure improper and its investigation of human-subjects ethics inconclusive.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph; Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Jerome 2020 row)
evidence.extracted: Across the studies reviewed to October 2023, conclusions were possible only for acute and short-term side effects, because insufficient data were available on longer-term risks beyond active treatment; the one included study that formally assessed long-term follow-up outcomes was the pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials by Jerome et al. (2020), which the PMC reference list now marks as retracted.

evidence.locator: Conclusion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Among the review's research priorities: longer follow-ups in clinical trials, because short-term outcomes, positive and negative, often change in the weeks and months after a typical trial ends.

risk_of_bias.note: Uncontrolled follow-ups with unblinded outcome assessment (in the first trial by a co-author paid by the sponsor), 16% not reassessed, co-treatment in most participants, an unvalidated questionnaire, and, for the pooled data, an expression of concern and analysis choices made after inspecting outcomes.

imprecision.note: 16 participants in the long follow-up; the 95% interval for the mean change runs from a 17.6-point improvement to a 15.9-point worsening.

publication_bias.note: Not rated down, but the programme's other long follow-up is retracted, so the published record is thin.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim about what was observed after treatment in two cohorts without comparison groups (METHODS §6.3: descriptive claims start low). Rated down once for risk of bias (unblinded and partly sponsor-paid assessment, missing data, co-treatment, an unvalidated questionnaire, an expression of concern on the pooled data) and once for imprecision (16 people in the long follow-up, with an interval compatible with large improvement or large worsening). The claim does not say that the benefit lasted because of MDMA: neither follow-up can separate the treatment's effect from later therapy, medicines or the natural course. Both follow-ups come from the same sponsor's phase 2 programme and share investigators, so their agreement is not independent replication.

statement: In the sponsor's pooled analysis of four phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic PTSD, as corrected (correction published online in December 2024: four participants of one site, treated by two therapists involved in an ethical violation, were removed, and the journal issued an expression of concern because the authors had not disclosed the violation at submission), full-dose MDMA compared with low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy was associated with a larger improvement in self-reported sleep quality 1 to 2 months after two blinded sessions: change on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (0 to 21, higher is worse) −3.5 against +0.5 points (Hedges' g 0.85, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.47; 44 and 14 participants), with an improvement of at least 3 points in 24 of 45 against 2 of 14. After open-label full-dose treatment for everyone, mean scores 12 months later were about 1 point lower than at the end of treatment (7.1 against 8.2), without a comparison group. The paper reports no check of whether participants could tell their dose, the outcome is self-reported, the analyses were not preregistered and the dose groups were defined partly after inspecting outcomes. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In four early trials run for the same sponsor, people with PTSD who had full doses of MDMA said they slept better a month or two later than people who had a very small dose: about 4 points better on a 0 to 21 sleep scale. A year later their sleep was a little better still, but by then everyone had had full doses, so there was nothing to compare with. No one checked whether people could tell which dose they had, and the results had to be corrected after an ethics breach at one site.
population: Adults with chronic PTSD in four of the sponsor's phase 2 trials (59 after the correction: 45 full dose, 14 low dose)
exposure: Two blinded sessions with full-dose MDMA within manualized psychotherapy
comparator: Low-dose MDMA with the same psychotherapy (no inactive placebo after the correction)
outcome: Change in self-reported sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) from baseline to 1 to 2 months after the blinded sessions; open-label change to 12 months
magnitude: Corrected blinded endpoint: PSQI change −3.51 (SD 5.08, n = 44) against +0.50 (3.25, n = 14), p = .008, Hedges' g 0.85 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.47); improvement of 3 points or more in 24 of 45 (53.3%) against 2 of 14 (14.3%). Corrected open-label, N = 58: PSQI least-squares means 12.59 at baseline, 8.18 at treatment exit, 7.09 at 12 months; exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029. Original (superseded) analysis: −3.53 against +0.56, g 0.88, p = .003.

evidence.locator: Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Original analysis, superseded by the correction: PSQI change −3.53 (SD 5.03) in the active group against +0.56 (3.05) in the control group (n = 16; active n printed as 46 in Table 2 and 47 elsewhere), p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 with a printed 95% CI of −0.27 to 2.03 that does not fit g; a drop of 3 points or more in 53.2% against 12.5% (N = 61).

evidence.extracted: Corrected blinded endpoint: PSQI change −3.51 (SD 5.08) in the active group (n = 44) against +0.50 (3.25) in the control group (n = 14), p = .008, Hedges' g 0.85 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.47); CAPS-IV −34.93 against −11.07, g 0.96 (0.33 to 1.59).

evidence.locator: Corrected Table 2, note b
evidence.extracted: PSQI fell by 3 points or more in 24 active participants (53.3%, of 45) and 2 controls (14.3%, of 14), p = .008; the footnote's counts and denominators do not fully agree (19 active without such a drop, n = 44 in the table).

evidence.locator: Corrected Table 3
evidence.extracted: Open-label (N = 58): PSQI least-squares means 12.59 at baseline, 8.18 at treatment exit, 7.09 at 12 months; change from exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029.

evidence.locator: Description and explanation for this correction; Summary of corrections made › In the abstract
evidence.extracted: The four MP-4 participants treated by the pair of therapists were removed; sample 63 to 59 (active 47 to 45, control 16 to 14); the removed participants were the only ones in the control group given no MDMA, so the control group now consists only of low-dose MDMA and the placebo label is dropped.

evidence.locator: Notice, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors had not notified the journal of the ethical violation at submission (December 2019), although it had been publicly announced in May 2019; the journal judged this improper and issued the expression of concern; its investigation of human-subjects ethics was inconclusive.

evidence.locator: Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Open Practices Statement
evidence.extracted: Doses pooled into control and active groups by the protocols' designations and by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores (citing the since-retracted pooled analysis by Mithoefer et al., 2019); independent-samples t tests; no power analysis; the analyses were not formally preregistered.

evidence.locator: Method › Measures › Sleep Quality, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Sleep quality was measured with the self-report PSQI (global score 0 to 21; a cut-off of 5 separates good from poor sleepers); the authors list the small, mostly White sample and self-reported outcomes as limitations; the paper reports no assessment of whether participants could tell their dose.

risk_of_bias.note: Very serious: self-reported outcome without any check of blinding; analysis not preregistered, with groups defined partly after inspecting outcomes and pooled without stratification; the data were corrected after an ethical violation at one site, under an expression of concern.

imprecision.note: 58 participants, 14 controls; the interval for g runs from 0.23 to 1.47.

grade.reasoning: The blinded comparison rests on randomization within each trial, so it starts high, but it is rated down twice for risk of bias (RoB 2 high on the study card: a self-reported outcome with no check of blinding, outcome-informed grouping, unstratified pooling, no preregistration, and the expression of concern) and once for imprecision. The relation is an association rather than a causal verb because the pooled comparison does not preserve each trial's randomization. The 12-month figures are uncontrolled and are given only as a description. This is one pooled analysis whose per-trial results are not reported, hence single study.

statement: For conditions other than PTSD, evidence is insufficient to say whether MDMA-assisted therapy helps. The systematic reviews read here (searches up to March 2024) found only small studies outside PTSD: one randomized trial each in anxiety related to a life-threatening illness (18 people), social anxiety in autistic adults (12) and tinnitus (13), an open-label study in alcohol use disorder (14), an uncontrolled study of couples in which one partner has PTSD (6 couples) and a Swiss case series. The Cochrane review rated the evidence in life-threatening illness very uncertain: in its one trial, MDMA against placebo changed trait anxiety by −14.7 points on a 20 to 80 scale (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05) and depression by −6.3 points on a 0 to 63 scale (−16.93 to 4.33). A network meta-analysis of depressive symptoms, whose MDMA trials were mostly in PTSD, found high-dose MDMA better than the placebo arms of psychedelic trials by 5.3 HAMD-17 points (95% credible interval 2.26 to 8.32) but not clearly better than the placebo arms of antidepressant trials (1.5, −2.79 to 5.78), a comparison made only indirectly. A critical narrative review found that, for MDMA, only the two phase 3 PTSD trials met its minimum standard (randomized, more than 15 people per group) and called MDMA for PTSD a signal needing replication. The reviews report that blinding was rarely achieved and that controlled follow-up was short. Certainty: very low. Status: single study (one trial per condition outside PTSD).
plain: The reviews up to 2024 found only a few very small studies of MDMA therapy outside PTSD: in people anxious about a life-threatening illness, autistic adults with social anxiety, people with tinnitus, people with alcohol problems and couples. Each had one small trial or no comparison group at all. The best review says the results for serious illness are very uncertain. So nobody can yet say whether MDMA therapy helps any of these conditions.
population: People with conditions other than PTSD: anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, social anxiety in autistic adults, tinnitus, alcohol use disorder, couples with one partner with PTSD, depressive symptoms
exposure: MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA in one to three sessions with psychotherapy)
comparator: Placebo or low-dose MDMA with the same therapy; none in open-label and uncontrolled studies
outcome: Condition-specific symptoms (anxiety, depression); number and design of the trials available
magnitude: Life-threatening illness (Cochrane, 1 trial, 18): STAI-T −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05), STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83), BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33), very low certainty. Depressive symptoms (network meta-analysis; MDMA trials mostly PTSD): high-dose MDMA against psychedelic-trial placebo 5.32 HAMD-17 points (2.26 to 8.32); against antidepressant-trial placebo 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78). Studies outside PTSD: randomized, 18, 12 and 13 participants; open-label, 14 (alcohol use disorder); uncontrolled, 6 couples.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Entactogens (MDMA) › Anxiety and Depression; Summary of findings 2
evidence.extracted: One trial (Wolfson 2020; 18 participants): STAI-T mean difference −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05) and STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83), both on 20 to 80 scales; BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33) on a 0 to 63 scale; 1 month after the second session; very low certainty, downgraded once for risk of bias and twice for imprecision.

evidence.locator: Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Ongoing studies
evidence.extracted: Searched on 30 March 2024: of six randomized trials in people with life-threatening diseases, one evaluated MDMA (18 randomized and analysed); seven ongoing trials, of psilocybin, LSD and ketamine, none of MDMA.

evidence.locator: Results › MDMA, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Other disorders rows)
evidence.extracted: Besides PTSD, randomized trials of MDMA in end-of-life anxiety (Wolfson 2020, 13 MDMA and 5 placebo), social anxiety in adults with autism (Danforth 2018, 12) and tinnitus (Searchfield 2020, 13), and an open-label study in alcohol use disorder (Sessa 2019, 2021; 14).

evidence.locator: Table 1
evidence.extracted: Of 13 studies to October 2023, the only randomized trial outside PTSD was in autistic adults with social anxiety (12); others outside PTSD were an open-label alcohol use disorder study (14) and a Swiss case series of various treatment-resistant disorders; the uncontrolled couples study (6 couples) enrolled dyads with one partner with PTSD.

evidence.locator: Fig. 2, upper and middle panels (values printed in the figure image); Results › Network meta-analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: High-dose MDMA against the placebo arms of psychedelic trials 5.32 HAMD-17 points (95% CrI 2.26 to 8.32); against the placebo arms of escitalopram trials 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78), the two parts of the network being joined only by one head-to-head psilocybin-escitalopram trial; participants in the MDMA trials were predominantly diagnosed with PTSD, those in the escitalopram trials with major depressive disorder.

evidence.locator: Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 3rd paragraph; Safety and Effectiveness of Psychedelic Drugs › MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 1st paragraph; Summary of Effectiveness Evidence for Psychedelic Medicines, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Standard: randomized trials in diagnosed disorders with more than 15 participants per condition; for MDMA only the two phase 3 PTSD trials, run by a consortium funded by MAPS, are discussed; because of absent successful blinding and likely expectancy effects, MDMA for PTSD is a positive signal that should not be taken as definitive without replication in methodologically stronger studies.

evidence.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 1st paragraph; Results › Effects of interventions, 2nd paragraph; Characteristics of included studies › Wolfson 2020 (risk-of-bias table)
evidence.extracted: Blinding could not be achieved in any included trial; in the MDMA trial more than 80% of investigators and participants guessed the assignment correctly and most outcomes were self-reported; all outcomes after more than 3 months were measured after crossover, without a comparison group.

risk_of_bias.note: Blinding not achieved in the trials; self-reported outcomes.

indirectness.note: Not rated down separately: the claim reports the depression estimates as coming from trials mostly in PTSD.

imprecision.note: One small trial per condition; intervals include no effect.

grade.reasoning: The underlying evidence for each condition outside PTSD is one small randomized trial or an uncontrolled study, as found by systematic reviews searched up to October 2023 and March 2024. Starting from randomized trials, rated down once for risk of bias (unblinding) and twice for imprecision, giving very low certainty, which matches the Cochrane rating for MDMA. The claim states insufficient evidence rather than no effect: the point estimates in the life-threatening-illness trial favour MDMA, but the intervals include no effect. Trials published after these searches (read by another reader) are for the editor to join.

statement: As described second-hand in one historical narrative review (Passie, 2018), whose estimates rest on a sparse literature and on information given to the author, a few dozen therapists in the United States, most in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy from the late 1970s until it was scheduled in 1985, while it was neither an approved medicine nor a controlled substance. The caseloads reported come mostly from the practitioners' own accounts, among them more than 80 patients treated by Greer and Tolbert from 1980 to 1985. The outcome evidence the review describes consists of practitioners' reports, a 1984 exploratory survey of 16 therapists, an unpublished 1980 study in which nine people had one MDMA session each, and a follow-up of 29 of Greer and Tolbert's patients, which found no serious side effects. Two therapists had sexual contact with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences. After the DEA recommended placing MDMA in Schedule I in July 1984, its administrative law judge concluded at the 1985 hearings that this was not required, and the DEA overruled the judge; the WHO's expert committee, when MDMA was scheduled internationally in late 1985, judged the therapeutic reports methodologically inadequate but urged research. Five applications to study MDMA submitted from 1986 to 1988 were put on clinical hold, and the first FDA-approved study of MDMA in humans, in healthy volunteers, began in 1992. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Before it was banned in 1985, a few dozen therapists in the United States used MDMA in talking therapy. Their reports were positive, but experts for the World Health Organization judged them not well enough designed to rely on, and two therapists had sex with patients during sessions. A US judge advised against the strictest ban, but the drug agency imposed it anyway. This history comes from one review based on old reports, memoirs and the author's own contacts.
population: Patients of psychotherapists in the United States who used MDMA before it was scheduled (late 1970s to 1985)
exposure: MDMA used in individual, couples and group psychotherapy
comparator: None (historical description)
outcome: Extent and nature of therapeutic use; outcome evidence of the period; documented misconduct; scheduling sequence
magnitude: A few dozen therapists, 1977 or 1978 to 1985; reported caseloads: Zeff about 4000 people over 12 years (from a memoir), Greer and Tolbert more than 80 patients (1980 to 1985), Ingrasci 100 patients in about 150 sessions, Harlow more than 200 clients; outcome reports: Greer and Tolbert follow-up of 29 (23 with positive changes lasting 1 week to 2 years, no serious side effects), ARUPA survey 15 of 16 therapists positive; two therapists lost their licences after sexual contact with patients during sessions; DEA recommended Schedule I on 27 July 1984, its judge concluded against in 1985, overruled; five research applications on clinical hold (1986 to 1988); first FDA-approved human study 1992.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: From the relatively poor data in the literature and information given personally to the author, a few dozen therapists, most in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy between 1977 (title and abstract) or 1978 (Discussion) and 1985, when it was neither an FDA-approved drug nor a controlled substance; a physician could use it legally if self-synthesized, with informed consent and a peer-reviewed protocol.

evidence.locator: George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 1st and 5th paragraphs; Leo Zeff—The Secret Chief, 2nd paragraph; Rick Ingrasci: MDMA in couples and patients with life-threatening illnesses, 1st paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Greer, a psychiatrist, and Tolbert, a psychiatric nurse, treated more than 80 patients from 1980 to 1985; their published follow-up of 29 patients found no serious side effects or negative after-effects and 23 with positive changes lasting from 1 week to 2 years; Zeff gave MDMA to about 4000 people over 12 years (from a memoir); Ingrasci treated 100 patients in about 150 sessions, one-third with couples; Harlow treated more than 200 clients before 1985.

evidence.locator: A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Kueny's 1980 study, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: A 1984 exploratory survey of 16 therapists for ARUPA: 15 judged MDMA valuable in augmenting psychotherapy and all claimed complications were negligible; it was used as evidence at the hearings; an unpublished 1980 study gave one MDMA session to each of nine people.

evidence.locator: Physical abuse in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Two therapists, Rick Ingrasci and Francesco DiLeo, initiated intimate body contact, sexual touch and intercourse with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences; a Maryland appeals court (1991) upheld damages to DiLeo's patient, later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety.

evidence.locator: Therapists opposed to the scheduling of MDMA in 1985, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th, 6th and 8th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The DEA recommended Schedule I on 27 July 1984; at the 1985 hearings its administrative law judge concluded that MDMA did not have to be placed in Schedule I; the DEA overruled the judge's decision; the WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, which scheduled MDMA internationally in late 1985, found the therapeutic reports intriguing but methodologically inadequate and urged research; five applications to study MDMA submitted from 1986 to 1988 were placed on clinical hold; after the FDA rejected a patient study and recommended a study in healthy volunteers, the first FDA-approved MDMA study in humans began in 1992.

risk_of_bias.note: One narrative review by a single author, relaying memoirs, interviews and proponents' documents without appraisal; the figures are second-hand.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive historical claim (starts low), resting only on a narrative review (METHODS §6.3: stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand), rated down once because the review relays unappraised sources. It describes the period; it makes no claim that MDMA-assisted therapy worked or was safe then. The primary documents of 1986 on the list (Greer and Tolbert; Downing; Grinspoon and Bakalar) should replace these anchors when saved.

statement: In three randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies of healthy adults with previous MDMA experience, a second dose taken 2 or 24 hours after the first raised plasma concentrations by more than the dose alone would predict, but did not raise the peak of the effects people felt. After a second 100 mg dose 24 hours later, exposure was 77% higher and peak concentration 29% higher than after the first dose, while pupil diameter, extraocular balance, one questionnaire subscale and prolactin did not change at all and the other effects rose only slightly (Farré et al., 2004). After 50 mg followed by 100 mg two hours later, peak concentration was about half as high again as after 100 mg alone (311 against 203 ng/mL), 12.8% above dose proportionality, yet heart rate did not rise in peak or area under the curve (it differed only at 2.3 and 5 hours) and none of the wanted subjective effects (euphoria, liking, stimulation) differed, while blood pressure, temperature and pupil diameter did rise (Peiró et al., 2013). In the largest and only registered study, a 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg raised peak concentration 1.5-fold and lengthened the subjective effect by about an hour (5.6 hours, SD 1.8, against 4.6, SD 1.2 in the abstract and text or 1.5 in the table) without raising peak ratings (83 against 85 for 'any drug effect'; 86 against 87 for 'good drug effect') or peak blood pressure, heart rate or temperature (Humbert-Droz et al., 2026). The authors read this as acute tolerance, or as consistent with it; in all three, effects subsided while plasma concentrations were still high. None of them modelled the relation between concentration and effect, so 'less than expected' is a judgement against dose proportionality, and the peak ratings in the booster study were already above 80 out of 100, where a rating cannot rise much further. All used 50 to 180 mg of known, pure MDMA in a quiet laboratory in 9, 10 and 23 people, two of the three studies in men only; no study has given more than two doses.
plain: If you take a second dose within a few hours or a day, the drug level in your blood goes up by more than the extra dose alone explains, because MDMA blocks the enzyme that clears it. The effects do not rise to match. In three laboratory studies the strongest feeling was no stronger after the second dose; what changed was how long it lasted, about an hour more. Heart rate hardly rose further, while blood pressure and body temperature did. The studies were small (9, 10 and 23 people), used pure MDMA in a quiet room, and none of them gave more than two doses.
population: Healthy adults with previous recreational MDMA experience in laboratory studies (9 men, 10 men, and 23 people of whom 11 were women), screened to exclude medical and psychiatric illness; two studies included only people who metabolize MDMA quickly
exposure: A second dose of MDMA taken 2 or 24 hours after the first (study conditions: 100 mg then 100 mg 24 hours apart; 50 mg then 100 mg 2 hours apart; 120 mg then 60 mg 2 hours apart)
comparator: The same people taking a single dose or placebo in a separate session, and their own first dose
outcome: Peak and duration of subjective effects, heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, pupil diameter, and plasma concentrations of MDMA and its metabolites
magnitude: Twenty-four-hour interval: exposure 2564 ng.h/mL (SD 762) after the second 100 mg dose against 1452 (SD 771) after the first, a ratio of 1.77; peak 232 ng/mL (SD 39) against 180 (SD 33), ratio 1.29 (both p<=0.001); peak systolic pressure rise 34 mm Hg against 25 and diastolic 20 against 10; pupil diameter, Maddox-wing, the amphetamine subscale and prolactin unchanged (Farré et al., 2004). Two-hour interval, 50 then 100 mg against 100 mg alone: peak concentration 311.16 ng/mL (SD 66.48) against 202.92 (SD 30.30), p<0.001, which is 12.8% above dose proportionality, with exposure 16.2% above; heart-rate peak 33.05 (SD 13.25) against 33.50 (SD 11.87) beats/min and area under the curve 69.98 against 57.75, neither significant; systolic area under the curve 72.96 (SD 22.12) against 49.35 (SD 24.28), p=0.029; no significant difference in any wanted subjective effect (Peiró et al., 2013). Booster: peak concentration ratio 1.50 (90% CI 1.43-1.57) and exposure ratio 1.47 (1.40-1.54); duration of 'any drug effect' 5.6 h (SD 1.8) against 4.6 (SD 1.5), p<0.01, with peak ratings 83 (SD 21) against 85 (SD 20) and 86 (SD 29) against 87 (SD 19), not significant; half-life 7.2 h in both conditions (Humbert-Droz et al., 2026).

evidence.locator: Table 2, MDMA and MDA rows (p. 370); Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 369, right column)
evidence.extracted: A second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first gave an area under the concentration-time curve of 2564 ng.h/mL (SD 762) against 1452 (SD 771) after the first, a ratio of 1.77 (77% higher), and a peak of 232 ng/mL (SD 39) against 180 (SD 33), a ratio of 1.29 (29% higher), both p<=0.001; the metabolite MDA rose 64% in exposure and 40% at peak. About 12 ng/mL of MDMA from the first dose was still present when the second was given.

evidence.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraphs on physiological parameters (p. 367, right column) and on Maddox wing and hormones (p. 369); Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The pharmacological effects after the second administration' (starts p. 372, quoted text on p. 373)
evidence.extracted: Effects after the second dose were slightly larger on blood pressure (peak systolic rise 34 mm Hg against 25; diastolic 20 against 10), heart rate (22 against 16 beats/min, significant only at 40 minutes) and cortisol (peak 49% higher), but unchanged on pupil diameter, the Maddox-wing measure, the amphetamine subscale and prolactin; the authors read the unchanged measures as 'the possible appearance of some degree of tolerance' and note that in no measure did effects exceed what the concentrations predicted.

evidence.locator: Table 1, HR and subjective rows (p. 887); Table 2, MDMA rows (p. 889); Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 889)
evidence.extracted: Taking 50 mg two hours before a 100 mg dose raised peak MDMA concentration to 311.16 ng/mL (SD 66.48) from 202.92 (SD 30.30) with 100 mg alone (p<0.001), 12.8% above dose proportionality in peak and 16.2% in exposure, with half-life unchanged (10.48 h against 10.41). Heart rate did not differ in peak or area under the curve with the added dose (peak 33.05, SD 13.25, against 33.50, SD 11.87; area under the curve 69.98 against 57.75, neither significant), although it differed at 2.3 and 5 hours of the time course (p=0.004), and none of the wanted subjective effects differed in peak or area under the curve.

evidence.locator: Table 1, SBP, DBP, T and PD rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 888)
evidence.extracted: In the same study the measures that did track concentration were blood pressure (systolic area under the curve 72.96, SD 22.12, against 49.35, SD 24.28, p=0.029; diastolic 46.82, SD 27.82, against 18.81, SD 21.09, p=0.015), pupil diameter (area under the curve 11.92, SD 3.33, against 9.42, SD 1.83, p=0.037) and body temperature (differences at 2.3, 2.6 and 3 hours), none of which differed significantly at the peak.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1, 'Any drug effect' and 'Good drug effect' rows; Table 3, MDMA rows
evidence.extracted: A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg lengthened the duration of 'any drug effect' to 5.6 h (SD 1.8) from 4.6 h with the single dose (SD 1.2 and p = 0.001 in the abstract and text; SD 1.5 and p<0.01 in Table 1) and raised the areas under several effect curves, while peak ratings did not differ (83, SD 21, against 85, SD 20 for 'any drug effect'; 86, SD 29, against 87, SD 19 for 'good drug effect'). Peak plasma concentration rose 1.50-fold (90% CI 1.43-1.57) and 9-hour exposure 1.47-fold (1.40-1.54), with half-life 7.2 h in both conditions.

evidence.locator: Results > Autonomic effects; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and body temperature rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo and lasted longer after the booster without a higher maximum; the authors say the unchanged maxima despite higher concentrations are consistent with acute pharmacodynamic tolerance, noting that effects subsided within the 9-hour session while the mean concentration at discharge after the booster exceeded the mean peak after the single dose. The numerical autonomic values are in a supplement that the first reader did not open.

evidence.locator: Results > Participants and blinding, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, Emax rows
evidence.extracted: Qualifications: blinding largely failed (every participant identified placebo correctly and 76% of MDMA sessions were identified correctly immediately afterwards), and the peak ratings against which the absence of an increase is measured were already 83-87 out of 100, so a ceiling on the scales cannot be separated from tolerance for the subjective measures.

risk_of_bias.note: All three are randomized or counterbalanced, double-blind, placebo-controlled within-person studies with objective pharmacokinetics; but blinding failed in the one study that measured it, two of the three tested about forty outcomes without correction and tabulate only the significant ones, and one has no placebo-only session. Downgraded one level rather than two because the concentration findings and the autonomic measures do not depend on the blind.

inconsistency.note: Two independent groups at three intervals (2, 4 in a related study, and 24 hours) report the same pattern: concentrations above proportionality with effects that do not rise in step.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the doses, intervals and settings studied, and says so.

imprecision.note: Nine, ten and twenty-three participants; no confidence intervals for the differences in effect, and the pharmacokinetic ratios are the only estimates with intervals.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled within-person laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give low. Status replicated: three studies from two independent groups, at different intervals and with different dose combinations, show the same dissociation between concentration and effect. The claim is worded as an observed dissociation; it does not state a size for the tolerance, because none of the studies fitted a concentration-effect model, and it names the ceiling of the rating scales as an alternative for the subjective peaks.

statement: The figures in this claim are second-hand: they come from one narrative review of the survey literature, and only one of the studies it cites has been read in full (below); the review itself reports that no laboratory study has ever given humans a series of MDMA doses, so chronic tolerance cannot be studied in people under blind, placebo-controlled conditions. In that review, most people who use ecstasy regularly say its wanted effects decline with repeated use: 596 of 1151 readers of a dance magazine reported tolerance (the review prints 58%; 596 is 52% of 1151), and about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reported a decline in subjective efficacy, with the first occasion often described as the strongest. Reported doses rise with past use: from 1.2 to 1.8 tablets a session in the same 430 people, from 100% of 109 people in a novice group reporting a usual dose of 1-2 tablets to 62% of 37 in the heaviest group, and from 0% to 35% reporting a maximum of ten or more tablets in a week. The one study read in full, by the reviewer and a colleague, asked 15 people with ten or more earlier occasions and 15 with one to nine to note what they took on one Saturday night at a London club: 1.80 tablets on average against 1.45. The review gives these figures correctly, but the paper calls the difference slight, prints no spread or test and did not check what the tablets held (Parrott & Lasky, 1998). One study ran the other way, with the longer-using group taking slightly fewer tablets per occasion. All of this is self-reported by people taking tablets of unknown content, compared across groups rather than followed over time, with about half the comparisons coming from the reviewer's own research group; the same surveys also report more problems attributed to ecstasy in the heavier-using groups, so nothing here separates tolerance from the other reasons people take more (Parrott, 2005).
plain: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well, and the first time is often described as the best. Across surveys, people who have used it more say they take more tablets. But these are answers on questionnaires, from people taking tablets whose contents nobody checked, comparing different groups of people rather than following the same people over time, so we cannot tell how much of this is the drug and how much is everything else. No laboratory has ever given people repeated doses over weeks, so there is no controlled study of this at all.
population: People who use ecstasy recreationally, in surveys and interview studies from Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States and continental Europe, in samples of 30 to about 1151 people, as summarized in one narrative review; its 30-person comparison (two groups of 15 at one London club) has been read in full
exposure: Repeated recreational use of tablets sold as ecstasy, over months to years, in amounts self-reported as tablets per occasion and lifetime occasions; the MDMA content of the tablets was not measured in any of the studies summarized
comparator: Groups of people with less past use in the same surveys, and each person's own account of their earlier use
outcome: Self-reported decline in the wanted effects, self-reported tablets per occasion and maximum tablets, and self-attributed problems
magnitude: Self-reported tolerance: 596 of 1151 people (printed as 58%); about 85-95% of 430 people using ecstasy regularly; 67% of those with six or more occasions in an earlier survey said positive effects decreased and negative effects increased. Dose: 1.8 tablets a session currently against 1.2 when starting (430 people); usual dose 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets and maximum ever 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7) across groups of 14, 14 and 11 people defined by lifetime use (maximum p<0.01; usual dose only p<0.10); a usual dose of 1-2 tablets reported by 100%, 84% and 62% of groups of 109, 136 and 37 people, and a maximum of ten or more tablets in a week by 0%, 9% and 35% (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, p<0.001). In the one primary study read in full, tablets noted on one Saturday night at a club: 1.80 on average in 15 people with ten or more earlier occasions against 1.45 in 15 with one to nine, with no spread or test printed. Against this, two groups differing in duration of use (3.9 against 10.9 years) and lifetime consumption (223 against 811 tablets) reported 2.5 against 2.1 tablets per occasion, not significantly different.

evidence.locator: The paragraph beginning 'The pharmacodynamic effects of single doses of MDMA' and the one following it (left column); Subjective reports of tolerance and diminishing responsiveness to MDMA, 1st-2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review states that no laboratory study has given a series of MDMA doses to humans and that chronic tolerance therefore cannot be investigated in humans under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions, so all human evidence comes from surveys of people who use ecstasy recreationally; in those surveys 58% (n=596) of 1151 people surveyed reported tolerance (596 is 52% of 1151, so what the 58% is a percentage of is unclear) and about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reported declining subjective efficacy, with an earlier survey finding 67% of those with six or more occasions reporting that positive effects decreased and negative effects increased.

evidence.locator: Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, 1st-2nd paragraphs; Table 1; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Reported dose rises with past use: 1.8 tablets a session currently against 1.2 when starting in 430 people; usual dose 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets and maximum ever 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7) across lifetime-use groups of 14, 14 and 11 people, with the maximum significant at p<0.01 and the usual dose only at p<0.10; and a usual dose of 1-2 tablets reported by 100% of 109, 84% of 136 and 62% of 37 people in novice, moderate and heaviest groups, with a maximum of ten or more tablets in a week reported by 0%, 9% and 35% (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, p<0.001).

evidence.locator: The paragraph beginning 'A related problem is the issue of dosage' (p. 72); Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, last paragraph (p. 75); Table 3 (p. 78)
evidence.extracted: Qualifications reported in the same review: one study found no dose escalation with longer use (2.1 tablets per occasion after 10.9 years against 2.5 after 3.9 years, not significant); average MDMA content per tablet in United Kingdom forensic samples fell about 20% across the mid-1990s (102 to 88 mg, then 75 to 73 mg) so falling tablet strength cannot be excluded for studies from that period; and in the same internet sample, problems attributed to ecstasy rose with lifetime use (depression 33%, 54% and 65%; memory problems 19%, 52% and 73%), so heavier use goes with more reported harm as well as with larger doses.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 261); Materials and methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 262)
evidence.extracted: Primary source of the review's Saturday-night figures, read in full. Three groups of 15 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30, recruited by word of mouth among people who regularly went to one large nightclub in north-east London: a regular group with ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, a novice group with one to nine, and a comparison group who had never taken it. Each person noted on a questionnaire the drugs taken that night: the regular group 1.80 tablets on average and the novice group 1.45, which the authors call slightly more; the comparison group took none. No spread, range or test of the difference is printed, no testing of the tablets is reported, and the paper does not discuss tolerance. Other drugs that night (comparison, novice, regular): alcohol 10, 5 and 6 people, cannabis 3, 1 and 2, cocaine 2, 2 and 4, amphetamine 1 novice. Editors' check against Parrott (2005), p. 74: the review gives 1.45 and 1.80 correctly and calls the record prospective (here a self-report on the night), but describes the regular group as more than 10 occasions, where this paper's Methods say ten or more.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional self-report of illegal drug use with no biological verification and no measurement of what the tablets contained, seen only through a narrative review with no search strategy, no selection criteria and no appraisal of the studies it cites, about half of them by the reviewer's own group.

inconsistency.note: Most surveys point the same way; the one study that does not is reported in the claim.

indirectness.note: The editors have read only one of the primary studies (two groups of 15 on one night, whose tablet figures match the review); every other figure is second-hand from the review (METHODS 6.3). Self-reported tolerance is also an indirect measure of a pharmacological change.

imprecision.note: The samples are large by the standards of this literature (hundreds to over a thousand); imprecision is not what limits this claim.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low. Risk of bias -2 for unverified self-report of unknown substances in unsystematically selected studies; indirectness -1 because the figures are second-hand from a narrative review and self-reported tolerance is an indirect measure. Certainty very-low. No upgrade for a dose-response gradient: the gradient here is between groups of different people, not within people over time, and the same gradient appears in self-attributed harms, which suggests shared reporting influences. The claim stays at draft and says in its first sentence that its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3).

verification.flag_note: Rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and is not shown in the at-a-glance box (METHODS 6.3). If the senior author wants this question on the page at a higher rung, the primary surveys (Verheyden et al., 2003a; Winstock et al., 2001; Scholey et al., 2004; Fox et al., 2001a and 2001b; Verkes et al., 2001; Topp et al., 1999) need to be read in full. Parrott and Lasky (1998) was read in full on 2026-10-23 (AI reader 94, card sc_parrott_1998): its tablet figures (1.80 against 1.45) match the review, but it prints no spread or test, calls the difference slight and defines the regular group as ten or more occasions where the review says more than 10; its anchor qualifies the claim, so the support still rests on the review alone and the claim stays at draft.

statement: In the laboratory studies of repeated MDMA dosing, the strain on the circulation followed the blood concentration even where the wanted effects did not. After a second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first, 8 of 9 men crossed 140 mm Hg systolic against 6 of 9 after the first dose, with episodes lasting on average 1.4 hours (range 0.5-3) against 1 hour (0.5-2), and the only two episodes of sinus tachycardia above 100 beats a minute both followed the second dose (Farré et al., 2004). In the study of a second dose two hours after the first, all 10 men met the study's criterion for high blood pressure at some point (the paper does not say in which condition), and blood pressure, temperature and pupil diameter rose with the added dose while peak heart rate and the wanted effects did not (Peiró et al., 2013). In the registered booster study, blood pressure, heart rate and temperature were prolonged but not raised at the peak, and no participant exceeded 180 mm Hg systolic or 40 degrees Celsius (Humbert-Droz et al., 2026). In these studies, the added dose added to the load on the heart and circulation without adding to the peak of the wanted effects. The numbers are small (9, 10 and 23 healthy screened people, two studies in men only), the doses are 50 to 180 mg of pure MDMA taken seated in a quiet room, and nobody has tested the hotter, more crowded, more active settings or the larger amounts described in surveys.
plain: When people take a second dose, the drug level in the blood rises more than the extra dose alone explains, and the strain on the heart and circulation goes up with it, even though the good feelings do not get stronger. In one study, 8 of 9 men went above a raised blood-pressure line after the second dose, against 6 of 9 after the first, and the two cases of a racing heart both came after the second dose. In another, all ten men went above that line. Nobody has tested this in a hot, crowded room or with the larger amounts people describe in surveys.
population: Healthy adults with previous recreational MDMA experience in laboratory studies (9 men; 10 men; 23 people of whom 11 were women), screened to exclude cardiovascular, other medical and psychiatric illness
exposure: A second dose of MDMA taken 2 or 24 hours after the first (study conditions: 100 mg then 100 mg 24 hours apart; 50 mg then 100 mg 2 hours apart; 120 mg then 60 mg 2 hours apart), taken seated in a quiet laboratory
comparator: The same people after a single dose or placebo, and their own first dose
outcome: Blood pressure and heart rate, the number of people crossing clinical thresholds, body temperature, and reported adverse effects
magnitude: Twenty-four-hour interval: isolated systolic hypertension (above 140 mm Hg) in 6 of 9 men after the first dose and 8 of 9 after the second; mean episode duration 1 h (range 0.5-2) against 1.4 h (range 0.5-3); two men met criteria for sinus tachycardia (above 100 beats/min), both after the second dose, lasting 15-30 minutes; peak systolic rise 34 mm Hg against 25 and diastolic 20 against 10 (Farré et al., 2004). Two-hour interval: all 10 men exceeded 140/90 mm Hg; systolic area under the curve 72.96 (SD 22.12) against 49.35 (SD 24.28), p=0.029, and diastolic 46.82 (SD 27.82) against 18.81 (SD 21.09), p=0.015, with heart rate unchanged (Peiró et al., 2013). Booster study: autonomic effects prolonged without higher maxima, no systolic pressure above 180 mm Hg and no temperature above 40 degrees Celsius; acute complaint scores 22 (SD 15) with the booster against 20 (SD 13) with the single dose, not significantly different, with vomiting in 3 of 23 (13%) against 2 (9%) (Humbert-Droz et al., 2026).

evidence.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'In reference to physiological parameters' (right column)
evidence.extracted: Criteria for isolated systolic hypertension (above 140 mm Hg) were met by 6 of 9 men after the first 100 mg dose and by 8 of 9 after the second dose 24 hours later, with episodes lasting a mean of 1 h (range 0.5-2) and 1.4 h (range 0.5-3); two men met criteria for sinus tachycardia (above 100 beats/min), both after the second dose, lasting 15-30 minutes. Peak rises were 34 mm Hg systolic and 20 diastolic after the second dose against 25 and 10 after the first.

evidence.locator: Table 1, SBP and DBP rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st paragraph (p. 887, bottom left into top right)
evidence.extracted: All ten men met the criteria for hypertension (above 140/90 mm Hg) in the study, a statement the paper does not tie to one condition; with 50 mg two hours before 100 mg, the systolic area under the curve over the 2-6 hour window was 72.96 (SD 22.12) against 49.35 (SD 24.28) for 100 mg alone (p=0.029) and the diastolic 46.82 (SD 27.82) against 18.81 (SD 21.09) (p=0.015), while heart rate did not differ in peak or area under the curve.

evidence.locator: Results > Autonomic effects; Table 2, List of complaints rows; Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 1st paragraph and the paragraph beginning 'Two participants dropped out'
evidence.extracted: With a 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg, blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and temperature lasted longer than with the single dose but did not reach higher maxima, and no participant exceeded 180 mm Hg systolic or 40 degrees Celsius. Acute complaint scores did not differ significantly between booster and single dose (22, SD 15, against 20, SD 13), although two of 25 participants, both women receiving the booster as their first MDMA experience, left the study after headache and nausea followed by weeks to months of mental instability (anxiety in both; confusion and impaired concentration in one, restlessness and tension in the other), and are excluded from that comparison.

evidence.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The changes seen in the concentrations between first and second doses'
evidence.extracted: The authors note that acute MDMA toxicity has been linked to high plasma concentrations and doses, that cardiovascular complications were more frequent after the second dose in their study, and that with further doses the contribution of each previous dose would grow because MDMA inhibits its own metabolism; they present this as speculation about what would happen beyond two doses, which was not tested.

risk_of_bias.note: Randomized or counterbalanced double-blind crossovers with instrument-measured blood pressure, heart rate and temperature, which the broken blinding affects little; but the threshold counts were not pre-specified outcomes and the studies tested many measures without correction.

inconsistency.note: Three studies agree that the circulatory load tracks concentration; they differ in whether the peak or only the duration rises, which the claim states.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the doses, settings and people studied, and says that hotter, more crowded settings and larger amounts are untested.

imprecision.note: The threshold counts are 6 of 9 against 8 of 9 and 10 of 10, with no intervals; a difference of two people in nine cannot support a quantitative statement about how much redosing raises the risk.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1: the measures that matter here are instrument-recorded, but the threshold counts are post-hoc descriptions rather than pre-specified outcomes. Imprecision -2: the counts come from 9 and 10 people and no intervals are given, so the claim can report what happened in those men but not a risk. Certainty very-low. The claim is deliberately worded as what was measured in these sessions, with the inference that redosing adds circulatory load without added wanted effect stated as the combination of two measured findings, not as a tested outcome.

verification.flag_note: Section 6 claim drawn from studies designed to measure pharmacology rather than harm; the senior author may prefer it merged into the acute-risks claim on cardiovascular effects once that exists.
