statement: Among people who use ecstasy, those who have used more of it have lower serotonin transporter binding, in most but not all of the studies that looked. In 23 people who had used MDMA, scanned with [11C]DASB, binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime tablets in every region but the midbrain: a doubling of lifetime tablets went with a fall of 0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), 0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), and about 0.07 in thalamus and amygdala (Erritzoe et al., 2011). Among 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair (47 in the cortical model), the only variables that predicted lower cortical binding were years of use and the largest dose taken in one session (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001), and years of use also predicted lower caudate binding (Kish et al., 2010). In 23 people, global binding was related to the typical monthly dose (r=-0.38 and -0.37 for the two tracers, p=0.04, one-tailed) (McCann et al., 2005), and in a SPECT study the relation with lifetime tablets held in women (r=-0.33, p=0.048) but not men (Reneman et al., 2001). Two studies found no relation: 13 people, where the correlations ran in the same direction but did not reach significance (r about -0.46, p=0.11 to 0.12) (Urban et al., 2012), and the prospective cohort, in which nobody had taken more than 80 tablets and most had taken one or two (de Win et al., 2008). All of these are relations within self-selected groups, measured against lifetime use recalled by the person, which in these samples ranges over two orders of magnitude; none is adjusted for other drug use, and heavier ecstasy use goes with heavier use of everything else. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: People who have taken ecstasy more often tend to show less of the serotonin marker on scans. Four studies found this link, and two smaller ones did not. The amounts come from what people remembered taking, sometimes hundreds of pills over years. People who take more ecstasy also tend to take more of other drugs, and none of these studies could separate the two.
population: Adults who use ecstasy recreationally, abstinent when scanned
exposure: More cumulative ecstasy use (lifetime tablets, years of use, typical monthly dose or largest dose in one session)
comparator: Lighter use within the same group
outcome: Serotonin transporter binding measured with PET or SPECT
magnitude: Per doubling of lifetime tablets: -0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014), -0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021), about -0.07 in thalamus and amygdala (Erritzoe et al., 2011; on a neocortical control mean of about 0.33 units, a doubling is roughly a 6% fall). Regression of cortical binding on years of use and maximum dose F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001 (Kish et al., 2010). Correlations: -0.38 and -0.37 with typical monthly dose, one-tailed p=0.04 (McCann et al., 2005); -0.33 with log lifetime tablets in women, p=0.048 (Reneman et al., 2001); -0.44 to -0.47, p=0.11 to 0.14, not significant, in 13 people (Urban et al., 2012). No relation in the prospective cohort, where the median was 2 tablets (de Win et al., 2008).

evidence.locator: Methods, 'Participants and drug use' (p. 563, the conversion of powder to tablets); Table 1 (p. 564, lifetime tablets); Methods, statistical analysis (p. 566, 23 participants for SERT binding); Results, 'SERT binding', 2nd paragraph (pp. 567-568) and Figure 3 (p. 568)
evidence.extracted: In 23 people who had used MDMA (of the 24 users of MDMA and/or hallucinogens), binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime MDMA tablets in every region except the midbrain: per doubling of tablets, -0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), -0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), -0.067 in thalamus (p=0.006) and -0.075 in amygdala (p<0.001). The printed upper limits for thalamus (0.022) and amygdala (0.045) contradict their p-values and appear to be missing a minus sign. Lifetime tablets were self-reported and ranged from 6 to 6590, with powder converted to tablets at 60 mg each.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 1785, lifetime tablets and maximum dose); Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 5th paragraph (p. 1787)
evidence.extracted: In a stepwise regression among the 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair (the degrees of freedom imply 47 people in the cortical model and 43 in the caudate model), entering demographic, drug-history, mood, subjective-effect and cognitive variables, the only predictors of lower binding across all cortical regions were years of use and maximum dose per session (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001); years of use also predicted lower caudate binding (F(1,41)=4.91, p=0.032). Lifetime tablets ranged from 4 to 922 (median 126) and maximum dose from 1 to 20 tablets (median 3), by self-report.

evidence.locator: Methods, Statistical methods (p. 1743, one-tailed tests); Table 1 (p. 1744, sample); Results, last paragraph (p. 1745, correlations); Discussion (p. 1748, the authors' caution)
evidence.extracted: In 23 people abstinent from MDMA, global binding (distribution volume ratio) was related to the typical monthly dose for both radioligands (r=-0.38 and -0.37, described in the text as inverse, p=0.04 for both), on one-tailed tests chosen in advance; the authors state the study was not powered for these correlations and call them preliminary.

evidence.locator: Results, last paragraph; Figure 3
evidence.extracted: With SPECT and [123I]beta-CIT, overall binding ratio correlated with the logarithm of lifetime ecstasy tablets in women (r=-0.33, p=0.048) but not in men (r=0.07, p=0.699). The page itself prints the coefficient as 'r=20·33', a misprint of the minus sign (a correlation cannot exceed 1), and the women's regression line in Figure 3 slopes downward. (the Lancet prints decimal points as middle dots.)

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (sessions: mean 142, median 50, range 15-1050) and 7th paragraph (correlations); Methods, last paragraph (the four use variables tested)
evidence.extracted: In 13 people, no correlation between binding and any use variable reached significance: with lifetime uses, dorsolateral prefrontal r=-0.46 (p=0.12) and parietal r=-0.46 (p=0.11); with duration of use, occipital r=-0.47 (p=0.12) and parietal r=-0.44 (p=0.14). Lifetime sessions ranged from 15 to 1050 (median 50).

evidence.locator: Results, 'Brain imaging', last paragraph (p. 2939); Discussion, limitations paragraph (p. 2943, the distribution of use)
evidence.extracted: In the prospective cohort, no relation was found between the cumulative number of tablets and any follow-up imaging measure; the authors suggest this could be because of the narrow range of use, since 54% had taken one tablet or less and only 17% ten or more.

evidence.locator: Results, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st paragraph (effect size ranges); Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st paragraph (animal and human exposure); Discussion, '3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine and additional drug use', 1st and 2nd paragraphs (de Win 2008b and Erritzoe 2011)
evidence.extracted: The review notes that human transporter studies have smaller effect sizes than animal studies (-0.05 to -2.17 against -0.38 to -20.03), that human exposure is estimated at 2-4 mg/kg for the one or two tablets typically taken (a person of 70 kg) against 20-141 mg/kg in the animal experiments, and that two studies suggest cannabis, cocaine and hallucinogen use do not account for the transporter findings. It records no pooled dose-response estimate.

risk_of_bias.note: Cumulative use is recalled by the person, spans two orders of magnitude within each sample and is not verified for amount; the relations are unadjusted for other drug use, which rises with ecstasy use; several are one-tailed or uncorrected, and all are within self-selected groups.

inconsistency.note: Four studies found a relation and two did not; one of the nulls had 13 participants with correlations of the same size as the significant ones elsewhere, and the other had almost no variation in dose, so the inconsistency is partly explained, but it is not resolved.

indirectness.note: Measured exposure and measured binding, as worded.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded twice: the small samples are already counted under risk of bias and inconsistency.

dose_response.note: Not applied: a dose-response gradient cannot upgrade the claim that there is a dose-response gradient.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias (self-reported lifetime use, unadjusted for other drugs, some one-tailed and uncorrected tests) and for inconsistency (two of six studies found no relation). The direction is the same wherever a relation appears, which is why the claim is made at all; its size is not estimable from these data.

verification.flag_note: Anchors are ai-located and need a second reader. The relation rests on within-group correlations and regressions; no study has measured exposure other than by recall, so a quantitative dose-response cannot be given.

statement: Whether serotonin transporter binding returns to normal after people stop using ecstasy has not been established, because no study has scanned the same people during use and again after a long break. Three findings are read as recovery: in 12 men who had not used MDMA for at least a year (mean 2.7 years), binding did not differ from that of men who used other drugs or none (F=1.22, p=0.31), although only one cortical region was measured and there was no group of people currently using (Selvaraj et al., 2009); in 23 people who had used MDMA, scanned once, binding was higher in those whose last dose was longer ago in pallidostriatum (0.14 binding-potential units per doubling of days, 95% CI 0.05-0.23), amygdala and thalamus but not in neocortex, from which the authors extrapolate a return to the comparison group's average after about 212 days, with a lower limit of 91 days and an upper limit beyond a human lifespan (Erritzoe et al., 2011); and in 23 people, global binding with one of two tracers was higher with longer abstinence (r=0.418 and 0.494, one-tailed p=0.026 and p<0.010) (McCann et al., 2005). Against these, two studies found no relation between binding and time since last use: 49 people abstinent a median of 38 days (range 11-194) (Kish et al., 2010) and 13 people abstinent 2 to 8 weeks (Urban et al., 2012); and a SPECT study in which the women who had stopped for at least a year had higher binding than the women still using heavily (difference 0.137, 95% CI 0.046-0.227) and did not differ from the comparison group, while remaining non-significantly lower in the two posterior cortical regions, compared separately recruited groups rather than the same people (Reneman et al., 2001). All of these comparisons are between people, so they cannot separate recovery from a difference between those who stop and those who do not, and the regions said to recover are not the regions where the difference is largest. A review of this literature nonetheless summarizes it as recovery within 40 to 200 days (Vegting et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Nobody knows whether the serotonin marker goes back to normal after people stop using ecstasy. No one has been scanned both while using and again years later. Three studies compared different people and found more of the marker in those who had stopped longer ago. Two others found no link with time since the last dose. People who stop may also be different from people who keep going, and the deeper parts of the brain, where the marker looked more normal, are not where the difference is biggest.
population: Adults who formerly used ecstasy, or who are abstinent for weeks to years when scanned
exposure: Longer time since the last dose of ecstasy
comparator: People still using ecstasy, or shorter abstinence, or people who have not used it
outcome: Serotonin transporter binding measured with PET or SPECT
magnitude: Not estimable within a person, since no one has been scanned twice. Between people: +0.14 binding-potential units per doubling of days since last use in pallidostriatum (95% CI 0.05-0.23), +0.12 in amygdala (0.04-0.21), +0.11 in thalamus (0.002-0.22), and +0.005 in neocortex (-0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67), with an extrapolated return to the comparison average at about 212 days (lower limit 91 days, upper limit beyond a lifespan) (Erritzoe et al., 2011); correlations of global binding with months abstinent r=0.418 and 0.494, one-tailed (McCann et al., 2005); no relation at all in two studies with abstinence windows of 11-194 days and 2-8 weeks (Kish et al., 2010; Urban et al., 2012); and no difference from controls in 12 men abstinent at least a year, with no estimate or interval printed (Selvaraj et al., 2009).

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 356, time since last use); Results, 'SERT binding', 2nd paragraph and Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 357); Figure 1 (p. 358)
evidence.extracted: 12 men who had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions and had stopped for a mean of 2.74 years (range 390-1825 days) did not differ in [11C]DASB binding from 9 men who used other drugs and 19 who used none (group F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31; region-by-group F=0.36, p=0.81), with regional means and standard deviations shown only as bars in Figure 1 and no numeric estimates or intervals. The authors state the result can mean either that binding never differed or that it recovered, and prefer recovery; there was no group of people currently using MDMA, and neocortical analysis was limited to the frontal cortex (cingulate cortex and insula were also analysed).

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 564, the drug group); Results, 'SERT binding', 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 568-569); Figure 4 and its caption (p. 569)
evidence.extracted: Across the 23 people who had used MDMA (the paper does not state the n for this model), scanned once, binding was higher the longer ago the last MDMA dose was taken: per doubling of days, +0.14 binding-potential units in pallidostriatum (95% CI 0.05-0.23, p=0.004), +0.12 in amygdala (0.04-0.21, p=0.008), +0.11 in thalamus (0.002-0.22, p=0.046), and no relation in neocortex (+0.005, -0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67). Adjusted for lifetime tablets, pallidostriatum (p=0.02), amygdala (p=0.02) and midbrain (p=0.02) held and thalamus did not. From a log-logistic model, pallidostriatal binding in a person with the median lifetime use would reach the comparison average after about 212 days, with a lower 95% limit of 91 days and an upper limit beyond a human lifespan.

evidence.locator: Methods, Statistical methods (p. 1743, one-tailed tests); Table 1 (p. 1744, abstinence); Results, last paragraph (p. 1745, correlations, 'exploratory'); Discussion (p. 1748, 'not powered')
evidence.extracted: In 23 people abstinent a mean of 4.7 months (SD 8.7), global [11C]McN5652 binding was higher with longer abstinence (specific distribution volume r=0.418, p=0.026; distribution volume ratio r=0.494, p<0.010), on one-tailed tests; no such correlation is reported for [11C]DASB. The authors call these analyses exploratory and underpowered.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 1785, days withdrawn); Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 5th paragraph (p. 1787); Discussion, 'Preferential SERT changes…' (p. 1792)
evidence.extracted: In 49 people abstinent a median of 38 days (range 11-194), there was no significant correlation between withdrawal time and brain binding (no regional detail given); the authors say the question of recovery could not be addressed because typical withdrawal was only 1-2 months, and cite the study of people abstinent about 2.7 years as suggesting any reduction might be reversible in some people.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd (abstinence mean 5.7 weeks, range 2-8), 7th and 10th paragraphs; Discussion, 8th paragraph
evidence.extracted: In 13 people abstinent 2 to 8 weeks (mean 5.7), no correlation between length of abstinence and transporter or 5-HT2A binding reached significance; the authors note their narrow range of abstinence, and say the null result in 12 former users whose last use was over a year before the scan suggests the lower binding might be reversible, but urge caution before adopting that conclusion because that study had no group of people currently using and because cortical measurement with this tracer is noisy.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 1865, time since last tablet); Table 3 (p. 1866); Table 4 (p. 1867); Results, 6th paragraph (p. 1867, ex-users); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 1867) and reversibility paragraph (p. 1868, prospective design needed)
evidence.extracted: With SPECT, 16 people who had used at least 50 tablets and had stopped for at least a year (mean 29 months) were compared with separately recruited groups: among women, overall binding was higher than in those still using heavily (difference 0.137, 95% CI 0.046-0.227, p=0.004) and did not differ from the comparison group (0.031, -0.067 to 0.129, p=0.524), while remaining non-significantly lower in parieto-occipital (p=0.059) and occipital cortex (p=0.107). Nobody was scanned twice; the Discussion states that a prospective design would be needed to establish reversibility. (the Lancet prints decimal points as middle dots, so these values appear in the PDF as 0·168 and so on.)

evidence.locator: Discussion, 'Recovery'; Concluding remarks, 'Current knowledge'
evidence.extracted: The review summarizes the field as showing that transporter binding recovers after 40 to 200 days, without saying where the figures come from: the only 40-day figure in its text is a baboon study in which binding rose after the 40-day scan in pons, midbrain and hypothalamus but stayed low in cortex, and the 200 days matches the cross-sectional extrapolation for the pallidostriatum in a study that found no recovery in neocortex. It then asks whether recovered binding means functionally intact neurones, noting a study in which people who had stopped for over a year had control-level binding but memory-test deficits similar to current users, and concludes that the cause of any recovery is unknown.

risk_of_bias.note: Every estimate compares different people: those who have stopped may differ from those who continue in how much they used, in why they stopped and in everything else they take. Abstinence is self-reported except for the weeks before scanning, two of the analyses are one-tailed, and the study of people abstinent for a year prints no estimates or intervals.

inconsistency.note: Three studies report a relation with time since last use and two find none; the regions in which binding looks recovered (pallidostriatum, amygdala, thalamus) are not those in which the difference is largest, and the one study of long abstinence measured only one cortical region.

indirectness.note: Not downgraded again: the between-person design is already counted under risk of bias.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded again; the width of the one published extrapolation (91 days to beyond a lifespan) is stated in the claim.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is downgraded for risk of bias (all comparisons are between people, with self-reported abstinence and one-tailed tests) and inconsistency (two studies find no relation with time since last use, and the regions that look recovered are not the ones most affected). The claim is worded as insufficient evidence, which is what the designs support: absence of a difference in people who stopped long ago is not evidence that binding recovered in them.

verification.flag_note: Anchors are ai-located and need a second reader. The two longitudinal studies the review cites (Buchert et al., 2006, and Thomasius et al., 2006, in which some people were scanned more than once) have not been read; they should be obtained before this claim is shown, since they are the only designs that could answer the question from within people.

statement: In the one study that scanned people before they had ever used ecstasy and again afterwards, starting to use it in small amounts did not change serotonin transporter binding. 188 people who had never used ecstasy were imaged; about 17 months later, 59 who had begun using (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2; last tablet a mean of 18.7 weeks earlier) and 56 matched people who had not were imaged again (complete transporter data for 57 and 53). Transporter binding with [123I]beta-CIT did not differ at follow-up in any region (midbrain 0.036, 95% CI -0.068 to 0.140; thalamus -0.001, -0.077 to 0.076; frontal -0.003, -0.036 to 0.31 as printed; occipital -0.018, -0.051 to 0.015; temporal -0.009, -0.053 to 0.35 as printed, the last two upper limits almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035), nor did brain metabolites, and a voxel-by-voxel analysis found nothing. Four smaller differences did appear, each under 5% and within the normal range of the age group: lower fractional anisotropy in thalamus and frontoparietal white matter, higher anisotropy in globus pallidus, a higher apparent diffusion coefficient in thalamus, and lower relative cerebral blood volume in globus pallidus and putamen. The two groups did not differ on any imaging measure, substance use or transporter genotype before anyone had used ecstasy, which is the one direct check on the objection that differences seen in people who use ecstasy were there beforehand. The transporter result cannot be read as showing that heavier use leaves binding unchanged: the doses were very low, the tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and the authors judge it too insensitive for small changes, 32 comparisons were made without correction, and the group that started also increased its use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: One Dutch study scanned young people before they had ever taken ecstasy, then again about a year and a half later. By then some had started, but most had taken only one or two pills. Their serotonin marker had not changed, and nor had the chemical measures. A few small differences showed up in other brain measures, all under 5%. Before anyone had used ecstasy the two groups' scans looked the same, which matters because people often ask whether the differences seen later were there all along. The doses here were tiny and the scan used an older, less exact marker, so this says nothing about heavier use.
population: Young adults in the Netherlands who had never used ecstasy and were judged likely to start
exposure: Starting to use ecstasy, a median of 2 tablets over about 17 months
comparator: The same people before any use, and matched people from the same cohort who did not start
outcome: Serotonin transporter binding with [123I]beta-CIT SPECT, brain metabolites, diffusion measures and cerebral blood volume
magnitude: Transporter binding at follow-up, adjusted for baseline (regression coefficients, 95% CI): midbrain 0.036 (-0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal grey matter -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed; the frontal and temporal upper limits appear to be misprints for 0.031 and 0.035). The binding ratios themselves are 1.1 to 1.3 in midbrain and thalamus but 0.01 to 0.05 in cortical grey matter, so the cortical intervals, although narrow in absolute units, do not exclude a large proportional change. Differences that did appear were under 5%: fractional anisotropy -8.16 (-15.30 to -1.02) in thalamus and -8.23 (-14.35 to -2.10) in frontoparietal white matter, +23.19 (3.65 to 42.73) in globus pallidus (all x1000); apparent diffusion coefficient +3.68 (0.67 to 6.69) x10-5 mm2/s in thalamus; relative cerebral blood volume -0.083 (-0.154 to -0.012) in globus pallidus and -0.058 (-0.110 to -0.006) in putamen.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 2940, exposure); Table 2, SPECT and 1H-MRS rows (p. 2941)
evidence.extracted: Prospective cohort: 59 people who started using ecstasy (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2) and 56 who did not, imaged before any use and about 17 months later (complete data: SPECT 57 users and 53 non-users, spectroscopy 52 and 51). Transporter binding at follow-up, adjusted for baseline: midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal grey matter -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed; the frontal and temporal upper limits are almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035, checked on the rendered page). All nine metabolite ratios were also unchanged.

evidence.locator: Results, 'Brain imaging', 2nd paragraph (p. 2939); Methods, 'Statistical analyses' (p. 2939, models 1 and 2); Table 2, DTI and PWI rows (p. 2941); Figure 2 (p. 2942)
evidence.extracted: Differences that did appear (each group's change from baseline under 5%), adjusted for baseline scores in Table 2; the authors report that all remained significant after further adjustment for sex, baseline verbal IQ, age, education and use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine and tobacco, but print no estimates for that model: fractional anisotropy lower in thalamus (-8.16, 95% CI -15.30 to -1.02, x1000) and frontoparietal white matter (-8.23, -14.35 to -2.10) and higher in globus pallidus (+23.19, 3.65 to 42.73); apparent diffusion coefficient higher in thalamus (+3.68, 0.67 to 6.69); relative cerebral blood volume lower in globus pallidus (-0.083, -0.154 to -0.012) and putamen (-0.058, -0.110 to -0.006). Part of each difference comes from change in the group that did not start.

evidence.locator: Results, 'Characteristics of the sample and substance use' (p. 2939); Table 1 (p. 2940); Table 2, baseline columns (p. 2941)
evidence.extracted: Before anyone had used ecstasy the two groups did not differ on any imaging parameter, on substance use or on serotonin-transporter genotype. Over follow-up the group that started increased its use of alcohol (p=0.036), cannabis (p=0.029), amphetamines (p=0.047) and cocaine (p=0.017) more than the other group, and their interval between sessions was shorter (15.9 vs 18.3 months, p=0.024).

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraph on the SERT result (p. 2942, animal studies on SPECT sensitivity); Discussion, limitations paragraph (p. 2943: power, multiple comparisons, reversibility)
evidence.extracted: The authors state that statistical power may have been insufficient for SPECT and spectroscopy given the low doses, that the tracer may be too insensitive to detect mild changes (animal work shows it underestimates MDMA-induced transporter loss), that no correction for multiple comparisons was applied in order to limit false negatives, and that the observed effects may be reversible adaptations rather than permanent neurotoxicity.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 728, sample); Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (p. 731); Table 2, RAVLT immediate row (p. 732); Comment, 1st paragraph (p. 732)
evidence.extracted: In the same NeXT cohort, at an earlier follow-up (58 who started using ecstasy, mean 3.2 tablets and median 1.5, against 60 who did not; not the same 59 and 56 as in the imaging follow-up), verbal learning improved less in those who had started using ecstasy (immediate recall +0.86 against +3.90 words; adjusted difference 2.23, 95% CI 0.17 to 4.29, p=0.03), while overall test performance in both groups stayed within the normal range for the general population.

evidence.locator: Table 4, de Win et al. (2008a) row and footnotes (only significant P values are shown); Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter', 2nd paragraph (14 of 16 studies) and 3rd paragraph (Urban et al.'s near-zero binding)
evidence.extracted: The review's Table 4, which prints only significant P values, shows none for this cohort, consistent with its count of 14 of 16 human transporter studies with a significant reduction (the review does not name the two that lacked one), and reports for it an occipital change of -40% (effect size -0.21), which follows from follow-up binding ratios of 0.05 against 0.03 (de Win et al. 2008, Table 2, p. 2941; the ratios are not printed in the review); the review does not flag that these near-zero values make the percentage meaningless, although it makes that point about another study's figures.

risk_of_bias.note: Not randomized: people chose whether to start, and those who did also increased their use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine and were re-tested sooner. Exposure is self-reported and tablet content unverified. The pre-use measurement removes most of the usual confounding, which is why only one level is taken.

inconsistency.note: A single cohort; nothing to compare it with, since no other prospective imaging study exists.

indirectness.note: The exposure is a median of 2 tablets, far below that of the people in the cross-sectional studies, and the tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and is judged by the authors too insensitive for small changes; so this bears only indirectly on what ordinary or heavy use does.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded again: the intervals are reported and the claim states what they do and do not exclude. In cortical regions the binding ratios are near zero, so the intervals are narrow in absolute units but wide in proportion.

dose_response.note: Not applied: no dose-response was found, and the range of use was too narrow to test one.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low, downgraded for risk of bias (self-selected starters with more other drug use and a shorter interval between sessions) and indirectness (a median of 2 tablets, measured with a tracer the authors call too insensitive). The claim is worded as no detectable change at this exposure and states the limits that stop it being read as no change at any exposure.

verification.flag_note: Anchors are ai-located and need a second reader. The companion paper on the thalamus from the same cohort (de Win et al., Br J Psychiatry 2008;193:289-296, doi 10.1192/bjp.bp.106.035089) has not been read and has no reference record; it reports the same cohort's thalamic findings and should be added before this claim is shown.

statement: In two randomized or counterbalanced, double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies of healthy adults, an antidepressant of the SSRI type (a medicine that blocks the serotonin transporter) taken before MDMA lowered the effects that people rated and that were measured; in the one study that took blood samples, the MDMA level was not lower. In 16 volunteers (3 of whom had tried ecstasy before) given citalopram by infusion before MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg), ratings of the altered state that MDMA brings on, taken 2 hours later, were lower on 10 of the 13 item clusters that MDMA had raised, by about 55 to 80 percent (editors' calculation from the printed means; the authors say about 60 percent); the rises in self-confidence and extroversion were lowered, those in emotional excitability and sensitivity were not, and no blood samples were taken (Liechti et al., 2000). In 12 men given paroxetine daily for 3 days before MDMA 100 mg, the rises in systolic pressure (12 mm Hg lower at the peak), heart rate (14 beats a minute lower at the peak, though not by the area test), pupil width (3.33 to 1.23 mm) and temperature (0.3 degrees lower) were smaller, ratings of euphoria, 'high' and liking were lower, ratings of bad effects, fear and low mood did not change (they did not change with MDMA alone either), and no serious adverse event occurred; the peak MDMA level was 16% higher (246.6 against 212.7 ug/L), the exposure to 21 hours 22% higher, and the level of its metabolite HMMA 49% lower at the peak and 39% lower in exposure (Farré et al., 2007). As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), a third SSRI, fluoxetine, lowered ratings of liking, 'high' and 'stimulated' in 8 people, and the review reports no serious adverse effects of any of these combinations in the trials. So in the one study that measured it, feeling less came with more MDMA in the blood, not less. Some people feel little from an amount, for reasons that include a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ and, as here, a medicine that blunts the effect, and some of them take more. Neither study gave more MDMA once the effects were blunted, so what happens then was not measured; the authors of the paroxetine study and of a probe-drug study suggest, without testing it, that it could add risk (Farré et al., 2007; O'Mathúna et al., 2008). Both studies used healthy volunteers, one infusion of citalopram or 3 days of paroxetine, and one fixed amount of MDMA by mouth, and the review found no trial in which people had taken an SSRI or a similar medicine for months before MDMA. Other antidepressants, reports of harm and monoamine-oxidase inhibitors are covered in separate claims.
plain: In two lab studies, healthy volunteers who first took an SSRI antidepressant (citalopram or paroxetine) felt much less from MDMA. With citalopram they rated the effects about 60 percent lower; with paroxetine the rises in the upper blood pressure number, heart rate and pupil size were smaller. The MDMA level in the blood was not lower. With paroxetine it was about 1 in 6 higher at the peak, so feeling less did not mean less MDMA in the body (citalopram's blood levels were not measured). Some people feel little from an amount and take more. The reasons can be a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect, as here. No study gave more MDMA to people on an SSRI, so what happens then is not known; the paroxetine authors suggest it could add risk. The volunteers were healthy, had the SSRI for 3 days at most, and got one fixed amount of MDMA.
population: Healthy adult volunteers in two laboratory studies: 16 people in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 3 had tried ecstasy, 13 had not) and 12 men in Barcelona (all with earlier MDMA use and normal CYP2D6 function), screened for health
exposure: An SSRI taken before a single dose of MDMA (study conditions: citalopram 40 mg by infusion over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg by mouth; paroxetine 20 mg a day for 3 days, then MDMA 100 mg on day 3)
comparator: The same people given a dummy treatment before MDMA, and (citalopram study) dummy before dummy and citalopram alone
outcome: Rated altered-state and mood scales, euphoria and liking ratings, heart rate, blood pressure, pupil width, body temperature, and (paroxetine study only) blood concentrations of MDMA and its metabolite HMMA
magnitude: Citalopram, 16 people (Liechti et al., 2000): altered-state item clusters, percent of maximum, MDMA alone against citalopram then MDMA: positive basic mood 40.1 against 16.4, derealization 32.7 against 12.6, thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6, changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1 (ten of the 13 raised clusters lowered, three not); interactions F(1,15) 22.47 for oceanic boundlessness and 23.04 for anxious ego dissolution; no blood levels. Paroxetine, 12 men (Farré et al., 2007): peak systolic pressure 12 mm Hg lower (P=0.001), pupil widening 3.33 to 1.23 mm (P<0.001), temperature rise 0.3 C lower (P=0.041), euphoria scale peak 7.27 to 4; MDMA peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and exposure to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L (both P<0.01); HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and exposure 1189.47 against 1923.32 (both P<0.01); the paper's text gives MDMA +16 percent (peak) and +22 percent (exposure), HMMA -49 percent and -39 percent. Editors' calculation from the printed means: citalopram clusters 55 to 80 percent lower (the authors say about 60 percent overall); HMMA exposure -38 percent. Fluoxetine, 8 people, as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022): liking 31.2, 'high' 47.6 and 'stimulated' 40.1 percent lower (P<.05).

evidence.locator: Materials and Method › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Substances and Dosing, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Study Design, 1st paragraph (pp. 514-515)
evidence.extracted: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person study of 16 volunteers (12 men and 4 women, aged 21 to 39) in four counterbalanced conditions at least 14 days apart: placebo then placebo, citalopram then placebo, placebo then MDMA, citalopram then MDMA. Citalopram 40 mg (or saline) was infused over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) was taken by mouth, and ratings were made 120 minutes after MDMA. Six volunteers had tried recreational drugs before: two ecstasy, three a hallucinogen and one both. Editors' count: 3 of the 16 had tried ecstasy and 13 had not.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (pp. 515-516); Figure 1 (p. 516); Table 1 (p. 517)
evidence.extracted: MDMA raised all three altered-state scales against placebo (Rao R(3,12)=7.25, P<.005) and citalopram pretreatment lowered them (pretreatment by treatment: oceanic boundlessness F(1,15)=22.47, anxious ego dissolution F(1,15)=23.04, visionary restructuralization F(1,15)=12.80). Item clusters, percent of maximum, MDMA alone against citalopram then MDMA: positive basic mood 40.1 against 16.4, derealization 32.7 against 12.6, thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6, changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1; of the 15 item clusters, MDMA significantly raised 13, and citalopram significantly lowered 10 of those 13 but not frightening derealization, synesthesia or facilitated recollection. Editors' calculation from the printed means: the ten lowered clusters fell by about 55 to 80 percent.

evidence.locator: Results, last paragraph (p. 516); Figure 2 (p. 518); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 517) and the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (pp. 517-519)
evidence.extracted: On the mood scales, citalopram lowered the MDMA-induced rises in self-confidence (P<.04) and extroversion (P<.01) to the level of citalopram alone, and efficiency-activation under MDMA (P<.03; MDMA alone had not raised it above placebo); the fall in heightened mood did not reach significance (P=.06), and the rises in emotional excitability and sensitivity were not lowered at all. Citalopram alone lowered some scale scores against placebo, which the authors put down mostly to its side effects (fatigue, headache and nausea; nausea in 6 of 16).

evidence.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 515); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Another interesting finding' and the continuation of the paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (p. 519)
evidence.extracted: MDMA's subjective effect lasted a mean of 3 hours; after citalopram it was markedly reduced but lasted a mean of 5 hours, stated without a method, spread or test. No blood concentrations were taken. The authors put the lowering at about 60 percent and note that all received the same 40 mg whatever their weight, with no correlation between dose per kilogram and the size of the lowering; in a pilot, two people given 60 or 80 mg of citalopram had MDMA's effects blocked to a degree comparable with 40 mg.

evidence.locator: Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 955)
evidence.extracted: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 healthy men (mean age 24; all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; MDMA taken on at least 5 earlier occasions). Two 3-day sessions 15 days apart: paroxetine 20 mg a day or placebo on days 1 to 3, with MDMA 100 mg on day 3, 3 hours after that day's capsule. A 13th man was withdrawn after two paroxetine doses (insomnia, restlessness, anxiety) and never took MDMA.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 957); Results › Physiological Effects and Subjective Effects (p. 957); Figs. 1 to 3 (pp. 958-960)
evidence.extracted: Paroxetine lowered MDMA's effects: peak systolic pressure 12 mm Hg lower (Emax F=22.20, P=0.001), diastolic 5 mm Hg and heart rate 14 beats/min lower, pupil widening from 3.33 to 1.23 mm (F=70.35, P<0.001), temperature rise 0.3 C lower (P=0.041); ARCI euphoria scale (morphine-benzedrine group) peak 7.27 to 4; VESSPA anxiety 5.55 to 2.7, sociability 3.0 to 0.58, activity 5.91 to 1.21; visual-analogue 'stimulated', 'high', 'any effect', 'good effects' and 'liking' lower (all P=0.003 or less at peak). By Table 1 the diastolic area (P=0.613) and peak (P=0.213) and the heart-rate area (P=0.093) were not significant.

evidence.locator: Results › Plasma Concentrations of MDMA and HMMA (pp. 957-958); Table 2 (p. 961)
evidence.extracted: MDMA with paroxetine against placebo (n=12): peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and area to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L, both P<0.01; HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and area 1189.47 against 1923.32, half-life 13.10 against 9.54 hours (all P<0.01); MDMA half-life 8.34 against 7.88 hours. The paper's own text gives MDMA 22 (exposure) and 16% (peak) higher and HMMA 39 (exposure) and 49% (peak) lower. Editors' calculation from the printed means: HMMA exposure -38%.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 954); Table 1 and Results › Subjective Effects (p. 957); Results › Plasma Concentrations of MDMA and HMMA (pp. 957-958); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 959); Table 2 (p. 961); Discussion, final paragraph (pp. 961-962)
evidence.extracted: Ratings of bad effects, fear, and depression or sadness did not change significantly with paroxetine (nor with MDMA alone), and no hallucinations, psychotic symptoms or serious adverse events were seen. The authors write that the marked decrease in positive effects may lead to higher MDMA doses (they give people with depression who take SSRIs as an example) and so to potentially life-threatening toxicity; no extra MDMA was given in the study, so this is their inference. The abstract gives the rise in MDMA level as 30%, a figure taken in the Discussion from an earlier 7-man analysis; the trial's own figures are 16% (peak) and 22% (exposure to 21 hours).
evidence.quote: could lead users to take higher doses of MDMA

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 529)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that a single recreational dose of MDMA inhibits CYP2D6 rapidly and completely whereas several prescription doses of paroxetine are needed, that citalopram and paroxetine block the positive effects of MDMA, and that people taking an SSRI together with multiple doses of MDMA should know that the metabolism of both substances is compromised, with a possible increase in the risk of acute adverse effects already reported for poor metabolizers. The reference given for people taking SSRIs to change MDMA's effects is a rat study. No SSRI was given with MDMA in this study.

evidence.locator: Table 6, citalopram, fluoxetine and paroxetine rows; Results › MDMA › Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand summary. SSRIs lowered the rated and measured effects of MDMA. Citalopram (n=16): oceanic boundlessness about 60% lower, anxious ego dissolution about 63% lower (both p<.05), heart rate 12.3% lower at 60 minutes (p<.05), acute complaints about 46% lower (p<.01). Fluoxetine (n=8; Tancer and Johanson, 2006, not read): drug liking 31.2%, 'high' 47.6% and 'stimulated' 40.1% lower (all p<.05), heart rate 14.6% lower (p<.05). Paroxetine (n=12): liking about 62%, 'high' about 68% (p<.001), systolic pressure about 41% (p<.001) and heart rate about 42% lower (p<.05). The review summarizes this as 30 to about 80% lower subjective effects and, for physiological effects, about 6 to 14% lower (about 40 to 60% for paroxetine), and says that with fluoxetine and paroxetine, both strong CYP2D6 blockers, plasma MDMA was increased despite the attenuated effects (Table 6 gives no blood-level figure for fluoxetine). Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 1st paragraph; Table 5
evidence.extracted: No trial gave an SSRI or SNRI for months to people who take one as treatment: participants were young healthy adults given the medicine once or, rarely, for up to 14 days (the longest, escitalopram with psilocybin; for MDMA 3 to 11 days: paroxetine 3, fluoxetine 5 to 11), some by the less common intravenous route (citalopram). The authors write that no serious adverse effects of these combinations were observed in clinical trial settings and that, because the trials show smaller physiological effects, the odds of serotonin syndrome may be reduced at least with acute SSRI dosing (their inference, not tested); they also write that modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first.

risk_of_bias.note: Both studies are rated 'some concerns' on the RoB 2 crossover checklist (study cards): about 32 and 45 outcomes tested without correction, ratings that partial unblinding (side effects, obvious MDMA effects) could shift, no blood levels in the citalopram study, an unclear day-3 baseline in the paroxetine study. One level, not two, because the physiological and blood-level results do not depend on the blind.

inconsistency.note: Two groups in two countries agree in direction, as does the fluoxetine trial as summarized.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for healthy volunteers, one infusion or 3 days of an SSRI, and one fixed MDMA amount, and says that people on long-term treatment were not studied.

imprecision.note: 16 and 12 people; no confidence intervals for the differences in effect.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized or counterbalanced within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give low. Status replicated: two independent laboratories, using different SSRIs and different measures, show the same lowering of effects; the rise in MDMA level rests on the paroxetine study alone, because the citalopram study took no blood samples. The claim states what was measured and what was not (no study gave more MDMA, none treated people for long); it gives no advice on amounts. Anchors from the review are second-hand and marked as such.

verification.flag_note: Review-only statements are marked 'as summarized'. No reference record exists for Tancer and Johanson (2006, fluoxetine; DOI not captured). MAOI evidence (Vuori 2003, Silins 2007) is with reader 55 and is not used here. The paroxetine paper's abstract states a 30% rise in MDMA; the trial's own figures are 16% and 22%. The editor may join this claim with the claim on other antidepressants.

statement: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), three other antidepressants were each tested before MDMA in one laboratory trial of 16 healthy adults, and they did not all act alike. Duloxetine (which blocks the serotonin and norepinephrine transporters) lowered nearly every effect ('any drug effect' 61.7% lower, drug liking 57.7% lower, closeness to others 83.1% lower, heart rate 57.4% lower), and reboxetine (a norepinephrine transporter blocker) lowered 'any drug effect' by 20.7% and heart rate by 26.2% but did not significantly lower drug liking or 'good drug effect'; with both, the MDMA peak was higher (duloxetine +14.6%, reboxetine +17.8%). Bupropion (which blocks the norepinephrine and dopamine transporters), taken for 7 days, did not lower the ratings: the areas under the curves of 'any drug effect', 'good drug effect', 'high' and liking over 8 hours were 36.7 to 46.1% higher, and the review says it prolonged the effects, while heart rate was 38.7% lower; the MDMA peak was 14.3% higher, the 24-hour exposure 33.1% higher and the peak of the metabolite HMMA 75.9% lower. So where the ratings were lowered (duloxetine, reboxetine) the peak MDMA level was still 15 to 18% higher, and where they were not (bupropion) the exposure over 24 hours was 33.1% higher. The review's authors say it is plausible, without data, that bupropion with MDMA raises the risk of seizures, stimulant toxicity or serotonin syndrome, since both are stimulants that lower the seizure threshold and raise each other's blood levels. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that blunts the effect) and some take more; none of the trials gave more MDMA once the effects were blunted, so what happens then was not measured. The percentages are the review's, partly read off graphs; the three trials come from one laboratory group and were not read for this library; and none followed people on long-term treatment.
plain: Other antidepressants did not all act alike. In single lab trials of 16 healthy people each, duloxetine and reboxetine muted MDMA's effects, and the MDMA level in the blood was a little higher (about 15 to 18 percent at the peak). Bupropion did not mute the effects: ratings were as high or higher than without it, and the MDMA level was higher too (about 14 percent at the peak and 33 percent over the day), while heart rate rose less. Some people feel little from an amount and take more, for reasons such as a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, bodies that differ, or a medicine that mutes the effect. No trial tested what happens then. The review's authors guess, without data, that bupropion and MDMA together might raise the risk of seizures. These numbers come second-hand, from a 2022 review.
population: Healthy adult volunteers in three single laboratory trials of 16 people each, as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022)
exposure: An antidepressant taken before MDMA (study conditions as listed in the review: duloxetine or reboxetine as a single dose or two doses within a day; bupropion for several days; MDMA by mouth)
comparator: The same people given a dummy treatment before MDMA
outcome: Rated effects of MDMA, heart rate, blood pressure, catecholamines, and blood concentrations of MDMA and its metabolite HMMA
magnitude: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), changes against placebo before MDMA: duloxetine 'any drug effect' -61.7%, liking -57.7%, closeness -83.1%, heart rate -57.4% (all p<.001), MDMA peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%, HMMA peak -40.5%; reboxetine 'any drug effect' -20.7% (p<.01), heart rate -26.2% (p<.05), liking -10.0% and good drug effect -15.2% (not significant), MDMA peak +17.8%, exposure to 24 hours +8.1% (p<.05); bupropion area under the curve of ratings over 8 hours +34.0 to +46.1% (p<.05), peak ratings +5.6 to +17.1% (not marked significant), heart rate -38.7% (p<.001), MDMA peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak -75.9%.

evidence.locator: Table 6, duloxetine and reboxetine rows; Results › MDMA › Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Reboxetine and MDMA
evidence.extracted: Duloxetine (n=16) lowered nearly every effect of MDMA: 'any drug effect' 61.7%, drug liking 57.7% and closeness to others 83.1% (all p<.001), heart rate 57.4% and systolic pressure 63.5% (p<.001), and acute complaints 122.5% (p<.01; above 100% because, as the review says, complaints with duloxetine and MDMA were below the pre-drug baseline). Reboxetine (n=16) lowered 'any drug effect' by 20.7% (p<.01), closeness by 38.6% (p<.05), heart rate by 26.2% (p<.05) and systolic pressure by 46.5% (p<.001), but drug liking (-10.0%) and good drug effect (-15.2%) did not change significantly. Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

evidence.locator: Table 6, pharmacokinetic rows (Cmax, AUC) for each medicine; Results › MDMA, the paragraphs on bupropion, serotonin reuptake inhibitors, duloxetine and reboxetine
evidence.extracted: MDMA blood levels were higher with these medicines; with duloxetine and reboxetine the effects were lower at the same time, whereas with bupropion the rated effects were not lower (heart rate was). Duloxetine: peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%, HMMA peak 40.5% lower. Reboxetine: peak +17.8%, exposure to 24 hours +8.1% (p<.05). Bupropion: peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak 75.9% lower. For comparison, carvedilol (+4.7%), clonidine (-2.9%), doxazosin (-1.6%) and methylphenidate (-3.5%) changed the peak by 5% or less, and memantine's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower. Table 6 has no blood-level row for citalopram or fluoxetine.

evidence.locator: Table 6, bupropion rows (Physiological; Circulating catecholamines; Subjective); Results › MDMA › Bupropion and MDMA; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Bupropion XR (n=16; taken for 7 days, with the amount stepped up, as listed in Table 5) did not blunt the rated effects: peak ratings of any drug effect, good effect, 'high', liking and 'stimulated' were 5.6 to 17.1% higher (no significance marks), and the areas under the rating curves over 8 hours were 36.7 to 46.1% higher for any drug effect, good effect, 'high' and liking (p<.05) and 34.0% higher for 'stimulated' (no mark), while heart rate was 38.7% lower (p<.001) and norepinephrine 65.6% lower (p<.05). The Results say bupropion significantly prolonged the positive mood effects of MDMA, and the Discussion that it prolonged the subjective effects and heightened the positive mood effects, and calls it plausible, without data, that bupropion with MDMA raises the risk of seizures, stimulant toxicity or serotonin syndrome because both are stimulants that can lower the seizure threshold and raise each other's blood levels. Its surveillance paragraph gives bupropion the highest unadjusted odds ratio of death of any antidepressant (2.82; see the claim on reports).

evidence.locator: Methods > Percent change calculation; Table 5; Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The 13 MDMA trials in Table 5 had 8 to 16 healthy adults each, nearly all double-blind counterbalanced crossovers; the medicine was given as a single dose or two doses within a day in 9 of the 13 and for 3 to 11 days in the other 4 (doxazosin, paroxetine, bupropion, fluoxetine). The Discussion says the trials came primarily from one laboratory group, that participants were young healthy adults, and that the studies are limited in their extrapolation to settings where medicines are taken daily for months or years. The percentage changes are the review's own calculation, and the review did not appraise the risk of bias of any included study.

risk_of_bias.note: The primary trials were not read for this library; the review that reports them appraised none of them and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (study card); some values were read off graphs.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: each medicine rests on one trial.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: numbers come through a review, from healthy volunteers given the medicine for hours to days.

imprecision.note: 16 people per medicine; the review gives no intervals.

grade.reasoning: The primary trials are double-blind, counterbalanced crossovers and start high (METHODS 6.3); the claim reaches them only through a systematic review that did not appraise them, so risk of bias -1 (not appraisable) and indirectness -1 (second-hand) are applied, with imprecision -1 for 16 people each. Certainty very low. Status single-study: each medicine was tested once, three trials from one laboratory group. Stays at draft because it rests only on the review (METHODS 12, brief). The claim says what was measured, never what to do.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Sarparast et al. (2022) as summarized, until the primary trials are read: duloxetine (Hysek et al., 2012, doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0036476), reboxetine (Hysek et al., 2011, doi 10.1038/clpt.2011.78) and bupropion (Schmid et al., 2015, doi 10.1124/jpet.114.222356) have no reference records. The editor may join this claim with the claim on SSRIs.

statement: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), reports from people who took ecstasy together with prescribed medicines point to more harm with some combinations, but they cannot show cause. In 946 reports of recreational ecstasy use to the US adverse event reporting system between 2000 and 2020 (mean age 28; 70.1% men), reports that also named an antidepressant had higher odds of a fatal outcome than reports that did not (adjusted odds ratio 1.62, against 8.17 for muscle relaxants, 7.13 for anesthetics, 3.05 for amphetamines and stimulants, 2.25 for benzodiazepines, 2.05 for opioids and 2.03 for alcohol); without adjustment the odds ratios were 2.82 for bupropion, 2.36 for sertraline, 1.97 for venlafaxine, 1.92 for citalopram and 1.86 for olanzapine, all 18 reports that named metoclopramide ended in death, and no death was reported with risperidone or lithium (Cohen et al., 2021). In a survey of 216 adults who had taken ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug in the previous 6 months, 76% of those who combined it with an antidepressant still felt euphoria, and they reported higher rates of muscle rigidity, involuntary eye movements, dizziness, headache and heavy sweating, but antidepressants were not separated by class and included monoamine-oxidase inhibitors (Copeland et al., 2006). The review gives no intervals, no numbers of deaths and no denominators; voluntary reports cannot show how many people took each combination, what else they took, or how much; and neither study was read for this library. The review's authors suggest, without data, that effects blunted by an SSRI may lead some people to take more, which could explain the higher odds.
plain: Besides lab studies, there are reports. In a US database of voluntary reports about ecstasy (946 reports), the ones that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often than those that did not. In a survey of 216 adults, people who mixed ecstasy with an antidepressant still felt euphoria, and reported more sweating, headache, dizziness and muscle stiffness. Reports cannot show cause: nobody knows how many people took each mix, what else they took, or how much. The review's authors guess that people who feel little may take more, but no data show it. Both studies come second-hand, from a 2022 review.
population: People who took ecstasy together with prescribed medicines: 946 reports to a US adverse event reporting system (2000 to 2020; mean age 28; 70.1% men) and 216 adults in a cross-sectional survey (mean age 26; 63% men; mean 11 days of ecstasy use in 6 months), as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022)
exposure: Taking ecstasy together with an antidepressant, or with another named prescribed medicine, as reported (no doses or timing given)
comparator: Reports or respondents involving ecstasy without that medicine
outcome: A fatal outcome in a report (odds ratios); euphoria and physical symptoms in a survey
magnitude: Cohen et al. (2021), as summarized: fatal outcome, adjusted odds ratio with a drug class also named: antidepressants 1.62, benzodiazepines 2.25, opioids 2.05, ethanol 2.03, amphetamines and stimulants 3.05, anesthetics 7.13, muscle relaxants 8.17; unadjusted odds ratios: bupropion 2.82, sertraline 2.36, venlafaxine 1.97, citalopram 1.92, olanzapine 1.86; metoclopramide 18 of 18 reports fatal; risperidone and lithium no deaths. No intervals, deaths or denominators given. Copeland et al. (2006), as summarized: among people combining ecstasy with antidepressants, 76% still felt euphoria; higher rates of muscle rigidity, nystagmus, dizziness, headache and heavy sweating (percentages in the review are paired without labels).

evidence.locator: Results › Epidemiologic studies, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Surveillance study (Cohen et al., 2021, as summarized here): 946 unique reports of recreational ecstasy use in the US adverse-event database, 2000-2020 (mean age 28, 70.1% men). Adjusted odds ratios of a fatal outcome when a drug class was also reported: MDMA metabolites or analogs 8.71, muscle relaxants 8.17, anesthetics 7.13, amphetamines and stimulants 3.05, benzodiazepines 2.25, opioids 2.05, ethanol 2.03, antidepressants 1.62. Unadjusted odds ratios for single psychiatric medicines: bupropion 2.82, sertraline 2.36, venlafaxine 1.97, citalopram 1.92, olanzapine 1.86; all 18 reports with metoclopramide ended in death; risperidone and lithium odds ratios could not be calculated because there were no deaths. No intervals, numbers of deaths or denominators are given.

evidence.locator: Results › Epidemiologic studies, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Survey (Copeland et al., 2006, as summarized here): 216 adults who took ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug in the past 6 months (mean age 26, 63% men, mean 11 days of ecstasy use in 6 months). Of those who took antidepressants with ecstasy, 76% still felt euphoria, but rates of muscle rigidity (0% vs 45%), nystagmus (0% vs 33%), dizziness (19% vs 42%), headache (21% vs 62%) and heavy sweating (28% vs 53%) were higher; antidepressants were not analysed by class and included MAOIs. Group sizes and the order of the paired percentages are not stated.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Trends in case studies, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review's authors write that the blunted subjective effects of SSRIs may lead people to take escalating doses and so explain the higher odds of death in the surveillance data, and that benzodiazepines were associated with a higher adjusted odds ratio of death than antidepressants, opioids or alcohol; no data on amounts taken are given. The review found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA, and notes that the surveillance study concerns unregulated ecstasy use in non-clinical settings.
evidence.quote: may drive individuals to take escalating drug doses to achieve effects

risk_of_bias.note: Voluntary adverse-event reports and a retrospective survey; no denominators, no way to know what else was taken; individual-medicine odds ratios are unadjusted.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: the two studies measure different outcomes.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: neither study was read; the review gives no intervals, counts or class sizes, and the paired survey percentages are unlabelled.

imprecision.note: No intervals; small numbers behind several odds ratios cannot be seen.

grade.reasoning: Observational reports start low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level, and the result is very low. Status single-study: each outcome rests on one study. Stays at draft because it rests only on the review as summarized (METHODS 12, brief). The claim is worded as an association in reports and states that cause, amounts and denominators are unknown; it gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Sarparast et al. (2022) as summarized. No reference records exist for Cohen et al. (2021, Sci Rep, doi 10.1038/s41598-021-85389-x) or Copeland et al. (2006, Addict Behav, doi 10.1016/j.addbeh.2005.05.025); build them, read them, and replace these second-hand anchors. Reader 56's claim on deaths involving MDMA and medicines (coroners' cases) covers related ground; the editor may join them.

statement: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), a few other medicines were each given before MDMA to 14 to 16 healthy adults in single controlled trials. Haloperidol (an antipsychotic, 1.4 mg intravenously; 14 people) did not change the heart-rate, blood-pressure or temperature responses to MDMA but made the state more dysphoric (well-being about 31% lower, state anxiety about 47% higher at 75 minutes, oceanic boundlessness about 59% lower). Methylphenidate (a stimulant; 16 people) delayed MDMA's time to peak by 45.8% without changing its peak (-3.5%) or exposure (+3.2%), raised heart rate by 15.1%, the rate-pressure product by 16.8%, acute complaints by 86.5% and later complaints by 191.9%, and added no psychoactive effect. Carvedilol (a heart and blood-pressure medicine) cut the rise in heart rate by 79.0%, in systolic pressure by 76.9% and in temperature by 42.0% with little change in ratings (any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%) while epinephrine and norepinephrine rose; pindolol, another heart medicine, lowered the peak heart rate by about 17.6% and the overall altered-state score by about 27%; clonidine and doxazosin lowered blood pressure (doxazosin: mean arterial pressure 6.8% lower, with heart rate 9.6% higher); memantine did not change MDMA's memory impairment or mood. The review's table of controlled trials has no entry for MAOIs, mood stabilizers (which include lithium) or anxiolytics with MDMA, and its text says it found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, as with the delayed peak under methylphenidate; tolerance; a weaker or different product; bodies that differ; a medicine that blunts the effect) and some take more; none of the trials gave more MDMA once the effects were blunted or delayed, so what happens then was not measured. The percentages are the review's, partly read off graphs; the trials were not read for this library; modern MDMA-therapy trials excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first; and none of the trials followed people on long-term treatment.
plain: The controlled studies on other psychiatric medicines are few, small (14 to 16 healthy people each) and second-hand, from a 2022 review. Haloperidol, an antipsychotic, left heart rate and blood pressure alone but made people feel worse: less well-being and more anxiety. Methylphenidate, a stimulant, delayed MDMA's peak by about 46 percent, raised heart rate and brought more complaints, with no stronger drug effect. Carvedilol, a heart medicine, cut the rises in heart rate and temperature while ratings stayed about the same. The review lists no controlled study of MAOIs, lithium or benzodiazepines with MDMA. A slow start (methylphenidate delayed the peak) or a medicine that mutes the effect can leave a person feeling little, and some people then take more. None of these trials tested what happens then.
population: Healthy adult volunteers in single laboratory trials of 14 to 16 people each, as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022)
exposure: A psychiatric or cardiovascular medicine taken before MDMA (study conditions as listed in the review: haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously; methylphenidate; carvedilol, clonidine, doxazosin, pindolol; memantine 20 mg; MDMA by mouth)
comparator: The same people given a dummy treatment before MDMA
outcome: Rated mood and drug effects, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, complaints, catecholamines and MDMA blood concentrations
magnitude: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), changes against placebo before MDMA: haloperidol well-being -31% (p<.05), state anxiety +47% at 75 minutes (p<.01), oceanic boundlessness -59% (p<.05), no change in heart rate, blood pressure or temperature; methylphenidate time to peak +45.8% (p<.05), peak -3.5%, exposure +3.2%, heart rate +15.1% and rate-pressure product +16.8% (both p<.001), epinephrine +54.6% (p<.01), acute complaints +86.5% (p<.01), subacute complaints +191.9% (p<.001), any drug effect -1.4%; carvedilol heart-rate rise -79.0%, systolic -76.9% (both p<.001), diastolic -39.2%, temperature -42.0% (p<.05), any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%; pindolol peak heart rate about -17.6% (p<.001), global altered-state score about -26.7% and oceanic boundlessness about -31.9% (both p<.01); clonidine mean arterial pressure -4.5% by the area measure (p<.05); doxazosin mean arterial pressure -6.8% and heart rate +9.6% (p<.05); memantine no effect on memory impairment or mood.

evidence.locator: Table 6, haloperidol rows; Results › MDMA › Antipsychotics and MDMA
evidence.extracted: Haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously (n=14) did not change cardiovascular or thermogenic responses to MDMA or the startle response, according to the review, but made the state dysphoric: well-being about 31% lower (p<.05), state anxiety about 47% higher at 75 minutes (p<.01), oceanic boundlessness about 59% lower (p<.05). Table 6 lists heart rate 13.7%, systolic pressure 5.0%, diastolic pressure 2.3% and temperature 1.4% higher at 120 minutes, with no significance marks. Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.

evidence.locator: Table 6, methylphenidate rows; Results › MDMA › Psychostimulants and MDMA; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 4th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Methylphenidate (n=16) delayed MDMA's time to peak by 45.8% (p<.05) without changing its peak (-3.5%) or exposure (+3.2%), raised heart rate 15.1% and the rate-pressure product 16.8% (both p<.001) and epinephrine 54.6% (p<.01), and raised acute and subacute complaints by 86.5% (p<.01) and 191.9% (p<.001), without adding psychoactive effects (any drug effect -1.4%).

evidence.locator: Table 6, adrenergic-agent rows (carvedilol, pindolol, clonidine, doxazosin); Results › MDMA › Adrenergic agents and MDMA, 2nd to 5th paragraphs; Discussion › Pharmacodynamic interactions-MDMA, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Adrenergic agents (n=16 each): carvedilol lowered the heart-rate rise 79.0%, systolic 76.9% (both p<.001), diastolic 39.2% and temperature 42.0% (p<.05), as changes from baseline, with little change in ratings (any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%) while epinephrine (+204.3%) and norepinephrine (+789.7%) rose (both p<.001); pindolol (men) lowered peak heart rate by about 17.6% (p<.001), the global altered-state score by about 26.7% and oceanic boundlessness by about 31.9% (both p<.01) and 'dreaminess' by about 95% (p<.05), with no effect on mean arterial pressure or temperature; clonidine lowered mean arterial pressure by 4.5% by the area measure (p<.05; 27.2% at the peak, not marked significant) and norepinephrine; doxazosin lowered mean arterial pressure 6.8% at the peak (p<.05) but raised heart rate 9.6% (p<.05), and lowered the area of heightened-mood ratings (marked significant). Table 6 gives carvedilol's vital signs as changes from baseline and pindolol's and doxazosin's as raw peaks; values with a tilde were read off graphs. The Discussion calls the effect of clonidine and doxazosin on physiology minimal.

evidence.locator: Table 6, memantine rows; Results › MDMA › Memantine and MDMA
evidence.extracted: Memantine 20 mg (n=15) had no effect on MDMA-induced acute memory impairment or on mood, per the review. Table 6 lists, without significance marks, changes of 0.4 to 13.6% on memory tasks and 0.7 to 41.1% on mood scales, and a 'subjective high' rating 20.9% and 70.3% higher at 90 and 120 minutes; MDMA's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower.

evidence.locator: Table 4; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Table 4, which lists the controlled trials of psychiatric medicines by class, has no entry in its MDMA column for MAOIs, mood stabilizers (the class that includes lithium) or anxiolytics. The review says it found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA. Modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first; the review notes that tapering carries its own risks of relapse and discontinuation symptoms. Online communities were described as encouraging olanzapine as a way to end a distressing psychedelic experience; the review says it is unclear whether an atypical antipsychotic would be an appropriate approach.

risk_of_bias.note: The primary trials were not read for this library; the review that reports them appraised none of them and is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (study card); some values were read off graphs.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: each medicine rests on one trial.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: numbers come through a review, from healthy volunteers given one dose of the medicine, some by the intravenous route.

imprecision.note: 14 to 16 people per medicine; the review gives no intervals.

grade.reasoning: The primary trials are double-blind, counterbalanced crossovers and start high (METHODS 6.3); the claim reaches them only through a systematic review that did not appraise them, so risk of bias -1 and indirectness -1 are applied, with imprecision -1 for 14 to 16 people each. Certainty very low. Status single-study: each medicine was tested once. Stays at draft because it rests only on the review (METHODS 12, brief). The claim says what was measured and what was not found, never what to do.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Sarparast et al. (2022) as summarized, until the primary trials are read. The reference records for these trials do not exist. Benzodiazepines, lithium and MAOIs: no controlled study was found by the review; MAOI case reports and deaths are with reader 55; the surveillance odds ratios for olanzapine, risperidone, lithium and benzodiazepines are in the claim on reports.
