statement: In healthy volunteers, whether the liver enzyme CYP2D6 works changed MDMA's blood level only a little, and medicines that block the enzyme raised it by a similar small amount; the authors link this to MDMA itself switching the enzyme off, which a probe-drug study found lasting for days. In a pooled analysis of eight double-blind, placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 139 people, the 7 with no working CYP2D6 (poor metabolizers, all given the higher dose) had a peak MDMA level 15% higher than the 111 with normal function (mean ratio 1.15), a peak of the active metabolite MDA 50% higher and a peak of the inactive metabolite HMMA 50 to 70% lower; the MDMA difference was confined to the first 3 hours, and their effects came sooner but were not larger at the maximum (Schmid et al., 2016). In 15 men with normal CYP2D6 given a test drug (dextromethorphan) before and after one dose of MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, the test drug's blood exposure rose roughly 9-fold (editors' calculation from the printed means; the authors say approximately 10-fold), the urinary ratio of the test drug to its product rose from 0.006 to 0.43, 67% (10 of the 15 men, by the editors' count) crossed the cut-off for poor metabolizers, and the ratio had not fully recovered after 10 days (recovery half-life 47 hours on one fit, 103 hours on another); the first test dose came 4 hours after MDMA and there was no placebo session, so, in the editors' reading, early competition for the enzyme cannot be told from its inactivation (O'Mathúna et al., 2008). In 12 men, paroxetine, which blocks CYP2D6 as well as the serotonin transporter, raised the MDMA peak by 16% and the exposure by 22% and lowered HMMA by 39 to 49% (Farré et al., 2007). As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), duloxetine, reboxetine and bupropion raised the MDMA peak by 14 to 18%, and ritonavir, a strong enzyme blocker, was named as having caused significant toxicity with MDMA (reports not read here); a 2012 narrative review by authors of the probe-drug and paroxetine studies says that the genotype and CYP2D6-blocking medicines may matter less for acute toxicity than once thought (de la Torre et al., 2012). Bodies that differ are one reason people can feel little from an amount and take more, alongside a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product and a medicine that blunts the effect; here the difference between bodies was small and early, and the effects came sooner, not stronger. What happens when people then take more was not tested, but the authors of the probe-drug study infer that a second dose taken while the enzyme is still switched off would reach higher concentrations (O'Mathúna et al., 2008). Only 7 people lacked CYP2D6 function, the probe-drug study included men only, and none of these studies gave a second dose of MDMA.
plain: The liver enzyme CYP2D6 helps clear MDMA, and bodies differ in how well it works. In a pooled lab analysis, the 7 people with no working CYP2D6 had only about 15 percent more MDMA in the blood at the peak, in the first 3 hours, and felt effects sooner, not stronger. The authors link this to MDMA switching the enzyme off itself: in 15 men a single MDMA dose pushed 10 of them into the range of people with no working enzyme, and it had not fully recovered after 10 days. Medicines that block the enzyme, such as paroxetine, raised MDMA by about 15 to 20 percent at the peak. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; bodies that differ are one reason, next to a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, or a medicine that mutes the effect. These small studies in healthy volunteers did not test that: none gave a second dose of MDMA. The authors of one study think that a second dose taken while the enzyme is still switched off would reach higher blood levels.
population: Healthy adult volunteers in controlled laboratory studies: 139 people (70 men, 69 women; 7 poor, 19 intermediate and 113 extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers) pooled from 8 studies; 15 men who were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers at screening; and 12 men, all extensive metabolizers
exposure: No working CYP2D6 (poor-metabolizer genotype); MDMA itself (a single dose, followed by a CYP2D6 probe drug); or a CYP2D6-blocking medicine (paroxetine for 3 days) (study conditions: MDMA 1.5 mg/kg or 100 mg; doses in the pooled analysis are in a supplement that was not read)
comparator: People with normal CYP2D6 function; the same men before MDMA (a control session with the probe drug alone, always first, no placebo MDMA); the same men after placebo instead of paroxetine
outcome: Peak and exposure of MDMA and its metabolites MDA and HMMA; blood levels of a CYP2D6 probe drug and the urinary probe-drug to metabolite ratio as measures of CYP2D6 activity, and time to recovery of that ratio; early effects
magnitude: Pooled genotype comparison (Schmid et al., 2016): peak MDMA 15% higher in 7 poor metabolizers (mean ratio 1.15 against 111 extensive; peak F(2,136)=4.19, P=0.02; area to 6 hours F(2,136)=5.25, P<0.01), peak MDA +50% (P<0.01), peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower (P=0.03), early systolic pressure rise and liking higher at 0.6 hours, maximal effects not different. Probe drug (O'Mathúna et al., 2008, n=15): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL and area 15.7 to 149.1; dextrorphan peak 464.6 to 31.9; urinary ratio 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848), 67% above the 0.3 cut-off; recovery half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8) one-phase, 103.0 hours (SD 70.3) two-phase; not fully recovered at 10 days. Paroxetine (Farré et al., 2007, n=12): MDMA peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and exposure to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L (both P<0.01); HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and exposure 1189.47 against 1923.32 (both P<0.01). As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022): duloxetine peak +14.6%, reboxetine +17.8%, bupropion +14.3% with exposure to 24 hours +33.1%.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, limitations paragraph
evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of eight double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies in 139 healthy people (70 men, 69 women): 7 CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, 19 intermediate and 113 extensive metabolizers (111 extensive in one Discussion comparison). Doses and study details are in a supplement that was not read; all seven poor metabolizers were in the high-dose group, and the authors state that an analysis of the high-dose group alone gave similar results (no figures are given in the text).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph
evidence.extracted: Genotype altered MDMA levels only in the first 3 hours (absorption and distribution), not after: genotype main effect on peak MDMA F(2,136)=4.19, P=0.02, with higher peaks in poor than extensive metabolizers (P=0.049); area under the curve to 6 hours F(2,136)=5.25, P<0.01 (poor higher than extensive, P<0.01). Peak MDMA was 15% higher in poor metabolizers (abstract) and the mean ratio was 1.15 (7 poor against 111 extensive).

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph
evidence.extracted: The active metabolite MDA was higher and the inactive metabolite HMMA lower in poor metabolizers: peak MDA +50% (F(2,136)=8.82, P<0.01; area F=9.09, P<0.001); peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower (F(2,73)=3.50, P=0.03; area F=5.22, P<0.01), HMMA exposure to 6 hours about a quarter (24%) of extensive metabolizers'; MDMA to HMMA ratios higher in poor metabolizers (F(2,73)=10.98 and 10.08, P<0.001). The HMMA tests rest on fewer people than the MDMA and MDA tests: N=76 in the HMMA correlation and F tests with 73 error degrees of freedom, against 136 for MDMA and MDA.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Main text, 4th paragraph; Fig. 2 legend; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph
evidence.extracted: Poor metabolizers had faster early effects but not larger ones: systolic pressure rise greater than in intermediate (P=0.02) and extensive (P=0.01) metabolizers at 0.6 h (F(2,135)=3.50, P=0.03), 'any drug effect' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.05) and 'drug liking' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.001) and 1 h (P<0.01); maximal effects did not differ and there was no genotype effect on heart rate or temperature. The authors read the small, short-lived difference as the result of MDMA inhibiting CYP2D6 itself, turning all people into functional poor metabolizers within about 1 hour; they cite a model estimating a rise of only 36% in peak MDMA with no CYP2D6 function, and say medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 raised peak MDMA by 15 to 20% and exposure by 10 to 30%. They also note that poor metabolizers were not over-represented among ecstasy deaths (their reference 11), that severe or fatal toxicity with high MDMA exposure occurred with ritonavir, which blocks CYP2D6, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 (more than one enzyme system), and suggest that other enzymes and CYP3A4 inhibition may matter more than CYP2D6 genetics; no toxicity outcome was measured in the analysis.

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 525); Materials and Methods › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 526); Drugs, 1st paragraph (p. 526); Study Design, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 526-527)
evidence.extracted: Fifteen healthy men (mean age 26, range 19 to 33; on average 26 previous MDMA experiences) who were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers at screening, recruited by word of mouth and paid. Open, fixed-order design: session 1 (control, dextromethorphan 30 mg with caffeine 100 mg), then at least 3 days later session 2 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, 75 to 100 mg, with caffeine and dextromethorphan 30 mg at 4 hours and later); the dextromethorphan schedule was 4, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 168 hours in the first 3 men and 4, 24, 72, 96, 168 and 240 hours in the other 12, because the ratio had not recovered by 168 hours; results pooled. No placebo MDMA session.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 528)
evidence.extracted: Plasma probe drug after MDMA against the control session (Table 1, n=15): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL (SDs 3.6 and 18.5) and area over 8 hours 15.7 to 149.1; dextrorphan peak 464.6 to 31.9 and area 1877.1 to 179.1; 3-hydroxymorphinan peak 164.1 to 16.6 and area 764.2 to 97.5 (all P<0.05); 3-methoxymorphinan not significantly changed. The authors say the dextromethorphan peak and area increased approximately 10-fold. MDMA peak 194.3 ng/mL (SD 30.9) at 2.0 hours (SD 1.0). Editors' calculation from the printed means: 8.5-fold for the peak and 9.5-fold for the area.

evidence.locator: Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
evidence.extracted: The urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio rose from 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848), which the authors call almost 100-fold; 67% of the men had a value above 0.3, the cut-off for assigning the poor-metabolizer phenotype, after MDMA; no correlation of the ratio with urine pH (r=0.049) or creatinine (r=0.214). Recovery fitted one exponential curve: rate constant 0.016 (SD 0.005) per hour, recovery half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8), r2=0.791. Editors' calculation: the ratio of the printed means is 71-fold, and 67% of 15 men is 10 men.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (pp. 528-529); 3rd paragraph (p. 529)
evidence.extracted: The ratio had not recovered fully to its basal level at 10 days; the half-life corrected for MDMA's own residence time is 37.4 hours (SD 11.6), and the authors think it underestimates recovery because activity had not recovered even at 10 days; a two-phase fit gives 103.0 hours (SD 70.3), corrected 93.7 (SD 70.4), though variability and few time points question the biphasic model. Editors' reading: the first probe dose after MDMA was given 4 hours after it, when MDMA was near its peak, so competition for the enzyme cannot be separated from its inactivation in the early hours.

evidence.locator: Results › Plasma Concentrations of MDMA and HMMA (pp. 957-958); Table 2 (p. 961)
evidence.extracted: MDMA with paroxetine, an inhibitor of CYP2D6 as well as of the serotonin transporter, against placebo (n=12): peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L and area to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L, both P<0.01; HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 and area 1189.47 against 1923.32, half-life 13.10 against 9.54 hours (all P<0.01). The paper's own text gives MDMA 22 (exposure) and 16% (peak) higher and HMMA 39 (exposure) and 49% (peak) lower. Editors' calculation from the printed means: HMMA exposure -38%.

evidence.locator: Table 6, pharmacokinetic rows (Cmax, AUC) for each medicine; Results › MDMA, the paragraphs on bupropion, serotonin reuptake inhibitors, duloxetine and reboxetine; Discussion › Pharmacokinetic interactions-MDMA, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand summary. Duloxetine: peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%; reboxetine: peak +17.8%; bupropion: peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak 75.9% lower; carvedilol, clonidine, doxazosin and methylphenidate changed the peak by 5% or less (memantine's level at 1 hour was 1.0% lower). The Discussion names the strong enzyme blocker ritonavir as having caused significant toxicity with MDMA (Papaseit et al., 2012, not read).

evidence.locator: Introduction > MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Discussion > Pharmacogenetics and MDMA, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Second-hand summary of Schmid et al. (2016): people with only non-functional alleles (*3, *4, *5) had a peak MDMA level 19% higher and early exposure (to 6 hours) 25% higher than people with only *1 and *2 alleles, with faster onset and higher blood pressure; the review's 19% and 25% are for a narrower genotype comparison than the paper's headline 15% and are not reconciled with it (the paper's supplement was not read). Pooled trial data are said to show that effects follow plasma concentration and that higher CYP2D6 activity scores predict lower MDMA levels (Studerus et al., 2021, not read).

evidence.locator: MDMA CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibition and the phenocopying phenomenon, paragraph 1; Abstract; Concluding remarks, 2nd and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Narrative review, second-hand. It says MDMA inactivates most liver CYP2D6 within about 2 hours and activity returns to its starting level only after at least 10 days (citing studies from 2008 and 2011), that phenocopying (the enzyme behaving as in a poor metabolizer whatever the genotype) was seen in 67% of male subjects in one study and 100% of females in another, and that the polymorphism and co-administered CYP2D6 inhibitors may have less impact on the risk of acute toxicity than previously thought. The 67% is 10 of 15 men in the 2008 study read for this library, whose first probe dose was at 4 hours and whose ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days; the 100% for women (2011) was not read. The Concluding remarks also say carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects, which the review's body does not support with numbers.

risk_of_bias.note: The genotype comparison is observational and pooled across eight studies with unequal doses (ROBINS-E, some concerns; supplement not read); the probe-drug study is open, fixed-order and without a placebo MDMA session (RoB 2, high); the paroxetine trial is randomized (some concerns).

inconsistency.note: The studies point the same way; the review's 19% and 25% for a narrower genotype comparison differ from the paper's 15% headline.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for healthy volunteers and for single doses; it says no second dose was given.

imprecision.note: Seven poor metabolizers, 15 men and 12 men; no confidence intervals for the main contrasts.

grade.reasoning: The central contrasts (genotype group, before and after one dose) are not randomized comparisons, so the claim starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status replicated: three independent lines (a pooled genotype analysis, a probe-drug study and CYP2D6-blocking medicines in a randomized trial and, as summarized, in others) agree that loss or blocking of CYP2D6 raises early MDMA levels by about 15 to 20 percent. The claim describes what was measured; it draws no conclusion about risk at any amount.

verification.flag_note: Carries the Mixing-page pair because it covers medicines that block CYP2D6; the editor may drop the pair if the claim should stay under pharmacology only. The narrative review (de la Torre et al., 2012) is a qualifying anchor only. Missing: Papaseit et al. (2012, ritonavir), Studerus et al. (2021) and the Yubero-Lahoz (2011) women's study have no reference records and were not read; the Schmid paper's supplement was not read. The reference record for O'Mathuna et al. (2008) gives pages 523-529 but the PDF prints 525-531; anchors here cite the PDF's printed pages.

statement: In eight men given MDMA 75 mg and 125 mg on separate days in a randomized, double-blind crossover, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak blood level 1.81 times higher (236.4 against 130.9 ug/L) and a 24-hour exposure 1.97 times higher (2623.7 against 1331.5 ug x h/L), so blood levels rose more than the dose did (de la Torre et al., 2000; ratios from the printed means). Clearance outside the kidneys fell from 74.0 to 38.1 L/h while clearance by the kidneys did not change, and across the five dose levels from 50 to 150 mg, with different men at 50, 100 and 150 mg, the same eight men at 75 and 125 mg, and only two men at each of the lowest and highest, the 24-hour exposure ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug x h/L, so differences between men are mixed in with the dose. The authors give two explanations, saturation of MDMA's breakdown (which they say cannot be excluded) and MDMA's blocking of the enzyme CYP2D6 that breaks it down, and state that the observations were retrospective and the studies were not designed to detect this. The authors' abstract goes further, concluding that this holds for the whole population whatever the CYP2D6 genotype and that small increases in the amount taken give disproportionate rises in blood level, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity; the dose comparison was made in men with normal CYP2D6 only and no toxicity outcome was measured. In a later study of 15 men, one dose of MDMA switched CYP2D6 off, and the enzyme's activity had not fully recovered after 10 days (O'Mathúna et al., 2008); this fits the second explanation, as does the small difference between people with and without a working enzyme (Schmid et al., 2016). The authors of the 2008 study infer, without giving a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. People can feel little from an amount for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts the effect, bodies that differ) and some take more. None of these studies tested people who took more because they felt little: the amounts were fixed and given to healthy men in a laboratory, and what they show is that a larger single amount gave a larger rise in blood level than the amount itself. Second doses taken 2 or 24 hours after a first are covered in the library's separate claim on acute tolerance.
plain: A bigger amount of MDMA gave more in the blood than the extra amount alone would explain. In 8 men, a dose 1.67 times larger gave a peak level 1.8 times higher and about twice the total exposure over the day. MDMA seems to switch off the liver enzyme that clears it, so more MDMA is cleared more slowly (the authors' explanation, not proven). The authors also say that small increases in the amount could raise blood levels out of proportion and so make acute toxicity more likely; the study did not measure toxicity. Some people feel little from an amount and take more, for reasons such as a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that mutes the effect, or bodies that differ. These studies did not test that: they gave fixed amounts to healthy men in a lab. What they show is that a larger amount gave a larger rise than the amount itself. Second doses are covered in the answer on tolerance.
population: Healthy adult men with earlier MDMA experience in laboratory studies: 14 men (8 in a randomized crossover at 75 and 125 mg; 6 in a pilot at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and, for the mechanism, 15 men in a probe-drug study
exposure: A larger single dose of MDMA (study conditions: 75 mg and 125 mg, and 50, 100 and 150 mg in the pilot, by mouth)
comparator: The same eight men at the smaller dose, with dose-normalized exposure as the yardstick
outcome: Peak and 24-hour exposure of MDMA in plasma, dose-normalized exposure, kidney and non-kidney clearance, and recovery of urinary MDMA and HMMA
magnitude: 75 mg against 125 mg, 8 men (de la Torre et al., 2000): peak 130.9 (SD 38.6) against 236.4 (58.0) ug/L; AUC(0-24 h) 1331.5 (646.0) against 2623.7 (572.9) ug x h/L; dose-normalized AUC 17.8 (8.6) against 21.0 (4.6), paired t test of AUC(0-infinity) P<0.03, 90% interval of the within-person ratio -0.3 to 89.3%; non-renal clearance 74.0 against 38.1 L/h (P<0.03); total clearance 86.9 (74.4) against 51.1 (14.1) L/h as printed; unchanged MDMA in urine 71.2 (13.7) against 169.6 (69.5) micromol. Across 50 to 150 mg, 24-hour exposure 100.1 and 813.9 (two men at 50 mg) against 5132.8 and 5232.0 (two men at 150 mg); Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized exposure P<0.1. Editors' calculation from the printed means: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the exposure.

evidence.locator: Methods > Patients and study design, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Abstract (Methods); Results, 3rd paragraph (last sentence)
evidence.extracted: Fourteen men took part: six in a pilot phase (two each at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and eight in a double-blind, randomized, Latin-square crossover of 75 mg MDMA, 125 mg MDMA, 40 mg amphetamine and placebo; all had used MDMA at least five times; in the second phase all were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers. The 150 mg volunteers had side effects that ruled out higher doses, and 50 mg was judged low.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (image; MDMA rows for 75 and 125 mg); Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: In the same eight men, 125 mg gave a higher dose-normalized exposure than 75 mg: peak 236.4 ug/L (SD 58.0) against 130.9 (38.6); AUC(0-24 h) 2623.7 (572.9) against 1331.5 (646.0); dose-normalized AUC 21.0 (4.6) against 17.8 (8.6); half-life 8.6 (3.2) against 7.7 (3.2) h. A paired t test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) gave P<0.03, and the 90% interval of the within-person ratio was -0.3 to 89.3%, so the authors judged the 125 mg dose not bioequivalent to the 75 mg dose scaled by dose. Editors' calculation: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the AUC.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (image; clearance columns); Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Urinary clearance of MDMA was roughly constant across doses (analysis of variance not significant) while non-renal clearance depended on dose (P<0.03) and, in the same eight men, was about halved at 125 mg (38.1 L/h) against 75 mg (74.0 L/h), which the authors read as impaired hepatic clearance; total clearance was 51.1 (SD 14.1) L/h at 125 mg against 86.9 (74.4) L/h at 75 mg. The SDs of non-renal clearance are cut off at the edge of the table image.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (image; 50, 100 and 150 mg rows); Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Across the five doses (50 to 150 mg, a 3-fold range), with different men at 50, 100 and 150 mg and the same eight men at 75 and 125 mg, the AUC(0-24 h) of MDMA ranged from 100.1 to 5232.0 ug.h/L (more than 10-fold): two men at 50 mg had 100.1 and 813.9 ug.h/L, two men at 150 mg 5132.8 and 5232.0, with peak concentrations 441.9 and 486.9 ug/L at 150 mg against a mean of 236.4 at 125 mg. A Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) across the five doses was only marginal (P<0.1).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors name two explanations: saturation of MDMA metabolism (the simplest, which they say cannot be excluded) and inhibition of CYP2D6-mediated demethylenation by MDMA, and perhaps by its metabolite HMMA, citing in vitro work showing MDMA is both a substrate and an inhibitor of CYP2D6. Their stated limits: the observations were made retrospectively, the clinical studies were not designed to detect the phenomenon, and bias cannot be excluded because the same individuals were not tested at each dose level.

evidence.locator: Abstract (Conclusions)
evidence.extracted: The abstract concludes that the lack of proportionality, in a window of doses the authors call compatible with recreational use, is a more general phenomenon concerning the whole population independent of CYP2D6 genotype, and that relatively small increases in the dose ingested give disproportionate rises in plasma concentration, so that people are more prone to acute toxicity. Editors' reading: the dose comparison was made in eight men who were all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers, so independence from genotype was not tested, and no toxicity outcome was measured.
evidence.quote: subjects are more prone to develop acute toxicity

evidence.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results › Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 528); Results › Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st paragraph (p. 528); Discussion, 1st paragraph (pp. 528-529)
evidence.extracted: In 15 men, a single MDMA dose of 1.5 mg/kg raised the exposure to the CYP2D6 probe drug dextromethorphan from 15.7 to 149.1 (area over 8 hours) and its peak from 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL, lowered the product dextrorphan from 464.6 to 31.9 ng/mL at peak, and raised the urinary probe-drug to product ratio from 0.0061 to 0.4322; the recovery half-life was 46.6 hours (SD 11.8) on one fit, and the ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 529)
evidence.extracted: The authors recall their own earlier study in which MDMA concentrations were increased beyond what accumulation predicts when a second dose was taken 24 hours later. They also write that people who use MDMA are known to take on average more than 1 pill per session (1.8 to 2.9 pills on average, up to 6 to 7 depending on the type of person, citing their reference 36, which was not read) and that many binge for several days, and infer, without having given a second dose, that a second dose taken up to a week later would give higher plasma concentrations and, they add, a higher risk of acute toxicity. No second dose, concentration-effect measure or toxicity outcome was studied here (editors' reading).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph (also the following paragraph on limitations)
evidence.extracted: The authors read the small and short-lived difference between people with and without CYP2D6 function as the result of MDMA inhibiting CYP2D6 itself, citing a physiologically based model that estimates a rise of only 36% in peak MDMA with no CYP2D6 function; they note that other enzymes and CYP3A4 inhibition may matter more than CYP2D6 genetics.

evidence.locator: MDMA pharmacology and metabolic disposition, 4th paragraph; Drug-drug interactions, 1st paragraph; Concluding remarks, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Narrative review, second-hand. MDMA is both a substrate of CYP2D6 (O-demethylenation to HHMA, then methylation to HMMA) and a potent mechanism-based inhibitor; the review gives metabolic clearance as about 75% of MDMA plasma clearance, with about 30% of its metabolism regulated by CYP2D6 (citing the 2000 non-linear paper and a 2005 paroxetine-probe study), written elsewhere as less than 30% and, for both drugs, lower than 50%.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 overall high on the study card, set by an unplanned retrospective analysis, the dependence of the wider dose range on two men per dose, statistical inconsistencies and a table misprint. One level, not two, because the 75 against 125 mg comparison is randomized and within-person and the concentrations are objective.

inconsistency.note: No contrary result in the studies read here; the editor should weigh the library's claim on acute tolerance, where a booster study reports a peak ratio close to the dose ratio.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for the doses and men studied and does not extend to other doses, women or settings.

imprecision.note: Eight men; the 90% interval of the within-person ratio reaches zero; the 50 to 150 mg range rests on two men per dose.

grade.reasoning: The 75 against 125 mg comparison is a randomized, double-blind, within-person crossover and starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -2 (eight men, an interval reaching zero, two men per dose in the wider range) give very low. Status single-study: one study shows the dose comparison; the probe-drug and genotype studies bear on the mechanism, not on dose proportionality. The claim describes the blood levels in fixed-dose laboratory conditions; it is not guidance on any amount.

verification.flag_note: Second-dose studies (Farre 2004, Peiro 2013, Humbert-Droz 2026) are anchored in the library's claim on acute tolerance, not here, and were not read for this claim; the editor may join the two claims. Note for the editor: that claim's booster study reports a peak ratio of 1.50 for a total dose ratio of 1.5, close to proportional, which may bear on inconsistency. Printed Table 2 value 40.9 in de la Torre et al. (2000) is probably 4.9 (see its card). The Table 1 and Table 2 values were read from the table images on the PMC page and were not checked a second time; the text confirms the 125 mg peak, the halved non-renal clearance and the more-than-10-fold range, and the dose-normalised AUCs reproduce from the AUCs and doses.

statement: The one study read here that counted birth defects after ecstasy use in pregnancy is a letter from a UK teratology information service, a prospective case series with no comparison group (it cites an interim report of 92 pregnancies from the same service and a Dutch series of 43, neither of which was read). From 302 enquiries (1989 to June 1998) it followed 136 pregnancies in which ecstasy was used (74 ecstasy only, 62 with other drugs, nearly all in the first 3 months); 135 enquiries (45%) were lost to follow-up and 31 (10%) had not finished. Of the 136, 11 ended in miscarriage and 48 in elective termination, and the other 77 gave 78 live-born infants (one pair of twins); 12 of the 78 (15.4%, 95% CI 8.2 to 25.4) had a congenital anomaly, which the authors call significantly higher than an expected 2 to 3% (no test is reported, the benchmark has no source, and the list includes minor findings such as a toe lying under its neighbour, a flat spot on the head, a drooping eyelid and clicking hips). Two infants had heart defects (26 per 1000 live births), both also exposed to other drugs by the table's grouping, and three girls had talipes (38 per 1000), all in the ecstasy-only group by the table's grouping; the authors say the series has too little statistical power to confirm a causal link with any anomaly, and no effect on the sex ratio was seen (McElhatton et al., 1999). A later cohort of 28 exposed women did not report a count of anomalies; one exposed infant had a rare genetic syndrome (Townes-Brocks), a spontaneous mutation that the authors say cannot be attributed specifically to maternal drug exposure (Singer et al., 2012). That cohort paper describes the 1999 letter as showing a 4 to 7 times higher risk, and a two-fold risk after allowing for higher-risk pregnancies; the letter prints neither figure and makes no such adjustment (editors' calculation: 15.4% against an expected 2 to 3% is a ratio of about 5 to 8).
plain: One study counted birth defects after ecstasy use in pregnancy. A UK information service followed 136 pregnancies. Of 78 babies born alive, 12 (about 15 in 100) had a birth defect, a mix of minor and major ones, more than the 2 to 3 in 100 the authors expected. But there was no comparison group, almost half of the enquiries were lost to follow-up, and 62 of the 136 pregnancies also involved other drugs. So the study cannot show whether ecstasy changes the chance of a birth defect. A later study followed babies of 28 women who used ecstasy but did not report a count of birth defects.
population: Women who used ecstasy in pregnancy and whose health professionals enquired to a UK teratology information service (136 pregnancies, 78 live births), and a cohort of 96 women of whom 28 used MDMA in the month before or during pregnancy
exposure: Self-reported ecstasy use in pregnancy, mostly in the first 3 months, alone (74 pregnancies) or with other drugs (62), reported second-hand by the enquirer; no doses or tablet contents
comparator: None in the case series (an unreferenced expected incidence of 2 to 3% was used); 68 comparison women in the cohort
outcome: Congenital anomalies in live-born infants, miscarriage, termination, prematurity, birth weight and sex ratio
magnitude: McElhatton et al. (1999): 12 of 78 live-born infants with an anomaly, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), against an expected 2 to 3% (no source); congenital heart disease in 2 infants, 26 per 1000 live births (95% CI 3.0 to 90.0), against 5 to 10 per 1000; talipes in 3 infants, 38 per 1000 (95% CI 8 to 109), against 1 per 1000. Miscarriage 11 of 136 (8%), elective termination 48 (35%), 8 premature births, 1 neonatal death, 3 term infants under 2.5 kg, no effect on sex ratio. 45% of enquiries lost to follow-up. No comparison group, so no risk ratio can be calculated. Singer et al. (2012): 1 of 28 exposed infants with Townes-Brocks syndrome (spontaneous SALL1 mutation per the authors).

evidence.locator: Research letter, 3rd paragraph (the summary above the text counted as the 1st; begins 'The UK National Teratology Information Service')
evidence.extracted: The UK National Teratology Information Service followed up 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with ecstasy exposure from January 1989 to June 1998; there were 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.

evidence.locator: Research letter, 5th and 6th paragraphs (begin '74 pregnant women reported' and '127 women')
evidence.extracted: 74 women reported ecstasy only and 62 ecstasy with other drugs of abuse (amphetamine 37, cocaine 20, cannabis 16, alcohol 13, LSD nine, other 13); acute toxicity from ecstasy in two mothers. 127 women (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs) were exposed in the first trimester, two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy.

evidence.locator: Research letter, 7th and 8th paragraphs (begin '11 pregnancies resulted in miscarriage' and 'There were 78 liveborn infants'); summary above the text; Table (Malformations reported after exposure of fetus to ecstasy and other drugs of abuse)
evidence.extracted: 11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage (8%, within the expected range) and 48 in elective termination (35%, higher than the UK average; one after prenatal diagnosis of malformations); no necropsy data on the other aborted fetuses; by subtraction (editors' arithmetic) the other 77 pregnancies gave the 78 live-born infants, one pair being twins. 78 live-born infants: 66 normal and 12 with congenital anomalies, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), described as significantly higher than an expected incidence of 2 to 3%, with no test or P value given; the summary calls this a possible association with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects; the table lists 13 anomaly findings (12 live-born, plus one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs), among them a toe under its neighbour, plagiocephaly, pyloric stenosis, ptosis, pigmentation of a thigh and clicking hips. No source is given for the expected incidence.
evidence.quote: may be associated with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects

evidence.locator: Research letter, 9th and 10th paragraphs (begin 'Eight infants were born prematurely' and 'No adverse effects were observed in the sex ratio')
evidence.extracted: Eight infants were born prematurely (25 to 36 weeks, including twins at 25 weeks; two fetal distress cases thought unrelated to ecstasy); one neonatal death in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy; no adverse effect on sex ratio; birthweights within the expected range for term infants, with only three under 2.5 kg.

evidence.locator: Research letter, 11th and 12th paragraphs (begin 'There were three female infants with talipes' and 'The spontaneous incidence of congenital heart disease'); summary above the text; Table (Malformations reported after exposure of fetus to ecstasy and other drugs of abuse)
evidence.extracted: Three female infants had talipes (38 per 1000, CI 8 to 109, against an expected 1 per 1000; the letter says idiopathic talipes is male-predominant 3 to 1 in the UK); two infants had congenital heart disease, ventricular septal defects (26 per 1000, CI 3.0 to 90.0, against an expected 5 to 10 per 1000). The authors say the small series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly but consider the data important. Editors' reading of the table: the three infants with talipes were in the ecstasy-only group, and both infants with a ventricular septal defect had other drug exposure.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; 4. Discussion, 9th and 12th paragraphs; Footnote 1
evidence.extracted: One infant in the MDMA-exposed group was diagnosed with Townes-Brocks syndrome, a rare genetic multiple-malformation syndrome of the gene SALL1, documented by genetic testing as a spontaneous (de novo) mutation; neither parent was a carrier. The authors say it would have occurred before conception and cannot be attributed specifically to maternal drug exposure; the mother had reported MDMA twice a month in the first trimester and none later, with cigarettes, alcohol and some cocaine. Results with and without this child did not differ. The paper does not report a count of other anomalies.

evidence.locator: 1. Introduction, 7th paragraph; 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The Introduction describes the 1999 series of 136 pregnancies as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk of congenital malformations and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies; the Discussion calls its 15.4% an increased risk, which echoes the letter's own summary. The letter reports a proportion (12 of 78 live births) compared informally with an unreferenced 2 to 3%, with no multiples printed, no adjusted analysis and no comparison group; it contains neither the 4 to 7 times nor the two-fold figure. Editors' calculation: 15.4% against an expected 2 to 3% is a ratio of about 5 to 8.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical on the study card: no comparison group, 45% of enquiries lost to follow-up, other drugs in 62 of 136 pregnancies, exposure and anomalies reported second-hand by the enquirer without definition or examination.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: one case series; the cohort does not count anomalies.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for what was reported to one service in the 1990s, not for current use or for tablet contents.

imprecision.note: Subgroup rates rest on 2 and 3 infants with intervals running from 3 to 90 and 8 to 109 per 1000.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim from a case series starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias -2 (critical, no comparison group) and imprecision -1 give very low. Status single-study. The claim is worded as insufficient evidence: the counts are reported with their limits, and the paper's own caution about statistical power is stated. It does not support a risk figure or a risk ratio, and the later cohort's mis-description of the letter is noted as a reporting error, not a finding.

verification.flag_note: Joins with the claim on infant development at 1 and 4 months (same exposure, different outcomes). The editor may keep them separate: the case series counts anomalies without a comparison, the cohort measures development with one.

statement: In a cohort of 96 women in the United Kingdom recruited in pregnancy through midwives, leaflets and magazine advertisements asking for women who used recreational drugs, 28 had used MDMA in the month before or during pregnancy (mostly in the first 3 months: on average 1.61 tablets a week in the month before pregnancy, 0.82 in the first 3 months, 0.08 in the second 3 months and 0.006 in the last, with a median of 0.13 a week across pregnancy; one woman used in the last 3 months; tablet contents were not tested) and 68 had not (32 of them had used before). At about 1 month (22 exposed and 60 comparison infants) no mean neurobehavioral score differed (two shifts in the spread of scores, toward more lethargic and less rigid behaviour, reached P<0.07). At 4 months (22 and 65 infants) the Bayley mental (99.1 against 98.6) and psychomotor (96.5 against 94.3) scores and the Alberta motor scale percentile (50.4 against 45.8; 14% below the 10th percentile in both groups) did not differ, but an assessor-rated motor quality score was lower in exposed infants (58.9 against 74.1, P=0.009) and still lower after adjusting for alcohol (beta -0.21, P<0.05); exposed infants were more often boys (71% against 46%; adjusted odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.2 to 8.2) (Singer et al., 2012). The women who used MDMA also used more cocaine (71% against 16% of women), cannabis, tobacco and amphetamine and more alcohol (9.1 against 6.6 units a week), fathers were not asked, and these are among many scores tested without correction in small groups, so the study cannot separate MDMA from the other exposures. The authors' dose-response rests on infants of the 13 women with heavier use scoring lower than infants of the 15 women with lighter use, while infants of the lighter-use group scored above the unexposed on two scales. Development after 4 months and exposure beyond the first 3 months were not studied.
plain: One study followed babies of women who used ecstasy in pregnancy, mostly in the first 3 months: on average about 1.6 tablets a week in the month before pregnancy and 0.8 a week in the first 3 months. At 1 month, average scores in 22 exposed babies and 60 others did not differ, though two patterns leaned toward more low-energy behavior (91 in 100 against 73 in 100) and less stiffness (9 against 27); neither passed the usual cut-off. At 4 months, standard mental and movement tests were also about the same. One rating of movement quality was lower in exposed babies (average score 59 against 74), and more of them were boys (71 in 100 against 46 in 100). The mothers also used more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, so the study cannot tell which drug mattered. The babies were followed only to 4 months.
population: Infants of 96 UK women recruited in pregnancy because they used recreational drugs: 28 exposed to MDMA in the month before or during pregnancy (22 seen at 1 and at 4 months) and 68 not exposed (60 seen at 1 month, 65 at 4 months)
exposure: Self-reported MDMA use in the month before or during pregnancy, mostly in the first 3 months (mean 1.61 tablets a week in the month before, 0.82 in the first 3 months), with no biological check and no testing of tablet contents
comparator: Infants of women who used recreational drugs but not MDMA in pregnancy (32 had used before pregnancy)
outcome: Neonatal behaviour at about 1 month (NNNS); Bayley mental and psychomotor scores, behaviour-rating motor quality and attention, and Alberta motor percentile at 4 months; birth measures and sex
magnitude: 1 month (22 against 60): no mean NNNS score differed (lethargy 3.14 against 2.63, P=.22). 4 months (22 against 65): Bayley mental 99.1 against 98.6 (P=.80); psychomotor 96.5 against 94.3 (P=.40); Alberta percentile 50.4 against 45.8 (P=.51), 14% below the 10th percentile in both; behaviour-rating motor quality 58.9 (SD 20.7) against 74.1 (23.8), t -2.61, P=.009, adjusted beta -.21 (P<.05) after alcohol. Three groups (none, lighter, heavier): motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (P<.04); Alberta percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (P<.03); psychomotor 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (P<.08). Male births 20 of 28 (71%) against 31 of 68 (46%), adjusted odds ratio 3.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 8.2). Other drugs in the exposed group: cocaine 71% against 16%, cannabis 82% against 54%, tobacco 86% against 62%.

evidence.locator: 2. Methods > 2.1.1 Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.1.2 Measures of MDMA Exposure and Covariates, 1st paragraph; 2.1.2.1 Prenatal Levels of Drug Exposure, 1st paragraph; 2.1.4 Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Recruitment of pregnant women who had used recreational drugs through midwives, leaflets at prenatal clinics and advertisements in pregnancy magazines (ecstasy, tobacco, cannabis, alcohol and cocaine named as examples); 126 responded, 5 did not meet criteria, 25 did not come to the first visit, leaving 96; 82 infants were seen at about 1 month and 87 at 4 months. Women were classed as exposed if they said they used MDMA during pregnancy or in the month before (28); women who had used earlier but not then (32) and women who had never used were the comparison (68 in all). 62 women were interviewed during pregnancy and 24 after birth; use was by self-report with no biological check.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 3rd to 7th paragraphs; Tables 2 and 4
evidence.extracted: Mean tablets a week for the 28 exposed women (Table 4): month before pregnancy 1.61 (SD 3.11), first trimester 0.82 (1.58), second 0.08 (0.38), third 0.006 (0.03); one woman used in the third trimester. Table 2: over pregnancy mean 0.6 (SD 1.1), median 0.13 (range 0.01 to 4.5). The text gives 3.2 tablets a week (SD 5.2) before pregnancy 'for those who used MDMA during pregnancy' and a mean total of 25 tablets over pregnancy and the month before (SD 43.7, range 0.45 to 180). Median split (0.14 a week): heavier 13 women, lighter 15; they differed mainly in the month before pregnancy (3.3 against 0.12 tablets a week, P<.007) and less in the first trimester (1.6 against 0.12, P<.12).

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Tables 1 to 3
evidence.extracted: The women who used MDMA were more likely to use cocaine (71% against 16% of women), cannabis (82% against 54%), tobacco (86% against 62%), amphetamine (18% against 3%), mushrooms (14% against none), LSD (11% against none) and ketamine (7% against none) in pregnancy, and used more alcohol (9.1 against 6.6 units a week; 96% against 91% of women); they had fewer previous births (parity 1.21 against 1.88) and higher drug-problem scores (DAST 7.7 against 4.6). The groups were similar in age, education, income, ethnicity and two intelligence subtests.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 5; 4. Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: All births were singletons. No group difference in gestation (40.0 against 39.5 weeks), birth weight (3537 against 3344 g), prematurity (1 of 28 against 1 of 68), length or head circumference (the last two with many missing values). Exposed infants were more often male: 20 of 28 (71%) against 31 of 68 (46%), chi-square 5.32, P=0.02; odds ratio of a male birth 3.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 8.2, P<.02) after controlling for other drug differences. The authors state that they cannot establish whether the sex-ratio difference is caused by MDMA.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.3 Neonatal Behavioral Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 6
evidence.extracted: NNNS at about 1 month (22 exposed, 60 comparison infants; mean age 33.6 days): no mean score differed (for example lethargy 3.14 against 2.63, P=.22; excitability 1.64 against 2.35, P=.15); trends in the score distributions for more lethargic behaviour (91% against 73%) and less hypertonicity (9% against 27%), both P<.069.

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 1st paragraph; Table 7
evidence.extracted: At 4 months (22 exposed, 65 comparison infants): Bayley mental index 99.1 (SD 6.4) against 98.6 (8.9), P=.80; psychomotor index 96.5 (10.0) against 94.3 (10.8), P=.40; behaviour-rating attention/arousal 71.2 against 70.9; Alberta motor scale percentile 50.4 against 45.8, P=.51, with 14% below the 10th percentile in both groups; behaviour-rating motor quality 58.9 (SD 20.7) against 74.1 (23.8), t -2.61, P=.009. After controlling for average alcohol exposure, MDMA still predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.21, P<.05); average tablets a week over pregnancy predicted it too (beta -.24, P<.042).

evidence.locator: 3. Results > 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 2nd paragraph; Table 8; 3.5 Other Drug Effects, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Three-group comparison at 4 months (none, lighter, heavier): behaviour-rating motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (F 3.6, P<.04); Alberta percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (F 3.8, P<.03); psychomotor index 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (P<.08); below the 10th percentile 14%, 0 and 27% (P<.18), so the lighter group scored above the unexposed on the psychomotor index and the Alberta percentile. Higher alcohol exposure predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.36, P<.005), and higher cannabis exposure poorer attention (beta -.28) and regulation (beta -.27) at 1 month (both P<.02).

evidence.locator: 4. Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs; Abstract; Highlights
evidence.extracted: Limitations the authors state: voluntary enrolment, self-reported use that may be unreliable, fetal exposure almost entirely in the first trimester, a small exposed sample, and fathers' use not asked. They conclude that the findings suggest risk to the developing child and warrant follow-up of the cohort to see whether the early motor differences persist or resolve. The abstract and highlights say exposed infants had poorer motor quality and lower milestone attainment, with a dose-response relationship; in the group comparison the Bayley psychomotor and Alberta scores did not differ.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high on the study card: the exposed women used much more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, fathers' use and weight gain are unknown; self-reported exposure; differential follow-up (79% against 88 to 96%); many outcomes without correction, and an abstract that features the significant ones.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: one cohort.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for UK women who used recreational drugs, mostly in the first 3 months, and infants to 4 months.

imprecision.note: 22 exposed infants; the three-group comparison rests on about 11 infants per group.

grade.reasoning: An observational cohort starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status single-study. The claim lists the null results first and the associations with their confounding, so it says no more than the anchors show; it is not a statement about cause or about any amount.

verification.flag_note: Joins with the claim on birth defects (same exposure). Reference record singer_2012 is metadata-verified; the cohort's later follow-up (beyond 4 months) was not found in the library's reference list.

statement: As summarized by a 2004 narrative review of tablet analyses (Parrott, 2004), what is sold as ecstasy has mostly held MDMA but not always, and the amount in a tablet has varied widely. The review's estimates, which it calls very approximate, put the share of tablets holding MDMA at 90 to 98 in 100 from the 1980s to the early 1990s (the rest generally MDA), 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid to late 1990s (5 to 30 in 100 held MDA or MDEA and 4 to 20 in 100 other drugs), 80 to 95 in 100 in the late 1990s and values approaching 100 in 100 in the early 2000s. They rest on three large series (a US laboratory to 1985, where 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy or MDMA held MDMA or MDA; Dutch monitoring from 1993; tablets in north-east Italy, 1995 to 2000) and on smaller surveys. In the Dutch series, 6 to 18 in 100 tablets in 1993 to 1997 held other drugs outside the amphetamine family, such as ketamine, atropine, caffeine or paracetamol; in Italy about 1 in 100 held nothing active. Other substances the review lists include opiates, dextromethorphan and 4-MTA, which the authors it cites say was implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands. The measured amount of MDMA also differed from tablet to tablet: 100 to 150 mg in most Italian samples; yearly UK averages of 90 to 102 mg (1991 to 1995) falling to 73 to 88 mg (1996 to 2001); and, within single small series, from under 20 mg to 140 mg (UK, mid-1990s) and from none (lactose) to 152 mg (Czech Republic). These are amounts measured in tablets, not amounts to take. For someone who felt little from a tablet, the analyses show that a tablet can hold much less MDMA than another, none, or a different drug. People in Australia who use ecstasy and were surveyed in 1998 to 2000 estimated that about 1 tablet in 4 or 5 was a dud, a ratio the review says is close to the more systematic survey data from Italy, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic. The review adds that jaw clenching, tooth grinding and the quality of mood changes are used to gauge a tablet's strength, and one qualitative study described early nausea as a sign; these are people's impressions, which the review does not compare with analyses. It says a tablet with MDA or MDEA in place of MDMA would probably not feel markedly different, except perhaps in how long it lasts. It does not look at other reasons for feeling little, such as tolerance, and has no data on what happens when people then take more; it says, without data, that tablets with a high amount may be especially risky for people new to MDMA. The limits are that no study used random sampling, most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins, seizures of uniform batches may overstate purity, a US service that charged $100 a pill probably over-represented unusual pills, and the data end around 2002, so they do not describe tablets now.
plain: Ecstasy is often MDMA, but not always, and one tablet can hold much more than another. A 2004 review of tablet tests put the share holding MDMA at about 90 to 98 in 100 from the 1980s to the early 1990s, about 50 to 80 in 100 in the mid-1990s, and nearly all by the early 2000s. The rest held related drugs such as MDA or MDEA, other substances such as ketamine, caffeine or paracetamol, or nothing active. The MDMA measured in tablets ran from none to about 150 mg (a measurement, not an amount to take). Some people feel a tablet did little. One possible reason, which these findings fit, is that it held less MDMA than the last one, or none. People in an Australian survey thought about 1 in 4 or 5 tablets was a dud. The review does not look at other reasons, such as tolerance, and has no data on what happens when people then take more. Its data end around 2002, the samples were not random, and it reaches us second-hand.
population: Tablets and capsules sold or submitted as ecstasy (or MDMA) and analysed in laboratories or by testing services in the USA (to 1985), the Netherlands (1993 to 1999), north-east Italy (1995 to 2000), the UK, the Czech Republic and a US website (to 2002), with surveys of people who use ecstasy on how they judged tablet quality, all as summarized in a 2004 narrative review
exposure: Being sold or submitted as ecstasy or MDMA; contents found by laboratory analysis (quick tests first in the Dutch series)
comparator: Earlier and later periods and different countries within the review; no random sample and no reference standard
outcome: Share of tablets holding MDMA, related drugs (MDA, MDEA), amphetamines or other substances; milligrams of MDMA per tablet
magnitude: Review estimates (very approximate), share of tablets holding MDMA: 90-98 in 100 (1980s to early 1990s; remaining 2-10 generally MDA); 50-80 (mid to late 1990s; 5-30 MDA or MDEA; 4-20 other drugs); 80-95 (late 1990s); approaching 100 (early 2000s). Dutch monitoring (several thousand tablets): MDMA alone 48-60 in 100 each year 1993-96, then 44 (1997), 75 (1998) and 81 (1999); each year 1993-96 MDEA alone 12-20, MDA alone 2-5, MDMA mixed 7-13, amphetamine alone 1-4, amphetamine mixtures 2-7; over 80 held an amphetamine-type drug; other drugs 6-17 (1993-96) and 18 (1997). Italy (at least 20,000 tablets, 1995-2000): MDMA 85-90, MDA or MDEA 8-10, inactive 1, others 1. Czech Republic (120 pills and capsules, 1998-2001): over 80 MDMA only. UK 2001 (136 tablets): all MDMA. US testing service 2002 (about 175 tablets): 88 MDMA alone or mixed, 4 MDA or MDE, 4 others, 4 no identifiable drug. US laboratory to 1985: 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy or MDMA held MDMA or MDA. Amount per tablet as measured: Italy mostly 100-150 mg (1995-2000); UK yearly averages 90-102 mg (1991-95) and 73-88 mg (1996-2001); one UK series some 100-140 mg, some about 50 mg, some under 20 mg; Czech series 30-100 mg with 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose) at the extremes; one UK seizure of 80 tablets 73-89 mg (mean 79). People surveyed in Australia (1998-2000) judged about 1 tablet in 4 or 5 a dud (their estimate, not an analysis; the review says it is close to the more systematic survey data). Amounts are contents of tablets, not amounts to take.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the 1970s to the early 1990s', 1st paragraph (p. 235); Table 1, Renfroe row (p. 236)
evidence.extracted: Renfroe (1986), as summarized: of 610 samples of MDA or MDMA among 20,721 street drug samples sent to a Californian laboratory between 1972 and 1985, 12% (89 samples) were submitted under the names MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy. The large majority of those 89 held MDMA or MDMA with MDA; only two held neither (a capsule from Honolulu with an amphetamine compound, and a largely empty plastic syringe from Miami labelled ecstasy/speed). Table 1 gives 97% (n=87) containing MDMA or MDA.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s', 1st paragraph (begins p. 235, ends p. 236); Table 2, Spruit (2001) 1993–1997 row (p. 236)
evidence.extracted: Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System, as summarized from Spruit (2001): set up in 1992; samples were not collected systematically, most being brought in by individual people who wanted to know what a pill held; each pill was quick-tested and those not identified were sent for laboratory analysis (on average more than 100 pills a week). In each year from 1993 to 1996 about 48–60% of pills held MDMA alone, 12–20% MDEA alone, 2–5% MDA alone, 7–13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or other drugs, 1–4% amphetamine alone and 2–7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA; over 80% held an amphetamine-type drug; 6–17% held other drugs outside that class (hallucinogens such as LSD and ketamine, atropine, caffeine, paracetamol or unknown compounds). In 1997 44% held MDMA alone, 14% MDMA plus another drug, 24% MDA, MDEA or amphetamine and 18% other non-amphetamine drugs; the review links the dip to difficulty in obtaining the chemical precursor. The share holding MDMA rose to 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999. Table 2 gives, for 1993–1997, 44–60% MDMA only, 9–25% MDEA or MDA only, 16–25% mixtures and 6–18% others.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 1st paragraph; Table 3, Schifano (2000), Spruit (2001) and Palenicek et al. (2002) rows (p. 237)
evidence.extracted: Italy, as quoted from Schifano (2000): forensic laboratories had examined at least 20,000 tablets in five years; about 85–90% of tablets seized in the north-east held MDMA as the active ingredient, in amounts of 100–150 mg a tablet; MDA and MDEA were usually in the remainder, phenylbutanamine occasionally, and dummy tablets about 1% of the material (Table 3: 85–90% MDMA, 8–10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others). Netherlands 1999: around 81% held MDMA (Table 3: 81% MDMA only, 19% all others). Czech Republic, Palenicek et al. (2002): 120 pills and capsules analysed between 1998 and 2002 (Table 3 says 1998–2001), over 80% held only MDMA; the rest held amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDEA, ketamine, ephedrine, MDA or mixtures (Table 3: more than 80% MDMA, 4% MDA, under 16% others and mixtures).

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Hansen et al. (2001) noted'; it continues on p. 238); Table 3, Winstock et al. row (p. 237)
evidence.extracted: Hansen et al. (2001), as summarized: people in Australia who used ecstasy and were surveyed between 1998 and 2000 estimated that about one tablet in every four or five was a dud; the review says this ratio is close to the more systematic survey data from Italy, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic. Winstock et al. (2001) surveyed 1151 dance clubbers in June 1999 about beliefs, consumption and perceptions of quality; Table 3 gives subjective reports of recent improvements in the quality of supplies.

evidence.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph, the part on p. 238 beginning 'The American website www.dancesafe.org' (the paragraph begins on p. 237); Table 3, Cole et al., Dancesafe and Ramsey (2003) rows (p. 237)
evidence.extracted: A US website, Dancesafe.org, listed tablets sent in for commercial analysis: about 175 tablets in 2002, of which 88% held MDMA alone or in combination and 4% held MDE or MDA (alone or in a combination without MDMA); Table 3 adds 4% others and 4% no identifiable drug. Ramsey et al. (2001): in samples from an amnesty bin at the entrance of a London dance venue, a high proportion of the tablets held MDMA and the powders were mostly amphetamine. Ramsey (2003), asked for later findings: the tablets in the bins were almost all MDMA. Cole et al. (2002): 136 tablets submitted to the Forensic Science Service in north-west England in 2001 all held MDMA by liquid chromatography.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has been described')
evidence.extracted: The review's own estimates of the share of ecstasy tablets holding MDMA: from the 1980s to the early 1990s around 90–98%, the remaining 2–10% generally MDA; in the mid to late 1990s between 50 and 80%, with around 5–30% holding MDA or MDEA and around 4–20% other drugs; in the late 1990s around 80–95% (citing Spruit and Winstock et al.); in the early 2000s values approaching 100% in the most recent surveys (citing Cole et al. and Ramsey).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'These estimates can, however, only be seen as very approximate')
evidence.extracted: The review calls its estimates very approximate because the empirical evidence is limited: only three reports covered large samples over a long period (a US anonymous testing service, Renfroe 1986; the Dutch monitoring project, Spruit 2001; northern Italy, Schifano 2000), and the smaller surveys largely confirmed them. It adds that no study used a randomized sampling procedure; most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins; police seizures of large batches of uniform tablets may overestimate purity (Cole et al. 2002); and a US service charged $100 for each pill analysed (Baggott et al. 2000), far more than its street value, which probably led to a preponderance of atypical drugs.
evidence.quote: no study has employed a randomized sampling procedure

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has practical consequences')
evidence.extracted: The review says that when a tablet holds MDA or MDEA, whose effects on brain chemistry are similar to those of MDMA, people would probably not notice any marked difference except possibly in how long the effect lasts or in subtle details of the experience (citing Hegadoren et al. 1999). In the Dutch data, even in the years with the lowest share of MDMA (1994 and 1997) the large majority of tablets still held MDMA, MDEA or MDA, and at other periods the match between ecstasy and MDMA was often around 90%.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'However, a substantial minority of ecstasy tablets')
evidence.extracted: The review states that a substantial minority of tablets held other compounds: between 1993 and 1997, 6–18% of Dutch samples held other drugs outside the amphetamine class. It says the effects of ketamine are so different from MDMA that taking it unknowingly could be extremely distressing, and reports that 4-methylthioamphetamine (4-MTA) was found in amnesty bins and, in the words of the authors it cites, had been implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands. A small proportion of tablets held weak substances (paracetamol, caffeine, placebo) and others held atropine, opiates, phenylbutanamine or dextromethorphan; the review says the acute effects of these could be unexpected and unpleasant.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'One intriguing question is why the supplies of ecstasy first became problematical')
evidence.extracted: The review says people who use ecstasy were fully aware of the quality problems of the mid-1990s and, when interviewed, can readily tell the occasions when they feel they have taken MDMA from their other experiences; jaw clenching, tooth grinding and the quality of mood changes are used to gauge the purity and strength of tablets, and one qualitative study described early nausea as a subjective sign. It adds that uncertainty over purity led many potential people to avoid illicit drugs, while regular ones often became more wary and took supplies only from friends. These are people's impressions; the review does not compare them with analyses of the tablets.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic', pp. 239–240)
evidence.extracted: Amounts of MDMA per tablet, as summarized: most Italian samples held 100–150 mg in 1995–2000 (Schifano 2000); UK annual averages were 90–102 mg between 1991 and 1995 and 73–88 mg between 1996 and 2001 (Cole et al. 2002). Small UK studies in the mid-1990s found amounts that were variable and often low: some tablets held 100–140 mg, others about 50 mg and some under 20 mg (Sherlock et al. 1999). In the Czech Republic tablets varied from 30 to 100 mg, with 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose) at the extremes (Palenicek et al. 2002). 80 white tablets from a large UK police seizure in 2001 held 73–89 mg, mean 79 mg (Cole et al. 2002). The Dutch monitoring met high-amount tablets occasionally in 1998. The review calls unknown amount a key area of uncertainty, says that high-amount tablets may be particularly dangerous for people taking MDMA for the first time because they could cause a severe serotonin syndrome reaction (no data given), and notes that two sources found no analytic evidence of toxic contaminants in MDMA batches (King 2000; Schifano 2000).

risk_of_bias.note: No random sampling; samples were brought in by people, taken from amnesty bins or seized, and a paid test service over-represented odd tablets; the review itself calls its estimates very approximate.

inconsistency.note: The series agree on the pattern (mostly but not always MDMA; amounts vary); shares differ by place and year, which the claim reports as ranges.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the primary analyses were not read, and the data end around 2002, so they do not answer what tablets hold now.

imprecision.note: Ranges without intervals; several series are small and the review's own estimates overlap.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive findings from observational analyses start low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level, and the result is very low. The qualitative finding (tablets sold as ecstasy are often but not always MDMA, and the amount varies) is better supported than any single percentage. Status replicated: independent series in the US, the Netherlands, Italy, the UK and the Czech Republic point the same way, and the review reports their direction (METHODS 6.4). Stays at draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim is worded as a description of the years covered and gives no advice; the amounts are tablet contents, not doses.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Parrott (2004) as summarized; none of the primary tablet analyses was read (Renfroe 1986; Spruit 2001; Schifano 2000; Cole et al. 2002; Palenicek et al. 2002; Ramsey et al. 2001), and none has a reference record here. SECTION: the brief put this claim in section 7, which only the senior author may write (the validator fails a section 7 claim whose drafter is not the senior author); it is staged in section 2, where METHODS 8 places drug-checking findings and adulterants. Move it if you prefer. VROLIJK 2022 (Vrolijk et al., Drugs, Habits and Social Policy, doi 10.1108/dhs-01-2022-0003) is still being obtained and was not used; it would add current years (2012 to 2021, against data here that end around 2002), a defined European sample (tablets sent to drug-checking services) and milligrams per tablet over time. RULE 0: the 'I barely felt it' paragraph is met for why it can happen (a weaker, empty or different tablet) but this review has no data on what happens when people take more; the editor may link the laboratory repeat-dose claim (cl_mdma_redose_cardiovascular) and the tolerance claim (cl_mdma_tolerance_chronic) from this one.
