statement: As summarized by a 2010 narrative review (Degenhardt, Bruno, et al., 2010), studies of people who use ecstasy have found that some meet criteria for dependence, but the share ranges from about 4 in 100 to 73 in 100 depending on who was asked, how, and over what period. In two US household surveys, 3.6 in 100 people who had used ecstasy in the past year (Wu et al.) and 3.8 in 100 of those who had started within the previous two years (Stone et al.) met criteria for hallucinogen dependence. In a German community study, 0.4 in 100 of all young adults met past-year criteria for ecstasy, hallucinogen or stimulant dependence, and 5.8 in 100 of people who had ever used ecstasy had ever met criteria (about 12 of 207 people, by our arithmetic from the table). In samples recruited differently, 19 in 100 of New York nightclub attendees and 22 in 100 of Taiwanese juvenile detainees who used ecstasy met past-year criteria, and 16 to 18 in 100 in convenience samples in Germany, the UK and Australia (195, 1,106 and 1,662 people) were counted as dependent or scored above a screening scale's cut-off. The highest figures, 43, 64 and 73 in 100 over a lifetime, came from three small samples: 52 adolescents and young adults in drug treatment and in the community who had used ecstasy at least 5 times, 185 people the review describes as regularly using ecstasy, and 59 rave attendees who had taken at least 250 tablets in their lifetime. The review says all the instruments were designed for other drugs, only one study used a clinician's assessment, assessment was mostly by self-report and lifetime recall, and most samples were recruited by convenience or snowball methods, so the figures cannot be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy; it adds that people often reported dependence symptoms despite relatively infrequent use and that it is unclear whether they understood the questions as intended, and that pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some dependence may be on another drug. Across studies, the symptoms most often reported included continued use despite problems, spending a lot of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal; in two studies the symptoms fell into a group about compulsive use and a group about escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended). In the one study that followed people (the German community study above), 93 in 100 of those who met criteria at the start no longer did just over three years later and 50 in 100 had stopped using ecstasy altogether; the review does not give the size of that group, which by our arithmetic was about 12 to 14 people. In Australia, fewer than 1 in 100 treatment episodes were for ecstasy. The review also describes animal studies in which MDMA is rewarding but may be less so than other illicit drugs, and notes a lack of case reports of severe withdrawal. It concludes that the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is thin in scope and design.
plain: Some people who use ecstasy meet the criteria for dependence, but studies disagree widely on how many. In two US national surveys, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently did. In club-goer, detention and volunteer samples, 16 to 22 in 100 did. In three small samples, including people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 tablets, 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. Most studies recruited volunteers and used questionnaires made for other drugs, so the figures may not fit everyone who uses ecstasy. The one study that followed people for over three years found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were; that group was small, about 12 to 14 people by our arithmetic. Tolerance (needing more for the same effect) was among the symptoms people reported most, and in two studies it went together with using more, or for longer, than meant. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug. This comes second-hand, from a 2010 review.
population: People who use ecstasy in studies summarized by a 2010 narrative review: US and German general-population surveys, New York nightclub attendees, Taiwanese juvenile detainees, and convenience samples in Australia, Germany, the UK and the US (26 to 1,662 people per study)
exposure: Use of ecstasy (pills sold as ecstasy, contents not tested), from a few lifetime occasions to hundreds of tablets
comparator: None in most studies; one study compared ecstasy with other hallucinogens; one followed people over time
outcome: Meeting criteria for dependence on questionnaires or interviews designed for other drugs (DSM-IV hallucinogen or amphetamine criteria, CIDI, the Severity of Dependence Scale and others), past year, past month or lifetime
magnitude: Share meeting criteria, as printed in Table 1: general population: 3.8% past year (Stone, N 1199, people who started within 2 years), 3.6% past year (Wu, N 652; text says 4%, another 11% with one or two symptoms), 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy (von Sydow, N 207; about 12 people, editors' arithmetic) with 0.4% of all young adults dependent in the past year; sentinel samples: 19% past year (Parsons, N 214), 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, N 200); self-selected or convenience samples: 18% past month (Bruno, N 1662, scale cut-off 4 or more), 17% (Winstock, N 1106, scale cut-off 5 or more, timeframe not specified in the table, lifetime in the text), 16% (Tossman, N 195, timeframe not specified), 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, N 154, probable dependence), 43% lifetime (Cottler, N 52), 64% lifetime (Topp, N 185), 73% lifetime (Thomasius, N 59, at least 250 lifetime tablets, clinician-rated); Hanson and Luciana (N 26): prevalence cell N = 2 but 14 met abuse or dependence criteria in the details column and text. Course (von Sydow, just over 3 years): 93% no longer dependent, 50% no longer using, 43% still using (group size not given; editors' arithmetic: about 12 to 14 people). Treatment: under 1% of Australian treatment episodes. No intervals are given.

evidence.locator: 2.1 Complicating issues in generalising laboratory research to recreational human use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The review notes that pills sold as ecstasy may not contain MDMA at all, so people developing regular or dependent use of ecstasy may not be taking MDMA, and that some or many pills may contain methamphetamine, so people may develop dependence on methamphetamine rather than, or as well as, MDMA. Some studies controlled statistically for other drug use, including methamphetamine, but that use was self-reported, not confirmed by laboratory testing.

evidence.locator: Table 1, rows Stone et al. to Bruno et al. (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: Population-based samples: Stone et al. (US National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse, 2000-2001; N 1199; six items matching DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria): 3.8% past year, among people who had started ecstasy within the previous two years. Von Sydow et al. (Germany, 1995-1999; representative sample aged 14-24; N 207; CIDI interview): 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy; less than 10% of those classed as lifetime dependent were past-year dependent at the 42-month follow-up. Wu et al. (US National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 2005; N 652; the same six hallucinogen items): 3.6% past year; another 11% reported one or two symptoms. Samples of sentinel populations: Parsons et al. (New York nightclub attendees aged 18-29 who had used ecstasy in the past 4 weeks; N 214; CIDI): 19% past year, with a median of 2.5 days of use in the past 4 months. Yen and Hsu (Taiwanese juvenile justice detainees who had used ecstasy; N 200): 22% past year. Self-selected sample: Bruno et al. (Australia, 2003-2004; N 1662; people using ecstasy at least monthly, recruited by purposive and snowball sampling; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 4 or more): 18% past month; among those screening positively, 49% used 1-2 times per week and 34% 1-2 times per month.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (continued), rows Cottler et al. to Thomasius et al. (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: Cottler et al. (US; adolescents and young adults in inpatient drug treatment and in the community, at least 5 lifetime occasions of use; N 52; computerised CIDI module): 43% lifetime; the most common symptoms were continued use despite problems (63%) and withdrawal (59%), and all dependent participants had tolerance or withdrawal. Hanson and Luciana (US students and community members; N 26; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): the prevalence cell reads N = 2 LT while the details column says 14 met the criteria. Scheier et al. (US and Australia; N 639; modified CIDI): no prevalence given, mean 227 lifetime pills. Topp et al. (Australia, 1997; N 185; CIDI): 64% lifetime; the authors questioned how withdrawal symptoms were endorsed. Tossman (Germany, 2002; N 195; people who used ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year): 16%, timeframe not specified. Yacoubian et al. (Washington rave attendees; N 154; a screening scale): 17% lifetime, 'probable' dependence. Thomasius et al. (Germany; rave attendees with at least 250 lifetime tablets, mean 794; N 59; clinical interview rated by clinical psychologists): 73% lifetime.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (continued), Winstock et al. row, and footnote; 3.2 Studies of ecstasy dependence among users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6)
evidence.extracted: Winstock et al. (UK, 1999; readers of a dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy; N 1106; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 5 or more): 17%, with a footnote that the timeframe was not specified; mean 160 lifetime occasions of use; tolerance and continued use despite problems with health, work or relationships were reported by more than half of the sample. Section 3.2: few studies have examined dependence among people who use ecstasy; all used instruments designed for other drugs, and just one (of a non-representative sample) involved clinician or psychiatric assessment. Topp et al. (1997): 64% of 185 people who regularly used ecstasy met lifetime criteria, typically during their heaviest use period, when 66% were using 1-2 times per week and 25% between 1 and 3 days per month; the authors questioned whether the withdrawal items separated comedown effects from dysphoria that eases with further use.

evidence.locator: 3.2, the paragraph beginning 'Two large survey samples of dependence' and the paragraph beginning 'Studies of dependence among ecstasy users in representative general population samples are limited'
evidence.extracted: Two large samples used the five-item Severity of Dependence Scale, which measures compulsion to use: in the UK survey of 1106 dance-magazine readers 17% screened positive for lifetime ecstasy dependence, and in the Australian interview-based study of 1662 people who regularly used ecstasy, 18% screened positive; of these 49% used ecstasy 1-2 times per week, 34% used 1-3 times per month and only 2% (n = 7) were using at least every second day, and financial, legal and work harms, sexual risk, overdose and help seeking were more common than among those who screened negative, independent of problematic methamphetamine use. In general population samples a German study found that past-year ecstasy/hallucinogen/stimulant dependence among all young adults was 0.4%; a US study found that 4% of people who had used ecstasy in the past year met DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria (another 11% reported one or two symptoms) (Wu et al.), and 3.82% of those who had started ecstasy in the previous two years had developed dependence (Stone et al.); some have argued that grouping ecstasy with the hallucinogens in DSM-IV may not fit the behavioural data.

evidence.locator: 3.3 The structure of ecstasy dependence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd begins on p. 7 and ends on p. 8)
evidence.extracted: Two studies of the structure of the symptoms, both in Australian samples (one also in US samples): Topp et al. (1997) found for ecstasy, unlike alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids, two separate components, compulsive use (use despite problems, giving up activities, unsuccessful attempts to stop, withdrawal, excessive time spent) and escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended); Bruno et al. (2009) found two related factors with the same names for the Severity of Dependence Scale. The review concludes that the dependence syndrome may not be of the same nature as for alcohol, opioids and amphetamine, and that behavioural reinforcement or learning may play a part for some people.

evidence.locator: 3.4 The course of ecstasy dependence; 3.5 Treatment seeking for ecstasy-related problems, 1st paragraph (p. 8)
evidence.extracted: Course: only one study has followed people who met DSM-IV criteria for ecstasy dependence (von Sydow et al., 2002; a German population-based study of young adults with a mean follow-up of just over three years): 93% were no longer dependent at follow-up; 50% were no longer using the drug at all, and of the 43% still using, the majority did not meet criteria for a use disorder; the authors suggested that ecstasy dependence might be a transient phenomenon. Treatment: routine data in Australia show very small numbers of treatment episodes for ecstasy (less than 1% of all episodes), consistent with surveys finding that treatment seeking is infrequent even among people who report concerns about their use.

evidence.locator: 3.6 Limitations of existing human evidence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; 4 Summary and implications, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 8)
evidence.extracted: Limitations: the studies are extremely heterogeneous in assessment methods and samples, which makes meta-analysis inappropriate; dependence was typically assessed by self-report without clinician verification, usually as lifetime retrospective reports; despite relatively infrequent use even at their heaviest, people very commonly reported dependence symptoms, and it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as the investigators intended; the prevalence cannot be extrapolated to all people who use ecstasy because most studies recruited people with recent use by convenience or snowball sampling; information on the natural history comes mostly from retrospective reports of convenience samples. Summary: the review judges the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome to be restricted in how much was studied and in how it was studied (see the quotation); animal evidence suggests MDMA may be a less potent reinforcer than other drugs but still has dependence potential; some people report problems controlling their use and concern about it, but there is a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal, which suggests physical symptoms play a more limited role than psychological ones; tolerance and withdrawal have been reported, mostly in questionnaires designed for other drugs; treatment presentations are uncommon compared with the prevalence of use but do occur.
evidence.quote: The evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is limited in both scope and design.

risk_of_bias.note: Mostly convenience and snowball samples, instruments designed for other drugs, self-report and lifetime recall; the review itself calls the evidence limited, and some figures differ between its table and text.

inconsistency.note: Shares range from 3.6 to 73 in 100; most of the spread follows who was sampled and the period asked about, which the claim reports as a range instead of one number.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through a narrative review; pills sold as ecstasy may not be MDMA; the criteria were built for other drugs.

imprecision.note: No intervals; the highest figures come from samples of 52 to 185 people, and the 93 in 100 remission figure from a group the review does not size (about 12 to 14 people by editors' arithmetic).

grade.reasoning: Descriptive prevalence from observational studies starts low (METHODS 6.3); each of risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision takes a level, so the result is very low. That some people meet criteria is better supported than any one percentage. Status replicated in direction only: every study finds some people meeting criteria, while the size varies widely, as the claim states (METHODS 6.4). Stays at draft because it rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim reports findings, makes no statement about risk for any one person and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Degenhardt et al. (2010) as summarized; none of the primary studies was read and none has a reference record here. The most useful to obtain, in order: von Sydow et al. (2002, German community study: the review does not size the group behind the 93% remission; 5.8% of 207 is about 12 and the 93, 50 and 43% fit 14, so it is a handful of people), Bruno et al. (2009, Australian SDS study), Stone et al. (2006, 2007) and Wu et al. (2008, US household surveys), Winstock et al. (2001), Topp et al. (1997). The review's table and text differ in places (Wu 3.6% in the table and 4% in the text; Bruno 1-2 against 1-3 times a month; Hanson and Luciana N = 2 in the table and 14 of 26 in the text; Winstock lifetime in the text but timeframe not specified in the table; Tossman's sample described as people who used ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year); the claim uses ranges and says so. The same text names 'escalating use' (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended) as one component, which is relevant to the 'I barely felt it' rule; the editor may link this claim to the tolerance claims.

statement: In one small echocardiography study of young adults in Belgium (Droogmans et al., 2007), heart valve findings that met the US Food and Drug Administration's criteria for valve disease caused by appetite-suppressant drugs (mitral regurgitation of grade 2 of 4 or more, or aortic regurgitation of grade 1 of 4 or more) were found in 8 of 29 people who had taken MDMA for at least 6 months (28 in 100; 95% interval 15 to 46, editors' calculation) and in 0 of 29 age- and sex-matched students who reported no drug use (Fisher's exact test, p = 0.0045). The people who had taken MDMA reported, by interview, a mean of 3.6 tablets a week (standard deviation 6.7) for a mean of 6.1 years (3.4), figures given for the 33 people recruited and not the 29 scanned. The leaks were usually mild to moderate. The clearest differences were in the tricuspid valve, with regurgitation of grade 2 of 4 or more in 13 of 29 against 0 (p < 0.001), and in stiffened (restrictive) mitral valve motion, 7 of 29 against 0 (p = 0.01). The two parts of the definition were not clear on their own: mitral regurgitation of grade 2 of 4 or more (4 of 29 against 0) and aortic regurgitation of grade 1 of 4 or more (4 of 29 against 0), p = 0.11 for each. Thin filaments called strands on the aortic valve were found in 5 of 29 against 0 (p = 0.05). People with higher grades had reportedly taken more tablets in total (943 against 242, p = 0.03; group sizes not given). The study cannot show that MDMA caused these findings: the valves were scanned once, so there is no scan from before MDMA use (one of the limits the authors state); the people who had taken MDMA came from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres and the controls from student advertisements, matched only on age and sex; other drug use is not reported although the authors note that substance use is mostly not limited to one drug; the amount came from interview and the paper reports no analysis of what the tablets held; 4 of the 33 people recruited were excluded after scanning; the study is small; and nobody had a history of heart disease or needed valve surgery, so it says nothing about symptoms or illness. The authors cite a cell-culture study (second-hand here) in which MDMA activated the 5-HT2B receptor and made human valve cells multiply, in a way the authors call fenfluramine-like; this study did not test that mechanism.
plain: In one small Belgian study, 8 of 29 young adults who had taken MDMA for at least six months (by their own account, on average about 4 tablets a week for about 6 years) had mitral or aortic valve findings that met a US definition of drug-related valve disease, against none of 29 students who reported using no drugs. Most of the leaks were mild or moderate. The biggest gap was in the valve on the right side of the heart (the tricuspid valve, which that definition does not cover), where 13 of 29 had a leak of grade 2 of 4 or more, against none. People with higher grades of leak said they had taken more tablets in total; the paper does not give the group sizes. This does not show that MDMA caused it: each person was scanned once and nobody before starting, the two groups were recruited differently (psychiatry departments and drug-help centres against student advertisements), other drug use is not reported, and the amount of MDMA came from what people said. The study did not check what the tablets held and says nothing about symptoms or illness.
population: Young adults in Brussels and Flanders (mean age about 24 to 26; 45% women): 29 who had taken MDMA for at least 6 months in the past year, recruited from psychiatry departments of two hospitals and from help centres for people with drug problems, and 29 age- and sex-matched students with no drug use; none with a history of heart disease or of ergot, appetite-suppressant or intravenous drug use
exposure: Self-reported MDMA use for at least 6 months, by interview (mean 3.6 tablets a week for 6.1 years among the 33 people recruited); tablets not analysed
comparator: 29 age- and sex-matched students who reported no drug use
outcome: Valve findings on echocardiography, read blind (the analysis used the independent observer's readings): FDA criteria for drug-induced valve disease (mitral regurgitation of 2/4 or more, or aortic regurgitation of 1/4 or more), regurgitation by valve, restrictive motion and strands
magnitude: FDA-criteria valve disease: 8 of 29 (28%; Wilson 95% interval 15% to 46%, editors' calculation) against 0 of 29 (upper 95% bound about 12%, editors' calculation), Fisher p = 0.0045 (the editors' recalculation reproduces the printed p values). By valve, MDMA group against controls (counts of 29): tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 13 (45%) against 0, p < 0.001, mean regurgitant area ratio 19% (SD 9.5) against 9% (SD 4.5), p < 0.001; mitral 2/4 or more 4 (14%) against 0, p = 0.11, mean area ratio 12% (SD 9.8) against 5% (SD 1.3), p < 0.007; aortic 1/4 or more 4 (14%) against 0, p = 0.11; pulmonary 1/4 or more 14 (48%) against 10 (34%), p = 0.42; restrictive motion mitral 7 (24%) against 0, p = 0.01, tricuspid 5 (17%) against 1 (3%), p = 0.19; strands aortic 5 (17%) against 0, p = 0.05, mitral 1 (3%) against 0. Cumulative tablets 943 (SD 1,162) in people with mitral or tricuspid regurgitation of 2/4 or more or any aortic regurgitation against 242 (SD 212) in the rest, p = 0.03. The printed relative risks (for example 1.68, 5.83) come from logistic regression, so they are odds-based and are not used as risk ratios.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 1442)
evidence.extracted: Recruitment: people who had taken MDMA in the past year were recruited from the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and from help centres for people with drug problems in Brussels and Flanders, Belgium, between December 2004 and February 2006; all took part voluntarily with written consent. Because substance use is mostly not limited to one drug, an experienced psychiatrist interviewed each person about current and past drug use (the paper does not report what the interviews found). People with a history of ergot-derived drugs, Chinese herbs, appetite-suppressant drugs, intravenous drugs or any drug known to induce valve disease were excluded, as were people with any past cardiac disease, congenital or degenerative valve disease (including mitral or tricuspid prolapse) found on echocardiography, or poor image quality. Controls were age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no drug use, with the same exclusions.

evidence.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph (p. 1442, right column: sonographers not told identities) and 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1443)
evidence.extracted: Examinations were done by experienced sonographers who were not told the person's identity; images were stored, randomized and read blind by one sonographer and one independent observer, whose agreement on the FDA criteria was excellent (kappa above 0.9); the independent observer's data were used. Valve disease was defined by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) criteria for appetite-suppressant-induced valve disease: mitral regurgitation of moderate or greater severity (2/4 or more) or aortic regurgitation of mild or greater severity (1/4 or more); Fisher's exact test was used for the FDA score. Results: 33 people who took MDMA and 29 controls were selected, none with a history of cardiac disease; 4 people in the MDMA group were excluded after scanning (3 for inadequate image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse), leaving 29; all had used MDMA for at least 6 months. 8 people (28%) who took MDMA met the FDA criteria and none of the controls (p = 0.0045); mitral, aortic and tricuspid regurgitation and shape abnormalities were more often seen in the MDMA group (Table 1).

evidence.locator: Table 1, Demographics and Echocardiographic findings
evidence.extracted: Controls against subjects taking MDMA (n = 29 against 33 for demographics, 29 against 29 for echocardiography). Demographics: women 13 (45%) against 15 (45%); mean age 25.6 (SD 2.6) against 24.3 (SD 3.1) years, p = 0.10; MDMA use in the MDMA group 3.6 (SD 6.7) tablets a week for 6.1 (SD 3.4) years. Echocardiography: mitral insufficiency 2/4 or more 0 against 4 (14%), p = 0.11; mitral regurgitant area ratio 5% (SD 1.3) against 12% (SD 9.8), p < 0.007; mitral restrictive motion 0 against 7 (24%), p = 0.01; mitral strand 0 against 1 (3%); aortic insufficiency 1/4 or more 0 against 4 (14%), p = 0.11; aortic strand 0 against 5 (17%), p = 0.05; tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 0 against 13 (45%), p < 0.001; tricuspid regurgitant area ratio 9% (SD 4.5) against 19% (SD 9.5), p < 0.001; tricuspid restrictive motion 1 (3%) against 5 (17%), p = 0.19; pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more 10 (34%) against 14 (48%), p = 0.42. The table also prints relative risks with intervals that the Methods say were calculated by logistic regression, without saying what each compares; they are not used here.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'In the MDMA group, subjects with valvular regurgitation')
evidence.extracted: In the MDMA group, people with mitral or tricuspid regurgitation of 2/4 or more, or any aortic regurgitation, had on average taken more tablets in total (943, SD 1,162) than those with lower grades (242, SD 212), p = 0.03; the group sizes and the way the cumulative number was calculated are not given.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1444)
evidence.extracted: The authors state that this is the first report of valve disease in young adults using or having used MDMA, that valve disease in young adults is very unusual and was not found in their controls, and that strands were seen in the MDMA group and not in the controls. They describe a cell-culture study (Setola et al.) in which MDMA bound to and activated human 5-HT2B receptors and caused prolonged growth responses in human valve cells, and suggest that this may explain valve disease with intermittent use; the present study did not test the mechanism.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (last sentence, p. 1445, top of left column), 6th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Although in our study, regurgitations were hemodynamically most often mild to moderate') and 7th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'This study has some limitations')
evidence.extracted: The authors write that the regurgitations were most often mild to moderate in their effect on blood flow. Limitations they state: MDMA is illegal and people were difficult to recruit, so the study is relatively small; information about the amount of use came from interrogating the people; there were no echocardiographic data from before MDMA use because a prospective evaluation was not possible for ethical reasons; and there is no pathologic evidence of the valve abnormalities because no valve surgery was needed. They say that further studies should help define the clinical significance and extent of the findings. (The paper also calls its findings of great clinical importance and suggests endocarditis prophylaxis; no data in the paper test those statements.)
evidence.quote: There were no echocardiographic data available before MDMA use

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card: confounding, exposure measurement and selection each rated high (people recruited from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres against student controls; use reported by interview; other drug use not reported).

inconsistency.note: One study; not rated.

indirectness.note: The claim names the people studied and the outcome measured, and states the limits.

imprecision.note: 8 events in 29 people with a wide interval (15% to 46%); several differences rest on 4 or 5 people and are not clear on their own.

grade.reasoning: A cross-sectional comparison starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias and imprecision each take a level, so the result is very low. No upgrade for a large effect (0 of 29 against 8 of 29) or for dose response (943 against 242 tablets) is applied, because confounding and selection are rated high and the dose figures cannot be checked. Status single-study: the paper presents itself as the first report, and this claim does not review later echocardiography studies. The claim is worded as an association in these 58 people, says that cause and any symptoms are untested, and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: One small study (58 people), cross-sectional although the paper calls it case-control (see the study card). The paper's relative risks and some abstract p values (mitral strand and 1/4 mitral regurgitation) cannot be traced to Table 1; the claim uses counts and Fisher p values only. Later echocardiography studies of people who have taken MDMA were not read for this claim and should be checked before it is published; the cell-culture study (Setola et al., 2003, Mol Pharmacol) has no reference record here.

statement: In a series of coroners' cases from Victoria, Australia (Pilgrim et al., 2011), MDMA was measured in postmortem blood above 0.02 mg/L in 106 of 14,682 deaths with full toxicology testing between 2002 and 2008 (78 in 100 men; ages 17 to 48, median 25; 60 in 100 by external injury such as hanging or a vehicle crash). Of the 106, 20 had MDMA alone or with MDA, 34 had MDMA with alcohol, 33 had other drugs judged unlikely to cause a drug reaction, and 19 had a combination that the authors rated as a risk of harmful interaction (4 major, all with moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type; 10 moderate; 5 minor). The 19 are a subset chosen by the authors for such combinations, so the counts below describe them and not all deaths involving MDMA. Among the 19, by editors' tally, blood held methamphetamine or amphetamine in 15, antidepressants in 13 (moclobemide in 4, others in 9), opioids in 12 (methadone, codeine and morphine in 5 each, tramadol in 1, and 6-MAM, a marker of heroin, in 3, so some opioids may not have been medicines), benzodiazepines in 8, paracetamol or ibuprofen in 4, cannabis in 5 and alcohol in 3; a benzodiazepine or an opioid was present in 14. Doctors or paramedics noted signs of serotonin toxicity before death in 3 of the 4 moclobemide cases (postmortem blood MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L); in other cases the authors think it more likely that it was overlooked or could not be diagnosed, which the data cannot show. Drug toxicity alone was recorded as the cause of death in 12 of the 19, injury plus drug toxicity in 2, and other causes (drowning, train impact, blood loss, hanging, carbon monoxide) in 5. Where the medicines came from was mostly unknown; in two moclobemide cases witnesses suggested a friend or family member. A narrative review reports, second-hand, 75 UK deaths attributed to ecstasy in 1997 to 2000 in which other drugs, mainly opiates and sedatives, were also found in 93 in 100 (Schifano et al., as summarized by Parrott, 2004). The limits are that a blood test after death cannot show who took what, when, how much or why, concentrations can change after death and are not doses, the series is one Australian state, and the risk groups follow a drug-information database and the authors' judgment.
plain: In one Australian study of 106 deaths with MDMA in the blood (2002 to 2008), 19 (about 18 in 100) also had a combination of drugs that the authors rated as risky. MDMA in the blood does not by itself show that MDMA caused a death: 6 in 10 of the 106 died of injuries such as hanging or a crash. Among those 19, 15 also had methamphetamine or amphetamine, 13 an antidepressant, 12 an opioid and 8 a benzodiazepine. Four had moclobemide, an antidepressant of the MAO-inhibitor type, and three of those four showed signs of serotonin toxicity before they died. These 19 were picked for risky mixes, so the numbers do not show how common any mix is in deaths with MDMA. A blood test after death cannot show who took what, when or why, and where the medicines came from was mostly unknown. A second-hand report of 75 UK deaths found other drugs, mostly opiates and sedatives, in 93 in 100.
population: People who died in Victoria, Australia, in 2002 to 2008 with MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood (106 of 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology; 78% male, median age 25, 60% death by external injury), of whom 19 (14 men, ages 21 to 45) were examined in detail; plus 75 UK deaths attributed to ecstasy in 1997 to 2000, second-hand
exposure: MDMA found in blood together with other drugs or medicines, grouped by the authors' rating of interaction risk (major: moclobemide; moderate: dothiepin, amphetamines, tramadol, venlafaxine, cocaine, methadone, fluoxetine; minor: doxylamine and some SSRIs)
comparator: The other 87 cases in the series (MDMA alone or with MDA, with alcohol, or with drugs unlikely to cause a reaction); no comparison with deaths without MDMA or with living people who took MDMA
outcome: Which other drugs and medicines were found in postmortem blood in the 19 cases, and the recorded cause of death
magnitude: Series: 106 deaths with blood MDMA above 0.02 mg/L among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology, 2002-2008; 83 (78%) men, ages 17-48 (median 25), 64 (60%) external injury. Of the 106: MDMA alone or with MDA 20 (about 19 in 100, editors' arithmetic), with ethanol 34 (32), with other drugs unlikely to cause a reaction 33 (31), examined in detail 19 (18). The 19 (14 men, ages 21-45, median 28): group 1 major 4 (all moclobemide; MDMA 1.0-2.6 mg/L, median 1.85; serotonin toxicity signs noted before death in 3), group 2 moderate 10 (MDMA 0.02-3.5, median 0.07), group 3 minor 5 (MDMA 0.2-1.4, median 0.2). Editors' tally of Table II, cases with at least one substance: methamphetamine or amphetamine 15; antidepressant 13 (moclobemide 4, other 9); opioid 12 (11 without 6-MAM); benzodiazepine or metabolite 8; benzodiazepine or opioid 14; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; cannabis 5; ethanol 3. Cause of death: drug toxicity alone 12, injury plus drug toxicity 2, other 5. Second-hand (Parrott, 2004, Table 3): 75 UK deaths attributed to ecstasy 1997-2000, other drugs also in 93% of cases, mainly opiates and sedatives. No intervals; the 19 are an author-selected subset, so no rate of any combination can be derived.

evidence.locator: Methods, Toxicological analysis (1st and 2nd paragraphs), Cohort selection, Data analysis, and Table I (p. 220)
evidence.extracted: Cases came from the Australian National Coroners Information System: all closed Victorian cases between January 2002 and December 2008 with a positive, quantified MDMA result above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood (femoral vein blood where possible, to limit redistribution). Toxicology used immunoassay screening and confirmation by gas chromatography with mass spectrometry, with a lower limit of quantitation for MDMA of 0.02 mg/L. The authors assessed each case's other drugs and the likelihood of a toxic reaction, including the risk of serotonin toxicity. Table I groups the drugs found: major interaction, moclobemide (a reversible MAO-A inhibitor; hypertensive crisis and serotonin toxicity); moderate interaction, dothiepin (a tricyclic antidepressant), amphetamine and derivatives (amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDA, MDEA), tramadol, venlafaxine and cocaine (serotonin toxicity), and methadone and fluoxetine (CYP2D6 inhibitors, raising MDMA concentrations); minor interaction, doxylamine and the SSRIs citalopram, sertraline and fluvoxamine.

evidence.locator: Methods, Data analysis, the paragraphs beginning 'Cases demonstrating a risk of ST' and ''Major' interactions were those' (p. 223); Results, Basic characteristics, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 223)
evidence.extracted: Cases showing a risk of serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction were examined more closely, and other cases (MDMA alone, or with drugs unlikely to produce a reaction) were excluded from further investigation because the cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only. Cases were grouped as major, moderate or minor interaction by risk of drug toxicity from a drug-information database and other references; fluoxetine and paroxetine were counted as moderate because their strong inhibition of the enzyme CYP2D6 can raise MDMA concentrations, and the weak inhibition by sertraline and citalopram was taken as unlikely to contribute to a fatal reaction. Results: 106 cases between 2002 and 2008 with quantified MDMA above the minimum level, among 14,682 coroners' cases that had full toxicological testing; 83 (78%) were male and 64 (60%) died by external injury (for example hangings, motor vehicle crashes); ages 17 to 48, median 25. Of the 106, 4 were a major risk, 10 moderate and 5 minor (Table II); these 19 were examined in detail. The other 87 were MDMA alone or with MDA as metabolite (20), MDMA with ethanol (34) or MDMA with other drugs not likely to cause an adverse drug reaction (33).
evidence.quote: this cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only

evidence.locator: Table II, the 19 cases (pp. 221-223): columns Cause of Death and Autopsy Findings and Postmortem Blood Drug Concentration
evidence.extracted: Table II lists each of the 19 cases by group with sex and age, cause of death and autopsy findings, the drugs found in postmortem blood with concentrations, and the specimen site and postmortem interval. Group 1 (cases 1 to 4): all four had moclobemide. Groups 2 (cases 5 to 14) and 3 (cases 15 to 19) held, besides the drugs that defined the group, combinations of methamphetamine, amphetamine, opioids (codeine, morphine, methadone, tramadol, 6-MAM), benzodiazepines and their metabolites (diazepam, alprazolam, temazepam, oxazepam, nordiazepam, 7-aminoflunitrazepam), other antidepressants (dothiepin, venlafaxine, fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, fluvoxamine, mirtazapine), paracetamol, ibuprofen, cannabis (THC) and ethanol, and in single cases ketamine, p-methoxyamphetamine, olanzapine, metoclopramide and frusemide. Editors' tally of the table's rows, cases with at least one: methamphetamine or amphetamine 15 (methamphetamine 14, amphetamine 7); antidepressant 13 (moclobemide 4, others 9); opioid 12 (11 without 6-MAM; methadone 5, codeine 5, morphine 5, tramadol 1, 6-MAM 3); benzodiazepine or metabolite 8 (cases 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, 19); benzodiazepine or opioid 14; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; cannabis 5; ethanol 3; blood MDMA 0.05 mg/L or less in 5 cases (6, 8, 9, 13, 14). Cause of death: drug toxicity alone in 12 (cases 1-5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 19), injury plus combined drug toxicity in 2 (13, 17), and drowning, train impact, hemorrhagic shock, hanging or carbon monoxide poisoning in the other 5.

evidence.locator: Results, Toxicology findings in the 19 cases of interest, 1st paragraph (begins p. 223, ends p. 224), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 224)
evidence.extracted: The 19 cases were mostly male (14), aged 21 to 45 (median 28). The four Group 1 cases all involved moclobemide, with postmortem blood MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L (median 1.85); clinical symptoms of serotonin toxicity were reported by a paramedic or physician in three of them (cases 1 to 3). Group 2 (10 cases) had fluoxetine, venlafaxine, methadone, dothiepin and tramadol with MDMA, and also paramethoxyamphetamine and methamphetamine, with MDMA 0.02 to 3.5 mg/L (median 0.07). Group 3 (5 cases) involved citalopram, fluvoxamine, sertraline and/or doxylamine, with MDMA 0.2 to 1.4 mg/L (median 0.2).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph and the paragraph beginning 'In this cohort, ST was reported'
evidence.extracted: Four cases involved moclobemide with MDMA, a combination associated with serotonin toxicity; the authors note that moclobemide was originally marketed as a safer alternative to older MAO inhibitors and that a search across Australia would probably find more such deaths. Serotonin toxicity was reported from symptoms witnessed before death in three cases (1 to 3); despite the possibility in many other cases, including moderate-risk cases with serotonin-active drugs, it was not reported. The authors consider it more likely that it was overlooked, or that the lack of symptoms before death (for example when the person was found dead) prevented a diagnosis, than that it did not occur.

evidence.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'In the Copeland et al. study' (begins p. 224, ends p. 225); Limitations paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 225)
evidence.extracted: In many postmortem cases the source of the drugs, licit or illicit, remains unknown unless a medicolegal investigation specifies it, which was unusual here; witness statements in a number of cases, including two of the moclobemide cases with fatal serotonin toxicity, suggested that the person may have obtained the medicines from a friend or family member. Limitations the authors state: postmortem redistribution may alter drug concentrations (some specimens were taken days after death, for example six days in case 18, or from non-peripheral sites such as cavity blood in case 10); missing information, including the source of the drugs (prescribing information) and clinical data such as temperature; people are usually found dead, so symptoms go unreported; and concentrations of drugs that produce tolerance, such as morphine, are hard to interpret. Conclusions: some people who use ecstasy may combine pharmaceutical drugs to strengthen the effect or ease the comedown, but this appeared to be a limited practice in Victoria in 2002-2008; people taking medicines for treatment who occasionally use ecstasy are at risk, particularly if unaware of interactions; many of the deaths were apparently unintentional drug toxicity, so knowledge of these interactions is likely to be limited.

evidence.locator: Table 3, Schifano et al. (2003) row (p. 237)
evidence.extracted: Parrott's Table 3, as summarized: Schifano et al. (2003), UK 1997-2000, toxicological analyses of 75 deaths attributed to ecstasy, XTC, MDMA or MDA: 91% MDMA, 9% MDA, other drugs also found in 93% of cases, mainly opiates and sedatives.

risk_of_bias.note: A case series: the 19 were selected by the authors for drug combinations they rated as risky, and the medicines were found in postmortem blood, which cannot show who took what or when; no comparison group.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: one series and one second-hand row that point the same way.

indirectness.note: The question is what else is found in deaths involving MDMA; the series answers it only for a selected subset of 106 deaths in one state, and the second series comes second-hand.

imprecision.note: 19 cases, no intervals, no denominators for any combination.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive case series starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level, and the result is very low. Status single-study: one primary series, with a second-hand row from a narrative review that points the same way. Stays at draft because it rests on a case series and a narrative review (brief; METHODS 6.3, 12). The claim describes what was found together in a selected set of deaths, not how common any mix is, and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Rests on one case series (Pilgrim et al., 2011) and one second-hand row from Parrott (2004). Stays at draft as the brief asks for case reports. Related ground is covered by the claim on voluntary reports of ecstasy with prescribed medicines (cl_mdma_medicine_reports, Reader 51), which the editor may join with this one. The abstract of the paper says 43 (41%) cases involved other drugs, but its Results give 19 + 33 = 52; the text counts four cases with pulmonary oedema against five in Table II and names chlorpromazine and chlorpheniramine, which no table lists; 'opioids' include 6-MAM (a heroin marker) in 3 cases and morphine and codeine that may come from heroin or from medicines. Schifano et al. (2003, BMJ), Silins et al. (2007; a reference record exists), Copeland et al. (2006) and Cohen et al. (2021) were not read here.

statement: In 166 healthy, screened adults aged 18 to 45 who took MDMA in a hospital research unit in Basel (nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies from one laboratory), a single dose raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo in the same people over the next 6 hours. At 125 mg (136 people) the average highest systolic pressure was 157 mm Hg against 133 on placebo, the average highest heart rate 95 beats a minute against 76, and the average highest ear temperature 37.7 degrees Celsius against 37.4. Systolic pressure went above 160 mm Hg in 38 in 100 people against 6 in 100 on placebo, and above 180 in 5 in 100 against none; heart rate went above 100 in 33 in 100 against 2; ear temperature went above 38 degrees in 24 in 100 against 9 (editors' calculation: with MDMA, 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38). The highest values were 196 mm Hg systolic, 145 beats a minute and 39.1 degrees; the paper reports no temperature above 40 degrees, no hypertensive urgency and no other sign of a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, shortness of breath, nosebleed). At 75 mg (30 people) the rises were smaller (systolic 145 against 131 mm Hg; temperature 37.2 against 37.0, not marked as significant); that comparison is between different people in different studies, and the difference between doses was significant for blood pressure but not for heart rate or temperature. Peaks came on average 1.7 to 2.4 hours after the dose. Laboratory studies from several groups, as summarized in a narrative review (second-hand), report a temperature rise that grows with dose (+0.1, +0.4 and +0.7 degrees on average at doses up to 1.0, 1.1 to 1.9 and 2.0 mg/kg), and one of 13 volunteers in an earlier study had a brief hypertensive crisis (240/145 mm Hg for 20 minutes). These sessions differ from real life: people rested, with a research assistant present, in a room at about 22.7 degrees Celsius; they took MDMA of known amount and no other drug, were healthy, four in five were new to MDMA, and no one took a second dose in the same session. Heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs, pills of unknown content and extra doses were not tested, and the study was too small to rule out events as frequent as 1 in 100 (for no temperature above 40 degrees in 278 sessions, the 95% interval runs from 0 to 1.3 in 100). Four people reported no effect of the drug and were left out of the analysis of when the felt effects began and ended; the paper does not say what their blood pressure, heart rate or temperature did. Everyone was given a fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in separate claims); the authors, citing earlier studies, argue that effects fade while MDMA is still in the body (acute tolerance) and that adding more may not lengthen the effect but may add adverse effects, which is their reading and not a result of this analysis.
plain: In a hospital laboratory, healthy young volunteers took one dose of MDMA and, on another day, a dummy pill. With MDMA (125 mg in the study) their blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature went higher than with the dummy pill. About 38 in 100 had a top blood-pressure number above 160, against 6 in 100 on the dummy pill; about 33 in 100 had a heart rate above 100, against 2 in 100; and about 24 in 100 had an ear temperature above 38 degrees, against 9 in 100. The highest temperature was 39.1 degrees. At a lower dose (75 mg) the rises were smaller, but that comparison used different people. The volunteers rested in a room at about 23 degrees with a staff member, took one pure dose and nothing else, and were healthy. Heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra doses were not tested. Four people felt no effect; the study does not say what their bodies did, and nobody took more.
population: 166 healthy adults aged 18 to 45 (equal numbers of women and men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA), psychiatrically screened, mostly recruited on a university campus and paid, in nine studies at one hospital in Basel: 30 people in the 75 mg study and 136 in the 125 mg studies
exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, taken at rest in a research unit with a research assistant present, room temperature 22.7 (SD 0.6) degrees Celsius (study conditions: 75 mg in 30 people; 125 mg in 136 people, 112 of whom took 125 mg a second time at least seven days later after a pretreatment medicine, a session not analysed here)
comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover); for the 75 against 125 mg contrast, different people in different studies
outcome: Highest blood pressure, heart rate and ear (tympanic) temperature in the 6 hours after the dose, and the number of people whose highest value crossed a clinical line (systolic above 160 or 180 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 beats a minute, temperature above 38 or 40 degrees Celsius)
magnitude: 125 mg (n = 136), average of each person's highest value in 6 hours, MDMA against placebo (SD): systolic 157 (15) against 133 (15) mm Hg; diastolic 93 (10) against 79 (8); heart rate 95 (17) against 76 (12) beats a minute; ear temperature 37.7 (0.5) against 37.4 (0.5) degrees Celsius; drug effect p < 0.001 for each. People above the line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 mm Hg 51 (38%) against 8 (6%); >180 7 (5%) against 0; heart rate >100 45 (33%) against 3 (2%); temperature >38 32 (24%) against 12 (9%). Highest single values: 196 against 175 mm Hg, 145 against 117 beats a minute, 39.1 against 38.7 degrees. 75 mg (n = 30): systolic 145 (14) against 131 (11); diastolic 84 (8) against 77 (5); heart rate 83 (17) against 69 (9); temperature 37.2 (0.3) against 37.0 (0.3), no significance mark; >160 mm Hg 3 (10%) against 0; heart rate >100 3 (10%) against 0; temperature >38 none. Dose-by-drug tests: systolic F 15.2 and diastolic F 17.9 (p < 0.001); heart rate F 2.38 and temperature F 2.43 (not significant). All 166 sessions: systolic >160 in 54 (33%), >180 in 7 (4%); heart rate >100 in 48 (29%); temperature >38 in 32 (19%); no temperature above 40 and no hypertensive urgency. Editors' calculation: at 125 mg, 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38 degrees with MDMA than on placebo. Laboratory studies summarized in a narrative review: peak rise in core temperature +0.1 (doses up to 1.0 mg/kg), +0.4 (1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg), +0.7 (2.0 mg/kg).

evidence.locator: Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph; Methods > Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph (p. 577, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies, all at the University Hospital Basel, in 166 psychiatrically screened, healthy European or Caucasian adults aged 18 to 45 (mean 24.5, SD 4), mostly recruited on the university campus and paid, equal numbers of women and men. 30 people took a single 75 mg dose; 136 took 125 mg (24 once; 112 twice, once alone and once after another drug, at least seven days apart, the pretreatment sessions being analysed separately). This paper analyses the 166 sessions of MDMA alone against placebo. Exclusions: psychiatric disorder, physical illness, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted), any in the last two months or during the study (urine tests before sessions). Fifty-nine people had tried a drug 1 to 5 times, 34 of them MDMA 1 to 4 times. The study drug was MDMA hydrochloride from a pharmaceutical supplier, in capsules.

evidence.locator: Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph (4 people left out of the timing analysis) and 2nd paragraph; Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph, 4th sentence on (doses not adjusted for body weight or sex) (p. 578, left column)
evidence.extracted: Four people reported no subjective drug effect and were left out of the analysis of when effects began and ended; the paper does not say what their blood pressure, heart rate or temperature did. Blood pressure and heart rate were measured in duplicate by an automatic oscillometric device after at least 10 minutes of rest, and temperature in the ear (tympanic thermometer), before the dose and at 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours; in the 75 mg study the 0.33 and 2.5 hour temperature points are missing, and in one 125 mg study (24 people) the 2 hour point. Lines used: systolic above 140, 160 and 180 mm Hg; diastolic above 90, 100 and 110; heart rate above 100 beats a minute; temperature above 38 degrees Celsius (hyperthermia) and 40 (hyperpyrexia). The dose was not adjusted for body weight or sex.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, one paragraph (p. 580, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: MDMA alone raised blood pressure, heart rate and body temperature (Table 2). Over the 166 sessions: systolic above 160 mm Hg in 54 people (33%) and above 180 in 7 (4%); heart rate above 100 in forty-eight people (29%); ear temperature above 38 degrees Celsius in 32 (19%), up to 39.1. Highest values 130 diastolic and 196 systolic; no hypertensive urgency and no temperature above 40 (the highest among all 278 sessions, with or without a pretreatment, was 39.1). Systolic pressure, heart rate and temperature peaked on average 1.7 (SD 0.9), 2.0 (SD 1.4) and 2.4 (SD 1.2) hours after the dose. The mean room temperature was 22.7 (SD 0.6) degrees Celsius. A significant dose-response effect was found for blood pressure but not for heart rate or temperature; the shares above 160 mm Hg, above 100 beats and above 38 degrees were higher at 125 than at 75 mg (p < 0.01, p < 0.05 and p < 0.01).

evidence.locator: Table 2, 125 mg block (n = 136): blood pressure, heart rate and temperature rows, MDMA and placebo columns, and the Drug column (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: Average of each person's highest value in 6 hours, MDMA against placebo, mean (SD): systolic 157 (15) against 133 (15) mm Hg; diastolic 93 (10) against 79 (8); heart rate 95 (17) against 76 (12) beats a minute; temperature 37.7 (0.5) against 37.4 (0.5) degrees Celsius; drug effect p < 0.001 for each (F 486, 292, 267 and 44.4). People above each line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 51 (38%) against 8 (6%); >180 7 (5%) against 0; heart rate >100 45 (33%) against 3 (2%); temperature >38 32 (24%) against 12 (9%). Highest single values, MDMA against placebo: systolic 196 against 175 mm Hg; heart rate 145 against 117 beats a minute; temperature 39.1 against 38.7 degrees. Editors' calculation from the printed percentages: with MDMA 32, 31 and 15 more in 100 people crossed the lines for systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 and temperature above 38 degrees than on placebo.

evidence.locator: Table 2, 75 mg block (n = 30): blood pressure, heart rate and temperature rows, MDMA and placebo columns (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: Average of each person's highest value in 6 hours, MDMA against placebo, mean (SD): systolic 145 (14) against 131 (11) mm Hg; diastolic 84 (8) against 77 (5); heart rate 83 (17) against 69 (9) beats a minute; temperature 37.2 (0.3) against 37.0 (0.3) degrees Celsius, the temperature difference carrying no significance mark in the table. People above each line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 3 (10%) against 0; >180 none; heart rate >100 3 (10%) against 0; temperature >38 none against none. Highest single values, MDMA against placebo: systolic 176 against 153 mm Hg; heart rate 134 against 95; temperature 37.6 against 37.7 degrees.

evidence.locator: Table 2, the Drug x dose columns (F and p); Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: Drug-by-dose interaction (the 75 against 125 mg contrast): systolic F 15.2 and diastolic F 17.9, both p < 0.001; heart rate F 2.38 and temperature F 2.43, both not significant. The 75 and 125 mg groups are different people in different studies. Average highest temperature on placebo was 37.0 (SD 0.3) in the 75 mg study and 37.4 (SD 0.5) in the 125 mg studies. Four in five of the participants had never taken MDMA before, and the rest had very limited experience (at most four earlier exposures).

evidence.locator: Discussion > 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 584, right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors read the vital-sign changes, in people at rest, as similar to moderate physical activity; transient systolic pressure above 180 mm Hg was seen in 5% of those given 125 mg, with no other sign of a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, shortness of breath or nosebleed); an earlier analysis of 74 people from laboratory studies had found systolic pressure at or above 160 in 32% and at or above 180 in 9%. Temperatures did not rise above 39.1 degrees Celsius. No controlled clinical study of MDMA has reported a temperature above 40, which the authors suggest may be because participants had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded place, unlike some recreational settings.

evidence.locator: Discussion > 2nd paragraph (p. 584, left column)
evidence.extracted: Onset of effects 33 minutes, peak 1.6 hours, duration 4.2 hours; the 75 and 125 mg doses did not differ in how long effects lasted. The authors attribute the short duration of effect, compared with the long time MDMA stays in the blood, to acute pharmacological tolerance, so that effects decline while MDMA is still in the body, and argue that adding more MDMA might not relevantly prolong the effect and may increase adverse effects (citing a separate study of second doses). This is their interpretation, not a result of this study: every session used a fixed dose.

evidence.locator: Discussion > 'The present safety data' paragraph (research assistant) and 'The present study has limitations' paragraph (p. 585, right column)
evidence.extracted: A research assistant was always present with the participants in the laboratory, similar to a therapy session. Only psychiatrically healthy, mostly young people were included. Blood sodium was not assessed. The sample (166 sessions of MDMA alone, 278 with or without a pretreatment) was too small to exclude infrequent (0.1 to 1%) or rare (under 0.1%) adverse events; with no temperature above 40 degrees Celsius in 278 sessions, the 95% interval allows up to 1.3%.

evidence.locator: Table 1, the 'Overall Mean' rows (p. 3); Section 8 > Overview, 1st paragraph (p. 7, right column)
evidence.extracted: In the review's table of placebo-controlled laboratory studies (several research groups; 4 to 16 volunteers per study; oral, ear, armpit and swallowed-sensor temperatures; doses given per kilogram or in mg), the peak rise in core temperature averaged +0.1 degrees Celsius at doses up to 1.0 mg/kg, +0.4 at 1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg. The review says the rise was related to dose, with low doses having minimal effects. Second-hand: a narrative review of small studies, not read in the original.

evidence.locator: Section 2 > Body temperature in laboratory studies, paragraphs on Vollenweider et al. (1998) and Mas et al. (1999) (p. 2, right column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: of 13 volunteers given 1.7 mg/kg by mouth (Vollenweider and colleagues), one had a brief hypertensive crisis (240/145 mmHg) lasting 20 minutes; in 8 men with earlier MDMA experience given 75 mg and 125 mg (Mas and colleagues) the peak rise in temperature was +0.4 degrees Celsius at both doses, about 2 hours after the dose, the review being unsure whether the peak was significant.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 is high overall on the card only because of the 75 against 125 mg contrast (different people in different studies, not randomised). The MDMA against placebo comparison in the same people, on which the claim rests, is at worst some concerns: the order of sessions is not described, blinding probably did not hold at 125 mg, some temperature time points are missing, and about 60 outcomes were tested without correction. The main outcomes are device readings and the effects are large (F 44 to 486), so one level, not two.

inconsistency.note: Nine studies from one laboratory agree; laboratory studies from other groups, seen second-hand, agree in direction for temperature. The dose difference is significant for blood pressure and not for heart rate or temperature, which the claim states.

indirectness.note: The claim is worded for healthy, screened volunteers at rest in a cool room and says that heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs and extra doses were not tested.

imprecision.note: 166 people; the 125 mg comparison with placebo separates clearly (SDs and F tests). The 75 mg group is small (30) and is described as such; no intervals are printed.

publication_bias.note: Nine registered studies, one unpublished, pooled by the team that ran them; no sign of selective omission.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that a single dose of 125 mg raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo in healthy volunteers at rest. The shares above each line are descriptive: they count people whose highest of many readings crossed a line, and 9 in 100 placebo sessions also crossed 38 degrees, so the lines show how many people went over them and not a threshold of harm. The 75 against 125 mg contrast rests on different people in different studies and is not tested for heart rate and temperature; the paper's abstract and Conclusion call all three shares significantly greater at 125 mg, and this claim follows the tests instead. Status replicated by the same team: nine studies, one laboratory and one analysis model; other groups are seen only second-hand through a narrative review. The claim gives no advice, does not say whether the changes are harmful, and does not generalise to settings that were not tested.

verification.flag_note: Other groups' laboratory studies (Vollenweider 1998, Mas 1999, Tancer 2003, Freedman 2005, Kolbrich 2008) have no reference record here and are seen only through a narrative review (Parrott, 2012); the pooled studies share one laboratory, hence replicated by the same team. The paper's Conclusion calls single-dose MDMA safe in healthy people in a controlled setting, which is broader than its data (heat, activity and crowding excluded; events under about 1 in 100 not excluded); the claim does not use it. The paper's recommendation of a fixed dose for women rests on comparing different studies and is not used. Table 2's 75 mg and 125 mg blocks come from different studies with different placebo temperatures (37.0 and 37.4). The repeated-dose laboratory studies are covered by the library's separate claim on repeated doses.
