statement: What makes body temperature rise more after MDMA is not settled. This claim rests on one narrative review (Parrott, 2012) of small studies, so its figures are second-hand and given as summarized by the review. In placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers each, the review puts the average peak rise in core temperature at +0.1 degrees Celsius at doses up to 1.0 mg/kg, +0.4 at 1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg, from studies using different body sites; in the one study of 8 men that gave 75 mg and 125 mg, the peak was +0.4 at both. In two small studies at 2.0 mg/kg in rooms at 18 and 30 degrees, the rise was +1.0 and +0.8 in 4 volunteers and +0.4 and +0.6 in 10, which the review describes as nearly identical or broadly similar in the two rooms, although its own table of factors lists a high room temperature as associated with a higher core temperature. The rise differs between people: in 8 volunteers the group average was +0.4 but one person peaked at +1.9; at a dance party the two people with the highest MDMA blood levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest rises (+1.0 and +1.6), while across 27 people the link between blood level and rise was borderline (r = +0.38, p = 0.058) and there was no night without MDMA to compare. In studies at dance clubs and parties, of 11 to 41 people each and with different comparisons, group peak rises ranged from +0.2 to +1.6 degrees (+1.8 on the skin in one), the largest in 11 people who took 6 tablets on average over a night; the review reports no comparison within them of amounts, dancing, room heat or crowding. It says data on dancing and on other drugs are very limited, that crowding and loud music have not been investigated, and that hydration, age, sex, genes and personality need to be investigated in people. Overheating to 40 degrees and above, some of it fatal, is known from hospital case reports, which cannot show how often it happens; in a UK report of 7 deaths and 4 further cases of this kind, plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which its authors said did not reflect high doses, and in another case a friend who took the same MDMA had no thermal reaction. How hot people feel also differs: in an Internet survey of over 200 people who take ecstasy, 16 in 100 did not feel hot, 41 slightly, 31 moderately and 12 strongly or extremely, and the review offers as a hypothesis for future study that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; the review notes continuous dancing and bingeing for over 48 hours without sleep in experienced people with greater tolerance, and calls the effects of that currently unknown. In 166 volunteers resting at about 22.7 degrees (a pooled laboratory analysis), 125 mg raised the average highest ear temperature by 0.3 degrees (37.7 against 37.4) and 24 in 100 crossed 38 degrees against 9 in 100 on placebo; the test of a dose effect between 75 and 125 mg was not significant. Those volunteers rested, took one pure dose and were not dancing, crowded or on other drugs, so the laboratory studies cannot show what heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or more MDMA do to temperature, and the party studies cannot separate them either.
plain: Nobody can yet say what makes some people get hotter than others with MDMA. In small lab studies of people at rest, body temperature rose by about 0.4 degrees on average at moderate doses and 0.7 at higher ones, and by 1.9 in one person. At dance parties the average rise ran from 0.2 to 1.6 degrees, but the studies compared different things, so heat, dancing, crowds, other drugs and extra tablets cannot be told apart. Overheating to 40 degrees or more is known from hospital case reports, which cannot show how often it happens. Not everyone feels hot: in one survey 16 in 100 did not. Some people feel little from an amount and take more; what that does to temperature has not been studied. This comes from one review of small studies, so the numbers are second-hand.
population: People given MDMA in placebo-controlled laboratory studies (4 to 16 volunteers each), people studied at dance clubs and house parties (11 to 41 each), and people treated in hospital for severe overheating (case reports and series), all as summarized in one narrative review; the 166 volunteers of one pooled laboratory analysis read in full as a qualifier
exposure: MDMA, by dose in the laboratory (study conditions: up to 1.0, 1.1 to 1.9 and 2.0 mg/kg; 75 and 125 mg) and by tablets taken over a night in party studies (1 to 6 tablets, other drugs sometimes taken); room temperature (18 and 30 degrees Celsius in two studies), dancing, crowding, other drugs and hydration as possible modifiers
comparator: Placebo in laboratory studies; an abstinent weekend, people not taking ecstasy at the same club, the evening before, or no comparison in the party studies
outcome: Peak rise in core temperature (rectal, swallowed sensor, ear, mouth or armpit), in degrees Celsius; severe overheating (40 degrees Celsius and above)
magnitude: Laboratory, peak change in core temperature, average across the studies in the review's table: +0.1 degrees Celsius (doses up to 1.0 mg/kg), +0.4 (1.1 to 1.9 mg/kg), +0.7 (2.0 mg/kg); different body sites, 4 to 16 volunteers per study, no intervals. In one study, 75 mg and 125 mg both +0.4 (8 men). Rooms at 18 and 30 degrees: +1.0 and +0.8 (4 volunteers) and +0.4 and +0.6 (10 volunteers). One study of 8 volunteers: group mean +0.4, highest individual +1.9. Dance clubs and parties, group peak change: +0.2 (27 people), +1.2 (32), +0.3 (12), +1.6 (11, 6 tablets on average), +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41); comparisons differ. One party study: blood level against rise r = +0.38, p = 0.058 (27 people). Internet survey of over 200 people: did not feel hot 16%, slightly 41%, moderately 31%, strongly or extremely 12%. Severe overheating (40 to 43 degrees): case reports and series only, no denominator. Laboratory study read in full, 125 mg against placebo (136 people): average highest ear temperature 37.7 against 37.4, above 38 degrees in 24% against 9%.

evidence.locator: Section 2 > Body temperature in laboratory studies, paragraphs on Tancer et al. (2003) (starting p. 2, right column) and Freedman et al. (2005) (p. 3, left column); Table 3, Sweating/perspiration row (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: 4 volunteers (Tancer and colleagues) and 10 volunteers (Freedman and colleagues) were given 2.0 mg/kg and placebo in rooms at 18 and at 30 degrees Celsius. Core temperature rose +1.0 and +0.8 degrees in the cool and warm rooms in the first study (rectal probes) and +0.4 and +0.6 in the second (swallowed sensor); the review says core temperature values were nearly identical in the two rooms in the first study and that the effects of MDMA were broadly similar under both room conditions in the second. In the second study the onset of sweating was delayed.

evidence.locator: Section 2, paragraph on Kolbrich et al. (2008) (starts p. 3, right column, continues p. 4, left column); Section 3 > Body temperature in dance club studies, 1st paragraph on Irvine et al. (2006) (p. 4, left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: in 8 volunteers given 1.0 and 1.6 mg/kg (Kolbrich and colleagues) the ear-temperature rise after MDMA (+0.3 and +0.4 degrees Celsius; temperature also rose under placebo) was not significantly different from placebo, but the link between blood MDMA and temperature rise was (p < 0.0001). At a dance party, 27 people (Irvine and colleagues) were measured the evening before, at 4 am and at 10 am: the rise was about +0.2 and not significant, there was no control night so the fall of body temperature during the night was not accounted for, 5 people had particularly high blood MDMA, and the two people with the highest levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest individual rises (+1.0 and +1.6 degrees); across the group the link between blood level and rise was borderline (r = +0.38, p = 0.058). Methamphetamine and cannabis were present in 41% and 33% of the group.

evidence.locator: Table 2 (p. 3, right column); Section 3 > Body temperature in dance club studies, paragraphs on Parrott and Young (2005), Parrott et al. (2008) and the third study (Parrott et al., 2007b) (p. 4, right column)
evidence.extracted: Group peak change in temperature at dance clubs and parties, as summarized by the review, with different comparisons: +0.2 degrees Celsius (27 people, no control night); +1.2 (32 people who had taken ecstasy that evening, against 26 controls at the same club who had not); +0.3 (12 people, ecstasy weekend against an abstinent weekend; the difference borderline, p = 0.08); +1.6 (11 people who took 6 tablets on average over a night, at house parties); +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41 people, Morefield and colleagues). Table 2 notes that the control conditions and procedures for statistical analysis varied across studies.

evidence.locator: Section 3, paragraph on Morefield et al. (2009) (starts p. 4, right column, ends p. 5, left column); Section 4 > Clinical hyperthermia and its treatment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 5)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: 41 people at dance parties in Australia took 1 to 5 tablets, 25% had blood levels in the toxic to lethal range by forensic guidelines, and the authors said these high doses were generally well tolerated. Severe overheating is known from case reports and series, with no denominator: 41.6 degrees Celsius 2 hours after 100 to 150 mg of MDMA powder in a woman whose friend took the same MDMA without a thermal reaction; a 16-year-old who took one tablet, her second time, had 0.424 mg/l MDMA and died after 36 hours; a UK poisons-unit report of 7 deaths with admission temperatures of 40 to 43 degrees and 4 further severe cases, in which plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l and the authors said the severe reactions did not reflect high dose levels.

evidence.locator: Table 3 (factors associated with the thermal effects of ecstasy/MDMA): rows on dance clubs, crowding, polydrug aspects, ambient temperature and other factors (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: The review's own table of factors: for dancing, the data are very limited; for crowding and loud music, effects have not been empirically investigated; for stimulant and sedative co-drugs, empirical data are very limited; for age, sex, genes, hydration and personality, they need to be empirically investigated; for the room, a laboratory row says high ambient temperature was associated with higher core temperature with complex combined effects. Dose and plasma level are listed with laboratory support (p < 0.0001 for plasma level) and, in a party study, a borderline correlation (p = 0.058). Editors' note: the text on p. 3 describes the effects as broadly similar at 18 and 30 degrees Celsius.

evidence.locator: Section 5 > Thermal self-ratings, 2nd paragraph (p. 6, left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review: in an Internet survey of over 200 people who take ecstasy (Parrott and colleagues, 2006), 16% said they did not feel hot when on MDMA, 41% felt slightly hot, 31% moderately hot and 12% strongly or extremely hot, which the review takes as showing wide variation in how hot people feel.

evidence.locator: Section 7 > Behavioural and environmental co-stressors, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 7, left column into right column); Section 8 > Overview, 1st paragraph (p. 7, right column)
evidence.extracted: The review says some people dance continuously and binge on MDMA for more than 48 hours without sleep, especially experienced people with greater tolerance, and that the effects of these periods are currently unknown. It lists as factors that would increase thermal stress higher single doses or successive binge doses, prolonged dancing, and crowded clubs with high ambient temperatures (citing surveys and observations), and says hydration needs to be investigated in people. It puts forward as a hypothesis for future study that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk. In the Overview, in 8 volunteers given 1.6 mg/kg (Kolbrich and colleagues) the group mean rise was +0.4 degrees Celsius but one volunteer peaked at +1.9.
evidence.quote: those with low thermal awareness might be most at risk from developing severe hyperthermia

evidence.locator: Table 2, 125 mg block (n = 136), temperature rows, and the Drug x dose columns (p. 582)
evidence.extracted: In the laboratory at rest, 125 mg of MDMA raised the average highest ear temperature from 37.4 (SD 0.5) on placebo to 37.7 (SD 0.5); 32 of 136 people (24%) went above 38 degrees on MDMA and 12 (9%) on placebo; the highest value was 39.1 against 38.7. The test of a dose effect on temperature between 75 and 125 mg (different people in different studies) was not significant (F 2.43).

evidence.locator: Discussion > 4th paragraph (p. 584, right column)
evidence.extracted: Temperatures did not rise above 39.1 degrees Celsius. The authors call a temperature above 40 rare and the most important life-threatening complication of recreational MDMA use, say no controlled clinical study has reported it, and suggest this may be because participants had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded place.

risk_of_bias.note: The review's methods are a personal collection of papers plus a PubMed search, and it cannot be appraised for bias (narrative review; high on the card on the editors' five-domain checklist). Its party studies lack comparable controls: no control night in one, a different comparison group in each of the others.

inconsistency.note: Party-study peaks run from +0.2 to +1.6 degrees Celsius with different comparisons and no explanation; the review's table says a warm room goes with a higher core temperature while its text says the effects were broadly similar.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through one review; most primary studies are not in the library. Laboratory studies at rest do not bear on dancing, crowding or heat, and party studies do not separate them.

imprecision.note: Samples of 4 to 41 people, no intervals; the large individual differences (+1.9 in one of 8) show that group means hide the spread.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: A claim seen only through a narrative review starts from the design of the primary studies the review describes (small placebo-controlled laboratory studies, uncontrolled party studies, case reports) and is downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness (METHODS 6.3). Observational start (low); down four levels in all (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision), bounded at very low. Relation: evidence is insufficient to say whether dose, heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or hydration change the rise, because no study separates them and the review says so itself. Status mixed: party studies disagree in size without an explanation, and the review's table and text disagree about room temperature. Draft: the claim rests only on a narrative review (METHODS 6.3); the pooled laboratory analysis read in full is a qualifying anchor, and the single quotation is the review's hypothesis, which it marks as untested.

verification.flag_note: Review-only claim. The primary papers (Grob 1996, Vollenweider 1998, Mas 1999, Tancer 2003, Freedman 2005, Irvine 2006, Parrott and Young 2005, Parrott 2007b and 2008, Kolbrich 2008, Morefield 2009, Henry 1992, Chadwick 1991, Brown and Osterloh 1987, Patel 2005) have no reference record here and were not read; their numbers are the review's. The review's Table 1 'overall mean' rows average studies that used different body sites and different dose units, and Table 2's comparisons differ by study. The review's Table 3 says a high room temperature goes with a higher core temperature; its text (p. 3) says the effects were broadly similar at 18 and 30 degrees.

statement: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. A later narrative review (Faria et al., 2020; second-hand, PubMed searched to October 2019 with one author mainly responsible) has 52 table rows about phenethylamine-associated cases, 50 labelled MDMA, and 21 outcomes labelled death. The 36 rows with sodium have lowest values 101–130 mmol/L; one of those rows also reports an earlier value 137, not an extra case. Two pairs of rows appear to repeat cases, although the primary reports were not read; one case cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper; three fatal rows report neither a numeric sodium result nor hyponatraemia among their effect labels; and one outcome is blank despite a death in the cited title. The authorless 2001 case is traceable, while another row's compound label conflicts with its reference title. Ten fatal rows come from the California series, so the review must not be added to it as an independent 52-person series. Amounts are unknown or blank in 30 rows, including 14 of 21 fatal rows. The review's single-dose statement is restricted to most reported deaths or permanent neurological injuries in women aged 15–30; its table cannot verify that statement. In the 10 fatal rows with sodium, values 109–126 mmol/L lie within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in the 24 recovery rows with sodium (editors' counts). The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. Faria also proposes sodium loss in sweat, while describing the drinking reports as anecdotal and the mechanisms as not fully understood. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, and the 2020 review bases its drinking discussion on anecdotal reports, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017).
plain: After MDMA, some young people have been treated in hospital because the salt (sodium) in their blood fell too low, causing fits and swelling of the brain. It started within hours of taking MDMA. In a UK group of 17 people aged 15 to 26, at least 10 had drunk a lot of fluid, and two died: both had taken one tablet, had been drinking a lot of water, and drank or were given more water after they felt ill. In California, 73 of 188 people who had their sodium measured had a low level, and 4 of them died. These are reports of people who became ill, so they cannot show how often it happens. Most of the UK group had taken one or two tablets, and no study has compared amounts. The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water; that part is not proven.
population: Mostly young people who became ill after taking ecstasy (MDMA) and came to a poison service or hospital: 17 patients aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (1993 to 1996); 545 poison-centre cases in California in 2000 to 2005 (mean age 21), 188 of them with a measured sodium; and published case reports as described in two narrative reviews (more than 25 reports to 2008; 52 tabulated cases to 2018, with errors)
exposure: MDMA sold as ecstasy tablets, content unknown (MDMA confirmed by laboratory tests in 8 of the 15 UK survivors and in both who died; in California by history, with urine screens in 103 of 188 and no specific method), with fluid intake recorded only for some: a large amount in 10 of the 17 UK patients; stated amounts of half a tablet to three tablets in 13 UK survivors; one published case took five tablets (study conditions as reported, not recommendations)
comparator: None for the UK series and the case reports; in California, cases with a sodium of 130 mmol/L or more or reported as normal (115 of 188)
outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L, seizures, coma, brain swelling, death, and the temperature recorded at hospital
magnitude: UK poisons service, 17 patients over 28 months (Hartung): day 1 sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l; symptoms within 12 hours of the drug in all; large fluid intake known in 10 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died), history not available for 5 of the 15; seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; 13 of the 15 recorded as recovering completely; temperature at hospital normal in 12 of 15 (37.5 in two, 34.8 in one); 12 of 13 with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to 3); 6 with biochemistry typical of excess antidiuretic hormone; 2 deaths (aged 15 and 18, both female, one tablet each, blood MDMA 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l, temperature 32.6 and 33 degrees Celsius at hospital). California poison control, 545 included cases 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson): sodium recorded in 188 (34.5%); below 130 mmol/L in 73 (about 39 in 100; the text once says 74), median 122 (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124); 13 deaths in 545 (2.4%), 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT and low blood pressure needing medicines; hyperthermia in 40 of 545 (7.3%), odds ratio for hyperthermia with low sodium against without 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; rave party the recorded site for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of 74 low-sodium cases. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 25 case reports, sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L; 32 tabulated cases, 16 deaths. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: Table 3 has 52 rows (1991–2018), not verified unique cases: 46 female, 21 labelled deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown and 1 blank outcome. Lowest sodium in 36 rows is 101–130 mmol/L, including one with an earlier value 137; 10 fatal rows have 109–126, within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in 24 recovery rows. Amount is unknown/blank in 30 rows, including 14/21 fatal rows. Probable duplicates, citation mismatches and unconfirmed fatal low-sodium labels limit interpretation; 10 fatal rows overlap the California series. No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.

evidence.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, last paragraph (p. 434, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: Retrospective series. All documented telephone enquiries to the London centre of the UK National Poisons Information Service from December 1993 to November 1995 were screened for MDMA use complicated by serum sodium below 130 mmol/l, advice cases to March 1996 were added, and a further fatal case was included. Of a mean 13 762 enquiries a month, 135 (1.0%) concerned ecstasy; over the 28-month study period 17 cases were identified (0.4% of all enquiries about ecstasy, a share of telephone calls and not a risk): seven male and 10 female, aged 15 to 26. Table 1 covers the 15 who recovered. Analytical confirmation of MDMA ingestion was obtained in eight cases. Eight patients were known to have ingested a large amount of non-alcoholic or alcoholic fluid; for five the history of fluid ingestion was not available. The pattern was uniform: vomiting and disturbed behaviour, then drowsiness, agitation and, in 10 patients, seizures; drowsiness, a mute state and disorientation lasted up to 3 days; clinical findings did not necessarily reflect the size of the fall in sodium; in six patients blood and urine tests were consistent with inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). In the two who died, symptoms of cerebral oedema began within 5 hours of one tablet, and in both an excessive amount of fluid had been drunk.

evidence.locator: Table 1, rows 1 to 15 (the table prints rotated; pp. 432-433)
evidence.extracted: The 15 who recovered. Day 1 serum sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l (lowest 107, highest 128). Amount of MDMA stated for 13: half a tablet (2 patients), 1 tablet (5), 1.25 (1), 1.5 (2), 2 (2), 3 (1); amount unknown for 2. Fluids recorded: beer (3 to 4 pints in one patient, 7 pints in another), soft drinks or water described as an excessive amount in several (13 bottles? in one), wine, lager and gin. Temperature at presentation recorded as normal in 12, 37.5 degrees Celsius in 2 and 34.8 in 1. Seizures (grand mal or tonic) in 10. Outcome: complete recovery recorded for 13 (one of them with pneumonia); difficulty in concentration and poor short-term memory at 2 months in one patient (extradural haematoma and skull fracture on CT), and aspiration pneumonia needing a tracheostomy in one. Editors' count: 12 of the 13 patients with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets; 12 of the 15 had a temperature recorded as normal.

evidence.locator: Table 2, both columns (p. 435)
evidence.extracted: The two deaths, both female and both having taken MDMA before. Patient 1, 15 years: one tablet at midnight; dancing, talking and drinking water (at least 3 litres) in rotation; ill and vomiting at 05.00 and given a considerable amount of water; on arrival GCS 3/15 and temperature 32.6 degrees Celsius; serum sodium 125 mmol/l at 12.00 after 1.5 litres of intravenous fluid in transport and 1 litre of 0.9% saline; diffuse cerebral oedema with herniation; brain dead on day 2; blood MDMA 0.05 mg/l. Patient 2, 18 years: one tablet at 19.45; talking, smoking cannabis, some alcohol, water from 22.00; ill at 00.15 and drank 6 to 7 cups of water, then vomiting, severe headache, loss of vision and rigidity; temperature 33 degrees; serum sodium 126 mmol/l; marked cerebral oedema; brain dead on day 3; blood MDMA 0.209 mg/l, MDA 0.029 mg/l, ethanol 0.8 g/l. The table's footnote says tablets of ecstasy usually contain 50 to 150 mg MDMA.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 434, right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that acute complications after MDMA may be under-reported but are relatively uncommon; that low sodium appears to be a result of water consumption in excess of the body's requirements, compounded by failure of the renal response to water loading; that all patients developed symptoms within 12 hours of taking the drug; and that the nervous-system signs were probably caused by a rapid fall in serum osmolar pressure with movement of water into cells and cerebral oedema, which post-mortem findings confirmed in the two patients who died.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (starts p. 434, right column; continues p. 435, below Table 2; ends p. 436, top of left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that the low sodium appears to involve inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin): in one earlier case plasma arginine vasopressin was inappropriately raised 9 hours after ingestion, and a recent report (not read here) showed a rapid rise in arginine vasopressin after MDMA in eight normally hydrated healthy male volunteers. They add that the mechanism by which MDMA causes this secretion remains to be established, and that acute stress and excessive visual and sound stimuli might contribute, as might nicotine (whether the patients smoked is not known).

evidence.locator: Discussion, the paragraph on early public messages about fluid (p. 436, left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors say that people who took MDMA were at first advised in underground magazines and the lay press to drink plenty of fluids, a message aimed at preventing collapse from overheating; that this did not say a high fluid intake could be harmful without prolonged exertion; and that it was later put right, especially after the publicity about the fatal cases.

evidence.locator: Methods > Methods of Measurement (p. 166, left column); Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results > Characteristics of Study Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 166, right column)
evidence.extracted: California Poison Control System records. 883 cases were excluded (267 treated at home and others), 5 more as miscoded and 3 with no sex recorded, leaving 545. Sodium values were recorded as given by telephone from the referring hospitals and not checked against medical records. Urine screening was documented in 103 of the 188 (54.8%) with a sodium: sixty-eight (66%) positive and 35 (34%) negative for amphetamines or derivatives; the 35 were still counted as MDMA intoxication on the history given. Of the low-sodium cases, 43 (58.9%) had urine screens. Sodium was documented in 188 (34.5%), with an exact value in 134 (71%) and 'normal' in the rest, similarly in women (105; 35%) and men (83; 33%). Among all 545: tachycardia 43%, agitation 32%, seizures 11%, intensive care one hundred fifty-three (28%), 13 deaths (2.4%). 'Rave party' was the site of ingestion for 50 (9.1%), including 3 of the 74 (4.1%) cases of low sodium. The paper reports no fluid-intake figures and no amount of MDMA (editors' reading of the full text).

evidence.locator: Table 1 and Table 2; Results, paragraph on low sodium among the 188 (starts p. 166, right column; ends p. 167, left column)
evidence.extracted: Table 1 (all 545): hyperthermia 40 (7.34%), coma 54 (9.91%), seizure 61 (11.2%), intensive care 153 (28.1%), death 13 (2.4%); mean age 21.2 (SD 6.8), the same in women and men. Among the 188 with a sodium, Table 2 gives low sodium in 55 women and 18 men; median sodium in the low-sodium group 122 mmol/L (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124). Editors' note: 55 plus 18 is 73, as in the abstract, while the last Results paragraph on p. 166 gives 74 (39.4%).

evidence.locator: Table 3; Results, paragraph on fatalities (p. 168, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: Table 3, odds ratios of each outcome with low sodium against without, within sex (women 55 of 105; men 18 of 83): hyperthermia 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; coma 3.93 (1.20 to 12.90) and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97); seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07); tachycardia 0.33 (0.14 to 0.81) and 0.13 (0.04 to 0.51); death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). There were 13 deaths in the 545; 4 were in the low-sodium group (3 women, 1 man), all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines; 2 had seizures, 1 arrived with a temperature of 34.4 degrees Celsius and 2 had fluid in the lungs. Of the 9 deaths without low sodium (6 women, 3 men), 3 had hyperthermia.

evidence.locator: Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (starts p. 168, right column; ends p. 169, right column)
evidence.extracted: Poison-centre data are passive reporting, subject to reporting bias. The authors say they may have missed cases and underestimated complications; that referral bias may produce spectrum bias, the series representing the more severe outcomes and possibly overestimating how often low sodium and poor outcomes occur; that exposure rests on a history from the patient or a witness and may include other substances sold as ecstasy; that laboratory confirmation of MDMA was lacking in a significant share and no gas chromatography with mass spectrometry was reported; that no sodium was recorded in 65.5% of cases, the timing of the sodium was not consistent, and low sodium may be relatively benign and self-correcting in some; and that differing body build, kidney function, hydration, coingestions and behaviour limit conclusions about how likely a given population is to develop low sodium.

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 1st paragraph (p. 1855, left column into right column) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1855, right column); Table 3 (p. 1855, foot of page)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review, second-hand: symptomatic low sodium (usually below 130 mEq/L) was first described by Maxwell and colleagues in 1993 and more than 25 separate case reports have been published since; sodium on presentation ranged from 101 to 130 mEq/L, and the vast majority of cases were in females aged 15 to 30 who took a single dose of ecstasy. The review attributes excess water intake in part to a harmful response to overheating (chill-out areas with free or cheap water or low-solute drinks), together with amphetamine-induced dry mouth and thirst; whether ecstasy gives a primary drive to drink is not known but has been hypothesized. Editors' count of Table 3: 32 published cases, 27 labelled F, 1 W and 4 M, 16 deaths, 15 recoveries and 1 not available; 10 rows are taken from the California series (reference 82 in the review).

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 2nd paragraph, the case report (starts p. 1855, right column; continues p. 1856, left column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: an 18-year-old woman came to an emergency department soon after taking five tablets of ecstasy, with severe headache and thirst and a serum sodium of 136 mEq/L; she then drank 1700 ml of water, her headache worsened and the repeat sodium was 130 mEq/L, with urine osmolality 335 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 101 mEq/L and plasma arginine vasopressin 33.7 pmol/L (normal below 5.6). The review reasons that ready fluids, severe thirst and advice to drink copiously are likely not enough on their own, because the kidney can usually excrete free water faster than it is taken in, so the kidney's water excretion must also be impaired, as the raised urine osmolality and vasopressin in this and other cases suggest.

evidence.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, paragraphs on vasopressin secretion and on sweat sodium (p. 1856, left and right columns)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: MDMA has been shown in case reports and controlled settings to induce vasopressin secretion. Henry and colleagues gave 40 mg (against a common street dose of 100 mg) to eight healthy volunteers and found vasopressin rose within 1 to 2 hours (from a baseline range of 1.14 to 1.88 pmol/L to 2.46 to 9.16) with a slight fall in serum sodium; several other controlled studies are said to show a rise within 1 to 2 hours, and the rise is said to correlate negatively with MDMA levels, suggesting a metabolite. Sweat sodium loss is judged likely marginal, the majority of case reports lack significant hyperthermia, and the review concludes that increased water ingestion with urinary water retention is the main driving force. None of these primary studies was read here.

evidence.locator: Discussion > 'The present study has limitations' paragraph (p. 585, right column)
evidence.extracted: Hyponatraemia, which the authors describe as frequently observed in ecstasy intoxications, was not assessed in the controlled laboratory sessions of 166 volunteers, so blood sodium was not measured there.

Outcomes are labelled Death in 21 rows, Recovery in 27, Unknown in 3, and are blank in 1. Numeric sodium appears in 36 rows and is absent in 16; the lowest reported value within each of the 36 rows ranges from 101 to 130 mmol/L. One of these rows reports 137 on day one and 129 on day three, so the range of all printed sodium values is 101-137 mmol/L, without adding a case. Ten Death-labelled rows report sodium, 109-126 mmol/L, within the 101-130 mmol/L range of the lowest per-row values in the 24 Recovery-labelled rows with sodium. Nine MDMA-labelled rows list at least one additional substance; six of these list an additional substance other than MDA, while the remaining three list MDA alone in addition to MDMA. risk_of_bias.note: Both series are ROBINS-I critical on their cards: cases are those that were reported to a poison service, exposure is by history (MDMA confirmed in only part), sodium was recorded in about a third of the Californian cases, and values were given by telephone. One level, not two, because the claim describes what was seen in these cases and gives no rate.

inconsistency.note: The UK and Californian series, from different countries, years and services, agree on the pattern (young people, within hours, seizures and brain swelling). They differ in the share of women (10 of 17 against 55 of 73 low-sodium cases), which the claim leaves to the separate claim on who is affected.

indirectness.note: Worded for people who came to a poison service or hospital, with the limits stated.

imprecision.note: Small counts (2 deaths in 17; 4 in 73), no intervals for any share, and an internal inconsistency in the Californian count of low-sodium cases (73 and 74).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the published case reports are selected by nature, and the claim takes no figure from them.

grade.reasoning: Case series start low (observational, no comparison group for the UK series). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3). The claim states what was recorded in two poison-service series and, as described in a narrative review, in published case reports, and that none could give a rate. Status replicated: two independent services in two countries show the same pattern; the 2008 review adds nothing independent, because its table draws on the California series and appears to include a UK case that is also in the first series, and the 2020 review (Faria et al.) is not an independent 52-person cohort: its table draws 10 of its 21 labelled deaths from the California series and contains errors (card sc_faria_2020), so it is cited for what it tabulates, with the errors stated. The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and as untested here; it is not part of what the claim asserts. No advice on fluid or on amounts is given.

verification.flag_note: Rests on two case series and one narrative review (METHODS 6.3 and 12), so it stays draft. A 2016 controlled study in healthy volunteers (Baggott et al., doi 10.1155/2016/2175896; seen only as a PMC abstract, not read, no reference record here) reports that a water load lowered sodium more after MDMA than after placebo while vasopressin and copeptin did not rise; if confirmed, the vasopressin explanation these papers give would be contested and the mechanism sentence should be revisited. The primary vasopressin papers (Henry 1998, Forsling and Fallon 2001-2002, Wolff 2006) and the case reports (Brvar 2004, Budisavljevic 2003) have no reference record here and were not read. The first UK death appears to be the Australian fatal case the UK authors include from an earlier report (Parr 1997); the review lists a 15-year-old female with sodium 125 who died. The UK abstract gives 14 complete recoveries and 11 with seizures (15 and 17 patients); Table 1 labels 13 of the 15 survivors as complete recovery.

statement: Among people reported to California poison control in 2000 to 2005 with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded blood sodium (188 of 545 cases; Rosenson et al., 2007), low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) was found in 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), an odds ratio of 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59), which is 31 more in 100 women than men among those tested (editors' calculation); sodium was recorded about as often in women (35 in 100) as in men (33 in 100). Within each sex, women with low sodium had higher odds of coma (odds ratio 3.93, 1.20 to 12.90) and of seizure (4.38, 1.74 to 11.00) than women without it, while in men the intervals for coma (0.78, 0.15 to 3.97) and seizure (2.21, 0.69 to 7.07) included 1. These are counts of people who became ill and were reported, not rates in people who take MDMA: sodium was recorded in only 35 in 100 of the cases, and the authors say that spectrum bias, incomplete laboratory data and differences between individuals prevent determining causality. The paper gives neither the amount of fluid drunk nor the amount of MDMA taken. The only comparison read of women and men given the same amount is described second-hand in a 2020 narrative review (Faria et al., 2020): in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study, 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women were given 125 mg of MDMA (study condition; the review does not specify the setting), and copeptin, a marker of the water-holding hormone, rose in the women but not in the men, while no significant differences were reported in the hormone itself or in blood sodium; the review does not identify that statistical contrast, so it cannot be treated as a demonstrated absence of a sex difference. The direction is the same, without a test, in the UK series in which 10 of 17 patients and both who died were female (Hartung et al., 2002), in an earlier series of 18 cases with 17 women that the California paper cites and that was not read, and, as described in a narrative review (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand), in more than 85 in 100 of published symptomatic cases, whose table draws 10 rows from the California series and so is not independent; the 2020 review's table of published cases (1991 to 2018) lists 46 female rows among 52 (88.5 in 100 by editorial calculation, whereas the review prints 89 in 100), from which it infers that women are predisposed, but the table appears to count two patients twice (conditionally 44 of 50, 88 in 100, editors' calculation, not a verified unique-patient count), cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper for one woman's case, draws 10 of its 21 deaths from the California series and sets no case count against the number of women and men who take MDMA. These series are of young people (mean age 21 in California; 15 to 26 in the UK series), so age cannot be compared. Reasons the authors and the reviews offer (metabolic and hormonal factors; oestrogen effects on water retention and on the brain's response to low sodium; lower muscle mass and body weight) were not tested in people who took MDMA; the 2020 review's main support for a greater risk to women once the brain swells comes from patients after surgery, among whom women who still menstruated were about 25 times more likely than men or women past menopause to die or have lasting brain injury (Ayus et al., 1992, as described in the review).
plain: In California poison-centre records, women with MDMA illness were more likely than men to have a low level of blood sodium: 55 of 105 women (52 in 100) against 18 of 83 men (22 in 100), among those who had their sodium measured. Women with a low level were also more likely to have fits or coma. The reports count people who became ill and were reported, not everyone who took MDMA, and sodium was measured in about a third of them, so this does not show how likely low sodium is in women or men who take MDMA. A review describes one small controlled study in 8 women and 8 men. A marker of the water-holding hormone rose only in the women; no clear differences in the hormone itself or in sodium were reported, but the review does not say which comparison that refers to. These were mostly young people (average age 21).
population: People with ecstasy intoxication reported to the California Poison Control System in 2000 to 2005 and given a serum sodium result: 188 of 545 included cases (105 women, 83 men; mean age 21 in both); descriptively, 17 UK patients aged 15 to 26 and published case reports tabulated in two narrative reviews; and, as described in the 2020 review, 16 healthy volunteers (8 women, 8 men) in one laboratory study
exposure: Female sex, among people who took ecstasy (MDMA) and became ill; amounts of MDMA and of fluid not recorded
comparator: Men with a recorded sodium; within each sex, people with low sodium against people without
outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L; coma and seizure among those with and without low sodium
magnitude: California poison control, people with ecstasy intoxication and a recorded sodium (Rosenson): low sodium (below 130 mmol/L) in 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%), odds ratio 3.97 (95% CI 2.08 to 7.59); of the 73 with low sodium, 55 (75.3%) were women, against 296 of 545 (54.3%) women among all cases. Sodium was recorded in 35.3% of women and 33.3% of men. Within each sex, low sodium against not: coma 3.93 (1.20 to 12.90) in women and 0.78 (0.15 to 3.97) in men; seizure 4.38 (1.74 to 11.00) and 2.21 (0.69 to 7.07); death 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70). Editors' calculation: 31 more in 100 women than men had low sodium among those tested (52.4 minus 21.7). UK series (Hartung): 10 of 17 patients and both deaths female. Earlier series cited by the California paper (not read): 17 of 18 women; 2 of 3 in an Israeli series of 32. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 85% of published symptomatic cases female. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: 46 of 52 rows female (88.5%, editors' calculation; review prints 89%; conditionally omitting two probable duplicates gives 44/50=88.0%, not a verified unique-patient count); controlled crossover, 8 men and 8 women given 125 mg MDMA: copeptin rose in women but not in men, no significant ADH/sodium differences reported, statistical contrast unspecified; postoperative patients with hyponatraemic encephalopathy (Ayus et al., 1992): menstruant women about 25 times as likely to die or have permanent brain injury as men or postmenopausal women. No rate in women or men who take MDMA can be derived.

Of the 115 with a higher sodium, 50 (43.5%) were women and 65 (56.5%) men. Among those with a sodium, female sex was associated with increased odds of low sodium (odds ratio 4.0, 95% CI 2.1 to 7.6). risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I critical on the card: the people are those who were reported and tested (spectrum and referral bias), sodium was recorded in about a third, the odds ratios are unadjusted for body weight, amount of MDMA, fluid intake or other drugs, and exposure is by history.

inconsistency.note: The UK series and the two reviews' case tables point the same way, though they are descriptions without a test and the tables overlap the California series. The small controlled crossover, described second-hand, reports no significant hormone/sodium differences without identifying the contrast; it concerns selected healthy volunteers under fixed study conditions, not on who was found among reported cases, so it qualifies the claim rather than contradicting it.

indirectness.note: Worded for people who became ill and were reported, which is what was studied.

imprecision.note: The main interval (2.08 to 7.59) excludes 1 but is wide; the within-sex odds ratios for coma and seizure have intervals up to 12.90 and 7.07.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the odds ratio (about 4) is large, but the people studied are those reported and tested, and unmeasured differences in body weight, amount taken and fluid drunk could produce or hide it (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: One poison-centre case series with a comparison inside it starts low (observational). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Relation: is associated with; the authors themselves say causality cannot be determined, and sex is bound up with body size, amount taken and fluid drunk, none of which was recorded. Status single study: only the California series tests the sex difference among reported cases; the UK series and the two reviews are consistent but do not test it, and both reviews' tables overlap the California series. The 2020 review (Faria et al.; card sc_faria_2020) infers a female predisposition from its case counts, but its table has errors and no denominators, and the only controlled comparison it describes (Simmler et al., 2011, not read) reports no significant hormone/sodium differences without identifying the statistical contrast; that study and the postoperative data (Ayus et al., 1992, not read) are second-hand. The answer to who is most at risk cannot be read from this claim: it gives who was found among reported cases with a sodium result, not who is at risk among people who take MDMA, and no age comparison is possible.

verification.flag_note: Rests on one case-series test of sex and descriptive series; stays draft (METHODS 6.3 and 12). The review misreports the California study twice: it cites reference 49 (a different 1998 case report) and says women had significantly higher death, which the study's Table 3 does not show. Within the California paper the text prints 74 low-sodium cases once (73 elsewhere) and 2.11 for an odds ratio the table gives as 2.21; the abstract gives 54.3% women and the Results 54.6%. Table 1 lists 8 women and 5 men among the 13 deaths, while the text and the appendix give 9 and 4 (not used here). The earlier 18-case series (Budisavljevic 2003, Am J Med Sci 326:89-93) was not read; DOI not checked.

statement: Kidney injury after MDMA is known from case reports, as described in two narrative reviews, so the figures here are second-hand and the claim cannot say how often it happens; the review of kidney effects writes that, because most of the data come from case reports, 'the absolute incidence of this complication cannot be determined' (Campbell & Rosner, 2008). As described in that review, most reported episodes of acute kidney injury followed muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) after seizures, extreme exertion or overheating, with creatine kinase, a marker of muscle injury, as high as 100,000 U/L or more, sometimes with disordered blood clotting, low blood volume and low blood pressure; the first case, in 1992, took three doses at a rave, and the review says that in the majority of such cases people had been exerting themselves excessively with inadequate hydration and had overheated. In a UK poisons-unit report of 7 deaths with overheating (admission temperatures 40 to 43 degrees Celsius) and 4 further severe cases, summarized in a second narrative review, the most severe cases showed overheating, disordered clotting, muscle breakdown and acute kidney failure together, and plasma MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which the report's authors said did not reflect high doses (Parrott, 2012). Other routes are described in single reports: loss of proximal tubule function in an 18-year-old, vasculitis with end-stage kidney disease in a 30-year-old man 10 days after use and loss of both kidneys from a donor with recent use, blockage at the bladder neck, kidney injury after accelerated high blood pressure, and kidney injury after liver failure; the review says no report of kidney injury after ecstasy has included a kidney biopsy that could show a direct toxic effect, and that causation is hard to attribute when people may have used other substances. In 164 healthy volunteers who took MDMA once or twice in controlled laboratory studies, creatinine (74 against 73 micromoles per litre) and estimated kidney filtration (122 against 125 mL/min) were unchanged on average at screening against about a month after the last dose (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017), but these people rested, were healthy, did not overheat or exert themselves, and had no test in the hours or days after the dose, so short-lasting changes are not excluded. The first reported case followed three doses, and none of the reports compares amounts, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk.
plain: Kidney injury after MDMA has been reported in single cases, and nobody can say how often it happens. In most reports it followed muscle breakdown after fits, very hard physical exertion or overheating. A few single cases involved blood-vessel inflammation, a blocked bladder outlet or very high blood pressure. In healthy volunteers who took MDMA once or twice in a laboratory, kidney blood tests were unchanged about a month later, but nobody tested them in the hours and days after the dose, and these people rested and did not overheat. No study compared amounts, so the reports cannot show whether taking more makes it more likely. This comes from reviews of case reports, so it is second-hand.
population: People who developed acute kidney injury after taking ecstasy (MDMA) in published case reports, as described in two narrative reviews; and, as a qualifier, 164 healthy volunteers in controlled laboratory studies who had kidney blood tests before and about a month after one or two doses
exposure: MDMA taken as ecstasy at parties and raves in the reports (first reported case: three doses at a rave); overheating, seizures and extreme exertion with inadequate hydration in the reported cases; in the laboratory, one or two doses of MDMA (study conditions: 75 or 125 mg, at least seven days apart) at rest
comparator: None in the case reports; in the laboratory, the same people's kidney tests at screening, before the study doses
outcome: Acute kidney injury and its reported routes (muscle breakdown, vasculitis, tubule dysfunction, bladder-neck obstruction, malignant hypertension, liver failure); in the laboratory, blood creatinine and estimated kidney filtration
magnitude: Case reports as described in the review (second-hand): no incidence can be given. First reported case 1992, three doses at a rave. Creatine kinase up to 100,000 U/L or more in some cases. Single reports: proximal tubule dysfunction (18-year-old), necrotizing vasculitis with end-stage kidney disease (30-year-old man, 10 days after use), graft loss from a donor with recent use, bladder-neck obstruction, malignant hypertension. UK poisons-unit report as summarized in a second review: 7 deaths with temperatures of 40 to 43 degrees Celsius and 4 further severe cases; plasma MDMA 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l; the most severe cases showed overheating, clotting disorder, muscle breakdown and kidney failure together. Laboratory studies read in full (Vizeli, 164 healthy volunteers, about 29 days after one or two doses): creatinine 74 (SD 13) against 73 (SD 12) micromoles per litre; estimated filtration 122 (SD 22) against 125 (SD 24) mL/min; not significant. No test was made in the hours and days after the dose.

evidence.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, 1st paragraph (p. 1854, left column into right column) and Table 2 (p. 1854, foot of left column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: acute kidney injury has been associated with ecstasy, mostly in case reports, so the absolute incidence cannot be determined. The first case report, in 1992, was a person who took three doses of ecstasy at a rave and developed kidney injury attributed to muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) after seizures and possibly a direct toxic effect on muscle, with disseminated intravascular coagulation. The review calls non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis the most common scenario and says that in the majority of such cases people had been exerting themselves to excessive levels with inadequate hydration, compounded by impaired temperature regulation and very high temperature; creatine kinase can reach 100,000 U/L or more, and volume depletion and low blood pressure add to the injury from myoglobin. Table 2 lists causes: muscle breakdown (from overheating, extreme exertion, or an unknown direct toxicity), necrotizing vasculitis (rare case reports), bladder-neck obstruction (one case report), malignant hypertension, proximal tubule dysfunction (one case report) and volume depletion.
evidence.quote: the absolute incidence of this complication cannot be determined

evidence.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, paragraphs on proximal tubule dysfunction, liver failure and vasculitis (p. 1854, right column); paragraph on bladder-neck dysfunction and malignant hypertension (p. 1855, left column)
evidence.extracted: As described in the review: transient glycosuria, phosphaturia and solute diuresis in an 18-year-old (a single report; mechanism unknown, with injury to proximal tubules shown in a rat model); acute liver failure with kidney injury through the hepatorenal syndrome; necrotizing vasculitis with end-stage kidney disease in a 30-year-old man 10 days after use, and graft loss from necrotizing vasculitis in both kidneys of a donor with recent ecstasy use; obstruction from bladder-neck dysfunction; kidney injury after accelerated or malignant hypertension. The review says no case report of kidney injury after ecstasy has had a kidney biopsy that could show a direct toxic effect, and that attributing causation to ecstasy in the vasculitis cases is difficult because the people may have used other substances.

evidence.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 1857, right column)
evidence.extracted: The review concludes that ecstasy use is associated with both kidney injury and low blood sodium, and that most of the episodes of kidney injury are due to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis associated with rhabdomyolysis.

evidence.locator: Section 4 > Clinical hyperthermia and its treatment, 2nd paragraph (p. 5, left column into right column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized by the review (Henry and colleagues, 1992, UK poisons unit, 1990 and 1991): 7 deaths with overheating, admission temperatures 40 to 43 degrees Celsius; the most severe cases showed overheating, disseminated intravascular coagulation, muscle breakdown and acute renal failure; the authors noted these severe reactions did not reflect high dose levels, with plasma MDMA from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, and other drugs were reported in only one case; four further severe non-fatal cases had temperatures around 40 degrees.

evidence.locator: Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit, 1st paragraph (p. 578, right column); Results > Effects of MDMA on kidney and liver function (p. 582, left column); Table 4 (p. 583)
evidence.extracted: Kidney tests in 164 of the 166 healthy volunteers (data missing for two), at screening and at an end-of-study visit on average 29 (SD 22) days after the last of one or two doses of MDMA (the Results text gives 30 +/- 22), 88 (SD 50) days between the visits: creatinine 74 (SD 13) against 73 (SD 12) micromoles per litre and estimated glomerular filtration rate 122 (SD 22) against 125 (SD 24) mL/min, neither significantly different. Liver enzymes were also similar, apart from a small fall in gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase.

evidence.locator: Discussion > 'The present study has limitations' paragraph (p. 585, right column)
evidence.extracted: The authors write that laboratory markers of liver and kidney function were assessed only at the end of the study, on average one month after the last dose, which does not exclude short-lasting transient changes; that only healthy, mostly young people were included; and that 166 sessions of MDMA alone (278 with or without a pretreatment) were too small to exclude infrequent or rare adverse events.

risk_of_bias.note: The reviews are narrative and cannot be appraised for bias (high on the cards on the editors' five-domain checklist); the underlying case reports have no comparison group and no kidney biopsies, and causation is hard to attribute.

inconsistency.note: The two reviews agree that the reported injury came mostly with muscle breakdown and overheating; the laboratory kidney tests concern a different situation and are a qualifier.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through two narrative reviews; the primary case reports were not read and have no reference record here.

imprecision.note: No incidence can be derived; the evidence is single reports, and the laboratory estimate rests on one test about a month after the dose.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; case reports are selected by nature, and the claim takes no figure from them.

grade.reasoning: A claim seen only through narrative reviews starts from the design of the primary studies they describe (case reports; low) and is downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness (METHODS 6.3); imprecision is also downgraded because no incidence can be given. Very low. Relation: describes (reported cases, no rate). Status single study: one review was read for the kidney findings, with one line from a second review; the primary reports were not read. Draft: the claim rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3); the laboratory kidney tests are a qualifying anchor, since they concern healthy volunteers at rest and a single test about a month later. The claim does not say that MDMA is or is not toxic to the kidney, and gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Review-only claim. The primary kidney case reports (Fahal 1992, Woodrow 1995 and others cited by Campbell and Rosner) and the UK poisons-unit report (Henry 1992) have no reference record here and were not read; DOIs not checked. The review's introduction also says the pattern of toxicity is not attributable to overdose and gives an estimated risk of death in people taking it for the first time of 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 50,000 (second-hand from one earlier paper); neither is used here because they are not about the kidney.
