statement: In healthy, screened adults given MDMA by mouth by researchers in laboratories, and a placebo on another day, MDMA raised ratings of the drug's effect, of a good effect and of feeling happy, and, in one study, of feeling open and close to others, and also raised ratings of a bad effect and of physical complaints, in the same sessions (five papers from Basel, Chicago, San Francisco and Zurich, not fully independent: the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers a senior author, and one author is on four of the five). In 166 volunteers aged 18 to 45 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel, four in five new to MDMA, the average highest self-rating of 'any drug effect' on a 0 to 100 line was 73 in men and 85 in women after 125 mg (136 people), against 4 on placebo, and lower after 75 mg (30 other people); of 'good drug effect' it was 77 and 82 after 125 mg, against 3 or 4. Four of the 166 reported no effect. The effect began on average 33 minutes after the dose (SD 24), peaked at 1.6 hours (SD 0.8) and lasted 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4 to 8.2); in 16 volunteers in Zurich it began 20 to 120 minutes after the dose and lasted about 3 hours. In a 32-person Basel study (probably within the 166), ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others rose (F(1,31) 121, 81 and 68; p < 0.001), as did scores for well-being, extroversion and activity, with no rise in anxiety; in Zurich, positive mood averaged 40% of the highest possible score against 0.6% on placebo and thought disorder 25% against 0, with no rise in aggression-anger, apprehension-anxiety or depressiveness. The social effects are less settled: a 'sociable' rating rose at 1.5 mg/kg in 9 people in Chicago (+19.7 points against -6.3; p = .04, which the authors call marginal) while a friendliness scale did not change significantly; closeness was rated higher in San Francisco than in Basel; peak ratings of drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ significantly between three sites (220 volunteers, partly overlapping the others; no means printed, and no significant difference is not proof of equality); and empathy and money-sharing tests rose in one Basel study, in men only on post hoc tests. The same sessions brought unwanted effects. 'Bad drug effect' averaged 13 in men and 24 in women after 125 mg against 2 on placebo, higher in women also after allowing for dose per kilogram and blood level (SDs of 22 and 24, so ratings varied widely). In the first 6 hours, MDMA against placebo in 166 people: lack of appetite 59%, dry mouth 55%, difficulty concentrating 46%, cold feet 42%, sweating 41% and jaw clenching 40% (of 134 asked), against 0 to 6%; at 24 hours, lack of appetite 31% (1% on placebo), lack of energy 30% (3%) and headache 33% (15%). Nine people reported anxiety, all after 125 mg; the authors say verbal support reduced it and no benzodiazepine was used. The paper reports no serious adverse event, depressed mood in 4% after 125 mg in the next one to two weeks, and 'flashbacks' (not defined) in 9%, 8 to 50 hours after the dose. Asked at the end of the study, 67% of 141 volunteers called the experience positive, 18% neutral and 15% disappointing or bad; 19% would probably not take MDMA again, 47% only in another controlled study and 34% perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known. Why people take MDMA was not studied: none of the five laboratory papers asked people who use ecstasy why they do or what they feel in real use (one small study outside the laboratory, below, measured what they felt); two say, citing other papers, that sociability and empathy are reasons for recreational use. Some people feel little from an amount. Of the reasons usually given, these studies show a start that ranged up to 120 minutes in Zurich; a lowering of Zurich ratings by about 60% by an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion before MDMA; peak blood levels averaging 1.29 times higher in women than in men at the same 125 mg; and, in Chicago and less clearly San Francisco, a lower 'any drug effect' rating with more earlier MDMA use (not for other ratings, and the other way round in Basel); a pill of different content was not tested, as every capsule held a known amount. No one took a second dose within a session, so what happens when people take more was not measured here (controlled second-dose studies are covered in a separate claim). The sessions differ from real life: healthy, screened volunteers (mostly new to MDMA in Basel and Zurich; earlier use in Chicago and San Francisco) took a known capsule and nothing else, at an amount set by the researchers, in a hospital or laboratory room (22.7 degrees Celsius in Basel) with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco; in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis people were alone and gave higher 'anxious' ratings than at the other sites, which the authors suggest, untested, may reflect company. The end-of-study answers came from people given MDMA by researchers, not from people who chose it, and heat, crowds and other drugs were not part of the MDMA sessions. Outside the laboratory, one small study with no placebo followed 45 people aged 19 to 30, recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub, from a drug-free session before a Saturday night out to the club and then 2 and 7 days later: 30 who had used ecstasy before (15 of them ten or more times) took tablets of untested content by their own choice that night, and 15 who had never taken it, 10 of whom drank alcohol, went to the same club (Parrott & Lasky, 1998). At the club all three groups rated their mood as good and the ecstasy groups' ratings were not clearly better (sad 9 against 20 out of 100, p < 0.10; good tempered about the same), though they felt more 'abnormal'; the authors had expected better moods and point to the setting and expectation, the comparison group's drinking, ratings already near the top of the scale and a mood list with no items on elation or empathy. Two days later both ecstasy groups rated themselves sadder (56 and 53 against 22), more unsociable and more 'abnormal', and the novice group also more depressed, more unpleasant and less good tempered (in the regular group these three reached only p < 0.10); seven days later the groups rated these moods alike again. These are self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims and their own group, with means only, many comparisons and no correction, and sleep and drug use after the night were not recorded, so the study shows what this group reported over that week, not what MDMA alone did.
plain: In hospital studies, healthy volunteers took MDMA on one day and a dummy pill on another, without being told which. In the biggest set (166 people, four in five new to MDMA; 136 had 125 mg), the average highest rating of how strong the effect was came to 73 to 85 out of 100, against 4 after the dummy pill, and of how good it was to 77 to 82 (3 or 4 after the dummy pill). It began about half an hour after the dose and lasted about four hours; 4 of the 166 reported no effect. Volunteers also felt happy, open and close to others, though the findings on closeness are less sure. The same sessions brought unwanted effects. The average highest rating of a bad effect was 13 to 24 out of 100 (2 after the dummy pill). In the first 6 hours, each of these affected 40 to 59 in 100 people: less appetite, a dry mouth, trouble concentrating, cold feet, sweating and a clenched jaw (0 to 6 in 100 after the dummy pill). A day later, 33 in 100 had a headache (15 after the dummy pill) and 30 in 100 low energy (3). Asked at the end of the study, 67 in 100 called the experience positive and 15 in 100 disappointing or bad. Some people feel little from an amount: the studies show a slow start in some people, a much weaker effect after an antidepressant given first, and higher blood levels in women than in men at the same amount. Nobody took more in a session, so that was not tested. The volunteers were healthy, mostly new to MDMA, took a known amount and had researchers with them. Outside the lab, one small study at a London club, with no dummy pill and pills nobody tested, found that people who had taken ecstasy felt about as good on the night as other clubbers, most of whom had been drinking; two days later they felt sadder and less sociable than the others, and a week later they felt like the others again. No paper asked why people take MDMA.
population: Healthy, screened adults, aged 18 to 45 in the largest set, in research laboratories: 166 in nine studies at one hospital in Basel (83 women, 83 men; mean age 24.5; four in five new to MDMA; 30 people took 75 mg and 136 took 125 mg), 32 in a Basel study probably within them (22 new to MDMA), 16 in Zurich (12 men, 4 women; 13 had never taken MDMA), 9 in Chicago with earlier ecstasy use (7 men, 2 women; 2 to 300 occasions) and, in a three-site pooled analysis that may overlap the others, 220 (Basel 80, Chicago 95, San Francisco 45; lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions; 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory); outside the laboratory, 45 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30 recruited by word of mouth around one London nightclub: 15 with ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, 15 with one to nine and 15 who had never taken it
exposure: A single oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride in capsules, given double blind by researchers in a hospital or laboratory (study conditions: 125 mg or 75 mg in Basel; 1.5 mg/kg in Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco; a fixed 125 mg in the Basel part of the three-site analysis; 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order in the Chicago brain-imaging study), with researchers present in Basel and San Francisco, people alone in the Chicago sessions of the three-site analysis, no other drug, and ratings made at set times; in Zurich, MDMA after an antidepressant (citalopram) infusion was also tested; outside the laboratory, tablets sold as ecstasy taken by people's own choice at a club, content not tested (study condition, self-reported: 1.80 tablets on average in the regular group and 1.45 in the novice group), with alcohol, cannabis or cocaine taken by some in every group
comparator: Placebo in the same people on another day (double-blind crossover; in Chicago the placebo session was placed at random among ascending doses); sites and earlier-use groups are compared across different people; in Zurich, MDMA after a citalopram infusion in the same people; outside the laboratory, people at the same club who had never taken ecstasy (10 of 15 drank alcohol that night), and each group's own drug-free session before the night
outcome: Self-ratings of drug effects on 0 to 100 lines (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, feeling happy, open, close to others, sociable, stimulated, anxious) and mood and altered-state scales; time to onset, peak and end of the effect; physical complaints on a 66-item list up to 6 hours and at 24 hours; end-of-study answers on the overall experience and on taking MDMA again; empathy and money-sharing tests as secondary outcomes; outside the laboratory, 16 single-item mood self-ratings (0 to 100) before the night, at the club, and 2 and 7 days later
magnitude: Basel pooled analysis (166 people; 125 mg n = 136, 75 mg n = 30), highest self-rating on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo, at 125 mg: any drug effect women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); good drug effect women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); bad drug effect women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); at 75 mg any drug effect 59 (29) and 56 (32), good 60 (28) and 57 (33), bad 35 (33) and 7 (11). Drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44 (p < 0.001); women's bad-effect ratings stayed higher after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0) and blood level (F 21.5), both p < 0.001. Four of the 166 reported no effect; onset 33 (SD 24) minutes, peak 1.6 (0.8) hours, duration 4.2 (1.3) hours (range 1.4 to 8.2). Complaints, MDMA against placebo (of 166), up to 6 hours: lack of appetite 59% against 2%, dry mouth 55% against 2%, difficulty concentrating 46% against 6%, cold feet 42% against 4%, sweating 41% against 0, jaw clenching 40% against 1% (134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, heart palpitations 24% (each 0 to 1% on placebo), nausea 11% against 1%, anxiety 9 people (printed as 6%; 9 of 166 is 5.4%, editors' calculation) against 0, headache 25% against 16% (not significant); at 24 hours: lack of appetite 31% against 1%, headache 33% against 15%, lack of energy 30% against 3%. No serious adverse event; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg; flashbacks 12 of 141 (9%) at 8 to 50 hours. End of study (141 asked): experience positive 95 (67%), neutral 25 (18%), disappointing or bad 21 (15%); would probably not take MDMA again 27 (19%), only in another controlled study 66 (47%), perhaps in a recreational setting if identity, purity and dose were known 48 (34%). At 125 mg women's peak blood level averaged 1.29 times men's. Basel, 32 people: feeling happy F(1,31) 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52 (p < 0.001); well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, activity 24.48; anxiety not raised; empathy test explicit F 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047), men only on post hoc tests; money sharing F 4.42 (p = 0.044), men p = 0.008. Zurich, 16 people, mean % of the highest possible score (SE): positive mood 40.1 (6.6) against 0.6 on placebo; derealization 32.7 (7.0) against 0.4; thought disorder 24.8 (6.0) against 0.0; onset 20 to 120 (mean 45) minutes; about 60% lower after citalopram (authors' figure). Chicago, 9 people: 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (1.5 mg/kg against placebo p = .04, marginal); friendliness scale F 1.3, not significant. Three sites, 220 people: peak ratings of any drug effect, liking and stimulation did not differ by site (p = 0.07 to 1.00; no means printed); earlier use and the any-drug-effect rating: 6.8 points lower per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7), 13.5 higher in Basel (CI 1.63 to 25.3; fewer than three earlier uses). Outside the laboratory (Parrott & Lasky, 1998; 15 people per group; 0 to 100 self-ratings, means only; Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group): at the club good tempered 85 (comparison), 90 (novice) and 88 (regular); sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); 2 days later sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); 7 days later none of these differed (sad 22, 25 and 21; depressed 37, 37 and 39). Group by session interactions: p < 0.001 for sad, depressed and abnormal; p < 0.01 for unsociable and unpleasant; p < 0.05 for good tempered.

evidence.locator: Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph; Methods > Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph (p. 577, into p. 578)
evidence.extracted: Pooled analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies, all at the University Hospital Basel and all registered (the registrations listed include NCT01386177 and NCT01465685), of 166 psychiatrically screened, healthy European or Caucasian adults aged 18 to 45 (mean 24.5, SD 4; equal numbers of women and men; mean weight 69 kg), mostly recruited on the university campus and paid. 30 people (15 men, 15 women) took a single 75 mg dose and 136 took 125 mg (68 men, 68 women; 24 once, 112 twice, once alone and once with another drug at least seven days apart); this paper analyses the sessions of MDMA alone against placebo. Excluded: psychiatric disorder, physical illness, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted) and any in the last two months or during the study (urine tests). 59 had earlier drug experience of 1 to 5 times, 34 of them with MDMA (1 to 4 times). MDMA hydrochloride in gelatin capsules (25 or 100 mg), not adjusted for body weight or sex: 1.7 mg/kg on average (SD 0.4; range 0.8 to 2.7). The authors state that similar amounts are found in ecstasy pills (citing another paper, not read).

evidence.locator: Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph and 3rd paragraph; Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit, 1st paragraph (p. 578)
evidence.extracted: Self-ratings on 100-mm lines (0 to 100%) from 'not at all' to 'extremely': 'any drug effect', 'good drug effect' and 'bad drug effect', before and at 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours after the capsule (some time points missing in two studies). Onset, offset and duration were taken from each person's 'any drug effect' curve with 10% of their own peak as the threshold; four people who reported no subjective effect were left out of that analysis. Complaints: a 66-item List of Complaints (bruxism added, used in 134 people), asked 3 to 6 hours (acute) and 24 hours (subacute) after the dose; adverse events from 24 hours to 14 days were also asked about. At the end-of-study visit, on average 29 days (SD 22) after the last of one or two MDMA sessions (with or without a pretreatment drug), volunteers were asked to rate the duration of the response, whether the experience was positive or negative, whether the clinical setting influenced it, whether they would take MDMA again and in what setting, and whether they had 'flashbacks'; these questions were put to 141 volunteers. The paper does not say which session the answers refer to.

evidence.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph; Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (p. 580); Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph (p. 578; four people with no effect excluded)
evidence.extracted: Time course of 'any drug effect' after MDMA alone (four people who reported no effect were left out): onset 33 minutes (SD 24), peak 1.6 hours (SD 0.8), duration 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4 to 8.2), with no sex or dose difference in duration; at the end-of-study visit volunteers recalled the duration as 4.0 hours (SD 2.9). MDMA raised 'any drug effect' and 'good drug effect' above placebo, both more at 125 than at 75 mg; a drug-by-sex interaction that was nearly significant: women tended to give higher 'any drug effect' ratings. MDMA also raised 'bad drug effect' ratings, not dose-dependent and higher in women than in men, still with dose per kilogram as a covariate (F(1,162) 20.0, p < 0.001) and with peak blood level as a covariate (F 21.5, p < 0.001). The mean room temperature was 22.7 degrees Celsius (SD 0.6).

evidence.locator: Table 1, rows 'Any drug effect', 'Good drug effect' and 'Bad drug effect' (all columns)
evidence.extracted: Highest self-rating after the dose, mean (SD), MDMA against placebo; 125 mg (68 women, 68 men) then 75 mg (15 and 15). Any drug effect: women 85 (20) against 4 (8) and 59 (29) against 3 (6); men 73 (24) against 4 (13) and 56 (32) against 6 (9). Good drug effect: women 82 (25) against 3 (10) and 60 (28) against 6 (13); men 77 (23) against 4 (15) and 57 (33) against 7 (12). Bad drug effect: women 24 (24) against 2 (10) and 35 (33) against 4 (13); men 13 (22) against 2 (10) and 7 (11) against 6 (16). Drug effect F(1,162): any 652, good 585, bad 44 (p < 0.001); drug-by-dose: any 20 (p < 0.001), good 20 (printed p < 0.01), bad 0.001 (not significant); drug-by-sex: any 3.4 (p = 0.068), good 0.9 (not significant), bad 16 (p < 0.001); drug-by-dose-by-sex for bad 3.6 (p = 0.059).

evidence.locator: Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 580, 2nd paragraph continued on p. 582); Table 2, rows 'List of complaints score' (p. 582); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 584)
evidence.extracted: Rise in the total List of Complaints score, MDMA against placebo, mean (SD): acute (up to 6 hours) 8.8 (5.9) in women and 6.4 (6.8) in men, subacute (24 hours) 5.4 (5.5) and 3.0 (5.0); the sex difference held after allowing for dose per kilogram or blood level (p < 0.05). Table 2, MDMA against placebo: 125 mg acute 10.0 (6.6) against 1.7 (2.3), subacute 5.7 (5.6) against 0.9 (2.2); 75 mg acute 5.6 (4.5) against 1.6 (2.1), subacute 2.9 (4.1) against 0.9 (1.5). Acute anxiety was reported by nine people (6%) after 125 mg and none after 75 mg. No serious adverse events were reported. From 24 hours to 7 to 14 days: headache 6% after 125 mg, 7% after 75 mg and 5% after placebo; depressed mood 4% after 125 mg (0% otherwise); none reported significantly more often after MDMA than after placebo. In the 125 mg studies 12 people (9%) reported 'flashbacks' 1 to 3 times (one eight times), on average 26 hours (SD 15; range 8 to 50) after the dose, with no sex difference; the Discussion says all 12 were within 8 to 50 hours and that no persisting perceptual change was found in this controlled setting.

evidence.locator: Table 3, all rows; columns 'Placebo' and 'MDMA', 'Up to 6 h' and '24 h'
evidence.extracted: Complaints, MDMA against placebo, n (%) of 166: up to 6 hours lack of appetite 98 (59%) against 3 (2%); dry mouth 91 (55%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 76 (46%) against 10 (6%); cold feet 69 (42%) against 7 (4%); sweating 68 (41%) against 0; jaw clenching 54 (40%, of 134 asked) against 1 (1%); restless legs 62 (37%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 57 (34%) against 2 (1%); hot flushes 52 (31%) against 0; heart palpitations 40 (24%) against 2 (1%); lack of energy 38 (23%) against 23 (14%); nausea 19 (11%) against 2 (1%); anxiety 9 (6%) against 0; headache 42 (25%) against 27 (16%), not significantly different. At 24 hours: lack of appetite 52 (31%) against 1 (1%); dry mouth 37 (23%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 35 (22%) against 4 (2%); headache 55 (33%) against 25 (15%); lack of energy 49 (30%) against 5 (3%); jaw clenching 19 (14%) against 1 (1%); hot flushes 12 (7%) against 0; restless legs 12 (7%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 12 (7%) against 3 (2%); heart palpitations 11 (7%) against 1 (1%); cold feet 10 (6%) against 2 (1%); nausea 9 (6%) against 1 (1%); sweating 7 (4%) against 0; anxiety 3 (2%) against 0, not significant. Both doses are pooled (total n = 166).

evidence.locator: Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (p. 582, right column, continued on pp. 583 and 584)
evidence.extracted: Asked at the end of the study: 80% were new to MDMA, the rest had at most four earlier exposures. Of 141 volunteers asked whether they would consider taking MDMA again, 27 (19%) probably not under any circumstances; 66 (47%) not recreationally but possibly in another study under controlled conditions; 48 (34%) possibly in a recreational setting but only if identity, purity and dose were known, 24 of these 48 (50%) having taken illicit drugs before, including MDMA; only 13 considered a club setting. Overall experience: 95 (67%) positive, 25 (18%) neutral, 21 (15%) disappointing or bad, with no sex differences. The controlled setting had no impact for 51 (36%) and was important for the type of experience, reassuring and made them feel safe for 90 (64%); women rated the setting as more important than men (F(1,139) 12.4, p < 0.001).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 584, left column)
evidence.extracted: The authors read their data as clearly greater positive than negative acute subjective effects and a state of predominantly positive mood across laboratories (citing other papers, not read), with one exception; modest apprehension anxiety in some volunteers, reported as an acute adverse effect by 7% after 125 mg and not after 75 mg (the Results say nine people, 6%); anxiety could be reduced by verbal support in all of the volunteers and no benzodiazepine was used; no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks; psychological distress minimal (no distress measure is reported apart from the 'bad drug effect' rating and the one-item anxiety complaint); overall positive experiences retrospectively in two-thirds and 15% disappointed or with bad experiences. They contrast this with panic attacks and agitation or aggression described in people who use ecstasy and present to emergency departments (cited from other papers, not read).

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 584, right column); Discussion, 9th and 10th paragraphs (p. 585)
evidence.extracted: The authors suggest that no controlled study has reported a body temperature above 40 degrees possibly because volunteers had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded environment, unlike some recreational settings. In their research setting a research assistant is always present, similar to a therapy session and unlike some other experimental settings; participants typically had no or very little earlier MDMA experience; the response may differ in people with psychiatric disorders compared with volunteers screened to be psychiatrically healthy; limits: only psychiatrically healthy and mostly young volunteers; hyponatraemia, neurocognitive function and long-term problems not assessed; 166 sessions of MDMA alone (278 counting those with a pretreatment drug) too few to exclude infrequent (0.1 to 1%) or rare (below 0.1%) events.

evidence.locator: Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph (p. 578); Table 1, rows 'Cmax' (p. 581); Results > Plasma concentrations of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 582); Discussion, 8th paragraph (p. 585)
evidence.extracted: Dose per kilogram at 125 mg: 1.7 (SD 0.2) in men and 2.1 (SD 0.3) in women. Peak blood MDMA level (Cmax) at 125 mg: women 252 (SD 40) and men 195 (SD 37) ng/mL; at the same 125 mg women had on average 1.29 times the Cmax and 1.26 times the 6-hour exposure of men. The authors say the 1.29 could be explained mainly by women's 1.24-fold lower body weight, and that subjective 'bad drug effect' ratings and other adverse effects were greater in women than in men, also after correcting for dose per kilogram or blood level.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Methods and Materials > Procedure, Dependent Measures, and Drug, 1st paragraph; Results > Participants, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Three laboratories pooled, 220 volunteers (44% women; age 25.4, SD 5.2; weight 68.8 kg): San Francisco 45 (20 women, 25 men; 1.5 mg/kg; researchers present; 11 am), Chicago 95 (37 women, 58 men; 1.5 mg/kg; people alone; 9:30 am; told they might receive a stimulant, sedative, cannabinoid or placebo) and Basel 80 (40 women, 40 men; a fixed 125 mg, 1.89 mg/kg (SD 0.33); researchers present; 8 to 9 am; told MDMA or placebo); oral capsules, double blind. Lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions: San Francisco 32.8 (SD 37.0), Chicago 13.1 (13.5), Basel 0.6 (0.6); 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory. The authors say some of the data were published earlier (Harris 2002, Bedi 2010, Hysek 2012) and some not (San Francisco, Chicago).

evidence.locator: Results > Acute Effects of MDMA across Sites, 1st paragraph; Figures 1 and 2
evidence.extracted: MDMA raised heart rate and blood pressure to a similar degree at the three sites (site comparisons p = 0.15 to 1.00) and gave similar reports on most subjective ratings; peak ratings of 'any drug effect', 'drug liking' and 'stimulated' after MDMA did not differ between sites (p = 0.07 to 1.00). Minor differences: after MDMA Chicago volunteers gave higher peak 'anxious' ratings than San Francisco and Basel volunteers, and San Francisco volunteers higher 'closeness to others' than Basel volunteers (p < 0.05 for each); after placebo Chicago volunteers gave higher peak 'any drug effect' and 'drug liking' than the other two sites (p < 0.01). The values are in figures that were not extracted; the text prints no means or effect sizes, and no significant difference is not proof of equality.

evidence.locator: Results > Relationship between acute drug-related effects and MDMA use history, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
evidence.extracted: The 'any drug effect' rating after MDMA related to lifetime MDMA use differently by site (use-by-site F(2, 218) = 4.74, p = 0.010). It fell by 6.8 points (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7) per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago, by 5.8 (CI -1.00 to 12.53; p = 0.094) in San Francisco and by 6.1 (CI 2.18 to 10.0) in the two together; in Basel, where people had used MDMA fewer than three times or not at all, it rose by 13.5 (CI 1.63 to 25.3). No other relation between earlier use and an acute effect reached significance. The log base is not stated, so the slopes cannot be converted to points per additional use.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 1st, 3rd, 5th and 6th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The authors describe the use-history finding as modest evidence of tolerance in people with heavier use (1st paragraph). They suggest, without testing it, that having researchers in the room (San Francisco, Basel) may have raised prosocial ratings and lowered negative ratings compared with being alone (Chicago), and note that closeness ratings fell with earlier use in San Francisco at trend level (p = 0.07) (3rd paragraph). They call the data the strongest support so far for repeated use weakening the subjective experience, and little support for a much stronger first experience; in Basel, responses reflected only the first to third experience, and people may come to identify the drug effect more accurately across those first experiences (5th paragraph). Other explanations they offer: people with heavier use may also use other potent drugs, tolerance may be specific to the setting, and the 'any drug effect' item is a global rating that may be more sensitive than the others (6th paragraph).

evidence.locator: Introduction, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state, citing earlier papers that were not read, that there is some evidence that chronic tolerance develops to the 'positive' subjective effects of MDMA, and that apparent decreases in effect may instead result from changes in the purity of MDMA tablets over time or place. No new data.

evidence.locator: Abstract (random-order); Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Experimental protocol, 1st paragraph; Study drug, 1st paragraph; Measures > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 32 healthy volunteers (16 men, 16 women), mean age 25 (SD 3; range 20 to 31), from the University of Basel campus; excluded: a personal or first-degree-relative history of psychiatric disorder or chronic or acute physical illness, smoking, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted) and any in the last 2 months (urine tests); 22 completely new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier uses; 19 had used cannabis more than five times and 15 other illicit drugs one to four times; women were tested in the follicular phase. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, random-order crossover; MDMA 125 mg (mean 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30) and identical placebo capsules, at least 10 days apart; registered (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685); paid. Visual analogue scales for 'happy', 'open' and 'close to others', and the 60-item Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS); repeated measures were expressed as the peak change from baseline.

evidence.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
evidence.extracted: MDMA raised visual analogue ratings of feeling happy (F(1,31) = 120.59), open (80.77) and close to others (67.52), all P < 0.001, and AMRS scores for activity (24.48), inactivity (7.72, P = 0.009), extroversion (40.58), introversion (10.05, P = 0.003), well-being (37.00), emotional excitation (28.46) and dreaminess (25.48), the rest P < 0.001, but not for anxiety. A sex-by-treatment interaction for 'happy' (F(1,31) = 10.49, P = 0.003), but no difference between men and women after MDMA on post hoc tests; no other sex-by-treatment interaction. The text prints no means; they are in Figure 1 and in Supplementary Table S1 (not read).

evidence.locator: Results > Empathy, 1st paragraph; Results > Social Value Orientation, 1st paragraph; Results > Facial emotion recognition, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Empathy test: MDMA raised explicit and implicit emotional empathy ratings across all volunteers (F(1,31) = 6.05, P = 0.019; 4.29, P = 0.047), significantly for positive scenes (8.60, P = 0.006; 5.02, P = 0.032) and not for negative scenes; interaction with sex for implicit empathy (4.68, P = 0.039) and a trend for explicit (3.03, P = 0.092); post hoc, the rises were significant in men only (P = 0.025 explicit, 0.022 implicit); cognitive empathy unchanged. Money allocation (Social Value Orientation): the prosocial angle rose (F(1,31) = 4.42, P = 0.044) with a sex interaction (5.52, P = 0.026); post hoc significant in men (P = 0.008) and not in women; the inequality-aversion index tended to fall, analysed only in the subjects with a prosocial orientation (F(1,20) = 3.39, P = 0.079). Face recognition: accuracy fell overall (F(1,31) = 28.63, P < 0.001), for fearful (14.90), angry (18.60), disgusted (5.81, P = 0.022) and surprised (9.79, P = 0.004) faces but not happy faces (0.27, P = 0.607); the fall was significant in women and not in men.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph
evidence.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: one dose only, relatively high with obvious subjective effects; although the design was double blind with identical placebo, most volunteers realised which treatment they had been given, so unblinding may have biased task performance; the evaluation of many aspects of social cognition required a relatively large number of statistical comparisons. They say the dose was chosen to correspond to those typically used in recreational settings (citing another paper, not read) or in clinical trials; lower doses and an active placebo could be used in future studies.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors state, citing earlier laboratory and clinical papers rather than surveys of people who use ecstasy (not read), that MDMA produces subjective prosocial feelings and that enhancing empathy and sociability is also considered a major reason for the recreational use of MDMA and for its therapeutic effects in psychotherapy. This paper presents no data on why people take MDMA.

evidence.locator: Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Protocol, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 9 healthy, right-handed volunteers (7 men, 2 women; mean age 24.0, SD 3.2; range 18 to 29), recruited by on-line advertisements and word of mouth, with earlier ecstasy use of 2 to 300 occasions (mean 63.9, SD 94.9; 4 of 9 in the past year; last use 0.5 to 24 months earlier); all had used cannabis, 8 stimulants and 7 hallucinogens; in the past month 5 smoked cigarettes daily. Three-session double-blind design within people: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order and placebo placed at random, at least 6 days apart; sessions began at noon; lactose capsules; abstinence from cannabis for 7 days, alcohol for 24 hours and other drugs for 48 hours, checked by urine, saliva and breath tests; after the capsule volunteers stayed in hospital at least 4.5 hours, in a comfortable laboratory environment.

evidence.locator: Results, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Table 2
evidence.extracted: Peak 'feel drug' rating (Drug Effects Questionnaire; change from before the capsule) 14.5 on placebo, 57.1 at 0.75 mg/kg and 91.8 at 1.5 mg/kg (F(2,16) 98.6; each dose above placebo and 1.5 above 0.75 mg/kg on post hoc tests, threshold p < .01); peak systolic pressure rose 4.8, 34.8 and 48.1 mm Hg and heart rate -5.3, 19.7 and 35.3 beats a minute; no serious adverse effects. 'Sociable' (visual analogue scale), change from baseline at 135 minutes: -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 mg/kg and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg (drug-by-time F(8,64) 3.1, partial eta-squared .28; at 135 minutes F(2,16) 7.3); 1.5 against 0.75 mg/kg t(8) 3.8 (p < .01); 1.5 mg/kg against placebo t(8) 2.5 (p = .04, called marginal against the paper's p < .01 threshold for post hoc tests); 0.75 mg/kg against placebo not different (t(8) 0.5). The Profile of Mood States Friendliness scale showed a similar pattern that was not significant (F(2,16) 1.3). Accuracy and speed of recognising emotional faces did not change.

evidence.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The authors write that increased sociability and decreased defensiveness are cited by people who use ecstasy as a motivator to use it (citing Sumnall 2006, not read here) and that people who use ecstasy recreationally describe feeling sociable after it (Discussion, citing the same paper); they also cite controlled human studies of raised sociability ratings, and say that advocates of psychotherapeutic use argue MDMA increases openness to the therapeutic process (citing Parrott 2007, not read here). This paper's own data do not address why people take MDMA.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 8th to 11th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: The drug increased subjective sociability only at the higher dose (1.5 mg/kg), while at the lower dose (0.75 mg/kg) it raised the ventral striatum response to happy faces without changing sociability ratings. The authors call the findings preliminary: the sample was small (9) and replication in a larger sample is needed; only two brain regions were chosen in advance; MDMA may have blood-flow effects on the signal; all volunteers had earlier ecstasy exposure, varying widely (they found no correlation between use variables and the brain signal); doses were given in ascending order for safety, which may have influenced outcomes, with at least 6 days between sessions (average 10.72, SD 7.15) and no effect of session order found; no plasma MDMA was measured.

evidence.locator: Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Substances and Dosing, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Study Design, 1st paragraph (p. 514, continued on p. 515); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 515)
evidence.extracted: 16 healthy volunteers (12 men, 4 women; aged 21 to 39, mean 27.4, SD 4.4) recruited at the University Hospital and the Medical School of Zurich, high-school educated, all but one university students or physicians; six had earlier recreational drug experience, three of them with ecstasy, so 13 had never tried it. Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person design with four counterbalanced conditions at least 14 days apart (placebo-placebo, citalopram-placebo, placebo-MDMA, citalopram-MDMA); citalopram 40 mg (or saline) by infusion over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) or placebo capsules by mouth; psychometric ratings once, 120 minutes after MDMA. MDMA alone mainly produced a state of positive mood, moderate derealization, heightened sensory awareness and a slight rise in psychomotor drive; the subjective effect began 20 to 120 minutes after intake (mean 45), peaked 15 to 30 minutes later and lasted a mean of 3 hours. After citalopram the effect was markedly reduced but lasted a mean of 5 hours. Side effects and cardiovascular changes from the same sessions are to be reported separately.

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 516)
evidence.extracted: Adjective Mood Rating Scale after MDMA against placebo: raised 'heightened mood' (p < .03), 'self-confidence' (p < .02), 'extroversion' (p < .01), 'introversion' (p < .05), 'emotional excitability' (p < .01), 'sensitivity' (p < .03) and 'thoughtfulness-contemplativeness' (p < .002); 'tiredness' lowered (p < .05) and 'dazed state' raised (p < .02); no change in 'aggression-anger', 'apprehension-anxiety' or 'depressiveness'; 'efficiency-activation' not raised, although a moderate rise in psychomotor drive was shown. The authors' summary: a state of enhanced mood with happiness, euphoria and in some volunteers mania-like experience, increased self-confidence and extroversion; moderate derealization, depersonalization and thought disorder (accelerated thinking, thought blocking and impaired decision making) without anxiety or panic reactions; no evidence of delusional thinking; no hallucinations but an intensification of visual, tactile and acoustic perception and changes in the meaning of the surroundings; only a slight rise in psychomotor drive.

evidence.locator: Table 1 (all rows and columns)
evidence.extracted: Altered States of Consciousness scale item clusters, mean percent of the highest possible score (SE), n = 16, placebo then MDMA then citalopram-MDMA: positive basic mood 0.6, 40.1 (6.6), 16.4; derealization 0.4, 32.7 (7.0), 12.6; depersonalization 0.0, 24.5 (6.7), 10.5; alterations of the sense of time 0.8, 30.9 (7.6), 13.1; mania-like experience 0.3, 26.6 (6.2), 6.7; frightening derealization 0.0, 8.5 (3.7), 2.1; thought disorder 0.0, 24.8 (6.0), 8.6; delusion 0.0, 10.4 (5.6), 1.5; loss of thought control 0.0, 14.1 (5.6), 2.8; loss of body control 0.2, 11.9 (3.6), 5.3; hallucinations 0.1, 9.7 (3.1), 3.6; synesthesia 0.0, 12.8 (4.6), 8.0; changed meaning of percepts 0.6, 37.3 (7.2), 14.1; facilitated recollection 0.0, 18.4 (6.2), 7.6; facilitated imagination 0.7, 27.2 (8.7), 6.6. MDMA raised most clusters above placebo (p < .05) but not delusion or hallucinations; citalopram pretreatment lowered most of the MDMA-induced scores (p < .05).

evidence.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (begins foot of p. 517, continues p. 518 into p. 519, left column); paragraph beginning 'Another interesting finding' (p. 519, right column); concluding paragraph beginning 'In conclusion' (p. 519, right column, into p. 520)
evidence.extracted: The authors say citalopram attenuated the effects of MDMA by about 60 percent, not fully, which they do not put down to too little citalopram: all volunteers received 40 mg whatever their weight, with no correlation between dose per kilogram and the size of the lowering, and in a pilot study two people given 60 or 80 mg had the effects of MDMA blocked to a degree comparable to 40 mg. They also say citalopram prolonged the effects by up to two hours compared with MDMA alone and offer two possible reasons (a metabolic interaction, or competition at the uptake site).

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 262); Assessment measures, 3rd paragraph (p. 262); Procedures and ethics, 1st paragraph (pp. 262-263) and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 263)
evidence.extracted: Field study with no placebo and no random allocation: unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30 (regular, novice, comparison: group means 21.4, 22.8 and 21.3 years; women/men 8/7, 8/7 and 10/5), recruited by word of mouth among friends and acquaintances who regularly went to one large nightclub in north-east London, in three groups of 15: ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use, one to nine, and never. Each rated 16 moods on 0 to 100 lines on a hand-held computer at a drug-free session at their own or the experimenter's home before the night out (no MDMA for at least 1 week and no other illicit drug for over 24 hours, by their own account), at the club 2 to 8 hours after taking their tablets (8 of the 30 at 8 to 16 hours; the comparison group at equivalent times), and 2 and 7 days later. Drugs taken that night were self-noted on a questionnaire; no testing of the tablets is reported. In the comparison group 10 of 15 drank alcohol (5.0 drinks per drinker), 3 smoked cannabis and 2 took cocaine; in the novice and regular groups 5 and 6 drank (2.7 and 3.7 drinks), 1 and 2 smoked cannabis, 2 and 4 took cocaine, and 1 novice took amphetamine. The aims of the study were described to each person beforehand; the study was approved by the University Ethics Committee.

evidence.locator: Table 1, mood-scale rows (p. 263); Table 2, mood-scale rows, all four sessions (p. 264)
evidence.extracted: Means only, no spread, with Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group at each session (comparison, novice, regular). At the club: good tempered 85, 90 and 88, no difference; sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); the comparison group less sober (46 against 78, p < 0.05, and 67) and less steady (50 against 76, p < 0.05, and 71, p < 0.10). Two days later: sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); energetic 72, 62 and 56 (regular p < 0.05). Seven days later none of these differed (sad 22, 25 and 21; depressed 37, 37 and 39; unsociable 22, 18 and 18; good tempered 86, 84 and 87); both ecstasy groups were less drowsy than the comparison group (28, p < 0.05, and 25, p < 0.01, against 38). Before the night the novice group was already sadder than the comparison group (31 against 22, p < 0.05). Group by session interactions in two-way analyses of variance: p < 0.001 for abnormal, depressed and sad; p < 0.01 for sober, unpleasant and unsociable; p < 0.05 for good tempered and steady; not significant for the other eight scales; no F values or degrees of freedom printed.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs (p. 266, the 7th continued on p. 267) and 9th paragraph (p. 267)
evidence.extracted: The authors call the absence of better moods in the ecstasy groups than in the comparison group on the night unexpected and give four possible reasons: earlier studies mostly had no comparison group of other clubbers, who would also be expected to feel good on their Saturday night out; the comparison group had taken other drugs, mainly alcohol, and a drug-free group is needed in future studies; ratings such as good tempered were already near the top of the scale in the comparison group; and the scales had no items on elation or empathy. They describe a range of negative moods two days later and marked swings over the week in depression, sadness, calmness, pleasantness and sociability in the ecstasy groups against fairly stable levels in the comparison group, attribute the low moods to serotonin depletion, which was not measured, and conclude that the good moods of all the clubbers show the importance of context and expectancy.

risk_of_bias.note: The comparison that carries the claim, MDMA against placebo in the same people, is at worst some concerns on the cards (session order is not described in the Basel pooled paper, the three-site paper or the Chicago paper), but the ratings are self-reports by volunteers who could tell what they had been given: the effects are obvious, the Basel authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had, and no paper tested the blind. The Basel papers also tested about 40 to 60 outcomes without correction. The size of the differences (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 for a good effect at 125 mg in 136 people) limits how much expectation can explain, so one level, not two. The social, empathy, sex-specific and earlier-use findings are worded as weaker and are not rated separately.

inconsistency.note: The direction agrees at Basel, Zurich, Chicago and San Francisco for ratings of drug effect, liking and good effect. Where results differ (closeness higher in San Francisco than in Basel, 'anxious' higher in Chicago, sociability marginal and only at the higher dose, earlier use opposite in Basel), the statement says so and does not rest on them.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the statement describes volunteers in laboratory sessions and says where they differ from real life (healthy, screened, mostly new to MDMA, a fixed known amount, a hospital room with researchers present). It does not say why people take it, which none of these papers measured; what people felt in real use comes from one small observational study (Parrott & Lasky, 1998), described with its limits and not part of this rating.

imprecision.note: 166 people for the main ratings, with differences far larger than their spread (SDs of 20 to 33 around averages of 56 to 85, against 3 to 7 on placebo). The smaller samples (16, 9, 32) carry the secondary findings and are described as such; no intervals are printed for the ratings.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: the Basel and three-site papers are pooled analyses by the teams that ran the studies, the three-site pool is not registered, and the registry records of the Basel studies were not read. No sign of selective omission, but unpublished studies cannot be excluded.

grade.reasoning: Placebo-controlled double-blind within-person laboratory studies start high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias -1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Moderate for the statement that, in healthy volunteers in laboratory sessions, a single dose of MDMA raised self-rated drug effect and good effect above placebo (about 80 against about 4 out of 100 at 125 mg, in 136 people), began within about an hour, lasted about four hours, and was accompanied by bad-effect ratings and physical complaints in the same sessions. The parts that rest on one small study or on marginal or post hoc tests (sociability in 9 people, the empathy and money-sharing tests, face recognition, the earlier-use relation, the effect of citalopram) are worded as such and would be rated lower on their own; a separate claim could carry them. The certainty does not extend to real use or to why people take MDMA, which the laboratory studies did not measure. The real-life sentences rest on one observational study of 45 people with no placebo, self-chosen tablets of untested content, unblinded self-ratings and no spread printed (ROBINS-E very high on its study card); they qualify the claim and are not part of the moderate rating, and on their own would be very low (observational start, risk of bias -2, imprecision -1). Status replicated: the direction agrees at four places, but the Basel papers probably share volunteers, the two Chicago papers share a senior author and one author (Liechti) is on four of the five papers (the Basel pooled paper, the Basel empathy paper, the Zurich paper and the three-site paper, which also includes the Chicago senior author), so the four places are not fully independent. The claim gives no advice on amounts or timing, and describing the effects people rated as good is a finding, not encouragement.

verification.flag_note: Sumnall et al. (2006) and Boys et al. (2001), the two papers meant to say why people take MDMA from their own accounts, were not read (their PDFs had not been saved when this was drafted), so 'why people take MDMA' rests on two papers' second-hand statements only and the claim says that none of the papers read asked; redraft when both are read. The Basel overlap is probable but not stated: both registrations of the 32-person study are on the pooled paper's list of nine, and the three-site paper's Basel 80 may sit inside the 166. The Chicago 9-person study and the Chicago part of the three-site paper share a senior author, and the three-site paper says some of its data were published earlier (overlap with the 9 not stated). Liechti is an author of four of the five papers (Basel pooled, Basel empathy, Zurich and the three-site paper). The three-site paper prints no means (figures not read) and its use-history slopes have no stated log base; the 32-person paper's supplementary table was not read; the 9-person paper's abstract states the sociability result against placebo more strongly than its own post hoc threshold (p = .04 against .01). The sociability, empathy and earlier-use findings are single-study and could be split into their own claim. The sc_liechti_2000 card was written by AI reader 51; these anchors were located from the PDF by this reader. The Basel pooled card was extended (additive; staged in _incoming/mdma/) with the ratings, complaints and end-of-study findings. 2026-10-23: Parrott and Lasky (1998), read in full by AI reader 94 (card sc_parrott_1998), adds the only real-life mood data (a club night and 2 and 7 days later, against other clubbers who mostly drank alcohol); its three anchors are qualifiers awaiting a second reader; no other field study of the days after was read (Curran and Travill, 1997, cited by this paper, has no reference record).

statement: In 7 adults with recreational MDMA experience (one double-blind, placebo-controlled sleep-laboratory study with counterbalanced sessions), a single dose of pure MDMA taken before a night in the laboratory, compared with placebo, is associated with about two hours less sleep that night (311 against 437 minutes), mainly because falling asleep took much longer (112 against 15 minutes), and with REM (dreaming) sleep almost disappearing (3.5% against 19.2% of sleep); light sleep rose slightly and deep sleep did not change. On the following night, with placebo, REM sleep was 22% against 21% after the placebo session, and no difference between the sessions was found that night. REM sleep was also lower than after a night of shortened sleep, so the REM loss was not only a result of sleeping less. The study had 7 people, one dose, and a quiet laboratory with a bedtime earlier than the participants' usual one (which the authors judged unlikely to change the comparison with placebo), unlike nights out with dancing, heat, other drugs or no sleep at all. The abstract also reports less deep sleep after MDMA, which the study's own results do not show. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a sleep laboratory, seven people slept about two hours less after a dose of MDMA than after a dummy pill, mostly because they took much longer to fall asleep, and their dreaming (REM) sleep almost disappeared that night. A night of short sleep without MDMA did not remove dreaming sleep in the same way. The next night, sleep was back to normal. Only seven people took part, with one dose in a quiet lab, which is very different from a night out.
population: Adults aged 19 to 34 (5 men, 2 women) with at least three recent recreational MDMA uses (lifetime mean 27), screened free of psychiatric disorders and drug or alcohol dependence
exposure: A single oral dose of pure MDMA given by the researchers before a night in the sleep laboratory (amount and timing are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's placebo night; as a positive control, a placebo night with a shortened time in bed
outcome: Polysomnographic sleep that night and on the following night: total sleep, time to fall asleep, sleep stages including REM sleep
magnitude: Treatment night, MDMA against placebo (mean, SEM): total sleep 310.6 (45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes, F(1,6) = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, P = 0.038; REM 3.5% (2.1) against 19.2% (2.0), P = 0.009, drug by night interaction P = 0.003; stage 1 8.4% against 6.6%, P = 0.022; stage 3/4 not different (P = 0.119). REM after MDMA also lower than after shortened sleep (19.3%; post hoc P = 0.004). Following night: total sleep 403.6 against 431.9 minutes; REM 22.2% against 20.6%.

evidence.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3, treatment column
evidence.extracted: MDMA against placebo (2-factor analysis over treatment and recovery nights, df 1 and 6), treatment-night values: total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes, F = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, F = 7.0, P = 0.038; stage 1 8.4 against 6.6%, F = 9.49, P = 0.022; REM 3.5 (2.1) against 19.2 (2.0)%, F = 14.28, P = 0.009, reduced on the treatment night only (interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003); no effect on wake after persistent sleep, stage 2 (P = 0.267), stage 3/4 (P = 0.119) or REM latency (P = 0.589).

evidence.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 legend; Table 3
evidence.extracted: On the treatment night, REM percentage after MDMA was lower than after both shortened sleep (19.3%; P = 0.004) and placebo (P = 0.004) (F(2,12) = 15.036), which the authors read as a specific REM-suppressing effect beyond sleep loss.

evidence.locator: Table 3, recovery column; Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Recovery night with placebo after the MDMA session: total sleep 403.6 (SEM 34.4) minutes and REM 22.2% (1.5), against 431.9 minutes and 20.6% on the recovery night of the placebo session; no main effects of night and no night-by-drug interactions except for REM percentage, reduced on the treatment night only.

evidence.locator: Methods › Experimental Procedures, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 9th paragraph; Abstract › Measurements and Results
evidence.extracted: Only 7 completed; two withdrew and the 12-sequence Latin square was incomplete; the laboratory schedule was earlier than the participants' usual sleep times, which the authors judged unlikely to affect the MDMA-placebo comparison. The abstract states that MDMA reduced stage 3/4 sleep, which the drug comparison does not show (P = 0.119).

risk_of_bias.note: Incomplete Latin square, two of nine withdrew, blinding of a noticeable drug not checked; objective outcomes.

inconsistency.note: Single study.

indirectness.note: Worded for one laboratory dose with a full night in bed.

imprecision.note: Seven participants; no confidence intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for one study.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory study with counterbalanced order starts high. Risk of bias -1 (incomplete counterbalancing, two withdrawals, blinding not checked, a misreported result in the abstract). Imprecision -2 (7 people, one study, no intervals). Very low, although the REM effect is large and plausible. Single study.

statement: In the same 7 adults with recreational MDMA experience (one double-blind, placebo-controlled sleep-laboratory study), the evidence is insufficient to say whether a single laboratory dose of MDMA makes people sleepier the next day. On next-day nap tests, sleepiness after the MDMA night did not differ significantly from the placebo night, but it did not differ from a night of shortened sleep either, which clearly made people sleepier than placebo, according to the Results text (the paper's figure legend instead reports the shortened night as different from both, and in the figure MDMA sits close to placebo); on the day after the recovery night, the three conditions did not differ. The values for each condition are shown only in a figure, 7 people are too few to rule out a real difference, and the study measured no next-day mood, thinking or tiredness ratings. The authors' conclusion that MDMA's sleep loss did not produce daytime sleepiness rests on this non-difference. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: The day after a night in a sleep lab, people's sleepiness was measured with short nap tests. After a short night of sleep without MDMA they fell asleep much faster than after a dummy pill. After MDMA they were somewhere in between and not clearly different from either, so this small study cannot say whether MDMA makes you sleepier the next day. Mood and thinking were not measured.
population: Adults aged 19 to 34 (5 men, 2 women) with at least three recent recreational MDMA uses (lifetime mean 27), screened free of psychiatric disorders and drug or alcohol dependence
exposure: A single oral dose of pure MDMA given by the researchers before a night in the sleep laboratory (amount and timing are study conditions in the study card)
comparator: The same people's day after a placebo night and day after a placebo night with shortened time in bed
outcome: Next-day objective sleepiness (multiple sleep latency test: mean sleep latency and sleep-onset REM periods)
magnitude: Treatment by day interaction F(2,12) = 4.63, P = 0.032; post hoc, shortened sleep gave a shorter mean sleep latency than placebo (falling to about 6 minutes), while MDMA differed from neither placebo nor shortened sleep (condition means only in a figure); sleep-onset REM periods 1.43 after MDMA, 1.00 after placebo and 2.14 after shortened sleep, not significantly different.

evidence.page: Results › Effects on the MSLT; Figure 4
evidence.locator: Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

statement: In two small field studies of young adults who took ecstasy tablets of unknown content at a weekend, the day after was marked by tiredness and short sleep, while mood was no lower than in the comparison groups. In London (Curran & Travill, 1997), 12 people who said they had taken ecstasy at a club rated themselves the next day as more lacking in energy and more physically tired than 12 people recovering from a night of heavy drinking (on 0-100 scales, 82 against 66 and 79 against 65), and made fewer correct subtractions in two minutes (14 against 27; they were lower on every test day, including mid-week; the authors could not say whether this was a direct drug effect or whether lack of sleep also contributed), while their depression questionnaire scores were the same as the drinking group's (8.7 against 8.3). In Melbourne (Scott et al., 2013), 34 people who took ecstasy slept about two hours less that night than 21 people who also use ecstasy but abstained that week (5.9 against 8.1 hours), yet the next day, against each person's own baseline a week earlier, the two groups did not differ in distress, mood ratings or clinician-rated depression, anxiety and hostility. Neither study tested the tablets or measured sleep objectively, people chose what they took, in London the assessor knew who had taken what, and there was no measurement before the drug night, with next-day tests at home in the afternoon rather than in the club at night. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Two small studies followed young people around a weekend. The day after taking ecstasy, people felt much more tired and low on energy, and had slept about two hours less, than people who had not taken it. Their mood that day was no worse than that of people recovering from heavy drinking, or of people who also use ecstasy but skipped it that weekend. Nobody tested the pills or measured sleep with a machine.
population: Young adults who use ecstasy, recruited at one London club (aged 20 to 27) or through advertisements in Melbourne (aged 18 to 35), studied around a weekend of use
exposure: Ecstasy tablets taken at a weekend, by self-report; contents not tested (amounts are study conditions in the study cards)
comparator: People who drank alcohol but took no illicit drug that night (London); people who use ecstasy but chose not to that weekend, each compared with their own baseline (Melbourne)
outcome: Next-day tiredness and energy, hours of sleep, depression and mood ratings, clinician-rated symptoms, a subtraction test
magnitude: London, day 2 (0-100 mm scales): lack of energy 82.2 (SD 11.4) against 65.8 (8.5) and physical tiredness 78.9 (11.7) against 64.5 (5.9), group x day p<0.001 for both; correct subtractions 14.2 (6.7) against 26.6 (10.7), group p<0.01; Beck Depression Inventory 8.7 (3.8) against 8.3 (5.2). Melbourne: sleep 5.85 h (2.14) against 8.06 h (1.93), p<0.001; no group or group x time effect on Kessler-10 distress or 1-10 mood; clinician-rated change scores p>0.05.

The text says the ecstasy group went from high energy on day 1 to marked lack of energy and tiredness on day 2, persisting somewhat to day 5.

risk_of_bias.note: Both observational: self-chosen exposure, untested tablets, self-reported outcomes; the London study has no pre-drug measurement and an unblinded assessor (ROBINS-E very high), the Melbourne study a baseline but self-selected groups (high).

inconsistency.note: Both studies agree that next-day mood did not differ from the comparison group and that the night cost sleep or energy.

indirectness.note: Worded for real-world weekend use in the samples studied.

imprecision.note: 12 and 12, 35 and 21 people; no intervals; a small next-day mood difference cannot be excluded.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. Status replicated: two independent field studies, in London and Melbourne with different comparison groups, both found tiredness or lost sleep and no lower mood than the comparison group the next day. The worse subtraction scores in London cannot be attributed to the drug night, because that group scored lower on every day.

statement: Whether ecstasy is followed by lower mood a few days later, the so-called mid-week low, is not settled; the evidence is insufficient to say. In a London field study (Curran & Travill, 1997), 12 people who said they had taken ecstasy at a club scored higher on the Beck Depression Inventory four days later than 12 people who had drunk alcohol (mean 11.8, SD 7.2, against 6.9, SD 4.1) and rated themselves sadder, more depressed, anxious, agitated and irritable; the paper says some were in the mild to moderate depression range but gives no count, there was no measurement before the drug night, and on the editors' calculation the day-5 difference taken alone was borderline (p = 0.053). In a Melbourne study with a baseline a week before (Scott et al., 2013), the 30 people who took ecstasy and were seen three days after use (Day 3) did not differ from the 17 seen who also use ecstasy but abstained, in distress or mood ratings; mood dropped a little in both groups, and across both groups fewer hours of sleep went with more distress and restless sleep with lower mood. The studies differ in their comparison groups (people who drank against people who use ecstasy), measures and timing, and both are small and observational. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Some people say they feel low a few days after taking ecstasy. One small London study found that people who had taken ecstasy felt sadder mid-week than people who had only been drinking. A Melbourne study, which also measured people a week before, found no difference from people who use ecstasy but skipped it that weekend; in both groups, people who slept badly felt worse. Two small studies disagree, so nobody can yet say how often a mid-week low happens.
population: Young adults who use ecstasy, at one London club (aged 20 to 27) or recruited by advertisement in Melbourne (aged 18 to 35)
exposure: Ecstasy tablets taken at a weekend, by self-report; contents not tested (amounts are study conditions in the study cards)
comparator: People who drank alcohol but took no illicit drug that night (London, no pre-drug baseline); people who use ecstasy but abstained that weekend, against each person's own baseline (Melbourne)
outcome: Depressive symptoms, mood, anxiety, irritability and distress three to four days after use
magnitude: London, day 5: Beck Depression Inventory 11.8 (SD 7.2) against 6.9 (4.1), group x day interaction p<0.001, group main effect not significant; editors' calculation for day 5 alone: difference 4.9 points, 95% CI -0.1 to 9.9, p = 0.053, d = 0.84; depression rating 56.3 (24.4) against 20.7 (13.6) on a 100 mm scale. Melbourne, Day 3: Kessler-10 13.47 (3.68) against 12.59 (1.91) with baselines 13.43 and 14.14; mood (1-10) 5.93 (1.76) against 6.44 (1.27) with baselines 7.06 and 7.10; no group or group x time effect; K10 of 17 or more in 7 of 30 against 2 of 17 (editors' Fisher test p = 0.45).

The text gives the day-5 mean as 11.75, cites scores below 9 as normal and above 16 as indicating clinical depression, and says some in the ecstasy group scored in the mild to moderate range, without a count.

risk_of_bias.note: London: no baseline, unverified intake, unblinded assessor, differing comparison group (ROBINS-E very high). Melbourne: self-chosen exposure, groups differing in age, sex and drug use (high).

inconsistency.note: One study found a mid-week difference and the other none; the different comparison groups and baselines may explain it, but this was not tested.

indirectness.note: Real-world weekend use in the samples studied.

imprecision.note: 24 and 56 people; the London day-5 difference has an interval touching zero (editors' calculation) and the Melbourne null has no interval.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision each -1 give very low (the floor). Status mixed: two studies disagree and the reason is not established. Insufficient evidence because neither a mid-week effect nor its absence is shown with precision. A third field study with a drug-free baseline (Parrott & Lasky, 1998; card sc_parrott_1998) measured mood two and seven days after a Saturday night and should be added by the editor from its card.

statement: In 194 healthy, screened volunteers aged 18 to 45, four in five new to MDMA, who took MDMA by mouth lying in a quiet hospital ward in Basel, with a placebo on another day (10 double-blind crossover studies pooled by the laboratory that ran them; a single dose in each analysed session, 125 mg for 164 people and 75 mg for 30, the same for women and men, as study conditions; 112 of them also took MDMA in another session after a medicine given first, which was not analysed; Studerus et al., 2021), the amount taken per kilogram of body weight and the blood level went most with how strongly the effects were felt, as the volunteers rated them. Without adjustment, the blood level was associated with the rating of any drug effect (standardized beta 0.48), and in penalized models dose per kilogram was selected for 21 of 25 effects and ranked first for 12, among them any drug effect, good drug effect, high mood, feeling stimulated and liking, but mattered less for unpleasant or anxious reactions. At the same dose per kilogram, genetically lower activity of the liver enzyme CYP2D6 went with a higher blood level (beta −0.19), older age with a smaller rise in heart rate (−0.27), higher openness with more closeness to others (0.28) and oceanic boundlessness (0.22), higher neuroticism (rated at screening) and trait anxiety with more dread of ego dissolution (0.32 each) and impaired control (0.26 each), and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before the dose with more anxiety (0.25 and 0.23); oceanic boundlessness, dread of ego dissolution, impaired control and anxiety were rated on a questionnaire at the end of the session, looking back over it. Each of these associations survived correction for multiple testing and was modest, explaining 5 to 12% of the variation (semi-partial R2). For a rating of a bad drug effect, older age, trait anxiety and anxious-depressed mood before the dose ranked highest in the penalized models, but the association with age did not survive correction for multiple testing in the main models. Women and men did not differ significantly once dose per kilogram was allowed for; because everyone took a fixed amount and women weighed less, women received more per kilogram, so sex and dose per kilogram went together and cannot be cleanly separated in these data (dose per kilogram varied from 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg across the volunteers). The authors note that this does not confirm earlier studies that found differences between women and men even after adjusting for body weight, and they cite others, among them an earlier report on safety data from these studies (Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), suggesting that women may be more prone to unpleasant effects, while a three-laboratory study of 220 people detected no differences between women and men. Previous MDMA use showed no association, but no one had used it more than five times before the study. Expectations were not among the measures, and the setting, highly standardized, could not be studied. So differences between bodies went with feeling more or less from the same amount: at a fixed amount a lighter body meant more per kilogram, which went with stronger effects, and genetically lower enzyme activity went with a higher blood level; each analysed session had one fixed dose, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested here (controlled studies of a second dose are covered in a separate answer). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In laboratory studies of healthy young adults, how much MDMA they got for their body weight, and how much reached the blood, went most with how strongly they felt it. People with more anxious personalities, or who felt anxious and low just before, said at the end of the session that they had felt more anxious, and more open people felt closer to others; these links were modest. Women and men did not clearly differ once body weight was allowed for, although an earlier report from the same laboratory suggested women may feel more unpleasant effects. Each session had one fixed amount, so what happens when someone who feels little takes more was not tested.
population: Healthy, screened adults aged 18 to 45, mostly new to MDMA, given MDMA in a hospital ward in 10 pooled laboratory studies (194 people)
exposure: Dose per kilogram and, without adjustment, blood level; characteristics measured before dosing: sex, age, CYP2D6 genetic activity score, previous MDMA use, personality at screening, trait anxiety (timing not stated) and mood just before the dose
comparator: Volunteers with lower or higher values of each characteristic, at the same dose per kilogram (placebo sessions in the same people)
outcome: Self-rated and physical effects of MDMA (visual analogue scales over the session; 5D-ASC rated at the end of the session, looking back; Adjective Mood Rating Scale; blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, blood level)
magnitude: Unadjusted: blood level and any drug effect beta 0.48. Penalized models: dose per kilogram selected for 21 of 25 responses, first for 12. Adjusted for dose per kilogram and corrected for multiple testing: CYP2D6 genetic activity score and blood level −0.19 (R2 0.10); age and heart-rate rise −0.27 (R2 0.07); openness and closeness 0.28 (R2 0.08), oceanic boundlessness 0.22 (R2 0.06); neuroticism and trait anxiety and dread of ego dissolution 0.32 each (R2 0.12 and 0.11), impaired control 0.26 each; anxious-depressed and introverted mood before the dose and 5D-ASC anxiety 0.25 and 0.23 (R2 0.06 and 0.05). Age and bad drug effect: first in the penalized model, not significant after correction. Sex and previous MDMA use (at most five times): no significant association after adjustment.
