statement: These studies do not establish a blood-MDMA cutoff that separates death caused by MDMA from other deaths or survival. They show overlap, while differing in population, specimen and sampling time. A Sheffield department reviewed 77 autopsies with MDMA or related compounds detected in 1992–2008. Of the full series, 17 deaths were attributed principally to MDMA, 30 to several drugs and 28 to trauma, with 2 other deaths. The blood-value subsets were 13, 22 and 24 respectively. Femoral-blood MDMA ranged 0.478–53.9 mg/L (median 3.49), 0.04–41.5 (median 0.76) and 0.035–4.81 (median 0.483). The toxicity median was about 7.2 times the trauma median; at least 7 of 13 toxicity values fall within the trauma range (editors’ calculations from the order statistics and ranges, not individual data; Milroy, 2011). The author concludes that concentration needs the history and full autopsy findings. He treats trauma deaths as a proxy for ordinary-use levels, but no living ordinary-use group was measured and MDMA could have contributed to a collision, fall or drowning. Certifiers, attribution rules and their knowledge of concentrations are not reported. If high levels influenced classification, the observed separation could partly reflect that decision; this is the editors’ possible-bias explanation, not Milroy’s documented method. He also notes possible low levels after water intoxication through dilution (Milroy, 2011). A striking specimen comparison cited by Milroy belongs to Elliott’s separate study of deaths after hospital admission, not the Sheffield 77. In one case sampled 2 days after death, heart blood 28.39 mg/L was about 3.9–4.6 times the two femoral values 6.19 and 7.25; an earlier serum value 4.33 had been taken a day before death. These are second-hand values from different sites, times and matrices, not an isolated measure of redistribution (Milroy, 2011, reporting Elliott). Henry et al. reported 7 deaths aged 16–21 among London poisons-service enquiries in 1990–1991. Recorded temperatures were 40–43°C. The tables label concentrations as plasma MDMA, but a fatal entry and the first two severe-survivor entries have missing or faint decimal points in the supplied scan. If the conventional decimal readings are correct, 5 quantified fatal values span 0.11–1.26 mg/L and 8 survivor values span 0.05–0.97 mg/L; the survivors include 5 after severe complications (one a child’s accidental exposure) and 3 after road accidents, and all 5 severe-case values lie within the fatal range (conditional editors’ comparison of Tables I–III). Clearer source images are needed to confirm those decimal readings. The headers do not establish the collection setting or timing for every value, so they cannot all be called hospital samples taken during life. These selected clinical and accident cases do not measure healthy ordinary use. The separate 7.72 mg/L case has only a short description of hangover, tachycardia and hypertension, with sampling time and detailed follow-up unstated; it cannot define a tolerated range (Henry et al., 1992). A previously checked Finnish source extraction records 57 medico-legal autopsies of all causes with MDMA in femoral blood in 2000–2010, median 0.30 mg/L and 97.5th percentile 4.0; its table prints 0% fatal poisoning with MDMA as the main finding (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014; primary full text unavailable in this continuation). That category excludes other possible contributions. With 57 cases, one would round to 2%, so ordinary whole-percent rounding is consistent with none in that specific category (editors’ arithmetic), not proof of no MDMA contribution. A narrative review relays one published lethal-MDMA range of 40–8,500 µg/L, equivalent to 0.04–8.5 mg/L (Ferner, 2008, second-hand). Borra et al. report higher femoral MDMA after death than earlier plasma or serum, without effect sizes; elimination before death, incomplete absorption or distribution, possible later administration, hospital selection and specimen differences prevent attributing each difference solely to redistribution (2026). None of these findings supplies a validated ordinary-use comparison or fatal cutoff. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: What blood level of MDMA is fatal? These studies do not establish a cutoff. In Sheffield, levels in deaths attributed to MDMA overlapped with levels in people who died of injuries. In the London paper, the table values for 8 survivors overlap those for 5 fatal cases if unclear decimal points in the scan have been read correctly. Some survivors had been severely ill; these were not healthy people after ordinary use. The London tables say plasma but do not establish when or where every sample was taken; the Sheffield comparison used blood taken at autopsy. The Finnish table concerns poisoning mainly attributed to MDMA, not every possible contribution. A concentration needs the rest of the case evidence.
population: 77 deaths with MDMA, MDEA or MBDB found at full autopsy in Sheffield, England, 1992–2008; 7 deaths and 5 severely ill survivors among enquiries to the London poisons information service, 1990–1991; 57 Finnish medico-legal autopsies of all causes with MDMA in femoral blood, 2000–2010
exposure: MDMA concentration in femoral blood after death, or in plasma in hospital
comparator: Deaths from injuries or from several drugs with MDMA present; one person with a higher level and mild symptoms; deaths not certified as MDMA poisoning
outcome: Whether an MDMA level separates deaths caused by MDMA from other deaths and from survival
magnitude: Sheffield 1992–2008: 77 autopsies, full-category totals 17 MDMA/30 polydrug/28 trauma/2 other; blood subsets 13/22/24. Femoral-blood ranges (mg/L)/medians: 0.478–53.9/3.49; 0.04–41.5/0.76; 0.035–4.81/0.483. Editors calculation: median ratio 7.2, at least 7 of 13 toxicity values within trauma range. Henry 1990–1991: 7 deaths; conditional on conventional readings of unclear scan decimals, 5 quantified plasma values 0.11–1.26 mg/L and 8 survivor values 0.05–0.97, with all 5 severe-complication survivor values inside the fatal range. Plasma headers do not establish collection setting or timing for every sample. Brief separate 7.72 case has limited clinical/timing data. External Elliott case via Milroy: heart/femoral ratio 3.9–4.6, not Sheffield. Inherited Finnish 57 cases, median 0.30, 97.5th percentile 4.0 mg/L, 0% fatal poisoning with MDMA main finding; 1/57=1.75%≈2% if rounded (editors calculation). Ferner secondary range 40–8,500 µg/L=0.04–8.5 mg/L. No individual prediction or use denominator.

statement: Among 116 adults in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once, surveyed in 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (Allott & Redman, 2006; 51 in 100 women, mean age 26.5), every respondent reported at least one thing they did to avoid ecstasy's negative side effects, chosen from a list: most often drinking water (96 in 100), limiting the amount of ecstasy (71 in 100), taking breaks or chilling out (62 in 100), a healthy lifestyle (60 in 100) and vitamins or natural products (53 in 100); 30 in 100 took other illegal drugs and 16 in 100 prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown in the days after, 4 in 100 had no strategy, and to avoid brain damage, 18 in 100 had none. 41 in 100 had taken pharmaceuticals or natural products before ecstasy ('preloading') and 47 in 100 after it ('postloading'): among those who listed them, half took multivitamins and 41 in 100 took 5-HTP (a building block of serotonin) before, followed by magnesium and fruit or juice, and 46 in 100 took 5-HTP and 44 in 100 multivitamins after; among those who gave reasons, 46 in 100 did it to ease the comedown and 33 in 100 to reduce brain damage. About 39 in 100 had ever tested their pills (61 in 100 never had; editors' calculation), and 53 in 100 had changed how they used ecstasy because of something they disliked about it, most of them by using it less often. Every respondent had also used at least one other substance with ecstasy, most often alcohol (91 in 100 before and 81 in 100 during use) and amphetamines (60 in 100 before and 66 in 100 during). Preloading and postloading were more common among respondents who had used ecstasy more than 50 times (preloading 55 against 30 in 100), among about 30 tests without correction. These figures describe one self-selected sample, not how common the practices are: respondents found through harm-reduction websites may be more interested in harm reduction, the response rate is unknown, the questionnaire was not validated, and how often each strategy was used was not asked. Whether any of these practices lowers harm was not studied: the authors note that the evidence that preloading protects comes only from studies in rodents given injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRI antidepressants or St John's wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome, which this survey did not examine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a 2004 survey of 116 people in Australia who had used ecstasy, almost all said they drank water to avoid side effects, and most said they limited how much they took or took breaks. About 4 in 10 had taken vitamins, 5-HTP or other products before ecstasy, and about half afterwards, mostly to ease the comedown; about 4 in 10 had ever tested their pills. Many were found through harm-reduction websites, so this is not how common these habits are. Whether any of them lowers harm was not studied, and the authors warn that 5-HTP and some antidepressants taken with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.
population: 116 adults living in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once (51% women; aged 18 to 41, mean 26.5; 79% had used in the past 3 months), surveyed June to December 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances, their networks and an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter
exposure: Ecstasy use, and practices reported before, during and after it: strategies chosen from a list, pill testing, preloading and postloading with pharmaceuticals or natural products, changes in use, other substances used alongside (self-report, lifetime, on an unvalidated questionnaire)
comparator: None for the shares (descriptive); for the correlates, respondents who did and did not preload or postload
outcome: Share of respondents reporting each practice; products taken before or after ecstasy and the reasons given; other substances used with ecstasy

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_allott_2006, JBI prevalence checklist, high: no sampling frame; acquaintances, their networks and self-selected readers of two harm-reduction websites; unknown response rate; unvalidated, unpiloted questionnaire with strategies prompted from a list and endorsed for any time in life; denominators vary from 101 to 116.

inconsistency.note: One survey.

indirectness.note: One Australian sample in 2004; the practices and products people use may differ in other places and years, and lifetime endorsement says nothing about how often a practice is used.

imprecision.note: 116 respondents: shares near 40 to 50 in 100 have 95% intervals of about ±9 points (editors' calculation); the product lists rest on 46 to 55 people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive survey starts low; rated down for risk of bias (a self-selected sample likely to over-represent interest in harm reduction) and indirectness: very low. The claim gives what this sample reported, not population prevalence, and says nothing about whether any practice works, which the paper did not study. Section 7, findings only, held for the senior author: products are named as respondents reported them, with the authors' caution about serotonin syndrome, and no amounts or timings are given. One reason respondents gave for preloading, to increase the effects of ecstasy (21.8%), is left out under decision p-before-during-after (nothing on making a drug's effects stronger). The paper calls itself the first study of these practices, but its own introduction describes an earlier UK survey (Akram & Galt, 1999), not read. Later surveys of preloading (Copeland et al., 2006; Kelly, 2009) and the rat studies behind it (Sprague et al., 1994) are on the reading list and were not read. Status single study.
